articles.text: Lorrel Plimier was sworn into office on December 16 to join four other members of Piedmont’s City Council, and Conna McCarthy was confirmed for a second four-year term. The special city council meeting took place in the Community Hall and included the swearing in of three new school board members. The meeting began with a farewell video from City Staff as a thanks to outgoing mayor Jen Cavenaugh. The City Council voted to name Betsy Andersen as Mayor and Conna McCarthy as Vice Mayor. “I have been sharpening my scissors,” said Andersen, with hopes for cutting many ribbons in her upcoming mayoral term. Guests enjoyed a reception with light refreshments after the ceremony. The event was later broadcast on KCOM-TV and will be available for viewing on the City’s online video archive. Betsy Smegal Andersen speaks after being named Piedmont’s new mayor.
articles.title: Piedmont City Council members sworn in

articles.text: On Friday, December 13, Wildwood families pooled together dinner efforts for a potluck of cuisine to share family favorite holiday traditions and spirit in the school auditorium. Students at the 5-7 p.m. event wove their holiday weekend energy into finger knit and weaving projects, while making ornaments, and singing holiday cheer. Three PHS Jazz band members supplied the holiday soundtrack with live instruments, including two Wildwood alumni Eric Venner, Raiden Holt, with PHS Sophomore Deniz Radzik on the drums. Tables were set up for crafting in the MPR, including a station for making holiday cards for senior citizens. articles.text: The Piedmont School Board saluted its three outgoing members Cory Smegal, Veronica Anderson Thigpen and Hilary Cooper, at its meeting on December 11. Speakers said goodbye to and thanked them for their tenures guiding Piedmont’s school system as elected officials. “It is the last time that the five of us are going to be coming together to conduct business on behalf of the district. At the next meeting in January, a new board will convene to govern PUSD for the next two years,” said Anderson Thigpen. President of the Teachers Union and Piedmont High English teacher Elise Marks thanked the exiting board members. “I think I have, in some ways, a unique perspective on just how hard your job is,” Marks said. “I imagine, I may once or twice have been a bit of a thorn in your sides, but I do want to take a moment just to tell you how much I appreciate what you do. Because I do see just how impossible it is what you’re trying to do all the time.” Superintendent Hawn called Smegal “the institutional memory on this board.” Smegal was first elected to the board in 2016 and served two terms that endured through the COVID school closures and subsequent reopening. “Cory really taught me what it means to engage in a social contract with this community,” said Hawn. “It is a social contract, not just a job. articles.text: For the ninth consecutive year, the Piedmont Scout Council was first in the U.S to completely sell its stock of Christmas trees. This year the tree lot sold its last tree at 6 p.m. on Sunday, December 15, 10 days prior to Christmas. A total of 1800 trees were sold in good weather and with rain, tying the past sales record at the tree lot in 2018 and 2019. Noble firs were once again the top-selling tree on the lot this year. “As traditional, we did well with the noble firs,” said Tree Lot organizer Tom Smegal. “It’s always hit and miss with the silvertip trees. RELIGION CORNER Illuminating the darkest nights By Pastor Jim Hopkins “In those days a decree went out from Emperor Augustus…” (Luke 2:1a) Having gained power by force in a bitterly fought civil war, Augustus was aware that he could easily lose it again. He was prepared to use any tool at his disposal to strengthen his claim to the imperial throne and thereby make it harder for his enemies to overthrow him. An important part of this strategy involved religion. The Emperor of Rome was already the most powerful man on earth, but this wasn’t enough. Augustus wanted a piece of heaven too: he was determined that his people would see him as their supreme spiritual leader. Roman religion had many gods and spirits and Augustus was keen to join their number as a god himself. This was not unusual: turning political leaders into gods was an old tradition around the Mediterranean. There was also precedent in Roman history – Aeneas and Romulus, who had helped found Rome, were already worshipped as gods. Aside from their many gods, Romans were deeply superstitious, so when Augustus was handed a huge piece of luck, he took full advantage of it. Early in his reign, Halley’s Comet passed over Rome. Augustus claimed it was the spirit of Julius Caesar entering heaven. If Caesar was a god then, as his heir, Augustus was the son of a god and he made sure that everybody knew it. The above, from a PBS series on the Roman Empire, tells us the Emperor Augustus, born as Octavian, wanted to be known as a god. He wanted his star to shine brightly. Luke’s story of the birth of Jesus tells us that what shined even more brightly than the light of Emperor Augustus was the glory of God shining on the shepherds as they watched their flocks by night while the angels sang “Glory to God in the highest and on earth, peace.” Luke seems to be telling his audience, which includes us, that there are imperial values, like getting one’s visage on a coin, and heavenly values, like See Religion Corner on page 32 Firefighter EMT Brian Clupny and Firefighter Paramedic Brian Protheroe (right) help load a van to deliver to the U.S. Marine Reserves, sponsor of the toy drive nationally. articles.text: Everyone is invited to attend the annual free Christmas Concert presented by First Church of Christ, Scientist, in Oakland’s Montclair district. The 90-minute concert will be held at 2:30 p.m., December 22, 2024, at the Church, 1880 Mountain Blvd., Oakland. This year’s theme, “Celebrang the Light of the Christ,” will feature congregaonal caroling, Christmas favorites and new arrangements performed by talented Bay Area musicians: soprano Katy Stephan, mezzo-soprano Alexis Lane Jensen, tenor Darron Flagg, baritone Steve Rogino, guitarist Richard Flores, pianist/organist Michael Moran, pianist Frederick Hodges and violinist Shauna Revelli. Admission is free. Wheelchair accessible. Parking is available across the street from the church at Montclair Elementary School. Br ing you r neighbors, friends and the whole family! For more informaon, visit https:// christianscienceoakland.org/ events/ or call (510) 832-2364 For 25 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send photos with the Post from near and far for publication in Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. Send photos as jpg. files to: news@piedmont-post.com, and be sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken.

articles.text: Piedmont Garden Club welcomes the community to attend a discussion by Dr. Ari Novy, President and CEO of the San Diego Botanic Garden, on “Gardens for a Changing Planet: Towards a 21st Century Botanic Garden”. He will be the guest speaker on January 15 at 9:30 a.m. at Piedmont Community Hall. Botanic gardens are more than just beautiful public parks. They play important roles in plant science and conservation. Novy, an internationally recognized leader in the horticultural world, will show how botanic gardens are adapting as the climate changes, He will share how these important green spaces are the sites of research into medicinal, native, and food and agricultural plants. In addition to his role at the Garden, Novy is an active researcher, holding an appointment as Adjunct Associate Professor at Salk Institute for Biological Studies. He is the founding co-chair of the Food and Agriculture Professional Section of the American Public Gardens Association and has served on task forces and advisory panels for diverse groups including the White House Council on Environmental Quality, the Cornell Alliance for Science, Botanic Garden Conservation InternaDr. Ari Novy, President and CEO of the San Diego Botanic Garden tional, Rock Creek National Park, the Garden Club of America, the European and Mediterranean Plant Protection Organization, and many others. In 2024, he became an honorary member of the Garden Club of America. Piedmont Garden Club was founded in 1923 and has been a part of the Garden Club of America since 1926. Piedmont Garden Club members meet monthly to learn about garden-related topics including garden and floral design, garden photography, horticulture and environmental conservation. Other activities include hands-on workshops, field trips and work projects. open every day 8:30 am – 3 pm

articles.text: After five days and 14 rounds, the Piedmont Middle School Spelling Bee has concluded. Thirty-five daring students faced diabolically difficult words and spelled them decisively and bravely. All participants should feel proud of their accomplishments. In the end, however, only one student can be crowned champion. This year’s spelling bee champion is 8th grader, Blue Pinsky, who overcame a worthy opponent in runner-up, Ben Sorensen. Spectators gasped as both Pinsky and Sorensen correctly spelled numerous punishing, grueling words. Pinsky won by correctly spelling “chimerical.” Rohan Seshan, an 8th grader, and Maddie Gutman and LiAnne Carver, both 7th graders, tied for third place in the competition. After a brief respite, Pinsky will take the Regional Qualifier Test to try to advance to the Region 2 Local Bee. The winner of the Local Bee qualifies for the Scripps National Spelling Bee. Good luck, Blue. This article was written by Piedmont Middle School faculty member Ted Scherman. Ted Scherman presents a Spelling Bee Champion Certificate to 8th grader Blue Pinsky. articles.text: Over the last two years, Chabot Space & Science Center has undertaken a major restructuring of its youth development program through the creation a workforce development initiative. The program is designed to connect East Bay youth, particularly those from low-income partner high schools, with career employment in the space sector. Commencing with students in the tenth grade, the program continues two years after graduation, spanning the sometimes fragmented and challenging transition from high school to initial college and career experiences. Currently moving from pilot to full implementation, the historic Galaxy Explorer (GE) program has been expanded to include structured Inquiry Teams in Astronomy, Engineering, Digital Media, and Space Data and the Environment. Each provides foundational space-sector knowledge and career awareness to increase access to space-sector careers for GEs. The traditional work-based learning component of museum floor facilitation and visitor support empowers participants to grow from volunteering, to mentoring, to Internships at Chabot and NASA’s nearby Ames Research Center. This provides a dynamic, intergenerational environment for GE’s to learn from professionals and to teach and pass along what they learn to peers and younger students as the lead demonstrations and public programs at Chabot. Recently, participants in the GE program partnered with Friends of Joaquin Miller Park in the Oakland Hills where Chabot is situated. The partnership comprised research about invasive plant species in the Park. The GE’s collated data from observations on the ground and images from space to map species in the Park, assess, and begin planning for possible remediation. As the program evolves, Chabot plans to expand those partnerships to other space sectors and aerospace industry organizations. Both the Inquiry Teams and the Floor Facilitation are competency based, incorporating the research of America Succeeds on employer-valued career readiness skills. To learn more about Chabot’s growing Galaxy Explorers and workforce development initiative, visit chabotspace.org/education/ teen-volunteers-galaxy-explorers/ Photo courtesy Chabot Space & Science Center Youth participants in Chabot Space & Science Center recently presented the results of a research project about invasive plant species in Oakland’s Joaquin Miller Park to an audience of about 100 Chabot visitors.
articles.title: Chabot student volunteer program grows

articles.text: our beautiful son and brother Jack youth lacrosse and helped to mentor new athletes to the sport. Jack spent three spring breaks working to build houses in Tijuana, Mexico as part of the Piedmont Community Church Mexico service trip. As a leader he was known for his strong work ethic and supportive leadership. Jack was the middle of three children in the Nelson family and was a wonderful brother to his older sister Ashley and younger brother Rylan. Jack and Rylan played together on multiple high school sports teams and Jack was always known to “have Rylan’s back.” There were countless favorite moments like when Jack would assist Rylan for a “Nelson to Nelson goal.” As the older sister, Ashley set a strong example and was always a source of advice, reassurance, and love. The entire family felt the love of Jack who was so proud to be a Nelson. Jack had a strong faith throughout his life and was a confirmed Catholic and parishioner at Corpus Christi Church in Oakland. He would light up in a discussion about Christianity or the Catholic Church and always highlighted the importance of faith and making a positive impact on the world. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, free compostable bags are available at City Hall to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. Compostable bags are also available from Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) for a fee. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: Staff Photos Elsa Wallway scored against Cal High and also sent the game-winning cross for a 2-1 win. Piedmont High’s girls’ soccer team had a great week with a pair of wins at Witter Field. They claimed a 2-1 victory over California HS, a Division 1 North Coast Section program, on Thursday, December 12, and also a 2-1 win over Div. 4 opponent Cardinal Newman two days earlier. Both momentous wins came after strong second half performances. Piedmont’s game-winner against Cal came with just two minutes left in regulation, where Elsa Wallway launched a cross from a corner to the very front of the Grizzlies’ net, resulting in an own-goal for the Highlanders. Against Cardinal Newman, Samantha Ronen scored a late game-winner after nicking a ball off of the goal keeper and retaining possession to score. “Two great wins against really great schools, it’s exciting. We’re still dealing with a few injuries, but the girls are competitors and winners. They are finding ways to win games. You definitely see a step up in the second half; Cal is a good school and a difficult team,” coach Dan Chubbock said. Both goals against Cal High were a product of brilliance by Wallway. She scored the tying goal on a 27-yard shot near the right sideline, stealing possession and taking a few dribbles to the inside before uncorking a beautiful longshot. The game-winner, meanwhile, couldn’t have been more perfectly placed as the cross was nearly an Olympico – giving the defender no chance to clear it off her own line. “Elsa’s goals were just ridiculous. When you have players who can win games like that, it really makes a difference,” Chubbock said. Both games also showed the amount of talent Piedmont has at both winger spots with freshmen Kyla Williams and Ayla Blanford – often using speed and technical ability to create chances. Williams, notably, scored the initial goal against Cardinal Newman where she recovered a lazy clearance by the defense to take a leftSamantha Ronen scored the game-winner against Cardinal Newman. Kyla Williams, a freshman, holds off a Cal High defender. She scored Piedmont’s opening goal against Cardinal Newman. footed shot on her first touch past the outstretched arms of the keeper’s dive. The results set Piedmont up nicely at 3-0-2 (W-T-L) as they approach the New Year. They look ahead to hosting one more upper-division school, Las Lomas of D2, on Friday, December 20 for their last match before the New Year. 2-1 over Calif. High Both teams went into halftime scoreless with the Grizzlies controlling much of the offensive action. Piedmont goalkeeper Friedie Schickedanzmde made a big save in close quarters in the 30th minute, but aside from that, neither team produced anything overtly challenging. The intensity turned up in the second half. In the 57th, Williams had a shot on target, and then sent a dangerous cross in the 58th that was fumbled by the CHS keeper. Cal High then capitalized on a poor clearance in the 61st to score the game’s first goal. In the 66th, Wallway nearly scored on a free kick from around 30 yards, but her shot was a couple of feet high of the net. Then a minute later, Wallway pounced to steal possession in Cal’s defensive half near the right sideline before launching in a high-arching finesse shot into the net from about 27 yards out. Piedmont stayed on the front foot to keep the Grizzlies under pressure. Cal’s defense desperately conceded a corner in the 78th with a defender pleading to her goal keeper to rush out for the ball. It was a mistake that proved vital. Wallway sent her in-swinging cross, whipping it to the doorstep off a defender and into the net for the game-winner. 2-1 over Cardinal Newman Piedmont never looked outmatched by last year’s Div. 3 NCS

articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ basketball team continued its perfect record to start the season at 6-0, dominating both of its games in the 14th annual Paris Twins Classic in Piedmont on Thursday and Friday, December 12-13. The Highlanders defeated Damonte Ranch of Reno 72-25 on the opening day and followed up with an equally lopsided victory over Campolindo, 65-19. The pair of wins provided a glimpse of the potential coach Bryan Gardere has with a young roster that includes three freshmen, Andrea Martin, Jenelle Solis, and Savannah Dennig. “They are adjusting to high school pretty well,” said Gardere. “I think they are doing a solid job so far. They play hard; there’s obviously a lot to learn, but they are willing to learn and want to be coached up. That’s a sign of great players.” With only six players available for both games meant they stuffed the stat sheet and gained extra time building chemistry. Even with their limited time the freshmen along with junior Cleo Afsar and senior Shakila Zuberi showed the synergy of a veteran team. PHS is expected to add two more new players, Briana Webb and Taylor White, when it returns from winter break. “It’s going to be good to have more energy available. We kind of get tired near end of games, so to be able to have that energy coming off of the bench is going to be really good for our team,” Dennig said. Solis, a point guard, has a knack for whipping in slick passes to Martin. The two have an unmistakable understanding of each other’s game coming from their AAU team, West Coast Elite. “Over the season, I think we’re going to be really good,” Solis said. “We’re young and we can continue improving over a long period of time. Andrea is a big guard and she can do everything. When I’m driving, I’m always keeping an eye on her,” “We played together about 3-4 years. She hits me on the layups and knows how to pass really well. On and off the court, we have the same energy and take care of each other. Most importantly, we stay locked in,” Martin said. PHS now looks ahead to the San Diego Holiday Classic tournament at Torrey Pines High School from Thursday, December 26 through Saturday, December 28. Piedmont competed in last year’s tournament as well, and won one of three games. The tourney gives the Highlanders a chance to see how they shape up against tougher competition. 65-19 victory over Campolindo Piedmont led 19-3 through the first quarter and extended the gap to 31-9 by halftime. The Highlanders then allowed just two points in the third quarter while adding 25 to go up 56-11, adding nine more points in the fourth. In the first quarter, the Cougars didn’t get on the board until 51 seconds were left in the quarter. Similarly in the second, Campolindo didn’t score a single point until converting a pair of free throws over halfway through the quarter with 3:38 left. Piedmont continued the dominant display in the third, keeping Campo off Staff Photos Andrea Martin had 16 points and 13 rebounds against Campolindo. She was named Player of the Week by the Post last week. Jenelle Solis is proving to be a versatile playmaker for Piedmont.

articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont looks ahead after going 1-2 at Acalanes’ Chris Huber Memorial Invitational. Piedmont High’s boys’ basketball team traveled to Acalanes in Lafayette for the Chris Huber Memorial Invitational on Thursday through Saturday, December 12-14. The Highlanders won one of three games at the tourney, falling 48-34 to Woodcreek of Roseville on the opening day, beating Pleasant Grove of Elk Grove 66-56 the next day, and losing narrowly 49-43 to International of San Francisco on Saturday. Senior guard Ravi Silverberg had a strong tournament with 20 points against Pleasant Grove and Woodcreek, but International limited him to just six points. The batch of games brings Piedmont’s record to 5-3 overall. They have just one game before the start of winter break, hosting Campolindo on Saturday, December 21. 49-43 loss to International In the most recent game, International came out hot with a 17-10 lead in the first quarter. Both teams scored nine points in the second quarter, giving the Jaguars a 26-19 lead going into halftime. The Highlanders still couldn’t get the offense going in the third, being limited to eight points while International scored 11, putting PHS at a 37-27 disadvantage. Piedmont’s best performance came in the fourth as they worked to claw away at the Jaguars’ lead scoring 16 points, but conceded 12 toward the 49-43 loss. Junior guard Dillon Casey had a strong performance with 18 points. He scored five points in the second and another six in the third. Silverberg scored five of his six points in the fourth quarter with International doing well to limit the senior captain. Final scorers: Casey led with 18 points, Beach Lorin scored nine, Silverberg had six, Lucian Fang-Ring had five, and Nick Riordan had three. 66-56 win vs. Pleasant Grove Piedmont’s offense responded well to the lackluster performance the previous day, putting up 26 points in the first quarter to hold a 26-14 lead going into the second. PHS extended their advantage to 38-25 in the second quarter, while the Eagles inched back in the third down 51-40. The Ravi Silverberg scored 20 points against Woodcreek and Pleasant Grove. Dillon Casey led scoring against International with 18 points.

articles.text: Piedmont looks to regain steam after drawing 1-1 with San Lorenzo. The Highlanders’ boys’ soccer team came out of its last match unscathed, but dropped points in the standings with a 1-1 tie with o San Lorenzo at Witter Field on Friday, December 13. Piedmont out-shot the Grizzlies in Friday’s game, but San Lorenzo did well to convert one of its three shot attempts on a counter attack against the run of play. In matches this week before winter break, PHS travels to Dublin tonight, December 18, and then visits another WACC Shoreline team, Tennyson in Hayward, on December 20. 1-1 tie with San Lorenzo Piedmont had the first good scoring chance of the game in the ninth minute when Jacob Rodriguez played a pass to Logan Faucher charging past the Grizzlies’ back line, but SLZ’s goal keeper caught Faucher’s shot out of the air. Roman Ahearn also had a long shot go wide in the 12th. Freshman Robert Piniella scored the tying goal against San Lorenzo with a header. Niko Markopoulos had an assist on Robert Piniella’s goal. Staff Photos San Lorenzo broke the deadlock just two minutes later. Following a goal kick, the Grizzlies recovered possession around midfield. An SLZ central midfielder turned himself free and launched a long pass over Piedmont’s defense to their right winger, who took one dribble into the box for sending a low shot to his near post for the goal. Piedmont had another good chance at scoring in the 20th minute when Harper Mand sent a free kick from 40 yards out of goal to Bosco Lorin running unmarked toward the left post. However, his header attempt went narrowly wide of the opposite post. PHS goal keeper Tobias Tsai then made a big save on a looping header in the 29th to force a corner. After back-and-forth action in the second half, Ahearn sent another long shot narrowly high of the net in the 51st minute. Max Goldfarb had a shot on target in the 52nd, but he couldn’t make square contact on his attempt, followed by Ahearn having a shot go wide in the 54th. Ahearn had another attempt go wide in the 56th. Piedmont’s tying goal came in the 63rd minute at the end of a corner, where Niko Markopoulos sent a cross on the button to freshman Robert Piniella standing free a couple of yards in front of the net. Without anyone marking him, Piniella slammed in an uncontested header for the goal. With five minutes left in the game Ahearn took a nice attempt on the volley, but his shot was saved. Neither team could muster any more chances from there. NEXT UP Piedmont (1-2-3) heads to Dublin tonight, December 18, for a 7:00 p.m. game and plays at Tennyson on December 20 at 6:00 p.m.

articles.text: Photo by Judy Lin Purple Reign frisbee team: (front row) Naren Ramani (left), Ethan Grossberg, Xuan Tran, Ben McMurtry, (back row) coach Don McBirney (left), Gabriel Garrigues, Jack Shim, Spencer Tsai, Ryan McMurtry, Theo Cost, Kai Lopez, Aidan Stewart, and Coach Carolyn Stewart. The 5th Annual Chilly Bowl tournament hosted by Bay Area Disc Association took place on Sunday, December 8. Middle school ultimate teams from all over the Bay Area converged at Wilder Fields in Orinda for this one-day competition to wrap the fall season. Purple Reign, Piedmont Middle School’s ultimate team, competed in Division 1, seeded seventh out of eight teams. The team consisted of four returning Varsity players, five returning JV players, and 2 first year players. Behind scrappy offense and tenacious defense, the Scots went 3-0 in pool play and found themselves in the championship game against perennial powerhouse, Catch & Release, a middle school club team based in Berkeley. articles.title: The Night Before Christmas

articles.text: With a sleigh full of toys – and Saint Nicholas, too. And then in a twinkling, I heard on the roof ’Twas the night before Christmas, when all through the house Not a creature was stirring, not even a mouse. The stockings were hung by the chimney with care, In hopes that Saint Nicholas soon would be there. The children were nestled all snug in their beds, While visions of sugar plums danced in their heads; And mama in her kerchief, and I in my cap Had just settled our brains for a long winter’s nap. When out on the lawn there arose such a clatter I sprang from my bed to see what was the matter. Away to the window I flew like a flash, Tore open the shutter and threw open the sash. The moon on the breast of the new-fallen snow Gave a luster of midday to objects below; When to my wondering eyes should appear But a miniature sleigh and eight tiny reindeer. With a little old driver, so lively and quick, I knew in a moment it must be Saint Nick! More rapid than eagles his coursers they came, And he whistled and shouted and called them by name: “Now, Dasher! Now, Dancer! Now, Prancer! Now, Vixen! On, Comet! On, Cupid! On Donder and Blitzen! To the top of the porch, to the top of the wall, Now dash away, dash away, dash away all.” As dry leaves that before the wild hurricane fly, When they meet with an obstacle mount to the sky. So up to the housetop the coursers they flew, The prancing and pawing of each little hoof. As I drew in my head and was turning around, Down the chimney Saint Nicholas came with a bound. He was dressed all in fur from his head to his foot, And his clothes were all tarnished with ashes and soot. A bundle of toys he had flung on his back, And he looked like a peddler just opening his pack. His eyes, how they twinkled! His dimples, how merry! His cheeks were like roses, his nose like a cherry! His droll little mouth was drawn up in a bow, And the beard on his chin was as white as the snow. The stump of a pipe he held tight in his teeth, And the smoke, it encircled his head like a wreath. He had a broad face and a little round belly That shook when he laughed like a bowl fully of jelly. He was chubby and plump, a right jolly old elf, And I laughed when I saw him in spite of myself. A wink of his eye and a twist of his head Soon gave me to know I had nothing to dread. He spoke not a word, but went straight to his work, And filled all the stockings; then turned with a jerk, And laying a finger aside of his nose, And giving a nod, up the chimney he rose. He sprang to his sleigh, to his team gave a whistle, And away they all flew like the down of a thistle. But I heard him exclaim, ’ere they drove out of sight, “Happy Christmas to all, and to all a good night!”
articles.title: ’Twas the Night Before Christmas

articles.text: Can a crisis evoke from us a one-shot pinnacle of creativity? In the case of two Austrian villagers in 1818, the answer was an emphatic yes. It was in the small church of Oberndorf, Austria, near Salzburg, readying for the gala Christmas Eve service. The all-important pipe organ had broken with no chance for repairs being done in time. To compensate for the crisis, the young priest Josef Mohr pulled out his poetic text now known as the sacred lullaby “Silent Night,” calming words for the Christ child in the manger, “Sleep in heavenly peace.” He passed these along to the village school teacher Franz Gruber, who was suddenly the superfluous church organist. The very same day Gruber (1787-1863) produced the music to fit the voices – equally straightforward, but uniquely memorable. He scored it for a pair of soloists, chorus and the best substitute instrument available, the guitar. Gruber called his effort “a simple composition.” The parishioners crowded in that night were treated to the world premiere of a work with singers who had barely had time to rehearse. Later, the work was taken up by the Strasser Sisters singing group specializing in Tyrolean music, as well as the Rainers. It became a hit all over the touring itineraries, eventually attributed to the eminent composer Michael Haydn (brother of Franz Josef Haydn). Who, after all, would believe that two village nobodies could create great music? After 15 years, it was finally published, and another six years later was already being heard in New York City. For decades, uncertainty reigned about the carol’s creators. It took a courtroom trial 26 years after the premiere to establish the truth, when Gruber’s son brought in a copy of the original manuscript to prove the true authorship before a governmental investigation committee. Case closed. Any thoughts that Gruber-Mohr could become the Austrian Rodgers and Hammerstein, or Lerner-Loewe, would be sheer fantasy. After 1818, they went their separate ways, given the usual moves and transfers, and never produced other significant works. It was sheer coincidence that the two were together at all; Mohr (1792-1848) had been sent to Oberndorf from his earlier posting because his delicate health could not cope with a harsh climate. Shortly before the Millennium, the sole manuscript regarding the carol’s origins was discovered, written in Mohr’s handwriting, dating back to 1820 or thereabouts. He attested that he had written the texts in 1816, with the music composed by Gruber in 1818. The lesson here is profound and invaluable: The Mozarts and Leonardos of our world could be brilliant every single day. As for the rest of us, however mediocre in the greater scale of things, we can still rise up once in full flower, like a century plant. We can create something uniquely masterful, provided we possess the will, the faith and the motivation. From adversity comes the flowering of inspiration. And a catalytic pairing doesn’t hurt, either. Silent Night, Holy Night Mohr; English trans. by John Freeman Young. Silent, night, holy night, All is calm, all is bright. ’Round yon virgin, mother and child Holy infant so tender and mild, Sleep in heavenly peace, Sleep in heavenly peace. Silent night, holy night, Shepherds quake at the sight. Glories stream from heaven afar, Heavenly hosts sing Alleluia; Christ the Savior is born, Christ the Savior is born. Silent night, holy night, Son of God, love’s pure light. Radiant beams from Thy holy face, With the dawn of redeeming grace, Jesus, Lord at Thy birth; Jesus, Lord at Thy birth.
articles.title: The true history of Silent Night

It took a courtroom trial 26 years after the premiere to establish the truth, when Gruber’s son brought in a copy of the original manuscript to prove the true authorship before a governmental investigation committee. Case closed. Any thoughts that Gruber-Mohr could become the Austrian Rodgers and Hammerstein, or Lerner-Loewe, would be sheer fantasy. After 1818, they went their separate ways, given the usual moves and transfers, and never produced other significant works. It was sheer coincidence that the two were together at all; Mohr (1792-1848) had been sent to Oberndorf from his earlier posting because his delicate health could not cope with a harsh climate. Shortly before the Millennium, the sole manuscript regarding the carol’s origins was discovered, written in Mohr’s handwriting, dating back to 1820 or thereabouts. He attested that he had written the texts in 1816, with the music composed by Gruber in 1818. The lesson here is profound and invaluable: The Mozarts and Leonardos of our world could be brilliant every single day. As for the rest of us, however mediocre in the greater scale of things, we can still rise up once in full flower, like a century plant. We can create something uniquely masterful, provided we possess the will, the faith and the motivation. From adversity comes the flowering of inspiration. And a catalytic pairing doesn’t hurt, either. Silent Night, Holy Night By Franz X. Gruber and Joseph F. Mohr; English trans. by John Freeman Young. Silent, night, holy night, All is calm, all is bright. ’Round yon virgin, mother and child Holy infant so tender and mild, Sleep in heavenly peace, Sleep in heavenly peace. Silent night, holy night, Shepherds quake at the sight. Glories stream from heaven afar, Heavenly hosts sing Alleluia; Christ the Savior is born, Christ the Savior is born. Silent night, holy night, Son of God, love’s pure light. Radiant beams from Thy holy face, With the dawn of redeeming grace, Jesus, Lord at Thy birth; Jesus, Lord at Thy birth. articles.text: Smuin Contemporary Ballet’s annual holiday performance of “The Christmas Ballet” will be at San Francisco’s Yerba Buena Center for the Arts through Christmas Eve, December 24. “The Christmas Ballet” is a popular ensemble of 31 short dance pieces, ranging from classical to swing to step dance and Broadway. Most of the choreography is by the dance company’s founder, Michael Smuin, who died in 2007. Along with a return to Smuin’s original pieces, the company will also unveil new works by Artistic Director Amy Seiwert, company artist Brennan Wall, and choreographer Rex Wheeler, a Smuin alum. The first act, Classical Christmas, features a world premiere by Seiwert in addition to traditional favorites such as Michael Smuin’s “Bach Magnificat,” “Gloucestershire Wassail,” and “Licht bensh’n”. The second act features the premieres of Wall’s “Last Christmas” and Wheeler’s “Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas,” as well as a collection of contemporary festive numbers including Smuin’s tropical “Christmas Island,” and dancing conifers in “Droopy Little Christmas Tree.” Smuin’s beloved “Santa Baby,” featuring the “world’s longest feather boa” rounds out the performance. Smuin Ballet will host a pre-show talk by the company’s artistic staff at 1:15 p.m. prior to Saturday matinees. The company will also provide accessibility offerings for The Christmas Ballet including an ASL-interpreted performance (7:30 p.m., Saturday, December 21), a pre-show haptic tour (12:45-1:00 p.m., Wednesday, December 18), and performance with audio description (2:00 p.m., Wednesday, December 18). To purchase tickets and for more information visit https:// www.smuinballet.org/events/ smuins-the-christmas-ballet/. Smuin Ballet dancers in Rex Wheeler’s “Snow Day”

articles.text: Tower of Power, an R&B horn and section band hailing from Oakland, returns to their hometown to perform at the Fox Theater on Saturday, December 21. Tower of Power was formed in 1968 and since then has created music to back legendary artists including Otis Redding, Elton John, Santana, the Grateful Dead, John Lee Hooker, Aerosmith, and Bonnie Raitt. The band has had a number of lead vocalists since its inception, the best-known being Lenny Williams who fronted the band between early 1973 and late 1974 and led the outfit to commercial success. The 1970s was a boom period for the band, as it produced popular radio hits like “So Very Hard to Go” and “What Is Hip?” Tower of Power released its first full-length Christmas album in September, entitled It’s Christmas, which features holiday classics like “Hark the Herald Angels Sing,” “O Holy Night” and “Silver Bells.” “Reflecting on 56 years of Tower of Power, it’s mind-blowing to see the incredible outpouring of love for our music all around the world,” said the band’s founder Emilio Castillo. “This time, we’re bringing a little extra holiday spirit to the stage with our brand new holiday album It’s Christmas, and it’s going to be something really special. We’re excited to celebrate both the holidays and the hits that have defined us.” The concert begins at 8 p.m. Doors open at 7 p.m. Tickets are still available for purchase online by visiting https://thefoxoakland.com/events/ tower-of-power-24121. The legendary Tower of Power band will perform a concert at the Fox Theater in Oakland on December 21.

articles.text: An exhibition featuring the work of Impressionist painter Mary Cassatt remains on view at the Legion of Honor in San Francisco through January 26. Mary Cassatt at Work is the first North American retrospective of Cassatt’s work in 25 years. The exhibition, which includes 93 works on loan from institutions including the National Gallery of Art, Washington, DC, the Philadelphia Museum of Art, and the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston, focuses on the roles of women and children in the late 19th century. Cassatt’s paintings often depict ‘women’s work,’ including knitting and needlepoint, bathing children and nursing infants. “Mary Cassatt at Work disrupts any preconceived notion that Cassatt was a sentimental painter and sheds fresh light on her groundbreaking practice,” said Thomas Campbell, Director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. “It is fitting that this exhibition, which celebrates Cassatt’s daring and modernity, will open our yearlong centennial celebration of the Legion of Honor. The Legion of Honor was cofounded in 1924 by another intrepid female pioneer, Alma de Bretteville Spreckels, who shared Cassatt’s deep attachment to French culture and bold vision for the future of art in America,” Campbell explained. The exhibition presents a group of distinguished works, including Cassatt’s magisterial oil portrait of her mother and recently acquired pastels from the Fine Arts Museums’ collection. Organizing curator Emily Beeny said the mother-and-child theme was to Cassatt’s final decades what water lilies were to Monet’s or apples to Cézanne’s. “Because this motif is and was so freighted with gendered meaning, it’s been too easy to write these pictures off as sweet or sentimental, when in fact they’re formally rigorous, engaged in an ever-deepening conversation with tradition and an ever more experimental handling of paint,” Beeny said. “Given the social realities of Cassatt’s time, it’s perhaps useful to reflect on the fact that these works are all, in some sense, brought to us by Cassatt’s own childless state. The ambition and scope of her career were, alas, quite incompatible in the late 19th century with marriage and childbearing, even for a woman of her elevated social class.” Visit https://www.famsf. org/exhibitions/mary-cassatt?mc_cid=f4db3a4148&mc_ eid=573801a180 to learn more and to purchase tickets to the museum. Mary Cassatt at Work

articles.text: Oakland Zoo has opened its gates to nighttime visitors for the witner month in the form of: Glowfari, the illuminated lantern festival. The nocturnal event lets the zoo animals rest out of view but lets visitors view hundreds of all-new and larger than life animal lanterns. Walking through the displays of beautifully glowing lanterns gives off a feeling of Disneyland’s Main Street Electric Parade. The Rides Area is open too, as is the gondola to the top and the Express Train to Wild Australia. This year’s display features new all new themes, as visitors are transported on Africa’s longest river, the Nile, to view wading wildlife and ancient Egyptian structures. Glowfari will also have a down-on-the-farm feel as guests will see lanterns of barnyard favorites cows, sheep and chickens. The Glowfari display also includes ibex and alpaca, high altitude animals. The zoo’s winter wonderland will be enhanced by a visit from Santa Claus. who will be stationed in the Rides Area on weekends every night through December 23 from 6:00-8:45 p.m. Glowfari also will be open on select days in January. Purchase tickets in advance. Re-entry is allowed until 8:30 p.m. Oakland Zoo is located at 9777 Golf Links Rd, Oakland, 632-9525. Visit Oaklandzoo.org for more information. Oakland Zoo’s Glowfari has begun. The Cobra Tunnel at Glowfari

articles.text: The Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) is free to the public every first Sunday of the Month. Admission to OMCA’s Galleries of California Art, History, and Natural Sciences is free on Sunday, January 5, between 11 a.m. and 5 p.m. Tickets to special exhibitions in the museum’s Great Hall are offered at a discounted price of $6. Currently on view in the Great Hall are two exhibitions celebrating the work of indigenous people, including a retrospective by California-born photographer Dugan Aguilar and Calli: The Art of Xicanx Peoples, featuring multiple artists of Mexican descent who identify as queer. Aguilar was an important figure in the revitalization of Native traditions for more than from 1982 until his death in 2018. Born of the Bear Dance: Dugan Aguilar’s Photographs of Native California, honors and showcases moments of cultural significance in contemporary Native life. Aguliar’s images document Indigenous experiences from California landscapes such as Yosemite and Sutter Buttes to gatherings, ceremonies, and the artistry of basket weaving. Calli: The Art of Xicanx Peoples focuses on people who are indigenous to Mexico but have been displaced or migrated to California. The exhibition features original artworks, installations, sculpture, painting, photography, poetry, and more, that showcase and honor the stories of queer Mexican peoples across California. Featured artists include Consuelo Jimenez Underwood, Gina Aparicio, Melanie Cervantes, Irene Carranza, René Castro, Yreina D. Cervántez, Enrique Chagoya and more. Visit https://museumca.org/ first-sundays/ to learn more. Museum patrons view Calli: The Art of Xicanx Peoples at Oakland Museum of California.

Born of the Bear Dance: Dugan Aguilar’s Photographs of Native California, honors and showcases moments of cultural significance in contemporary Native life. Aguliar’s images document Indigenous experiences from California landscapes such as Yosemite and Sutter Buttes to gatherings, ceremonies, and the artistry of basket weaving. Calli: The Art of Xicanx Peoples focuses on people who are indigenous to Mexico but have been displaced or migrated to California. The exhibition features original artworks, installations, sculpture, painting, photography, poetry, and more, that showcase and honor the stories of queer Mexican peoples across California. Featured artists include Consuelo Jimenez Underwood, Gina Aparicio, Melanie Cervantes, Irene Carranza, René Castro, Yreina D. Cervántez, Enrique Chagoya and more. He defines meet-cute as two people who get into a NYC cab at the same time and look at each other, immediately ready to declare ownership, but suddenly sensing a spark of attraction. The Holiday opens with two young professional women who have issues with their boy friends. They agree to swap homes, feeling in need of a change. Iris (Kate Winslet) a Brit who owns a charming cottage takes up residence in Abby’s (Cameron Diaz) elegant Hollywood digs. Both insist that no man will interfere with their hiatus. Of course, The Holiday is a rom-com and so it’s just a matter of when things get complicated. Enter Iris’ brother Graham (Jude Law), a book publisher. He creates an unexpected meetcute moment when he surprises Amanda late at night, unaware that his sis is in California. A similar moment occurs for Iris when Miles (Jack Black), a local film songwriter arrives, looking for Amanda and finding Iris instead. Look for their very subtle meet-cute encounter. And so the narrative evolves, cutting from Amanda/Graham to Iris/Miles. Naturally there are speed bumps for both couples to sort out as they explore their nascent chemistry. And with director Nancy Meyer’s stories, things always get rom-com complicated, ending with a much-anticipated denouement. The Holiday, Directed by Nancy Meyers. articles.text: Historic Filoli House and Garden is dressed up for the holidays. Visit historic Filoli House and Garden in Woodside now through January 12 to see the 16-acre estate decorated for the holidays. Filoli’s team has installed and decorated 22 trees, 3,600 light strands that stretch more than 18 miles, with more than 7,000 luminescent ornaments, and 1,000 feet of festive garlands. The Reception Room’s 18-foot ceiling create an appropriate location for “The Grand Tree,” the tallest tree on display. The two-story historic mansion contains 56 rooms, including a ballroom and reception room designed to host concerts and debutante balls. Each room in the mansion is adorned with holiday decorations that complement the room’s original hues and aesthetics. The design team carefully recreated the original holiday placement used by Agnes and William Bourn, Filoli’s first owners. Original artifacts can be viewed throughout the home. Lurline Roth, who lived with her family in the mansion after the Bourns, was an avid collector of religious icons. Her Italian Murano glass nativity scene is now on display in the study. While holiday evenings at Filoli are truly a sight to see, the lighting enhancements glow just as festively during the day. Daytime admission allows visitors to explore the estate trail before sundown and admire the garden’s autumnal colors. Daytime hours are 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. The estate is open until 9 p.m. through January. To learn more about holidays at Filoli and to purchase tickets, visit https://filoli.org/events/holidays/.
articles.title: Celebrate the holidays at Filoli House & Garden

articles.text: Lightyear is a kid-friendly, action-adventure spin-off from Disney-Pixar’s Toy Story. And parents might consider the following: if your little guys have not been introduced to the Toy Story franchise, start there before Here is some backstory: In 1995, the year that the first Toy Story was released, it began with Andy, a boy who had a bevy of plastic toy-figures in his room. Buzz Lightyear was not one of them. What happened was that Andy went to the movies and watched a sci-fi action adventure film starring Buzz Lightyear, and he was smitten. Loved the character, which became an action figure. For Christmas, of course, under the tree was Buzz What Lightyear is not is a film about how Buzz ends up in Andy’s room, joining the gang of figures that come to life, so to speak. Instead, Lightyear is the film that captured Andy’s imagination. In other words, it’s sort of an origin tale that stands alone and is only referenced in Toy The question then begged is, what was there about this animated story that so captured Andy’s imagination? First, the tale unfolds with Buzz (Chris Evans), a charismatic, all-American, lantern-jawed space ranger and a crew of hundreds on board a Star Trek-like deep space star ship, akin to the iconic EnterA scene from Disney-Pixar’s Lightyear prise. In command is Alisha Hawthorne (Uzo Aduba). The ship is 4.2 million light years from Earth on a deep space mission; all have been in deep hibernation. Awakened, they decide to explore an unfamiliar planet named T’Kani Prime. Of course, stuff happens that provides excitement. The planet has breathable air; however the ship is damaged on landing, plus there are hostile, voracious insect-like creatures that threaten the crew. What allows the ship to travel at warp speed is a hyperspeed crystal that is also in need of repair. Of course, Buzz is the obvious choice to be the test pilot. This is when time travel comes into play and the story does get a bit convoluted. Buzz takes the crystal out for a very short test; however, when he returns he discovers that four years have passed on the planet. There’s also an evil emperor, Zurg (James Brolin), who threatens the new colony now established on T’Kani Prime. He has an army of robotic soldiers. There is also a scene-stealing robotic cat named Sox (Pixar;s Peter Sohn) who is Buzz’s close companion. Think of the critter as Buzz’s feline wingman and advisor. It’s all wonderfully animated, filled with lots of action and adventure, and a great introduction to Buzz Lightyear, a swaggering daredevil, dedicated to the mission no matter the breathtaking risk. Lightyear. Directed by Angus MacLane. Disney-Pixar animation. Voiced by Chris Evans, Taika Waititi, Keke Palmer. 1 hr., 40 min. Rated PG. Streaming on Fandango/Disney+. Released in 2022.

articles.text: Before discussing Star Trek Beyond, consider that it is the 13th movie in a 50-year-old franchise, which also includes six TV series and some 100 million books and comics sold during the last half century. Star Trek is now a cinematic senior citizen and this fact begs the question: why? What is there about these films, about these characters who spend most of time encapsulated in a large frisbee with enormous thrusters, daring to go where no travelers have gone before, into the final frontier — space. It’s a remarkable, pop culture phenom (now rebooted), supported by countless Trekies, some covert others nostalgically closeted, but all, by degree, fans of the premise. Which brings us to Beyond. And perhaps it offers up an answer as to why? This film, like most of its predecessors, is a solid, straightforward adventure story, packaged in 23rd century technology (much of it dreamy and ersatz but still cool, like, say, a phaser on stun). There is a heterogeneous crew, always a merciless villain – in the case of Beyond he’s a biped E.T. with a very bad complexion named Krall (Idris Elba), intent on putting the Federation astronauts in sustained jeopardy. In the initial set up, the Enterprise receives a distress call from a stranded ship and is lured by Krall into an ambush that turns out to be a swarm of metal “bees,” meaning tiny weapons Chris Pine, Sofia Boutella, and Anton Yelchin in Star Trek Beyond

From Bartók to Björk, from Palestrina to Paul Simon, Solstice shares the music they love from around the world and through the ages. They are committed to performing new works for women’s voices. Thursday, December 26, 6:30 p.m. Free Holiday Concert with Miles Graber Join us on Boxing Day for a gift of thanks to the community for its ongoing support of the Center. The free concert is made possible in part by a grant from the Piedmont Post. The musicians are led by pianist Miles Graber, featuring the brilliant young cellist Hannah Paulus, and flautist Amy Likar. The program includes works highlighting this unusual combination of instruments, to include Louise Farrenc’s Trio for Flute, Cello and Piano. Melanie Bonis’ Pièce, Op 189, will be paired with Claude Debussy’s Cello and Piano Sonata. Finally, Beethoven’s C Major Cello Sonata will be followed by the E Minor Cello Sonata of Johannes Brahms. Sunday, January 5, 2025, 4:30 p.m. In the Tradition Jazz and Pop Piano Trio Join Bill Jackman, Albert Brooks, and Michael Jones in our comfortable, relaxed classic jazz club to celebrate the New Year 2025 with some classics from the 20s, 30s, and 40s, along with eight of your favorite Beatles songs and, of course, sing along with Auld Lang Syne using Bill’s English translation of the traditional words, Enjoy complimentary refreshments with $25 tickets at https://bpt.me/6214927, or pay more at the door, cash/check Only. Devine, Robin Eschner, Dennis Hysom, Natasha Haugnes, Chris Smith, and John Tuttle. These eight group members bring dynamic vocal harmonies to original compositions and the arrangements with guitar, bass, keyboard, banjo, accordion, dobro, lap steel, and percussion. The songs lean toward Americana/Folk/Indie traditions. Advance tickets for this concert can be found at https://bpt. me/6383991. Doors will open at 4 p.m. Saturday, January 25, 7:30 p.m. Cristiana Pegoraro solo piano Returning to PCA after several years, Italian-born pianist and composer Cristiana Pegoraro will perform another inspired solo performance. Acclaimed as one of the most gifted musicians of her generation, she has released 30 CDs, including performances at Lincoln Center and Carnegie Hall. In addition to a full-time teaching schedule in Rome and New York, she has written books, is the founder of Narnia Arts Academy and Artistic Director of its annual Narnia Festival in her hometown of Narnia in Umbria, Italy. Tickets for this spectacular performance will be available soon. Sunday, January 26, 4 p.m. Mads Tolling, with Kenny Washington Danish-born jazz violinist Mads Tolling returns to PCA with jazz pianist John R. Burr and Grammy-nominated vocalist Kenny Washington in their first time performing together. Kenny Bay Area native Washington, one of the world’s premier jazz vocalists, is a frequent performer at Jazz at Lincoln Center. Jazz writer Andrew Gilbert has dubbed Kenny “The Superman of the Bay Area Jazz Scene.” They will perform American Songbook tunes by Duke Ellington, Thelonious Monk, and George Gershwin. Tickets for this performance will also be available soon.

articles.text: La Dolce Vita was one of the most famous films of all time. Let’s use the title as the impetus for an evaluation of the good things that happened musically this year and a look back in hisDo you have a favorite season of the year? In the old days things were much more difficult than they are today. The summer season was a time to relax and have a vacation. There were no concerts at all. Concert artists began to think about what they would play in the next season, and they prepared accordingly. Most likely the first concerts of the fall season began in small towns. The concert artists tried out the programs and had a chance to “get in shape”. After they were in shape, they went to the big cities. Life was very difficult before modern transportation. A group of musicians usually traveled together. There was a headliner and a few associate artists. When they arrived in a town, one of their representatives went to the local royalty and to the local church asking permission to present a concert. Without permission, they would not be allowed to perform. First, they performed a concert for the royalty in a palace. Then they performed three concerts for the general public. More often than not, royalty was very generous and presented the artists with beautiful gifts. These were usually in the form of jewelry, but sometimes they were given thoroughbred horses. Some of the gifts were rather outlandish. What would you do with a thoroughbred horse? In addition to arranging the logistics of the concert, the traveling artists had to arrange for publicity and engage an orchestra. After the last concert, they had to arrange transportation to the next city and then the process began all over again. These days, concert managers take care of all of the details. All the artist needs to do is arrive and perform. And that’s the way it was for the entire concert season. The year is closing in brilliant fashion. Performances of the Nutcracker are everywhere. San Francisco Ballet actually began the tradition of Nutcracker performances. You can attend the Dorrance Dance brings its Tap Dancing Nutcracker performance to the Bay Area.

Concert fees were a hit and miss proposition. One thing is certain… Royalty was always generous in their gifts. In Russia, the royalty usually gave jewelry made by the most famous jeweler, Fabergé. Men were given cufflinks and tie pins. Women received more flamboyant jewelry. Sometimes they wore the jewelry at their concerts as part of the act. These days, musicians seek other ways to be flamboyant. Jewelry does not figure so much in their outfits. But Fabergé was one of the great artists of all time. I visited jeweler friend Tom Hunt in San Francisco recently. He showed me some cufflinks made by Fauxberge …not Fabergé. Somehow, one of the cufflinks lost its crown. Tom thought that the cufflink should be restored so he replaced and improved one of the crowns and then did exactly the same thing with the other link. After the work was finished, it was almost impossible to tell the difference between the Fauxberge and genuine Faberge. It looked like a gift from the czar. If possible, try to take in one of the performances of the Nutcracker this season. Happy holidays. By Joseph Gold La Dolce Vita was one of the most famous films of all time. Let’s use the title as the impetus for an evaluation of the good things that happened musically this year and a look back in history. Do you have a favorite season of the year? In the old days things were much more difficult than they are today. The summer season was a time to relax and have a vacation. There were no concerts at all. Concert artists began to think about what they would play in the next season, and they prepared accordingly. Most likely the first concerts of the fall season began in small towns. The concert artists tried out the programs and had a chance to “get in shape”. After they were in shape, they went to the big cities. Life was very difficult before modern transportation. A group of musicians usually traveled together. There was a headliner and a few associate artists. When they arrived in a town, one of their representatives went to the local royalty and to the local church asking permission to presLa Dolce Vita ent a concert. Without permission, they would not be allowed to perform. First, they performed a concert for the royalty in a palace. Then they performed three concerts for the general public. More often than not, royalty was very generous and presented the artists with beautiful gifts. These were usually in the form of jewelry, but sometimes they were given thoroughbred horses. Some of the gifts were rather outlandish. What would you do with a thoroughbred horse? In addition to arranging the logistics of the concert, the traveling artists had to arrange for publicity and engage an orchestra. After the last concert, they had to arrange transportation to the next city and then the process began all over again. These days, concert managers take care of all of the details. pages.text: Wednesday, December 18, 2024 27 Features Walking on Wednesday Wed. Walkers head to Sea View Avenue By Dick Carter The Walking on Wednesdays group had a beautiful day for their walk last Wednesday. Some rain was forecast for the evening, but the morning was sunny and mild. The walkers try to get to every Piedmont street during the year but one street they hadn’t walked in its entirety was beautiful Sea View Avenue. There were wonderful homes and holiday house decorations to see, and the story of one of Piedmont’s most important founding fathers to be told. A strong turnout of 47 walkers, and one K-9 best friend was on hand. The walkers were asked what historical figures they could think of who have Piedmont streets or buildings named after them. Frank C. Havens, Walter Blair, and Hugh Craig came to mind, but Wallace Alexander was not named. Alexander made significant contributions to Piedmont, but there is no public recognition of him, and he is little remembered. A past article by Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi wrote about Alexander and his contributions to Piedmont. In 1912 he was instrumental in the construction of Piedmont’s first commercial center, which was just across the street from where the walkers were. In 1916 Alexander arranged for the purchase of land for the Piedmont Interdenominational Church, which became the Piedmont Community Church. Next, he organized the purchase in 1921 of land in Piedmont Park from the widow of Frank C. Havens. This saved it from residential development and provided land for Piedmont High School. He helped establish the Piedmont Boy Scout Council in 1921. Additionally, Alexander led a group of neighbors in the purchase of the land for Crocker/Bear Park. The group decided to walk to some of what Alexander created. They crossed Highland and went past the Piedmont commercial center that replaced the one Alexander developed. The walkers went on Highland Way to the Piedmont Boy Scout Council office and the Community Church. They then turned up Mountain Avenue and climbed up to Sea View Avenue where the Alexanders lived. The walkers went on Sea View to the northern edge of Alexander’s former estate, which ran from what is now 87 Sea View to Hampton Avenue. Alexander’s family was a leader in the Hawaiian sugar industry, and he was born in Maui in 1869. The family moved to the Bay Area so that Wallace could attend school in Oakland. He married an Oakland High School classmate Mary Baker in 1904, and they chose a large site on the corner of Sea View and Hampton, which was then called Union Street, for their home. The Alexanders built a three-story mansion that they named “Brown Gables” for its large, brown painted dormers. In 1911 Alexander’s mother built her own home across the street from Brown Gables at 92 Sea View, and Mary’s mother built a home further down the street at 236 Sea View. These homes are still there, but Brown Gables no longer exists. After Alexander died from a stroke in 1939 in Honolulu at the age of 70, his wife followed his wish that the mansion be torn down, and the land subdivided into 13 lots that were sold, so that more families could live in Piedmont. The group stopped at 92 Sea View, Alexander’s mother’s beautiful home, and a group picture was taken. An interesting reminder of the Alexanders is inlayed in the sidewalk. It’s the word “Kailani.” Lani means heaven, or heavenly in Hawaiian. So, Kailani means “heavenly sea”, or “heavenly seaside.” The walkers then crossed Hampton and continued up Sea View to see the former home of Mary’s mother. The group continued down Sea View, across La Salle Avenue to the Piedmont/Oakland city line at Clarendon Crescent where the street becomes Oakland’s Ashmont Avenue. They went on Ashmont to Mandana Boulevard. A few steps up Mandana got the walkers back into Piedmont on Crocker Avenue. The walkers passed Alexander’s Crocker Park and made their way back to the city center with a better understanding of Wallace Alexander and his contributions to Piedmont. His public service of 100 years ago continues to be experienced today. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Register at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. Among those participating in last week’s Walking on Wednesdays were Joyce Ahern, Leigh Sorensen, Bill Ahern, Jim Kellogg, Margaret Leunig, Chuck Oraftik, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Denny McGee, Alicia Rivera, Jim Kuo, Sheila Leunig, Melba Yee, Karen Palmer, Jack Fischrup, Sharona Fischrup, Elizabeth Richter, Joyce Hicks, Tom Lehrkind, Judy Sokoloff, Vicki Trimbach, Priscilla Wanerus, Stella Houston, Tina Shum, Noemi Alvarado, Leilani Ching, Dottie Hutch, Mark Davis, Claudine Bach, Michelle Yang, Sherry Jacobs, Ken Moy, Pat Nicholas, Phil Witte. Abha Kotari, Kat Lang, Lois Price, Lorek Haghnazarean, Alissa Quan, Albert Chen, Denise Frankoff with K-9 best friend Chester, Susan Anderson, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome Gail Truman, Mark Laemmle, and Martina Parrone who were walking with them for the first time. articles.text: Are you looking for an affordable, durable, and entertaining holiday gift? Look no further than a book published earlier this year by Piedmont author William Wong, Sons of Chinatown: A Memoir Rooted in China and America. Sons of Chinatown is an uplifting immigration success story that defied institutional racism. You can get it for the December holidays at a discount. pages.text: 28 Wednesday, December 18, 2024 BUSINESS SPOTLIGHT Vintage Rug Shop moves to 4th Street in Berkeley After five incredible years in the Temescal neighborhood, The Vintage Rug Shop has moved to a more expansive space at 1799 4th Street, Suite D, in Berkeley. The new location will allow it to grow alongside its loyal customers, offering an even wider range of curated collections of rugs, furniture, tabletop and home decor. “Temescal has been a wonderful home for us since day one, and we’ll always cherish the memories and the community we’ve built there. As our offerings and customer base have grown, we felt it was time to find a space that could grow with us, and 4th Street is the perfect place for that next step,” said founder Brittany Chinaglia. The new 4th Street location offers a thoughtfully designed showroom, allowing customers to experience the unique blend of contemporary and vintage pieces that have become The Vintage Rug Shop’s signature. With a focus on creating collected, meaningful homes filled with heirloom-quality goods, the new store continues to provide the same personalized shopping experience that customers have come to love. Grand Opening The 4th Street store officially opened its doors on November 5. “We’re so grateful for the incredible support over the years, and we can’t wait to welcome you to our new home on 4th Street,” Brittany said. The Vintage Rug Shop is a home decor destination (both online and in-person) offering a curated collection of rugs, furniture, and home accessories. Known for blending contemporary design with vintage pieces, the shop provides customers with heirloom-quality pieces that create meaningful, timeless homes. For more information, visit https://thevintagerugshop.com. Are you looking for an affordable, durable, and entertaining holiday gift? Look no further than a book published earlier this year by Piedmont author William Wong, Sons of Chinatown: A Memoir Rooted in China and America. It is at once an illuminating, educational, and absorbing read about a chapter in American immigration history that isn’t all that well known. Sons of Chinatown is an uplifting immigration success story that defied institutional racism. You can get it for the December holidays at a discount. Order it online at: https://tupress.temple.edu/books/sons-of-chinatown. At checkout, in the box “Enter promo code, insert T20P, hit “apply,” and the price of $28 should appear. Tax and shipping costs are extra. articles.text: On a rainy day November 21 twelve brave Piedmont Seniors plowed through the grim weather on a visit to West Sacramento to learn about the training facilities of the California Highway Patrol. As one might imagine security is tight to preserve the integrity of the cadets’ training. The group was fortunate enough to have a private guided tour led by retired CHP Sergeant Howard Clauson. The Academy is on 457 acres, which include the Emergency Vehicle Operations Course (EVOC), Administration Building, Dining Hall, Rec Building, Classrooms, Dormitories, Canine Course and Tactical Shooting Range. The academy was completed for full-time operation in July 1976 and is to this day very modern with pristine landscaping. Upon entering the administrative building, the Seniors saw an retired CHP Dodge vehicle as well as different types of motorcycles. At the Academy’s museum the Seniors saw a photograph of a helicopter and a stretcher used for mountain and sea rescues in a basket type apparatus that is lifted into the helicopter. The facility is staffed by approximately 200 full-time employees, including uniformed Piedmont Seniors at the entrance to the California Highway Patrol Academy. Pictured are Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein (left), Fred Pemberton, Lois Horwitz, Jim Ayotte, Nava Shaham, Mona Jamieson, Carole Jones, Sue Getreuer, Larry Hu, Tanya Hu, and Toni Robison. and non-uniformed personnel. The training facility houses 500 students in 168 dorm rooms, with three cadet classes. Janet Epstein (left), Carole Jones, and Mona Jamieson in front of a classic Highway Patrol Dodge Polara, a vintage car from the 1960s Piedmont Seniors Nava Shaham, Mona Jamieson, Tanya Hu, Larry Hu, and Sue Getreuer see a classic Highway Patrol vintage motorcycle at the California Highway Patrol Academy museum in West Sacramento. The Piedmont Seniors were fortunate enough to have the opportunity to eat lunch in the dining hall along with the cadets. It is very regimented with military-type methods, and when the Seniors wondered why the cadets don’t speak while eating it is because they only have 15 minutes before their training resumes. They are on site for 26 weeks/year and are allowed no visitors. They are trained to be polite and to say “hello ma’am” and “hello sir” when approached. The Seniors weren’t able to get close to the actual EVOC area as it is off-limits to visitors, but they were able to see the patrol cars driving and skidding through simulated wet weather conditions, with flooding and other hazardous road conditions. The Seniors also heard rifle shots at a nearby shooting range and got a look at a large pool where the cadets practice water rescues. It was a fascinating and unusual experience to visit the only facility of its kind in California. The cadets have to pass a written test, physical agility, written psychological test, psychological screening, medical/drug screening, background investigation and voice stress analyzer. It is quite a financial commitment to train each cadet, at a cost of approximately $100,000 spent on each applicant. To find out more about the Piedmont Seniors program, contact Janet Epstein at jepstein@ piedmont.ca.gov. The Seniors meet monthly on Wednesday mornings from 10 a.m. to noon at the Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue. They also go on monthly excursions throughout the Bay Area.

Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. By Cookie Segelstein Dear MacMama: I will be traveling over the holidays, and I would like to know what I should do to keep safe with my iPhone and computer. Do you have some pointers? Jeri, Piedmont Dear Jeri: This is a great question and one I’ve covered before and will do again. Because as time goes by, hackers are getting more and more sophisticated, so there are some things you can do to help prevent easy access to your data. 1. First and foremost, make sure your iPhone and computer are backed up on some kind of cloud back up like iCloud, or Dropbox. Or even more complete backup systems like Backblaze or Crashplan. If you are backing up to an external hard drive with cloning software and/or Time Machine, hide that external drive somewhere in your house, so if one of your devices get stolen, you can replace your files to a replacement machine. 2. Make sure that you do not do any banking or access any sensitive financial sites while you are on public Wi-Fi of either a hotel or airplane, or another public area. This is where most people get hacked when they’re traveling. They might be relaxing in their hotel room, and decide they want to check their credit card or their bank account. There are so many ways that nefarious hackers can create fake networks that look just like the hotel one and access your data. So, no banking while you are on public Wi-Fi. You might also consider using a VPN, which is a virtual private network. There are several companies that provide this way of connecting to public Wi-Fi or even your Wi-Fi at home, by putting a privacy fence around your Internet connection. There are also VPNs for your iPhone. One company that I like for the Mac is Nord VPN. Surfshark is another that I have heard good things about. 3. Make sure you have really good passwords; not your phone number, not your dog’s name, not your kids birthdays, but a good combination of letters, characters and numbers. Also, enable two factor authentication. This means that if you try to get into a password protected site, you will have to authenticate with a code sent to your phone or email. 4. Disable Bluetooth when you don’t need it. If you’re not using your Bluetooth capable earbuds or speaker, turn it off. 5. Either enable find my iPhone, and turn on location service on your phone, as well as your computer, or install some location software. With a Mac as well the iPhone, it’s all built in. You don’t really need another app to do that. 6. Get a privacy screen for your phone, and be careful when you type in passwords, make sure no one is standing next to you. 7. This may sound obvious, but keep your devices close to your body. If you’re in a cab or an Uber, don’t put it on the seat next to you. There have been so many cases when cars are stopped at a stoplight, some very quick thief reaches in through the window, or even breaks the window and grabs devices and purses on the seat next to the passenger. Also, it’s a good idea to have a protective case in case of falls or drops. 8. If you’re going to leave your computer or other devices in your hotel room, find a solid thing in the room, maybe a desk or something that’s bolted into the floor, and lock your suitcase to that with a strong packable cable lock, and keep your devices in the suitcase. And put a lock on your suitcase. Of course, if a thief really wants your things, they will likely get them get them. But if you do what you can to make it hard for them, then you will have less of a chance of having your vacation ruined by having your devices and worse, data or identity stolen. Cookie Segelstein is the MacMama, an Apple Certified Service Professional that provides Apple computer consultation and trouble-shooting in your home and office. Piedmont’s offense couldn’t get going in the third quarter, scoring just five points and conceding nine to fall behind 29-19. Both teams finally got the offense rolling in the fourth with Woodcreek outscoring the Highlanders 19-15 toward the 48-34 final score. Silverberg had a strong fourth quarter, scoring 11 of Piedmont’s 15 points in the final going. Why the attack is initiated has something to do with an Abronath, which holds the key to ultimate power, and is coveted by Krall, who is one very bad dude. When the Enterprise crashes on said planet, well, that’s when the games begin. It’s one set piece after the next of hyper-action, with Captain Kirk (Chris Pine) and Spock (Zachary Quinto), along with the crew, fighting for their lives. And, interestingly, a new character, Jaylah (Sofia Boutella), is introduced as one of the lone rebels fighting Krall. She’s fresh and resilient and interesting with kind of a goth, white face, zebra stripes look.
