East Bay Real Estate Update December 2024 2025 Industry Insights As we look ahead to 2025, we are curious to hear from some of our local industry experts about the trends they predict for the coming year. From mortgage lending, housing prices, and rentals to interior design, architecture, and the art market, we’ve gathered their thoughtful predictions on what’s next. Continue reading to learn more about what they expect in the coming year. Commercial Market "I believe we will see a rebound of real estate activity, especially in multifamily and office sectors. We will see an active push to get back to the office 5-days a week by the end of 2025. This will have a big impact on multifamily and office spaces in the urban core of U.S. cities. Also, if interest rates decline, we will see a rebound of asset values locally and nationwide. " -John Protopappas Housing Provider & Commercial Property Owner Design Trends “In 2025, home design embraces authenticity and soul, prioritizing spaces for connection and comfort. Expect libraries for quiet escapes, kitchens for communal cooking, and functional living rooms filled with natural materials and handcrafted details. Sustainability leads the way with locally crafted furniture and understated luxury, while bold art, calming neutrals, and biophilic touches create nurturing, personal sanctuaries. ” -Laura Martin Bovard Laura Martin Bovard Interiors Mortgage Rates The presidential election results suggest we could face a “higher for longer” period for mortgage rates, driven by several factors like a booming stock market, potential tax cuts, and inflation concerns that might make it harder for the Fed to cut rates aggressively. Despite challenges like higher rates and home prices, housing activity may increase in 2025 as people adapt to this “new normal. ” -Brady Thomas La Salle Mortgage Housing Prices and Inventory The dramatic rise in interest rates starting in March 2022 had a wide-ranging impact on real estate prices and transaction volume in 2023 and 2024. In 2025, for our local markets, I foresee a moderate increase in the number of total transactions and a marginal upward trend in sales prices. These trends are predicated on a relatively stable interest rate environment; a dramatic downward (or upward) adjustment in mortgage rates could have a more notable impact on prices and total sales volume. - Carrie McAlister Calia Homes Art Market “The middle-art market is likely to see prices stabilize after recent increases, but transaction volume remains uncertain. While high stock prices support activity, economic uncertainty dampens major purchases. Closely tied to real estate trends, this market faces challenges from reduced new construction and home sales, likely extending its current recession through 2025. ” -Danielle Fox SLATE Contemporary Gallery & Art Consulting Note: Homes over 900 sq ft and Oakland Zipcodes 94602, 94608-11, 94618-19 Calia Homes is not a financial advisor. articles.text: The Piedmont City Council approved at their meeting on Monday, December 2, an additional $2.8 million in funding to complete the new community pool. The money will come primarily from the City’s Facilities Capital Fund. This action brings the total project cost to $34.9 million, an increase of 79 percent from the original bond of $19.5 million approved by voters as Measure UU in November 2020. Since construction started in early 2023, the project has incurred significant new costs due to: • Project delays related to weather, utilities, and the discovery of two buried fuel tanks on the construction site • Additional costs associated with the complexity of pool electrification • Soil disposal, due to the presence of naturally occurring arsenic in the soil composition Additional costs have also come from construction adjacent to the pool site, including waterproofing of the Recreation Department building and the full-width repaving of Magnolia Avenue. George Sanen, Construction Manager on the project, expects construction on the sidewalk of Magnolia Avenue to be done by late January. Completion of the Magnolia sidewalk is dependent on PG&E submerging a gas line 12-16 inches lower. Pool architect Clarence Mamuyac speaking to City Council. Joining the meeting remotely was Griffin Construction President Jon Hughes (left) and Construction Manager George Sanen (right).
articles.title: Cost overrun soars to 79 percent

articles.text: Editor: A joyful thank you to everyone who came out to celebrate Lights Up! on the evening of December 4. Learning from John the Baptist By Rev. Jim Hopkins “And the crowds asked John, ‘What, then should we do?’” Luke 3:7-18 John the Baptist was a star. Crowds followed him. Rulers feared him. Seekers of truth revered him. If there had been paparazzi in his day, they would have stalked him. History remembers John kindly. Every third Sunday of Advent we read about him. We remember that his name means “God is gracious.” We remember that he preached and baptized in the wilderness. We remember that he fulfilled his mission to “Prepare the way of the Lord.” We remember that Jesus came to him for baptism. Beyond being fascinated by this powerful, complex and courageous individual, we do well to think about ways we can participate in his work of preparing a way for Jesus to be known in our lives and in our world. John did that work well but it did not end with him. It continues even now. Paying attention to what the gospel of Luke tells us about John’s words and deeds gives us some good ideas for ways in which we can prepare the way for Jesus to come into our world. The first thing John did was to go into the wilderness. This may mean that we need to get outside and appreciate nature. It can also mean that we can start preparing the way for Jesus by finding a quiet place, even if that quiet place is in our hearts and minds. We live in a noisy world. We prepare the way by literally, and figuratively, turning down the noise. The second thing John did was to ask the crowd that found him in the wilderness “What brings you here? Who warned you to flee the coming judgment?” In so doing, he teaches us that we prepare the way by considering carefully who and what we are listening to. What are the influences that shape us? What are the values that guide us? What are the teachings that form us? Who are the voices that call us? These are central questions in our work of preparing a way for Jesus. The third thing John did was to respond to the question “What then should we do?” He urged the people to share their possessions and not exploit others financially. He made it clear that we prepare the way for Jesus by caring about the well-being of others in tangible, helpful, “meet their basic needs” kinds of ways. We prepare the way for Jesus by making sure that our spiritual values are expressed in physical realities. This Advent, as we consider the ways in which John fulfilled his purpose, let us commit ourselves to preparing the way for Jesus. Rev. articles.text: The Piedmont Post asked Teachers Union President Elise Marks about the false report of a gunman outside the high school on November 12. Though later deemed to be a hoax it resulted in students and staff being put on lockdown for around 50 minutes. That event has since been overshadowed with the tragedy of three former PHS students being killed in an auto accident on November 27. But to not be forgotten, Marks describes the events from inside a Piedmont classroom when fear struck Piedmont campuses. – Elise Marks, Pres., PHS Teachers Union “The awful accident and loss of three Piedmont High graduates the day before Thanksgiving obviously eclipsed everything else,” Marks began. The following is Marks’ account of the lockdown on November 12 when a gunman was reported to be outside of Piedmont High School. Dr. Marks’ statement “Teachers got an email at 12:06 p.m. saying that a “shelter in place” was about to be initiated, but there was no detail given at the time. An announcement came over the loudspeaker right after that to go into shelter in place. Shelter in place is what we use when there might be a threat near the school so that we keep kids in our classrooms. It’s usually more for things like a gas leak a couple blocks away or something like that. We do lock our doors, close our windows and lower our blinds, and keep voices in the room quiet and tell kids they can’t go out to the bathroom. But we continue teaching, very quietly. Teachers were actually texting each other to double-check that we all knew what the protocols were. My classroom is right by the breezeway and when the first email alert came through, I locked my classroom door behind me so the kids were safe and ran a couple of steps into the hallway to pull the outside door closed and cut off access to the building. At that point, through the door windows, I could see a group of maybe half a dozen Piedmont police in tight formation hurrying onto campus. There were no other signs of trouble, so I hurried back into my classroom. On the teacher text chain, I’m seeing someone at 12:11 saying that “it’s a real warning from PPD,” but clearly not everyone An empathy board allowed students to add post-it notes about the experience of the school being on lockdown on November 12 under the fear of a gunman on campus. saw that text. I’m not sure how much time passed, maybe more than five minutes, before a second announcement came over the loudspeaker that this was now a “lockdown.” That’s the signal that there’s imminent threat on campus, presumably an active shooter. As soon as we knew it was lockdown, everyone moved fast. We’ve rehearsed this a lot, so it literally took just seconds for most students to shove desks aside and get down into the safest spot in the classroom, while a few volunteers and I quickly piled desks and stools in front of the door and used a trick we’ve learned to immobilize the door handle from the inside. Everyone was silent the entire time, not even a brief exclamation or questions to me about what to do. Somehow kids did manage to slide their phones from the phone holder, so they had them and were texting friends and family. At this point, we didn’t know what the threat was, though it was clear this wasn’t a drill. It was maybe another ten minutes before I saw the text alert from the police that a report had come in that said someone with an AR-15 was in front of the PHS Main Office threatening harm. That was definitely a frightening moment, seeing those actual words. But we all imagine this scenario enough that it wasn’t really a shock. We knew we were as safe as we could manage to be and that it was very unlikely that anyone could make it through the door. Everyone stayed very quiet. I texted teachers at Havens to see if they were in lockdown, but they weren’t. I also silently motioned kids to really squish together to be in the absolute safest part of the room to minimize the chance that if bullets were to come in through the door or windows that anyone would be in the direct line of fire. That’s an awful, awful thing to have to be calculating, but it’s something all teachers have to think about. At 12:37, we got the follow-up message that “This appears to be a wide-spread ‘swatting’ event across the county, but out of caution PMS, MHS, and PHS are in lockdown while the school is searched.” So we had to stay crouched and silent waiting for the all-clear, which we got via PUSD email at 12:47, though the police alert confirming it went out at 12:52, and we all decided on the text chain that we’d just stay put until we heard an official announcement over the PA, which came a few minutes later. So the whole thing lasted almost 50 minutes from our perspective. Kids seemed calm afterwards, but maybe it’s just being resigned. I gave them a few minutes to talk with each other and have a chance to get some water or use the bathroom. After that, it seemed like the best thing to do was just continue with the rest of class as if it was normal. At 1:03, someone said they heard a chopper circling. The next day someone posted a sign on a bulletin board in the STEAM building hallway where students could leave their thoughts on Post It notes. Some kids wrote notes about how scared they felt and how terrible it is that kids in school have to worry about this. We should have done more to help kids process it, but honestly even the adults don’t know what to say. We reacted fast to maximize safety, and everyone did that well.
articles.title: Dr. Marks describes lockdown at PHS

articles.text: Tonight’s December 11 school board meeting will take place at 7:00 p.m. in City Hall and will be the final board meeting for School Board members Cory Smegal, Veronica Anderson Thigpen and Hilary Cooper. Although much of the school community continues to cope with the recent deaths of three Piedmont High graduates, school business must go on. Important items on the agenda tonight include the first readings for six proposed new courses at Piedmont High School: AP Physics C and Honors versions of: Acting, Jazz Band, Orchestra, Symphonic Band, and Dance. First readings will also take place for board policies detailing: • Academic Honesty • Emerging Technology (AI) Another recent development is the announcement of Havens Principal Anne Dolid’s planned retirement at the end of the school year. The school board meeting agenda also includes an agreement between the district and Catholic Charities East Bay (CCEB) to “provide qualified mental health staff to support the school-based (PMS) mental health services through the Wellness Center.” The information and discussion item listed is the farewell to Board Members Smegal, Cooper, and Board President Anderson Thigpen. pages.text: Wednesday, December 11, 2024 5 SchOOLs Dr. Marks describes lockdown at PHS By Jay Russell The Piedmont Post asked Teachers Union President Elise Marks about the false report of a gunman outside the high school on November 12. Though later deemed to be a hoax it resulted in students and staff being put on lockdown for around 50 minutes. That event has since been overshadowed with the tragedy of three former PHS students being killed in an auto accident on November 27. But to not be forgotten, Marks describes the events from inside a Piedmont classroom when fear struck Piedmont campuses. “We’ve rehearsed this a lot, so it literally took just seconds for most students to shove desks aside and get down into the safest spot in the classroom.” – Elise Marks, Pres., PHS Teachers Union Preview of tonight’s School Board Meeting By Jay Russell Tonight’s December 11 school board meeting will take place at 7:00 p.m. in City Hall and will be the final board meeting for School Board members Cory Smegal, Veronica Anderson Thigpen and Hilary Cooper. Although much of the school community continues to cope with the recent deaths of three Piedmont High graduates, school business must go on. Important items on the agenda tonight include the first readings for six proposed new courses at Piedmont High School: AP Physics C and Honors versions of: Acting, Jazz Band, Orchestra, Symphonic Band, and Dance. First readings will also take place for board policies detailing: • Academic Honesty • Emerging Technology (AI) Another recent development is the announcement of Havens Principal Anne Dolid’s planned retirement at the end of the school year. The school board meeting agenda also includes an agreement between the district and Catholic Charities East Bay (CCEB) to “provide qualified mental health staff to support the school-based (PMS) mental health services through the Wellness Center.” The information and discussion item listed is the farewell to Board Members Smegal, Cooper, and Board President Anderson Thigpen. The board has benefited from Smegal’s eight years of experience on the board and Anderson Thigpen’s direction running meetings as President. New board members Michael Malione, Susy Struble and Max Roman will be sworn into their roles on December 16 along with new city council officials. To view the December 11 meeting agenda, see Simbli. e b o a r d s o l u t i o n s . c o m / S B _ Meetings/ViewMeeting.aspx- ?S=36030373&MID=34847 To stream and participate in the meeting remotely, see Zoom. us/j/83655029072. “The awful accident and loss of three Piedmont High graduates the day before Thanksgiving obviously eclipsed everything else,” Marks began. The following is Marks’ account of the lockdown on November 12 when a gunman was reported to be outside of Piedmont High School. Dr. Marks’ statement “Teachers got an email at 12:06 p.m. saying that a “shelter in place” was about to be initiated, but there was no detail given at the time. An announcement came over the loudspeaker right after that to go into shelter in place. Shelter in place is what we use when there might be a threat near the school so that we keep kids in our classrooms. It’s usually more for things like a gas leak a couple blocks away or something like that. We do lock our doors, close our windows and lower our blinds, and keep voices in the room quiet and tell kids they can’t go out to the bathroom. But we continue teaching, very quietly. Teachers were actually texting each other to double-check that we all knew what the protocols were. My classroom is right by the breezeway and when the first email alert came through, I locked my classroom door behind me so the kids were safe and ran a couple of steps into the hallway to pull the outside door closed and cut off access to the building. At that point, through the door windows, I could see a group of maybe half a dozen Piedmont police in tight formation hurrying onto campus. There were no other signs of trouble, so I hurried back into my classroom. On the teacher text chain, I’m seeing someone at 12:11 saying that “it’s a real warning from PPD,” but clearly not everyone An empathy board allowed students to add post-it notes about the experience of the school being on lockdown on November 12 under the fear of a gunman on campus. saw that text. I’m not sure how much time passed, maybe more than five minutes, before a second announcement came over the loudspeaker that this was now a “lockdown.” That’s the signal that there’s imminent threat on campus, presumably an active shooter. As soon as we knew it was lockdown, everyone moved fast. We’ve rehearsed this a lot, so it literally took just seconds for most students to shove desks aside and get down into the safest spot in the classroom, while a few volunteers and I quickly piled desks and stools in front of the door and used a trick we’ve learned to immobilize the door handle from the inside. Everyone was silent the entire time, not even a brief exclamation or questions to me about what to do. Somehow kids did manage to slide their phones from the phone holder, so they had them and were texting friends and family. At this point, we didn’t know what the threat was, though it was clear this wasn’t a drill. It was maybe another ten minutes before I saw the text alert from the police that a report had come in that said someone with an AR-15 was in front of the PHS Main Office threatening harm. That was definitely a frightening moment, seeing those actual words. But we all imagine this scenario enough that it wasn’t really a shock. We knew we were as safe as we could manage to be and that it was very unlikely that anyone could make it through the door. Everyone stayed very quiet. I texted teachers at Havens to see if they were in lockdown, but they weren’t. I also silently motioned kids to really squish together to be in the absolute safest part of the room to minimize the chance that if bullets were to come in through the door or windows that anyone would be in the direct line of fire. That’s an awful, awful thing to have to be calculating, but it’s something all teachers have to think about. At 12:37, we got the follow-up message that “This appears to be a wide-spread ‘swatting’ event across the county, but out of caution PMS, MHS, and PHS are in lockdown while the school is searched.” So we had to stay crouched and silent waiting for the all-clear, which we got via PUSD email at 12:47, though the police alert confirming it went out at 12:52, and we all decided on the text chain that we’d just stay put until we heard an official announcement over the PA, which came a few minutes later. So the whole thing lasted almost 50 minutes from our perspective. Kids seemed calm afterwards, but maybe it’s just being resigned. I gave them a few minutes to talk with each other and have a chance to get some water or use the bathroom. After that, it seemed like the best thing to do was just continue with the rest of class as if it was normal. At 1:03, someone said they heard a chopper circling. The next day someone posted a sign on a bulletin board in the STEAM building hallway where students could leave their thoughts on Post It notes. Some kids wrote notes about how scared they felt and how terrible it is that kids in school have to worry about this. We should have done more to help kids process it, but honestly even the adults don’t know what to say. We reacted fast to maximize safety, and everyone did that well. articles.text: Piedmont Girl Scouts brought cheer and plenty of holiday crafts inspiration to the tree lighting ceremony on Wednesday night, December 4. Beach Elementary 3rd Grade Brownie Troop 30981 and Piedmont 10th grade Senior Girl Scouts Troop 30713 set up a 20-foot long row of tables for making crafts and decorate holiday ornaments. Nearly 100 people wrote messages of kindness and positivity to hang as ornaments for the Senior Girl Scouts tree. It was part of their troop’s Take Action Project with a ‘Make the World A Brighter Place’ themed activity. The Brownie Girl Scouts are also working towards their “Take Action” Journey Badge and hosted a craft table for younger children to decorate a star, wreath or snowflake ornament or puppet. By the end of the evening, kids attending the event had made more than 100 pieces of artwork to take home. “I loved seeing all the little kids and helping them out,” said Brownie Troop member, Maeve Denison. Beach Brownie troop members Elena Dean (left), Maeve Denison, Lucia Jones & Essie Brezovec. Elena Dean (left) and Maeve Denison help a younger child use a glue gun for an ornament. The Senior Girl Scouts tree is adorned with messages from community members. “It was fun to see kids making up their own ideas,” said Troop member Essie Brezovec. All the materials were provided by the troops, with members planning and procuring the supplies in advance. “I’m enjoying all the activities for the kids,” said Anarjhya Vardhani, whose 2-year-old daughter, Ehime, glued sequins onto a star ornament. “It allows kids to exercise their creativity and I love that the Girl Scouts are running it. It shows great leadership on their part.” Piedmont High School sophomore Skye Baack, a member of Troop 30713 said that she and some of her fellow troop members have been participating in Piedmont’s holiday lights ceremonies since they were in Kindergarten. “I loved being able to share activities with the kids and do things together we find enjoyable,” she said. Being a role model for younger Girl Scouts was one of the highlights of the experience, she added. The 8- and 9-year olds in the Beach Brownie Troop were equally thrilled to be included in the event for the first time and help the community alongside the older Girl Scouts. “I really liked that all the Girl Scouts were working together,” said Brownie Troop member, Elena Dean. “It was really fun.”
articles.title: Girl Scout Troops lead the way with craft-making

articles.text: We’ve all done it: someone’s talking to us, and we’re nodding along, but we’re thinking about something completely different— like what’s for dinner or how we’ll escape this conversation to refill our drink. Sure, we heard them, but did we actually listen? As we head into the holiday season – family dinners, parties, gatherings – it’s easy to show up physically while staying checked out mentally. And yet, this is also the time of year when many people feel the most alone or isolated, even in a room full of people. Why? Because there’s a difference between being around people who hear you and people who actually listen to you. Hearing is the easy part. Hearing is passive. It’s the sound waves hitting your ears and your brain saying, “Yep, I caught that.” You hear the background music, the hum of conversation, and that one uncle who always talks a little too loudly. But hearing doesn’t mean you’re engaging. You can hear someone and still miss the point entirely—or worse, miss the person entirely. But the real gift is listening! Listening is active. It’s intentional. It’s the effort of tuning in, not just to someone’s words but to their meaning, their feelings, their humanity. When you listen, you’re saying, “I see you. I value what you have to say.” And let’s be honest: isn’t that what we all want, especially during the holidays? To feel seen and understood, even amidst the chaos of the season? How to Really Listen This Holiday Season Want to be the person who makes someone feel like they truly belong at the table? Here’s how to step up your listening game: 1. Put Down Your Phone: This one’s a no-brainer, but it’s harder than it sounds. Give the gift of your undivided attention. 2. Pause and Be Present: Before responding, take a beat. Listen not just to what they’re saying, but why they’re saying it. 3. Notice What’s Unsaid: Sometimes it’s about the tone, the hesitation, or the look in their eyes. Pay attention to the emotions behind the words. 4. Ask Thoughtful Questions: Show you care by asking questions that go deeper. “What’s been the best part of your year so far?” hits differently than, “How’s work?” 5. Reflect Back: Once you listen to what they say, reflect it
articles.title: The difference between listening and hearing

articles.text: Nikolas Markopoulos, a member of Piedmont Scout Council’s Troop 1, started his Eagle project to give back to the NIAD Art Center in Richmond (Nurturing Art through Artistic Development), which supports adults with disabilities. He was able to tour the area learn about the things NIAD needed. When he arrived in their office space, they told him that their bookshelves were too small and needed a bigger one. The shelves were needed for the artists’ personal files. “My vision was to create a bookshelf that held the files securely and that had extra space. Once my bookshelf was created it provided the office space with the ability to store more files and organize them more efficiently,” said Markopoulos. Building the bookcase The finished product

articles.text: On Tuesday, December 17, at 6:30 p.m. a thought-provoking film centering on mathematics in the modern world will be shown in Alan Harvey Theater. The showing of the 91-minute film Counted Out is open to the public, and will include comments from its filmmaker, Vicki Abeles. The community-wide event is hosted by Piedmont High School with support from Piedmont Education Foundation and PHS parent clubs. Counted Out investigates crises of political polarization, racial and economic inequity, a global pandemic and climate change through an unexpected lens: math. “In my quest to understand math’s critical role in our lives, I uncovered a movement of scholars, activists and educators who also see math as more than an academic subject. For them, math is a tool for understanding and harnessing the beauty, wonder and possibility of the world we live in,” said Abeles. This will be one of the first screenings of the film, and organizers are planning a panel discussion afterwards with the director and others in the greater Bay Area. The audience will be given the opportunity to ask questions. The screening is free, Register and RSVP on EventBrite at: Eventbrite.com/e/piedmont-unif ied-school- d ist r ict- cou nted-out-f ilm-screening-tickets-1092602506509?aff=oddtdtcreator Filmmaker Vicki Abeles will speak at the event; she previously directed Race to Nowhere and Beyond Measure.

articles.text: Piedmont Makers hosted a 2-day weekend of robotics events at Piedmont Middle School on December 7 and 8 with over 600 students and 150 parent coaches. Starting with the LEGO League Explore Festival on Saturday, the tournament continued on Sunday with the LEGO League Challenge Community Tournament. The LEGO League Explore Festival is an annual event for children ages six to ten to learn about STEAM (science, technology, engineering, arts, and math) through hands-on activities and challenges. At the festival, teams made presentations on a project related ocean exploration. They shared their LEGO models for their project solution, including code. “The LEGO League Explore Festival is a way to showcase the incredible creativity and problem-solving of our young teams. The teamwork is definitely the hardest part!” said Piedmont Makers Explore Co-commissioner Marta Lutsky. “We hope that this event will inspire the next generation of engineers and scientists.” This year’s festival set alltime records for participation and attendance, with 56 teams and over 500 attendees visiting Piedmont Middle School’s Buzz Redford Gymnasium on Saturday. According to event organizer Scott Miller, it was the biggest weekend in Piedmont Makers Robotics history. On Sunday, 35 LEGO League Challenge teams and 250 students took over the Middle School campus, filling the Redford Gym, Morrison Gym, several classrooms and the school plaza for judging during a full day of robotic competition. The LEGO League Challenge Community Tournament is a robotics competition for children ages nine to fourteen. Teams of up to eight kids design, build, and program LEGO robots to autonomously complete a series of challenges in a 2.5-minute match. The robots “The Ocean Explorers” from Beach Elementary School describe their LEGO model to a project judge. The “Axolotl Stars” from Beach Elementary and their coaches show off their ocean-themed project poster. Over 100 parent volunteers take part in mentoring and guiding teams throughout the fall season. The “Penguin Powerbots” from Wildwood Elementary, pose with their robot before showing it to a judge. The team later won the “Champion Award”, the top-prize of the weekend. The festival also included hands-on activities. Here, a team member shows off a day-of mechanical creation built from some of the thousands of LEGO Technic bricks that were available for free building. Students use visual code blocks from the Scratch programming language to learn the fundamental principles of software engineering as ages as young as kindergarten. The “Happy Robots” from Rheem Elementary in Moraga built a multistory model highlighting the layers of ocean exploration.
articles.title: Piedmont Makers hosts largest ever 2-day robotics event

Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ basketball team traveled to Reno, Nevada for the 2024 Winter TipOff Classic, and came home with the championship after winning all three games. PHS opened with a 46-34 win over Fernley on Thursday, December 5, then beat Spanish Springs 57-43 the next day, and closed it out with a dominant 64-18 win over Galena on the final day. “It was a good tournament for us. It’s great to have early-season road trips, especially for a young team like this to have that bonding experience,” coach Bryan Gardere said. Freshman Andrea Martin had a big performance with double-doubles in each game. “Andrea had a great tournament with three double-doubles. She was everywhere,” Gardere said. Freshman classmate Jenelle Solis also made a strong impression with 10 total 3-pointers throughout the three games. “Jenelle came out hot in the first game with three 3-pointers in the first quarter against Fernley. She has a great floor game Freshman Jenelle Solis knocked down 10 total 3-pointers at the Winter Tip-Off Classic. Freshman Andrea Martin had a big tournament in Reno with doubledoubles in all three games. and showed some dazzling passes and ball handling skills,” Gardere said. It marks the second time the Highlanders have won the Winter Tip-Off Classic, last claiming the title in 2022. The trio of games improves Piedmont’s record to 4-0 to start the year. They now look ahead to hosting the annual Paris Twins Classic at home. The opening game is with Damonte Ranch of Reno on Thursday, December 12. 64-18 win over Galena Piedmont got out to a fast 21-6 lead by the end of the first quarter and allowed just three points in the second quarter to extend the gap to 37-9 by halftime. PHS then scored 18 more points in the third to go up 55-17, then put up nine more points and conceded just a single point in the final going. Martin led the way with 28 points, including three 3-pointers. Junior Cleo Asfar and freshman Jenelle Solis both hit a pair of 3-pointers. articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ basketball team finished in third place at the annual Winter Classic, now hosted by the Highlanders for the 34th time. In the tournament. PHS defeated Envision Academy 74-36 in the first round on Thursday, December 5, followed by an 85-58 loss to Acalanes in the semifinals. They won third place with a 59-52 victory over HeadRoyce on Saturday, December 7. Northgate wound up winning this year’s Winter Classic by beating Acalanes. Piedmont’s win over Head-Royce was with a Division 4 North Coast Section foe. “We now have two D4 wins, which already sets us up nicely for NCS [post-season playoffs]. Because we’re in the league we’re in, you never know how things are going to go against those big, physical schools,” Although the Highlanders loss to Acalanes was by 27 points, they were in the game through three quarters, including an 11 point disadvantage early in the third quarter. PHS returned the following night to play stout defense for the win against the Jayhawks. “We’re young, so you’re going to see flashes of brilliance and times that we’re going to struggle. In terms of a loss like that, any time you come back and get a good win against a well-coached team, it’s a sign of growth for a young team,” Spencer said. It was a big performance on Saturday night for junior guard Dillon Casey, scoring 28 points. He finished the tournament with 17 points against Acalanes and 12 vs. Envision. “Last year we had Brit Burden have those big games. Since he’s gone, I’ve definitely had the chance to step up and have the ball in my hands. As the games go on, defenses will turn focus on me and I can kick out a pass to our new sophomores who are stepping up,” Casey said. Helping Piedmont put the game away against Head-Royce was new varsity starter, sophomore Lucian Fang Ring. He knocked down a 3-pointer with 50 seconds left in the game to sink the dagger. “The young guys are especially stepping up. The players we have, they are so much better than they get credit for and make veteran moves all the time. I remember being a sophomore, I was a bit more selfish in that regard and wasn’t truly focused yet. I feel like these guys are ahead of their time,” senior captain Ravi Silverberg said. 59-52 over Head-Royce It was a tight first half with Piedmont leading 10-9 at the end of the first quarter and 27-26 by halftime. PHS then outscored the Jayhawks 20-15 in the third to extend its lead to 47-41 to start the fourth quarter, adding 12 more in the fourth while allowing 11. Head-Royce remained within striking distance entering the final minute of the game down 56-49. But with slightly over 50 seconds left, Beach Lorin found Fang Ring sitting in the corner—knocking down the dagger 3-pointer to put the game away and give PHS a 10-point 59-49 lead. The Jayhawks hit a final 3-pointer with 6.2 seconds left. Staff Photos Dillon Casey goes in for a layup against Acalanes. He score 28 points against Head-Royce, and 17 in the game with Acalanes Lucian Fang Ring shoots a dagger 3-pointer to put Head-Royce away.

articles.text: Piedmont girls’ soccer team showed their potential on Saturday, December 7 in a 2-1 loss against Archbishop Mitty, the defending Division 1 CIF State champions. Despite the loss, the Highlanders battled to a 1-1 tie 10 minutes into the second half thanks to a penalty kick by Elsa Wallway. “It was great for the girls early in the seasons to see what the class of Northern California is and know they can hang with them. Just a little adjustment here and there and we can get to that level,” said assistant coach Tom Baudendistel filling in for head coach Dan Chubbock. Baudendistel named forward Ryo Woltag Piedmont’s player of the game after drawing the penalty to help knot things up. “We brought the wingers in a little tighter in the second half and Ryo totally adapted to that on the right side. articles.text: Staff Photos Nathan Bekele (left) celebrates with Jacques Saldanha after scoring the game-winning goal against Granada in the last minute. Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team pulled off a stunning 1-nil victory over Granada on Thursday, December 5 under the lights at Witter Field. In the final minute of the game junior Nathan Bekele scored the game-winner at the very end of regulation time The victory came against a team that reached the Division 1 North Coast Section playoffs last season. “First, it’s great to have all the players back from [their club teams]. It’s significant to have the seniors in the starting lineup. It’s great for the boys to get the win, but there’s still work to be done,” coach Ben Russell said. On the game-winning goal, Max Goldfarb sent a long free kick from about 50 yards away from the goal. His long pass sailed past Jacques Saldanha soaking up defensive pressure, bouncing off of the turf and perfectly for Bekele to head in the ball. Nathan had just entered the game as a substitute just a few minutes before scoring the winner. “We got a free kick and I just got into the game. The ball came flying and I managed to get my head on it. It was a good confidence booster,” Bekele said. “I knew it was going to be the last play of the game. I just made a run and I thought the ball was coming my way. I was right under it and the ball went over me, then I saw Nathan and his head was down. It bounced off of his head and goes in the goal, it was an act of God,” Saldanha recalled of the play. It was also a sentimental moment for the Highlanders following the tragic passing of former soccer players Soren Dixon and Jack Nelson. Saldanha, now a senior, was a sophomore on the squad when Dixon and Nelson were seniors. “It’s been a really hard week for the Piedmont community. We lost two amazing former players. That was the kind of goal Soren and Jack would’ve scored; they were the most clutch players and scored goals just like that. I made countless memories with them,” Saldanha reflected. top for an attempt on target, but Granada’s keeper did well to rush off his line to make the stop. Gianluca Bini then had a header trickle wide from a corner in the sixth minute. Bini had the best scoring chance of the first half in the 19th when one of his shot attempts rang off of the crossbar. From there, Granada had a shot go narrowly wide in the 24th, then goalkeeper Lucas Malecki had a big save on a shot in pointblank distance three minutes later. Both sides went into halftime in a 0-0 deadlock. In the second half, Bosco Lorin had a shot go wide two minutes into the half at 42’. Granada drew a free kick from a dangerous area just a couple of feet above the penalty area in the 53rd, but their shot attempt went into Piedmont’s wall of defenders. In at goal keeper for Piedmont in the second half was sophomore Tobias Tsai. He came up with a critical stop when rushing off his line in a 1-on-1 situation in the 71st minute. Both sides traded possession until Piedmont gained a free kick for the last play of the game, 3 minutes into extra time. Goldfarb’s long pass was inch-perfect, bouncing off the turf to lay up perfectly for Bekele’s header goal. Piedmont dog-piled onto Bekele in celebration. 1-0 victory vs. Granada Piedmont had the first action in the third minute, when Logan Foucher tracked a ball over the Max Goldfarb sends in the assist to Nathan Bekele for the gamewinner over Granada.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Chico State Athletics JoJo Murphy, PHS Class of 2022, is a junior on Chico State’s basketball team and is leading his conference in scoring. This week’s edition profiles three outstanding athletes, now in college. JOJO MURPHY Basketball Chico State JoJo Murphy, PHS Class of 2022, is a junior at Chico State and is an every-game starter for the Wildcats. So far this season, Murphy is leading the entire California Collegiate Athletic Association with an average of 19.4 points per game. The Wildcats are currently 6-2 overall with Murphy leading the team with 279 total minutes and 155 points. He’s converting 44 percent from the field and 34 percent from 3-pointers. He was named the CCAA’s Freshman of the Year in 2023 and was first-team All-CCAA. He was an honorable mention for All-CCAA in 2024. During his time at Piedmont High, Murphy earned Co-Player of the Year honors as a senior in 2022 and finished his high school career with 1,488 points. He was named the Posts’ 2020 Sophomore of the Year. NINA SCHWAB Diving Nina Schwab, PHS Class of 2024, is a freshman diver on Carleton College’s swim team and has already earned two MIAC Athlete of the Week awards. She recently won two events in the Rochester Invitational on December 7, scoring a 435.75 in the 1-meter dive and 432.70 in the 3-meter dive. On November 9, Schwab also won the 1-meter and 3-meter dives in a dual meet against Macalester College with scores of 258.85 and 248.45. Schwab was Piedmont High’s only diver and competed in the 2024 CIF State Swimming Diving Championship in the 1-meter dive. She finished 16th of 28 athletes with a score of 429.55. To get there, Nina finished fourth of 16 at the NCS Championships with a final score of 423.35. Carleton College Nina Schwab, PHS Class of 2024, is a freshman on Carleton College’s diving team in Minnesota. She has already earned two Athlete of the Week awards for the Minnesota Intercollegiate Athletic Conference so far this season. LUKE HARRIS Basketball Carleton College Luke Harris, PHS Class of 2021, is a senior at Carleton College. articles.title: Three former PHS athletes in college

articles.text: Staff Photo Dillon Casey earns Athlete of the Week honors after helping the Highlanders claim third place in the Winter Classic tournament. Andrea Martin, a freshman, earned Athlete of the Week honors after scoring a total of 57 points and grabbing 36 rebounds in the 3-day Winter Tip-Off Classic in Reno. This week, we’ve named Dillon Casey of the boys’ basketball team and Andrea Martin of girls’ basketball team our Athletes of the Week, while honorable mentions go to Jacques Saldanha of the boys’ soccer team and Elsa Wallway of the girls’ soccer team. Casey, a junior, is proving to be a leader on the basketball team. Last week he helped Piedmont go 2-1 at the Winter Classic and start its season with a 4-1 record. In the Winter Classic, Casey put up 28 points against Head-Royce to help his team claim third-place, while also scoring 17 in a loss to Acalanes and 12 in their opening round win over Envision. Andrea Martin is bursting onto the scene as a freshman star on Bryan Gardere’s girls’ basketball team. Last week she helped the Highlanders go undefeated in three games and win the Winter Tip-Off Classic in Reno. She recorded a total of 57 points and 36 rebounds in the weekend tournament. Honorable Mentions Soccer player Jacques Saldanha is proving to be an instrumental piece in coach Ben Russell’s system as a threeyear varsity player. Although he didn’t wind up on the score sheet in Piedmont’s big 1-0 win over Granada, he soaked up the defense’s attention to enable Nathan Bekele’s game-winning goal. He also bagged Piedmont’s only goal own a beautiful long shot in Piedmont’s 3-1 loss to defending D1 State Champion Archbishop Mitty. Wallway, a sophomore, earns our honorable mention for being a do-it-all player in Piedmont’s narrow 2-1 loss to Mitty, the defending D1 State Champion. Playing as a striker, she played as a False 9 as a playmaking passer and shooter. She scored Piedmont’s goal on a penalty kick. Staff Photo Jacques Saldanha was named honorable mention for his performances against Granada and Mitty. Staff Photo Elsa Wallway earned an honorable mention after being a key catalyst in Piedmont’s 2-1 loss to defending State champions, Mitty.

articles.text: The San Francisco Gay Men’s Chorus will perform its annual Holiday Spectacular! at Zellerbach Hall in Berkeley on Saturday, December 21. The San Francisco Gay Men’s Chorus is the world’s first openly gay chorus most often credited with creating the LGBT choral movement. The iconic ensemble will sing traditional holiday classics like “Little Drummer Boy,” “Sleigh Ride,” and “Deck the Halls” as well as holiday pop songs by George Michael, the Jackson 5, and the Manhattan Transfer for this Bay Area annual celebration. Beyond caroling, the evening will include satirical sketches, ugly Christmas sweaters, Santa outfits, and guest dancers and drag artists. Performance begins at 5 p.m. Call the Cal Performances box office at 510-642-9988 or visit https://calperformances.org to purchase tickets. The San Francisco Gay Men’s Chorus

articles.text: American Bach Soloists will return to the Herbst Theatre in San Francisco to perform an evening of Baroque pieces on New Year’s Eve, December 31. The program includes instrumental masterpieces by G.F Handel, J.P Rameau and C.H Graun performed by talented musicians, playing alongside soprano Maya Kherani and countertenor Eric Jurenas. Kherani recently showcased her debut with the New York Philharmonic in Handel’s Messiah, and Jurenas was an American Bach Soloist in 2011 where he sang the roles of Polinesso, Duke of Albany, in Handel’s Ariodante. The soloists are led by Artistic Director Jeffrey Thomas, recognized globally as a leading interpreter of Bach and Baroque music. Thomas co-founded American Bach Soloists in 1989 with the mission of introducing today’s audiences to Bach’s famous cantatas. The concert begins at 4 p.m. well before the midnight hour so guests will have opportunities to attend festivities afterward. Patrons are invited to the Soprano Maya Kherani is a featured performer with American Bach Soloists in its concert on December 31. Herbst Theatre Bar and Lounge on the lower-level for a welcoming reception prior to the performance. A selection of champagne, sparkling rose, red and white wines and cocktails named after Handel opera characters will be available. Visit https://www.cityboxoffice.com/eventperformances. asp?evt=3046 to purchase tickets. The theatre is located at 401 Van Ness Avenue in San Francisco’s Civic Center.

articles.text: Dorrance Dance, an awardwinning tap dance company based in New York City, will perform the classic Nutcracker Suite at Zellerbach Hall in Berkeley on December 14 and 15. Tchaikovsky’s iconic holiday score, The Nutcracker Suite, is reinterpreted by Dorrance Dance Artistic Director Michelle Dorrance, who has transforms the Sugar Plum Fairy into the “Sugar Rum Cherry. The “March of the Toy Soldiers” becomes a swinging brass “Peanut Brittle Brigade” performance, and collaborators Hannah Heller and Josette Wiggan give the original ballet’s pageant of national dances a 21st-century twist. The program features music by Duke Ellington and Billy Strayhorn’s jazz interpretation of Tchaikovsky’s classic score. Performances are Saturday, December 14 at 7 p.m., and Sunday, December 15 at 3 p.m. Tickets may be purchased by calling the Cal Performances Ticket Office at (510) 642-9988 or online at https://calperformances.org. Photo courtesy of Dorrance Dance Dorrance Dance performs The Nutcracker Suite with a tap-dancing twist.

articles.text: Dr. Suess’s greatest children’s stories come to life on the Berkeley Playhouse stage in the whimsical musical Seussical, performing through December 22. Directed by William Thomas Hodgson and choreographed by Leslie Waggoner, the musical is a collection of the writer’s most loved stories including Cat in the Hat, The Lorax and Horton Hears a Who. “I have such a fondness for this show,” said Berkeley Playhouse Artistic Director Kimberly Dooley. “I directed William in our production of Seussical in 2011 when he performed as Cat in the Hat. It’s an absolute delight to see him come full circle and get to be in the director’s seat.” Dooley added that the characters and cast this year “are zany and vibrant, and there are some really heartfelt moments that leave you feeling inspired.” Some cast members have family members performing, making Suessical “an intergenerational musical,” she said. The cast includes Stephen Kanaski as Cat in the Hat, Christian Arteaga as Horton the Elephant, No’Eau Kahalekulu as Gertrude McFuzz, and Andrea Rae as Mayzie La Bird. Hodgson said the musical is about “real deep human issues” that can be felt by all ages. “This is a family show, it’s a holiday show, it’s a feel-good show, it is a raucous show,” he said. “There’s a lot of dancing and colors and interaction.” Performances run Friday through Sunday and select weekday evenings. For tickets or more information, call the box office at (510) 845-8542 x351 or visit berkeleyplayhouse.org to purchase online.
articles.title: Berkeley Playhouse presents Suessical through Dec. 22

articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse’s newest production Waitress is playing onstage now through January 18. Susi Damilano’s revision of the motion picture Waitress, written by Adrienne Shelly, features music and lyrics by pop singer-songwriter Sara Bareilles. The play first premiered in 2015 at the American Repertory Theater in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and then transferred to Broadway in 2016, where it went on to receive 3 Tony Award nominations including Best Musical and Best Original Score. Waitress features protagonist Jenna, a diner waitress and expert pie maker, who is stuck in a small town and a loveless marriage. Jenna worries she will have to abandon her dream of opening her own bakery when she becomes unexpectedly pregnant, until she enters a baking contest and meets the soon-to-be love of her life. Ruby Day plays Jenna, and is supported by Zeke Edmonds, who plays Jenna’s love interest, Dr. Pomatter. Supporting characters include Louis Parnell, Dorian Lockett, Tanika Baptiste and Sharon Shao. Music Direction is by Dave Dobrusky and choreography by Nicole Helfer. Waitress is playing at San Francisco Playhouse through January 18, 2025. The venue is located at 450 Post Street in the heart of San Francisco’s Union Square theatre district. Performances are Tuesday through Sunday. Visit https://www.sfplayhouse. org/sfph/2024-2025-season/waitress/ to purchase tickets. Photo by Jessica Palopoli Tanika Baptiste, Ruby Day and Sharon Shao in San Francisco Playhouse’s production of Waitress
articles.title: Waitress on stage at SF Playhouse through Jan. 18

articles.text: A toy train made at Randall Museum during its annual Winter Crafts Day. The museum also hosts holiday-themed dance and magic performances, cookie-decorating activities, and seasonal photo opportunities throughout the month. Be sure to stop by the popular snow machine on the piazza, which emits non allergenic, nontoxic and non staining snow flurries every two hours. Afternoon tea at iconic hotels Afternoon tea has been a fixture at the Fairmont Hotel in San Francisco for ove100 years. Through December 28, families can book a reservation to sip steaming pots of fine loose-leaf tea with house-made scones and fruit-topped pastries. You can elevate the experience by booking an afternoon slot inside Fairmont San Francisco’s life-sized gingerbread house for up to eight guests at a time. Visit https:// www.fairmont-san-francisco.com to purchase tickets. Westin St. Francis Hotel The Westin St. Francis Hotel in Union Square also offers afternoon tea on December 14 and 15 only, with a twist: Young guests are invited to bring dollies and toys for Westin’s “Dollie and Me Holiday Tea” events, where adults can enjoy a full tea service and champagne, while children are served hot chocolate, sweet treats and assorted tea sandwiches to share with their best inanimate friends. Visit https://kitandsis. com/pages/dollie-me-holiday-tea to purchase tickets. Christmas tree in Golden Gate Park Christmas tree in Golden Gate Park The San Francisco Recreation and Park Department kicked off the holiday season on December 5 with its annual tree-lighting event in Golden Gate Park. Affectionately called “Norton” or “Uncle John’s tree,” in honor of Golden Gate Park’s designer and first park superintendent John McLaren, the 135-year old Monterey cypress in front of McLaren Lodge is once again adorned with 550 colorful holiday bulbs. The annual tree-lighting might be San Francisco’s oldest holiday tradition. According to city officials, McLaren had the tree lit for the holidays as a gift to The City’s residents who were enduring the Great Depression. The tree will be illuminated through the month. Nearby is the Solar Arch, Golden Gate Park’s newest public art installation. The 26-foot wide, 13-foot tall illuminated solar-powered arch towers over a handful of patio chairs and is a great spot to wrap up an evening stroll in the park. SF Ballet’s Nutcracker The San Francisco Ballet opened its 2024-25 season with Nutcracker, set in The City and honoring the company’s legacy as the first in the U.S. to present a full-length production of Tchaikovsky’s holiday classic. The company will host a sensory-friendly performance on December 29 in collaboration with the Autism Society San Francisco Bay Area. The Ballet’s familiar “Nutcracker” will be performed by principal dancers for audience members with autism, sensory disorders and sensitivities, or other physical, cognitive, or developmental disabilities. The performance takes place in a relaxed and shush-free setting that is appropriate for all ages, and designated quiet areas will be available for guests. Theater lights will remain at a low level for the entirety of the performance and guests are invited to bring their own sensory tools, including fidget objects, noise-reducing headphones and soft toys. Call the box office at 415-865- 2000 to purchase tickets, or visit www.sf ballet.org to purchase online. Celebrate Hanukkah at Pier 39 San Francisco’s tallest menorah will be lit at sundown on December 25, the first night of Hanukkah, at Pier 39. Each of the copper-sculpted menorah’s nine branches will be illuminated over the eight days of the holiday in the Entrance Plaza with insets of colored glass symbolizing the menorah’s traditional flames. The event is free and open to all ages.

articles.text: Ongoing through December 15 Andrew Wiener Photo exhibit “Living in the Abstract”, an exhibit of kinetic photography works by Andrew Wiener, will be on view on weekends from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. through December 15. Thursday, December 12, 6:30 p.m. Sacha Grippando Lecture on watches “It Doesn’t Just Tell Time, It Tells History” – A Journey Through the Fascinating World of Watches will explore the history of the human fascination with time and watches of the world, highlighting important watch makers and designers as well as specific models and collections. Admission will be by suggested donation. Just in time for Christmas, come learn about Cartier, Rolex, and Patek Philippe watches! Sunday, December 22, 4:00 p.m. Solstice Holiday Concert A remarkable group of seven women a cappella singers has enthralled audiences with their technically precise and passionate treatment of music since 1996. From Bartók to Björk, from Palestrina to Paul Simon, Solstice shares the music they love from around the world and through the ages. They are committed to performing new works for women’s voices. Discount tickets are available at https://bpt. me/6495389; full price at the door (cash/check only). Doors open at 3:30. Thursday, December 26, 6:30 p.m. Miles Graber Trio FREE Holiday Concert Join us on Boxing Day for a gift of thanks to the community for its ongoing support of the Center. The free concert is made possible in part by a grant from the Piedmont Post. The musicians are led by pianist Miles Graber, featuring the brilliant young cellist Hannah Paulus, and flautist Amy Likar. The program includes works highlighting this unusual combination of instruments, to include Louise Farrenc’s Trio for Flute, Cello and Piano. Melanie Bonis’ Pièce, Op 189, will be paired with Claude Debussy’s Cello and Piano Sonata. Finally, Beethoven’s C Major Cello Sonata will be followed by the E Minor Cello Sonata of Johannes Brahms. Doors will open at 6. Saturday, January 25, 2025, 7:30 p.m. Cristiana Pegoraro solo piano Returning to PCA after several years, Italian-born pianist and composer Cristiana Pegoraro honors Piedmont and PCA with another stellar, inspired solo performance on our Steinway grand piano! Acclaimed as one of the most gifted musicians of her generation, since her formal debut in Messina at age 10 she has received more than forty international awards, has released over thirty CDs, of which six are filled with her own compositions, and has performed with major orchestras and in renowned concert halls all over the world, including Lincoln Center and Carnegie Hall. articles.text: Visit historic Filoli House and Garden in Woodside now through January 12 to see the 16-acre estate decorated for the holidays. Filoli’s team has installed and decorated 22 trees, 3,600 light strands that stretch more than 18 miles, with more than 7,000 luminescent ornaments, and 1,000 feet of festive garlands. The Reception Room’s 18-foot ceiling creates an appropriate location for “The Grand Tree,” the tallest tree on display. The two-story historic mansion contains 56 rooms, including a ballroom and reception room designed to host concerts and debutante balls. Each room in the mansion is adorned with holiday decorations that complement the room’s original hues and aesthetics. The design team carefully recreated the original holiday placement used by Agnes and William Bourn, Filoli’s first owners. Original artifacts can be viewed throughout the home. Lurline Roth, who lived with her family in the mansion after the Bourns, was an avid collector of religious icons. Her Italian Murano glass nativity scene is now on display in the study. While holiday evenings at Filoli are truly a sight to see, the lighting enhancements glow just as festively during the day. Daytime admission allows visitors to explore the estate trail before sundown and admire the garden’s autumnal colors. Daytime hours are 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. The estate is open until 9 p.m. through January. To learn more about holidays at Filoli and to purchase tickets, visit https://filoli.org/events/holidays/. Historic Filoli House and Garden is dressed up for the holidays.

articles.text: Everlasting Moments is a remarkable film, unhurried and beautifully photographed: warm sepia images contrasted by stark winter scenes; a trolly car emerges out of the mist on a dark winter’s night; a summer picnic, lush and green and blue; the harrowing shadow of an enormous zeppelin floating overhead, darkening the neighborhood; a young woman, on a bitterly cold day, enveloped by slanting sunlight, walks out onto the thin ice, only to disappear into the fog; the face of Maria Larsson, briefly caught in agony is transformed as she finds resolve. It’s breathtaking. From beginning to end, Everlasting Moments is Swedish director and cinematographer Jan Troell’s film. Now 78, after 40 years of moviemaking, Troell has created a lovely, episodic, quietly told narrative set in the early 1900s. Mar ia Larsson (Mar ia Heiskanen), Finnish, marries Sigfrid (Mikael Persbrandt) and moves to Maimo, Sweden. Just prior to her marriage she wins a Contessa folding camera in a lottery and rather than sell it, she puts it away in a keepsake trunk. Only years later – now with children, coping with Sigfrid’s drunken episodes and abusive rages – does she remember the camera and takes it to a local studio to sell. At the shop she meets Sebastian Pedersen, proprietor, who encourages her to keep the Maria Heiskanen in Everlasting Moments camera and take pictures. Maria soon discovers that she has an eye. A new world is suddenly revealed and captured. Pedersen, looking at her pictures, tells her, “If you’re a person who sees, you have no choice but to do so.” The connection between them – her sensitivity and openness and his kindness and generosity – is palatable yet by unspoken agreement held in check. And so, like an undeveloped print dropped into a tray of solution, Everlasting Moments comes into focus. Slowly. Deliberately. Evocatively. Through seemingly pedestrian moments, the picture is brought into unyielding relief. It is a gorgeous thing to behold, subtle, nuanced and deeply human. The performances, led by Heiskanen and Persbrandt and Christensen, are so wonderfully rendered it becomes impossible to comprehend that they are acting. The verisimilitude of their circumstances is seamlessly convincing while Troell explores the resilience of love, the abrasive effect of resentment, even loathing, and the courage that is required of a woman who, constrained by the dictates of a narrow and fiercely judgmental world, manages to step forward and find herself. What Troell asks of the audience is to find a reflection of the human condition. He asks us to see, while never allowing sentiment or caricature to overwhelm the story. His film has a fragile yet enduring honesty. This is film as art, and is the work of a master. Everlasting Moments. Starring Maria Heiskanen, Jesper Christensen, Mikael Persbrandt and Ghita Norby. Directed by Jan Troell. Swedish with subtitles. 1 hr., 32 min. Not rated. Streaming on prime/apple tv. Released in 2017. articles.text: I’m reluctant to say that The Ghost Writer is the antidote to those fast-paced, intense “B” thrillers that are ever ubiquitous. Recent examples would be The Hurt Locker, The Green Zone, as well as the Bourne trilogy, all shot with the revolutionary handheld steadicam and the digital Red, creating a grainy, documentary style, jerky and intense – a gestalt of visual experience. Antidote is too strong a word, perhaps, even a bit disparaging of a genre that is superbly entertaining. The Ghost Writer, directed by Roman Polanski, does possess all of the intensity of a thriller; however, the narrative is conveyed not by action and physical confrontation, but through dialogue. This is a film of language, well written, with engaging set pieces wherein the characters reveal themselves and the plot – which is at first intriguing and then ever more complex. Told from the point of view of a thirty-something writer (Ewan McGregor) for hire (his name is never given. He’s referred to only as “Ghost” or “man”) who reluctantly agrees to edit the memoirs of Adam Lang (Pierce Brosnan), England’s recently resigned Prime Minister. Lang is now living in a stark, contemporary house on Martha’s Vineyard – the month is January, it’s cold, the sky and ocean a mix of wintry slate and teal, rain falling constantly. Everything feels ominous and unsettling; exactly Ewan McGregor in The Ghost Writer
articles.title: The Ghost Writer a fine film by Polanski

articles.text: A scene from Coraline everyone she meets has buttons instead of eyes. Something she is willing to overlook. So seductive is this new world, where f lowers bloom in the moonlight, where all is a kaleidoscope of colors, she begins to find it harder and harder to return to her real life and her real parents. And, of course, her new mother encourages her to remain forever. It all seems so perfect. But as a talking cat suggests, perhaps there is more to this parallel world than first meets the eye (or button). And perhaps all of this good will and attention is a bit suspicious. What child doesn’t fantasize about a world in which they are the center of attention, a world in which they feel powerful and have more than a modicum of control over their own lives. Or a world suddenly absent parents who draw boundaries and make rules and all seems so arbitrary. The culmination of this fantasy was captured perfectly in the film Home Alone, when Kevin wakes up in his house and discovers everyone is gone. He wished them gone, and suddenly his wish has come true. He quickly sets out to create a life in which he rules. It’s a rush until it isn’t. Like Kevin, Coraline is soon confronted with more than she can handle and what was a thrill becomes deeply frightening. Will she be able to find her way back to her real world and once again be able to embrace her parents? Nothing is certain. What is surprising about “Coraline” is that none of the characters are particularly attractive. Even Coraline herself is feisty and a bit ill-tempered. That’s not to say that she should

articles.text: Secretariat is a Disney film about a magnificent chestnut racehorse nicknamed Big Red, also known as Secretariat, thought by some to be the greatest racehorse of all time. In 1973, Red won, against all odds, the Triple Crown: the Kentucky Derby, the Preakness and the Belmont Stakes. It was then, and remains still, the Holy Grail of horse racing, a trifecta that is rarely attained. No one does movies about animals better than Disney and Secretariat is filled with excitement: tight shots of jockeys clutching the reins as horses weighing some 1,200 pounds charge around an oval track more than a mile long. It’s intense, even thrilling. Of course, it’s irresistible for Disney not to give Secretariat a sentient intelligence. In one scene, Penny Chenery (Diane Lane), owner of Secretariat, stands holding the horse’s bridle, looking the horse in the eyes, while he looks back and conveys to Penny that he’s ready to race. Disney loves to anthropomorphize animals (Bambi, et al); however, thankfully, director Randall Wallace shows restraint. A horse by any other name is still a horse. While the hub of the film is Secretariat and his ability to run, the focus throughout is on Penny, a Denver suburban housewife who tenaciously, with grit, takes a huge gamble on Secretariat Diane Lane stars in Secretariat For advance tickets, go to https://bpt.me/6383991 or use this QR code:

pages.text: Wednesday, December 11, 2024 19 MOVIES FOR KIDS Coraline – good and scary By Chris Honoré The animated stop-motion feature Coraline is a tour de force of imagination. Though originally made to be shown in stereoscopic 3-D, even in 2-D it is vivid and rich with a panoply of colors and strange and interesting characters but best suited for older children. It can be dark and sinister, the narrative taking a young girl’s fantasy and turning it into a gothic nightmare. Of course, all fairytales have a distinctly dark side to them. Dorothy follows the yellow brick road only to meet the Wicked Witch. Alice falls down the rabbit hole into a world while fanciful is not simply benign. And certainly Harry Potter, for all of his deft ability with magic, encounters evil that takes many forms and threatens his very existence. And so it is with Coraline. She and her parents have recently moved into a Victorian rooming house called The Pink Palace, filled with eccentric boarders. Feeling lonely and bored, and finding her parents distracted and cranky as they work intensely on a gardening catalogue (her mother is especially curt and preoccupied), Coraline sets out to explores the house. She soon discovers a hidden door in her room that opens into a narrow tunnel (a rabbit hole?) and a parallel world. In this mirror universe, however, her new parents are attentive to her every need, and her room wonderfully inviting. Along with windows which we discussed last time, doors make up the most common component of fenestration – the collective term for openings in the architecture of a building. Since the most prominent fenestration of a building is generally the entry side, it includes the most important door in the building, the entry door. This door and its place in the facade composition are essential elements of the style and quality of the entire building. Often “nested” in an architectural recess, the entry door likely includes architectural enhancements like surrounding tile work or plaster accentuation, and usually closely surrounding windows of various types. Among these are sidelights, which are vertical fixed (non-operable) windows adjacent to a door, and transoms which are horizontal windows above the door. Besides the door leaf (the actual hinged panel), the style, size and finish of hardware including locks, hinges, thresholds, stops, weather stripping, and address numbers are also important visual considerations for the appropriateness and quality of the door(s). (In a previous column on Porches and Entries, we mentioned a number of other components that work with the door itself to make a welcoming entry.) The process of designing door assemblies can be fairly complex. Desired swing direction (door “handing”) must be coordinated Doors and windows are always related on a building’s fenestration, especially at the main entry. Very different in scale, style and materials, both the traditional and contemporary designs shown in these Piedmont homes are well done. Note the deep recesses on the traditional (top left photo), and the matching door/stair rail material on the contemporary (top right photo). In this Craftsman style home, I would say the visually strong and nicely proportioned porch opening could also be considered a part of the architectural fenestration. Nicely proportioned and detailed, well designed garage doors such as these can be considered a fenestration feature on a home. Both the glazing (glass) and planting create a special character to both the double wide and paired single doors.

Exterior doors are generally only OK relative to energy efficiency, except at their perimeters where the necessary break between door leaf and jamb is a weak spot, necessitating weather stripping to meet energy standards. articles.text: Wednesday, December 4 was a beautiful, sunny, winter morning. During 2024 the Walking on Wednesdays group hadn’t gotten to Olive Avenue on the southwest side of town, so that was the day’s destination. Along the way, there was some Key System train history on Fairview Avenue to be shared too. Forty-two walkers and two K-9 best friends were at the Exedra to enjoy it all. The walkers went on Fairview and stopped for a group photo in front of a Victorian home built in 1896. Some history of the Key System was told. The transit system (bus, streetcar) began service in 1903 in Berkeley and in 1904 in what was to become the City of Piedmont. The No. 12 Line was originally called the “Grand Avenue & Hollis Street Line.” It initially went along a set of Oakland and Piedmont streets including Oakland, Fairview, Grand, Webster, 14th, Market, 24th, Adeline, 32nd, and Hollis to Yerba Buena. This line began on Grand and Wildwood Avenues, at Piedmont’s boundary, as a shuttle to Perry Street near where Oakland Avenue and the MacArthur Freeway are today. The line connected there with the Lakeshore Avenue line cars. The end of the line was extended from Grand up Fairview in 1915. The route had a few name changes over the years, but in 1928 its name was finalized as the “No. 12” line. However, on June 27, 1948 the No. 12 Grand Avenue streetcar service was abandoned, and buses replaced the streetcars. The group walked down Fairview past a long street median that was once a Key System right-of-way. They crossed Grand Avenue and climbed up Sunnyside to Olive Avenue where they enjoyed seeing many front yard gardens. Olive goes along the top edge of the Morcom Rose Garden below. The garden is in a 7.5- acre, natural bowl in Oakland, but when the City of Oakland purchased the site in 1911 the best park entrance was through land in Piedmont. The Piedmont City Council joined the effort to create the park by acquiring Piedmont lots at the southern corner of Olive and Oakland Avenues. The walkers went up Olive and passed a garage that is decorated as a bar with a sign proclaiming it to be “Tom’s Tavern Steak House.” The group crossed the Oakland Avenue bridge that Albert Farr designed in 1910 as a significant entrance to Piedmont. The bridge replaced a wood trestle that was built in 1890 for the cable cars that served what was to become Piedmont. Farr used the same Spanish design that he used for Piedmont City Hall. The bridge was built in 1911 as a reinforced concrete arch bridge over Linda Avenue with a 160- foot arch span and a total length of 343 feet. The relatively new lampposts and lights make the bridge a lovely entrance to the city, and guardrails make it safer for walkers. The improvements were made by the city in 2014. The walkers crossed Grand Avenue to Arbor Drive, where they discovered a hidden, 110- foot path between Arbor Drive and MacKinnon Place and Magnolia Avenue. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. On hand for last week’s Walking on Wednesdays were Charlene Louie, Adrienne Hamlin, Jim Kuo, Mark Davis, Brenda Ferrero, Karin Fetherston, Alan Goldhammer, Albert Chen, Stella Houston, Tina Shum, Tom Lehrkind, Jack Fischrup, Sherry Jacobs, Sharona Fischrup, Melba Yee, Kat Lang, Phil Witte, Joyce Hicks with K-9 best friend Mocha, Matt Gerhardt, Bob Wang, Leigh Sorensen, Michelle Yang, Alissa Quan, Abha Kotari, Karen Palmer, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Bill Ahern, Ken Moy, Leilani Ching, Greg Keller, Julia Chin, Phil Chin with K-9 best friend Rocky, Noemi Alvarado, Priscilla Wanerus, Bonnie Sherwood, Vicki Trimbach, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome Mary Worthington, Joan Skolnick, and Susan Anderson, who were walking with the group for the first time.

Full-bodied, rich, velvety it should provide thrilling drinking for over a decade. • 2022 Clos du Calliou Cotes du Rhone Vielles Vignes This wine overdelivers and exhibits textbook cherry, earth, olive, and underbrush as well as clean, balanced medium bodied red fruit profile on the palate. This solid, sturdy wine could challenge many more expensive Chateauneuf du Papes. This ripe muscular wine will benefit from time in the cellar. articles.text: The Rhone wine region of France is usually broken into two sub-regions, the North and the South. The north extends from just south of Orange to Valence and primarily focuses on the Syrah grape for reds and the Viognier and Marsanne grape for whites. I recently wrote an article focusing on the wines of the North region, so this month I will be focusing on the South region. It is a much harder task as the South Rhone region is huge compared to the north and produces a staggering number of wines. It ranges from Valence all the way down to the Mediterranean Sea. As the Rhone River progresses southward, the valley widens and the climate changes. The region is distinctly more Provencal with a Mediterranean influence in culture and climate. The summers are long and warm and the winters are mild. Rainfall is less than in the north and the famous Mistral wind is a major player. Another unique characteristic of these wines are the nuances of Garrigue – the wild resinous herbs that cover the landscape. If Syrah is the big boy of the North Grenache is king in the South and forms the foundation of the areas popular blends. You’ll also encounter Mourvedre, Cinsault, Counoise, Carignan, Grenache Blanc, Marsanne, Roussanne, Clairette, Bourboulenc and a host of minor players. The Southern Rhone’s most famous wine is Chateauneufdu-Pape, a blend containing up to 19 varieties of wine grapes as permitted by AOC rules. The other major AOC’s of the area are Gigondas, Lirac, Tavel, Vacqueyras and Ventoux. Some of the southern Rhone’s greatest values can be found under the Cotes du Rhone label. This is a massive region that produces vast quantities of wine and the prices are very reasonable and the wines can sometimes rival the higher priced AOC wines. The following wines are imported by North Berkeley Imports and are available online and at their retail store, North Berkeley Imports, 1505 Shattuck Ave. Berkeley. • 2022 Clos du Mont-Olivet Chateauneuf du Pape This CDP reveals a bouquet of violets, dark, wild berries, spices and garrigue accented by delicate notes of pepper. Medium to full-bodied, delicately juicy and round, with good depth at the core and framed by firm, structured tannins. A bit young to drink now, this wine will blossom with time in the cellar. • 2022 Clos du Mont-Olivet Cotes du Rhone Vielles Vignes This is the baby brother of the above wine. It shows hints of vanilla and baking spices to go along with the red plums and black cherries. It’s supple on the mid-palate and velvety on the finish, showing ample richness and length. Drink this delicious

Teams also presented a research innovation project that addressed the year’s theme. This year, the theme was problems faced by people that explore or research the world’s oceans. The weekend included a host of STEAM attractions for the community, including build stations with thousands of LEGOs, robotics presentations by FTC Circuit Breakers and FRC 8033, and a huge crowd-pleaser – the famed Makers’ t-shirt slingshot. “The LEGO League Challenge Community Tournament is a great opportunity for children to experience the joys and challenges of working as a team, public speaking and presentation, and using the engineering design process to build, code, and revise robot designs.” said Piedmont Makers League Commissioner Pat Holder. “We are always blown away by the creativity and ingenuity of our teams.” This year’s tournament was the largest robotics tournament ever held by the Makers, with 35 teams vying for the top prize – the Champion’s Award. Teams also took home trophies for best robot design, best innovation project, and even a coach/mentor’s award. The full list of awards and winning teams is listed below. The Piedmont Makers LEGO League Explore Festival and LEGO League Challenge Community Tournament are part of the worldwide FIRST LEGO League program, which aims to inspire children to pursue careers in STEAM. More information on the Makers is available at www. piedmontmakers.org. Team #55795, the “Sea Cucumbers” from Havens elementary won the “Motivate” award for embracing “the culture of FIRST LEGO League through team building, team spirit, and displayed enthusiasm.” The Champion’s Award was given to team #37487, the “Penguin Powerbots” for their high level performance in the robot game, robot design, innovation project, and demonstration of core values throughout the tournament.
