Instead of the usual mass-gathering at the Summit Pole, the pack never got more than 10—giving the Post a surprising opportunity to snap a few shots. 12 night-owls were still trekking their way up to the summit on our way back down, meaning we spanned an average of 29.5 hikers per mile in the 6.5 mile day. Senior hikers or beginners can find several places to stop on the way up to the 3.25 mile, 2,500’ peak. With a flashlight in hand, there was never a point when we would get too far ahead or too far behind other hikers—giving an assured feeling of safety under the night sky. Be sure to pack a good-sized water to stay hydrated, some granola or source of energy, and a charged battery for videos of an unforgettable sunset. Is Edge of Darkness violent? Definitely. In the Craven world you can have conversations, brief and to the point, and then the moment is quickly reached when the best response is simply to hit or shoot the bad guy. Sometimes these moments of carnage and gunplay, or the threat of carnage and gunplay, are connected to the plot by the slightest of threads. No worries, though, they’re a rush. News of the fatal event quickly spread. At 9:30 a.m. on Wednesday, November 27, Police Chief Jeremy Bowers and Fire Chief Dave Brannigan held a press conference for media outlets. “I really want to keep the focus on the victims and the families that have lost their loved ones,” Bowers said. “I will tell you that our women and men who responded to this call did everything they could.” Speed is believed to have resulted in the crash. Investigations are being conducted by the California Highway Patrol and National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. 1 classmate survives A fourth classmate, Jordan Miller, was removed from the wreck by a motorist that was following behind the Cybertruck. “There was a motorist that was traveling behind the vehicle that was involved in the collision, a significant distance behind that vehicle. And when they turned the corner they saw the vehicle in flames, [then] a person exited that vehicle and helped extract one of the involved parties out of the vehicle [on fire],” explained Bowers. “It’s good to know that somebody was willing to help. They probably saved a life,” said Brannigan. articles.text: Thanksgiving is almost here, and with it comes the 23rd Annual Piedmont Turkey Trot. The 5K run through Piedmont streets will take place on Thanksgiving morning, November 28 at 8:30 a.m. with the start and finish line located at the Exedra on Highland Avenue. The race has received 1300 registered entries and organizers anticipate that number to double by race day. Runners will be coming for more than 100 cities from cities as far away as Arlington, Virginia and Calstock Cornwall, England. Race rewards include a turkey for the overall men’s race leader and overall women’s leader, plus a pair of running shoes from Transport. Winners in each age division will receive a pumpkin pie, courtesy of Piedmont Grocery, a cap and a bouquet of flowers from J. Miller Flowers. The top three runners in each age group will also receive cards for Yellow Door café in Montclair. The 2024 race shirts, hats and swag bags have been delivered, with shirts in purple for the first time in over a decade. Race Shirt Pickup On Wed. Runners may pick up their race bibs the day before the race, Wednesday afternoon November 27, between 3:00-6:00 p.m. at the Veterans Hall. Dog bandanas will also be available during this time for $6. The first Tiny Tot Trot for children ages 3-6 will be taking registrations from 3:00-4:00 p.m. and their race will take place at Witter Field on Wednesday at 4:15 p.m. It will be a 1-2 lap race around the track. Race proceeds benefit Piedmont High School’s cross-country and track & field teams, as well as the PHS Boosters Club. They also benefit Piedmont Middle School’s cross-country and track teams, and the Piedmont Junior Running program led by Leonard Goldman. Race director Sandy Proctor said, “We are all squared away. We have our city permit in place. We’ve worked with the police and the fire department and City Works… Our sponsors are all lined up and they’ve got their signs ready to go, so it looks like it’s going to be a great year.” Entry fees are unchanged from last year: • Adults 13 & older: $50 • Children 12 and under: $30 Register at Piedmontturkeytrot.com Runners at the front of the pack at the last year’s Piedmont Turkey Trot.
articles.title: Turkey Trot kicks into high gear for annual 5k run on Thanksgiving

His sense of wonder was not misplaced for historians of the era such as Flavius Josephus and Tacitus commented on its beauty. Jesus, however, gave a shocking response. He informed everyone who was listening, “Before long, it will all come tumbling down.” When they were out of the city and looking at the temple grounds from the Mount of Olives, Jesus explained his comments to the leaders of his disciples. “Hard times are coming. It will seem like the world is coming apart at the seams. The scale of human suffering will be immense. Yet, mark my words, this is but the beginning of the birth pangs. Religion Corner - Main Low points and turning points By Pastor Jim Hopkins As Jesus and company were leaving the Jerusalem Temple one day, an unnamed disciple marveled at the magnificence of the temple complex. His sense of wonder was not misplaced for historians of the era such as Flavius Josephus and Tacitus commented on its beauty. Jesus, however, gave a shocking response. He informed everyone who was listening, “Before long, it will all come tumbling down.” When they were out of the city and looking at the temple grounds from the Mount of Olives, Jesus explained his comments to the leaders of his disciples. “Hard times are coming. There will be trouble at every turn. Supposedly trustworthy leaders will prove untrustworthy. Friends you thought you could count on will let you down. Your foundations will be shaken. It will seem like the world is coming apart at the seams. The scale of human suffering will be immense. Yet, mark my words, this is but the beginning of the birth pangs. This low point will be a turning point.” How can this be? How can our low points be turning points? It may be that low points can be turning points because they cause us to turn anew to the only one who can tell us who we are, the only one who can teach who we are born to be, the only one who holds us when the world breaks us, the only one who stills us when our foundations shake. Long before Jesus, long before there was a temple at Jerusalem, maybe even long before there was a Jerusalem, there was a woman of deep faith named Hannah. Hannah was broken. In a world that defined women by their ability to have children, Hannah did not have a child. She went into her temple at the old city of Shiloh and prayed earnestly, yet silently, for a son. The priest at the temple, Eli, observed her and rebuked her. “Go home. You are making a spectacle of yourself. Look at you. Drunk in a sacred space.” This low point for Hannah proves to be a turning point. Her longing to give birth serves as the birth pangs for a new way of being. She challenges Eli, who represents male dominated religion, “I am pouring out my heart and you accuse me of pouring in the wine. It is you who needs to repent.” She trusts God. “I believe you have heard me. articles.text: The following letter was sent to Piedmont City Council on November 15. Editor: I am writing to express my support for the proposed EV charging station at 29 Wildwood Avenue and to commend the Planning Commission’s recommendation to limit its hours of operation from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. This restriction, especially from the perspective of nearby residents, strikes a reasonable balance between community needs and maintaining neighborhood peace. I also appreciate the plan for an 8-foot soundproof wall along the property perimeter to help reduce noise impacts on adjacent homes. However, I am concerned about the effectiveness of relying solely on off-site camera monitoring to manage on-the-ground issues. During the Planning Commission meeting, Shell representative Matthew Lyons was unable to outline a specific plan to address safety concerns, disturbances, and noise. Without a clear, proactive management strategy, these issues may place an undue burden on nearby residents. Approving the Conditional Use Permit (CUP) without a comprehensive on-site plan or reliable off-site monitoring would be like driving with blinders on. Additionally, Mr. Lyons referenced 12 other EV charging sites with similar operational models, all still in development and data is available from these locations. Relying solely on cameras and remote management to secure
articles.title: The burden rests with Shell and Planning Commission

At the same meeting, proponents of 24/7 estimated that as many as 1000 Piedmont residents who, as emergency medical workers, could potentially benefit from overnight EV charging hub services. This apparent inconsistency in estimated usage demonstrates a deeper lack of insight into the risks v. rewards of a 24/7 operation. I wish there was more effort to examine the operating hours, locations, usage statistics of EV charging hubs within a 25=mile radius of 29 Wildwood Ave. That information could be helpful to make an informed decision going forward. The onus should be on Shell to provide reasonable estimates of usage, security risks and noise levels before they are given a 24/7 operating hours variance from the City. –Vanessa Oklejas The following letter was sent to Piedmont City Council on November 15. articles.text: The annual Toys for Tots drive has begun, with bins for donations at the entrance of City Hall. Community members are asked to donate new unwrapped gifts for children whose families have trouble affording holiday gifts. Donation bins will remain for donations through December 23. The drive is accepting all toys from dolls and action figures to books and board games. Toys for Tots is a national campaign operated by the U.S. Marine Corps Reserve. Observing a longstanding tradition, members of the City Council will each donate a toy during a ceremonial presentation at the December 2, 2024, Council meeting. Community members in attendance are welcome to contribute toys during the presentation as well. All toys collected will be distributed to families in Oakland and Alameda County. Toys dropped off before December 11 will be distributed through the Marine Toys for Tots Foundation. Toys donated after December 11 will be distributed at the annual Three Wise Men toy giveaway in Oakland’s Fruitvale neighborhood. Schoolmates employees and Fire Engineer Anthony Renteria with Schoolmates students from Havens School at last year’s Toys for Tots drive
articles.title: Toys for Tots drive is underway

articles.text: A book drive for the East Bay Children’s Book Project (EBCBP) will be held at the Piedmont Turkey Trot bib pickup on Wednesday, November 27, from 3:00-6:00 pm at the Veterans’ Memorial Building, 401 Highland Avenue. Volunteers will be collecting new and gently used children’s books, including board books. Books should be clean with no marks or stains. No textbooks, religious books, encyclopedias, magazines, adult books, or library discards please. Bring donated books in boxes for easy transport to EBCBP. The mission of EBCBP is to help build literacy by putting books into the hands of children who have little or no access to them. Working through individuals and organizations who help children in need, the organization has given out more than 2,000,000 free books since opening their doors in 2005. School Board and City Council members started this tradition more than 10 years ago. EBCBP volunteer and former Wildwood Elementary School librarian Ellen Reed notes that 570 books were donated last year during this event. “We are so grateful for the community’s contribution to our children’s literacy project year after year,” said Reed. Volunteers are needed to help receive donated books on Wednesday, November 27, from 3:00- 6:00 pm, and drive books to EBCBP at 2501 Harrison Street in Oakland. Those with an interest in maintaining this tradition are asked to e-mail Sarah Pearson at srpear@gmail.com. If you miss this opportunity to donate books, you may drop off books at EBCBP on Tuesdays 3:30-5:30 pm or on Saturday, December 7, from 10:00 am-1:00 pm. Donated children’s books may also be left Piedmont School Board member Lindsay Thomasson is shown donating books at last year’s Turkey Trot registration at the Veterans’ Hall during pre-race packet pickup. in the EBCBP box at the Piedmont Middle School library, 740 Magnolia Avenue, during school hours. About EBCBP Too many children in the Bay Area live in homes without books or attend schools and programs where books are in short supply. Encouraging reading is not enough when families and schools do not have books. East Bay Children’s Book Project’s books are given directly to children in need by teachers, social workers, health care professionals, community outreach groups, housing authority employees, and police officers. Some are used by schools, daycare and community centers, homeless shelters, and hospitals to create libraries at their sites. To learn more about the EBCBP visit eastbaychildrensbookproject.org/about/ Piedmont School Superintendent Jennifer Hawn donates books to PHS student Clea Villaluz at last year’s Turkey Trot Book Drive.
articles.title: Children’s book drive at Turkey Trot Bib Pick-Up

articles.text: The City of Piedmont and Piedmont Beautification Foundation will host the annual tree lighting ceremony on Wednesday, December 4, at 6:00 p.m. rather than the traditional 7:00 p.m. to better accommodate young people. Lights Up Piedmont continues Piedmont’s holiday tree lighting ceremony which dates to 1969. The event has been expanded to reflect winter light celebrations enjoyed by cultures across the globe. Piedmont Boy Scouts will be serving hot cider donated by Piedmont Grocery and hot cocoa courtesy of Heafey-Baum Group. The Recreation Department staff Piedmont High School Troubadours sing at the 2023 lighting ceremony. will be serving hot latkes donated by Chabad Jewish Center. The program will begin at 6:00 p.m. led by Beautification Foundation president Patty Dunlap. Music will be provided by the Troubadours, Piedmont High School’s a capella choral ensemble. A Make-A-Wish foundation recipient will flip the switch to light up the 80-foot tall redwood tree in front of the Community Hall.
articles.title: Lights Up ceremony returns December 4

articles.text: Meet Peanut, a two-yearold 85-pound Bullmastiff mix who is anything but tiny. Oakland Animal Services staff and volunteers describe Peanut as a gentle giant with a big heart. Once he is comfortable with a new person, which doesn’t take long, Peanut is affectionate, trusting, and a loyal companion. He is happiest being close to people and likes to rest his big head on laps or lean in for pets. You can see an adorable video of him getting a bath on the shelter’s website. Although he is strong, he doesn’t pull when walked on a leash, making for pleasant strolls. Peanut attends dog playgroups and his ideal home would either be with another mild-mannered dog or as the only dog. If you’re looking for a low-key, loving friend, come pay Peanut a visit and see if he is right for you. Peanut is available for a meet and greet at Oakland Animal Services this Thursday Peanut is a two-year-old Bullmastiff available for adoption at Oakland Animal Services. from 12 - 7 p.m., or this Friday, Saturday, or Sunday between 12 and 3 p.m. Potential adopters with a child younger than 12 or a dog that weighs 25 pounds more or less than Peanut must bring them to the shelter for the meeting. articles.text: The Piedmont Education Foundation’s (PEF) Giving Campaign has launched a new fundraising challenge called “Pop Up Participation.” It has set a goal of raising $4,000,000 and receiving donations from 75% of all families. Giving Campaign chairs Catie Osborn and Kim Hunter have announced that if 75% of families participate in the Giving Campaign the entire town will enjoy a community-wide pajama day. A chart by Mulberry’s Market is tracking progress so the city can watch as Piedmont works toward the ambitious target of 75% participation. “Imagine our whole community celebrating with a pajama day with even our city officials in their PJs!” said Osborn. “It’s a fun and lighthearted way to recognize the serious difference each donation makes, no matter the size.” PEF reminds the community that participation by residents is vital to supporting Piedmont schools and that donations signal a united commitment to bettering the education system for all students. articles.text: For the second year, the community thrift organization Dress Best for Less (DBFL), has donated a New York Times subscription to Piedmont schools. Last year, the online subscription was accessed over 200,000 times by Piedmont High and Millennium High students and staff. “When we heard that the PHS library was unable to renew their NY Times subscription because of budgetary cuts last year we jumped in to offer to renew it. We hope that this will provide broad access to a top-notch publication such as the NYT for our students,” said Sarah Berman, DBFL volunteer and board member. The cost of the annual subscription was $1,622. Dress Best for Less, a nonprofit organization, has benefitted Piedmont schools since 1982. DBFL donates most of its profits to the Piedmont Education Foundation. Over $1,000,000 has been donated over the past 40 years. DBFL also gives to the community at large and regularly donates to public schools in Oakland and Richmond, the SPCA, and Oakland Children’s Hospital. DBFL is operated by a passionate team of volunteers who care about recycling, repurposing, and promoting sustainable shopping. The DBFL retail store is located at 4020 Piedmont Avenue next to Piedmont Grocery. Donations may be brought to the DBFL location at First Congregational Church located at 2501 Harrison Street in Oakland. The church site also offers a monthly $10 bag sale. articles.text: It’s the giving season once again – that time of year when we exchange gifts and consider charitable contributions to nonprofit organizations that enhance our quality of life. Did you know there is science behind giving? It turns out that the human species is hardwired to help others. It’s part of our survival instinct according to psychologists, neurologists and anthropologists. Giving also makes us feel good by releasing endorphins, those chemicals produced by our brains to improve our mood, reduce pain, etc. You could say that making a charitable contribution feels as good as eating a plate of seasonal favorite cookies or a warm hug from a loved one. Psycholog y Today has reported on what it calls “The Happiness Trifecta”. Eva Ritvo, MD, writes, “Helping others triggers a release of oxytocin, which has the effect of boosting your mood and counteracts the effects of cortisol (the dreaded stress hormone). Interestingly, the higher your levels of oxytocin, the more you want to help others. When oxytocin is boosted, so are serotonin and dopamine!” It works at any scale, and everyone can do it. “When most people think of giving, they may have too narrow a focus,” according to Ritvo. “All giving works A donation box is located in the Chabot Space and Science Center atrium. wonders, not just cash given once or twice a year. How can you help others? Is there a cause you support? A friend that needs help? A stranger that needs a random act of kindness? You should fill every day with small acts of giving, as this is an effective way to bring happiness to yourself and others. Even just smiling at someone is an act of giving and will brighten both of your days.” This holiday giving season, be generous with your cash, your volunteer time and your kindness. Make a meaningful contribution to organizations that you feel connected to and that make you feel good. Science says it will make you feel good helping others. articles.text: On October 19, the 8th grade Piedmont Girl Scouts Troop 33587 went on their first overnight backpacking trip of the school year to Redwood Regional Park. They set up camp on Friday after school and immediately started preparations for dinner. At the start of the season, the troop welcomed three new members from a former Beach Girl Scout Troop. For some it was their first backpacking trip. The Girl Scouts planned and cooked Korean bulgogi and banchan for dinner. Additionally, the girls reviewed the “leave no trace” principles and discussed a project the troop will be completing this year to earn their Silver Award, which is given for outstanding community service and is among the Girl Scout’s highest honors. On Saturday the girls hiked down a trail near the camp to a small redwood grove before packing up and hiking out. This is the eighth year that Troop 33587 has had Scout adventures. Four members have been in the troop for all eight years. The troop has plans for future camping trips and projects like the Silver Award, with the possibility of attempting to earn the Gold Award next year, the highest honor in Girl Scouts. articles.title: Girl Scout Troop 33587 camps out in Redwood Regional Park

pages.text: Wednesday, November 20, 2024 9 Girl Scout Troop 33587 camps out in Redwood Regional Park By Junie Worthen On October 19, the 8th grade Piedmont Girl Scouts Troop 33587 went on their first overnight backpacking trip of the school year to Redwood Regional Park. They set up camp on Friday after school and immediately started preparations for dinner. At the start of the season, the troop welcomed three new members from a former Beach Girl Scout Troop. For some it was their first backpacking trip. The Girl Scouts planned and cooked Korean bulgogi and banchan for dinner. Additionally, the girls reviewed the “leave no trace” principles and discussed a project the troop will be completing this year to earn their Silver Award, which is given for outstanding community service and is among the Girl Scout’s highest honors. On Saturday the girls hiked down a trail near the camp to a small redwood grove before packing up and hiking out. This is the eighth year that Troop 33587 has had Scout adventures. Four members have been in the troop for all eight years. The troop has plans for future camping trips and projects like the Silver Award, with the possibility of attempting to earn the Gold Award next year, the highest honor in Girl Scouts. Over the years the troop has participated on organizing trash pickup and recycling for Wildwood Elementary School, and selling enough cookies to earn a VIP trip to Disneyland. articles.text: Staff Photos Inara Mehta with a forehand smash in her No. 3 doubles win over Marin Academy. Piedmont High’s girls’ tennis team finished their post-season on Friday, November 15, after losing to No. 4 No. 4 Marin Academy 5-2 in the North Coast Section team tennis championships. As the No. 5 seeded school, the Highlanders opened with a dominant 6-1 win over No. 12 Urban of San Francisco at home at the Corey Reich Tennis Center. After a rain-out on Thursday, PHS wound up hosted the next day in the loss to the Wildcats. “We had a good win over Urban and only lost one match. We had some close matches against Marin Academy, but could only win one match at singles and one match at doubles,” coach Jim Landes said. Against Marin Academy, the Highlanders battled to a 2-2 draw through the first four matches, but the Wildcats won the remaining three matches. Of the wins was at No. 3 doubles with Inara Mehta and Abigail Call, winning in three sets, 6-3, 4-6, 6-1. The match was Piedmont’s second win of the afternoon, which drew the Match Day at two apiece. “It’s very exciting to get an NCS win, but we still need those two more. It kind of puts you on the edge, but its great to get one of the wins for the team,” Call said. Call and Mehta won their first set but dropped the second before turning in a dominant 6-1 in in the third set. “Abby played great in the first set and was picking everything Abigail Call in her No. 3 doubles win against Marin Academy. up. Second set was closer, but we took the shots we could in the third set,” Mehta said. “We played Marin Academy before and we played really well, so I expected us to get a win. I think we got a little rushed in the second set and we just wanted to finish the third set quickly,” Call said. The loss to Marin Academy essentially ended the Highlanders’ tennis season aside from the D2 NCS Individual Tournament on Monday and Tuesday, November 18-19. Looking ahead to 2025, Piedmont will graduate No. 1 singles starter Carolina Romanczuk, No. 1 doubles starter Emma Eisemon, along with Alina Shahid and Call. Faith Chin sends a backhand in her No. 4 doubles win over Marin Academy.

articles.text: The Highlanders, the No. 3 seed in the North Coast Section post-season playoffs, beat No. 6 Fortuna 42-26 under the lights of Witter Field on Friday, November 15. articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ soccer team got its season started with a successful scrimmage against San Leandro on Thursday, November 14 at Witter Field. Piedmont outscored its opponent 4-1, though no official score is maintained in scrimmages. The Highlanders demonstrated their usual counter pressing and fluid action under new head coach Ben Russell in his season debut. “We’ve only had three sessions and just one on a full-sized fields. So running in bigger spaces is something we’re going to have to understand a bit more. We had some cramps, but the key components were the counter press and managing the game,” Russell said. While former coach Todd Sullivan was known for his vocal and exuberant demeanor on the sideline, Russell is the opposite – only using his voice when needed. “My sister had coach Russell when she was a senior and she only had good things to say about him,” said PHS senior Gianluca Bini. “I’m psyched to have him as a coach. He’s an absolute phenomenal coach.” The first goal could be a sign of things to come. Niko MarkoGianluca Bini sends in one of his two goals in a scrimmage with San Leandro. Niko Markopoulos sends an assist to Gianluca Bini. Staff Photos New boys’ soccer coach Ben Russell makes his Piedmont debut. poulos sent a cross from a free kick to Bini at the far post for a header goal and a quick 1-0 lead. . “We needed a right-footed player to send that ball in and I just tried to look for the tallest guy,” Markopoulos said. “We have a lot of big players and when we get set pieces and corners, we’re going to put the ball in the box to our tall players. When you have a fantastic player like Niko, we’ll be able to put the ball in the right spot,” Bini mentioned. It was a dominant night for the Highlanders, recording 15 shot attempts with eight on target. “Overall, it was a really happy first game with the boys. The fact we were able to work on two different formations was really impressive. We can see the areas we want to develop and understand,” Russell said. PHS got its season officially started on Tuesday against Campolindo. They look ahead to hosting Oakland Tech on Thursday, November 21. Match Recap After recording four shot attempts, including a header on target by Bini after receiving a pass from Markopoulos, Bini scored the game’s opening goal in the 21st minute after Markopoulos whipped in a pass from a free kick about seven yards outside the penalty area. Bini then scored again in the 34th minute when goal keeper Lucas Malecki launched a pass from Piedmont’s own box past midfield to Bini—who retained the ball after a faulty tackle by San Leandro, dribbling by the approaching keeper to slot in a shot in the 28th minute. San Leandro got one back in the 37th, making it 2-1 at halftime. Piedmont took just two minutes to score in the second half when Logan Faucher assisted Bosco Lorin for a goal in the 42nd. Lorin and Markopoulos also had shots on target in the 51st. PHS then scored by way of an own goal in the 63rd after sending in a long pass from a free kick, leading to the final 4-1 score. Final stats: Bini scored two goals. Markopoulos and Faucher had assists. Lorin scored once. Tuesday vs. Campolindo The Highlanders officially got its season started on Tuesday, November 19 when hosting Campolindo. See next week’s Post for match details. NEXT UP Piedmont hosts Oakland Tech on Thursday, October 21 for a 7:30 p.m. game.

articles.text: Staff Photos Coach Dan Chubbock and the girls’ soccer team return for the 2024- 2025 season. Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team returns for the 2024-2025 season this week with a game against Mt. Eden in Hayward tomorrow, Thursday, November 21. PHS finished last year with a 12-2-4 (W-T-L) record and reached the North Coast Section quarterfinals as the No. 7 seed. Although last year’s team graduated nine players, the current team has a healthy returning roster. Some won’t be available to compete until after their club seasons conclude in December. “We’re still putting things together and waiting on the pieces to the puzzle with club stuff and college showcases,” explained veteran coach Dan Chubbock. Leading the front line will be Miranda Liu, the Piedmont Post’s 2024 Sophomore of the Year, alongside Elsa Wallway, the Post’s Freshman of the Year. Ryo Woltag provides another attacking starter from last year. “When Miranda and Elsa are able to play, that will make the difference in us being able to challenge for [the league title],” CHubbock said. “Ryo has looked really sharp in practice.” At m id f ield , Ju lia n na Thornborrow, Elia Kwong, and Louisa Symkowick make a solid rotation with a mix of offensive fluidity and defensive stability. “Louisa will be the center of the midfield three. Elia and Julianna are in there; it’s a similar team as last year. Louisa is a great leader,” Chubbock said. Piedmont lost several starters on the back line when they graduated, but he team will have versatile defenders Darcy McKee and Eliza Hammond. “We have Eliza and Darcy coming back in the defense, so we still have the spine of the team there. I can see those two being our starters, but we won’t have a lot of coverage there if we have injuries. Samantha Ronen is someone we called up from JV,” Chubbock said. Piedmont finished second in the Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division last year narrowly two points behind Castro Valley. It’s shaping up to be another close race with the Trojans, Berkeley, and Bishop O’Dowd. CV, notably, graduated just six players from last year’s WACC Miranda Liu (left) and Elsa Wallway make up Piedmont’s premier attackers. Liu was the Post’s Sophomore of the Year last season, and Wallway was our Freshman of the Year. Louisa Symkowick is a key player in midfield for Piedmont.

articles.text: The Neon Champions, an Under-10 boys Piedmont Soccer Club team won their top bracket finals match at the Jack London Youth Soccer League (JLYSL) tournament held in Alameda Point on Saturday and Sunday, November 9-10. This is their second tournament championship, having previously won their finals tournament match the year prior in 2023. After an exciting regular season run this fall in which the team, yet again, remained undefeated (9-0), the Neon Champs entered into the JLYSL end of season tournament with high hopes. Those hopes suffered a brief setback after the first match of the weekend in which the team met with their only loss this fall by just one goal. However, the team roared back in their second tournament game later that day. After being down in the first half Colin Liou (left), Quincy Wells, Parker Johnson, James Budge, Leo Davis, Goalie Jack Gilwee, Blake Olson, Luca Ibarra, Ty Breitenbucher, Luca Maffei, Luke Shin, and Jack Olson. (not pictured: Theodore Brozowski-Schrader) of the game by a score of 2-0, the Champs found their usual stride and scored four unanswered goals, led by defender Parker Johnson’s three scores which included a pinpoint direct free kick. The Champs then fought their way to victory on Sunday with a 6-0 third match against Alameda’s Firestorm and finally, a 6-0 finals win against Alameda’s Red Bulls. Strikers and Midfield players led by Luca Ibarra, Luke Shin, Quincy Wells, Jack Gilwee, Luca Maffei, Theodore Brozowski-Schrader, Jack Olson, Leo Davis, and James Budge were all instrumental in racking up the points. They were backed by defenders Parker Johnson, Ty Breitenbucher, Colin Liou, and goalkeeper Blake Olson who were the anchor for the team and whose fearless defending resulted in two shut-outs for the tournament. Guiding the team throughout were Head Coach Brando Ibarra and Assistant Coach Brett Gilwee. Reflecting on the end of a terrific season, coach Brando said: “I am proud of the soccer players these boys have become, but I’m even more proud of the friendships they built, the unique personalities I got to know, and the bond we shared as a team. articles.text: On November 2 Piedmont’s JV girls’ tennis team participated in the Western Alameda County Conference Tournament at Castro Valley High School. Piedmont’s Leela Suvikumar wound up winning the 16-player Serena Williams singles bracket, and her teammate Amalia Sarti won the 32-player Venus Williams singles bracket. PHS had great representation in the entire tournament including performances by Amelia Oldrin and Nuala Price, Rabia Mahmood, Paige Chin, and Chloe Hong. Through the season the team became a close unit. All players worked hard on their groundstrokes, volleys, serves and overall game strategy. As the players gained match experience, the determination to improve their game (including mental toughness) was evident. Under coach Frannie Chinn, the team finished with a 7-6-2 record. They were backed by defenders Parker Johnson, Ty Breitenbucher, Colin Liou, and goalkeeper Blake Olson who were the anchor for the team and whose fearless defending resulted in two shut-outs for the tournament. Guiding the team throughout were Head Coach Brando Ibarra and Assistant Coach Brett Gilwee. Reflecting on the end of a terrific season, coach Brando said: “I am proud of the soccer players these boys have become, but I’m even more proud of the friendships they built, the unique personalities I got to know, and the bond we shared as a team. A woodpecker at Redwood Regional Park. Stream Trail from the Canyon Meadows Staging Area are bushels of ladybugs. Scientists determined that their behavior is a mechanism for the species to reproduce and cope with a limited food supply during the winter months—laying eggs on the underside of leaves. The Stream Trail is predominantly flat, so it’s a great location for children and senior walkers. To reach the location, there are a few options. For an easy walk, start at the Canyon Meadow Staging Area off of Redwood Road and take the Stream Trail which starts at the end of the parking lot. At 1.5 miles you’ll reach a bridge and intersection with the Mill Trail. Take the bridge to continue down the Stream Trail and .2 of a mile later you will encounter the swarms of ladybugs. Turning around from this point will end your day at slightly over three miles of hiking. Should visitors want to experience more of Redwood Regional and add a workout to their visit, park at the Redwood Bowl Staging Area off of Skyline Boulevard. Take the West Ridge Trail until it intersects with the Madrone Trail, traveling left. You’ll walk slightly less than a half-mile until reaching the Starflower Trail, which you will take all the way until reaching the Stream Trail about 0.8 mile away. From there, you’ll walk about a half-mile to reach the ladybug swarm. Returning to the Starflower Trail and hiking back to your car will take about 1.6 miles and top out your day around 850 feet in elevation gain. Another option is taking the Redwood Peak Trail and walking uphill to Redwood Peak—taking 1.2 miles from the ladybugs. Redwood Peak is possibly the best hidden treasure of the park, where you can find a collection of boulders with initials, names, and dates etched into its surface. It is a great location to relax and hydrate while you scour the boulders to find the oldest date. The oldest year I was able to find went all the way back to 1918. It’s worth mentioning that the Stream Trail is one of the most popular trails at Redwood Regional due to the ladybug swarm and the general easiness of the walk. On a Sunday around 11:00 a.m., we passed approximately 122 people on the Stream Trail as we made our way to the Tres Sendas Trail. On the Tres Sendas and Starflower Trails, we passed just 20 people on the way to Redwood Peak and passed another 41 people while on the West Ridge Trail. The Chown Trail was one of the most secluded and perhaps the most underrated, passing just six people in the mile descent. Back on the Stream Trail, we passed another 51 patrons while making our way back to the car for a total of 240 park-goers we encountered on the trails. The Stream Trail provides a staggering 173 of those numbers alone. The collection of boulders at Redwood Peak has names, initials, and dates from several generations etched into its surface. articles.text: The San Francisco Ballet’s 2024-25 season begins on December 6 with the holiday favorite Nutcracker, honoring the company’s legacy as the first in the nation to present a full-length production. This special production is set in San Francisco’s post-1906 earthquake era, with opening scenes featuring famous landmarks like the Painted Ladies at Alamo Square. Nutcracker is the longest-running production in the company’s history. San Francisco Ballet premieres the production every year and features a cast of more than 150 dancers to tell the classic story of the Sugar Plum Fairy. Artistic Director and principal choreographer Helgi Tomasson’s production is inspired by the city of San Francisco, accompanied by an orchestra performing Tchaikovsky’s familiar score. Photo of a past production of The Nutcracker by San Francisco Ballet A diverse array of instruments are played during performances, including a glockenspiel, triangle, suspended cymbal, crash cymbal, tambourine, snare drum, bass drum, castanets, tam-tam, ratchet, and timpani – all played by only three musicians. Sasha De Sola will dance the role of the Sugar Plum Fairy, and Jasmine Jimison and Fernando Carratalá Coloma perform the roles of the Queen and King of Snow. Scenic design is by Michael Yeargan and costume design is by Martin Pakledinaz. Performance times vary. Visit https://www.sf ballet.org/productions/nutcracker/ to purchase tickets.
articles.title: SF Ballet’s Nutcracker opens on December 6

articles.text: The Oakland Symphony, led by Conductor Kedrick Armstrong, will pay tribute to the legends of Disco in the annual Let Us Break Bread Together concert at the Paramount Theatre on Sunday, December 15. This seasonal celebration joins leading East Bay maestro Armstrong and the Bay Area’s most celebrated artists in what San Francisco Classical Voice calls an “inspired, multifarious, musical bash!” Tiffany Austin, Maiya Sykes and Christopher Tunerner are featured as vocal soloists alongside the Oakland Symphony chorus and interfaith gospel choir. The evening will also feature the Napa High School Chamber Choir, Dame Drummer on drums, Uriah Duffy on bass and Kelyn Crapp on guitar. Tickets range from $25 to $65 and $15 for youth under 18. articles.text: Ruth Bancroft Gardens’ annual holiday fundraiser and festival, Garden of D’Lights, begins this Friday, November 22. Garden of D’Lights is a fun outdoor holiday lights experience in Walnut Creek that is suitable for all ages. The event is even petfriendly, but keep in mind that all pets must be leashed. Thousands of lights and lasers transform the Garden’s cacti, succulents and trees into magical, multicolored botanical sculptures, unlike anything else in the East Bay. The holiday light and laser show highlights the 3-acre garden and its many succulents, cacti, and native flora. The gardens house plants from various hemispheres, so there is always something in bloom at Ruth Bancroft. Evenings are segmented into three time slots: at 5:30, 6:30 and 7:30 p.m. Time slots are enforced to ensure that guests have the ability to park onsite and enjoy a less crowded space. The holiday event runs through January 11. Visit https://www.ruthbancrof tga rden.org /ga rden- ofdlights/ to purchase tickets. Bancroft Garden is awash with holiday lights.
articles.title: Garden of D’Lights opens Friday at Bancroft Gardens

articles.text: Oakland Zoo opened its gates to nighttime visitors this week for the fifth year of Glowfari, the illuminated lantern festival. The nocturnal event lets the zoo animals rest out of view but lets visitors view hundreds of all-new and larger than life animal lanterns. Walking through the displays of beautifully glowing lanterns gives off a feeling of Disneyland’s Main Street Electric Parade. The Rides Area is open too, as is the gondola to the top and the Express Train to Wild Australia. This year’s display features all new themes, as visitors are transported on Africa’s longest river, the Nile, to view wading wildlife and ancient Egyptian structures. Glowfari will also have a down-on-the-farm feel as guests will see lanterns of barnyard favorites cows, sheep and chickens. The zoo’s winter wonderland will be enhanced by a visit from Santa Claus. who will be stationed in the Rides Area on weekends in November and every night from December 1 to 23 from 6:00-8:45 p.m. Glowfari also will be open on select days in January. Purchase tickets in advance. Re-entry is allowed until 8:30 p.m. Oakland Zoo is located at 9777 Golf Links Rd, Oakland, 632-9525. Visit Oaklandzoo.org for more information. Oakland Zoo’s Glowfari has begun. “Down on the farm” themed lanterns The Cobra Tunnel at Glowfari
articles.title: Oakland Zoo lantern festival Glowfari is now open

articles.text: Visit the Conservatory of Flowers in San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park on December 14 and learn how to make an ornamental holiday wreath under the mentorship of a local artist. Bay Area artist Robert Mahar leads this unique botanical workshop where visitors will learn how to create a festive seasonal wreath using locally-sourced evergreens and eucalyptus, alongside botanical accents collected from the garden grounds. The workshop is held from 10 a.m. to 12 p.m. on Saturday, December 14. Light refreshments will be served. Ticket purchase includes fresh greenery, a 12” round wire wreath form which creates an approximately 24” diameter wreath, and paddle wire with access to wire cutters. Guests may bring their own ribbon, bows, seasonal accents and garden gloves, if desired. SF Conservatory guests create holiday wreaths at this unique class. The workshop is for ages 7 and up. Children must be accompanied by an adult. Visit https://gggp.org/event/ botanical-wreath-making/ to purchase tickets.
articles.title: SF Conservatory of Flowers hosts wreath-making workshop Dec. 14

articles.text: The Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) recently previewed Born of the Bear Dance: Dugan Aguilar’s Photographs of Native California, an extensive collection highlighting California’s Indigenous people. articles.text: At first glance, Indianapolis is a typical Midwestern American city. The most famous thing here is the Indianapolis 500 automobile race. It is to automobile racing what powerlifting is in the Olympics. Strength versus strength. There is nothing like it anywhere else in the world. The buildings look Midwestern. People are friendly here. In the old days they used to talk with a slight southern drawl, but no longer But there is much more to Indianapolis, then incredibly fast cars, friendly people and Midwestern buildings. Everything is very clean. Eight of us arrived to attend a very special convention of the Violin Society of America. When we entered the downtown section of the city, we were greeted by an elegantly dressed marching band. They were dressed like soldiers from the time of Napoleon. It turns out that there were 113 marching bands, attending a competition. The bands were from every part of the United States. The Midwest has always been famous for its marching bands, and it was good to know that the marching band tradition continues both in the Midwest and other parts of the United States. As soon as we checked into the Marriott Hotel, I noticed that there were many parents who were eager to tell me of their exploits. The first ones told me about the band competition. Then I noticed some other parents who were there for a dance competition with dance groups from throughout the United States and kids from 5 to 18. I began to realize that Indianapolis is a real convention city. But that was just the tip of the iceberg. At the same time as these other conventions, there was a drum and percussion convention. MusiHundreds of violin makers and vendors were at the opening celebration of the Violin Society of America convention and competition. There was plenty of good food, lots of fun, and friendly violin makers. Rest assured, the spirit of Stradivarius is alive and well.

articles.text: Bosch and Bosch Legacy are two episodic series streaming on Prime, and based on the acclaimed novels of Michael Connelly (City of Bones, Echo Park and The Concrete Blonde). At the center of the stories is homicide detective Hieronymus (aka Harry) Bosch, assigned to the LAPD Hollywood Division. To follow this character in the novels is to form an image of the man, his style, his way of being. To be introduced to him in Bosch/ Bosch Legacy only adds a new dimension to his fictional persona. He is perfectly portrayed by Titus Welliver who is experienced, often abrasive, and laconic in the extreme. These qualities are not off-putting but well played as Harry moves in a world that is raw, gritty, and often deeply dark. As well, Bosch must carefully navigate the political/bureaucratic maze of the hierarchical LAPD. Nothing about him is a cliché. In the opening of Episode one he and his partner J. Edgar (Jamie Hector), are following a suspect. Fearing they will lose him, they split up (against department policy), and Bosch proceeds on foot, following the man down a side alley. It’s the middle of the night, and all is shadowed and obscured. The suspect, appearing from the back of a dumpster, confronts Harry, pulls a gun from his jacket pocket but is shot by Bosch. The narrative cuts to a courtroom two Titus Welliver as LAPD Homicide Detective Harry Bosch years later where Harry and the department are involved in a civil suit over fatal shooting. And so begins the many episodes that introduce a panoply of characters as well as setting up Harry and J. Edgar’s next case regarding the possible murder of a young boy whose bones are discovered in the hills of Laurel Canyon. As Bosch and J. Edgar gather evidence, visit the crime scene, interview those who are in some tangential way connected to the skeletal remains of the boy, they encounter a panoply of ancillary participants. Harry spends time on site with a medical examiner (Alan Rosenberg) who is also a philosopher of sorts. The doctor engages Bosch, asking the detective how he deals with the spiritually harrowing world he confronts daily, his days a perpetual reveal of the damage people inflict on one another or themselves with a finality that is all but inexplicable. This reality is a through line connecting Bosch and Bosch Legacy. In the aggregate this is superb storytelling, unremittingly hardedged, grim, and can’t look away watchable. If you enjoy wellmade, character-driven police procedurals, you will be solidly entertained by these two series, and likely wish for a Season 3. Bosch and Bosch Legacy. Television series (crime drama). Streaming on Prime. Core cast: Titus Welliver, Jamie Hector, Amy Aquino, Madison Lintz, Lance Reddick. Rated TV-MA.

articles.text: Broken Embraces was written and directed by Pedro Almodovar, the best-known and most successful Spanish filmmaker of the last four decades. His most memorable film, at least in the U.S., was Volver (Return), and starred, as does Broken Embraces, Penelope Cruz, often referred to as Almodovar’s muse. It is unusual for male directors to explore and celebrate the resilience of women and their will to survive and even prevail. Volver is about women, young and old, women who are buffeted by the vagaries of life, by the inexplicable and by the unexpected. The narrative is compelling as are the complex characters. Broken Embraces is a love story with a strong woman at its center: the stunningly beautiful Elena (Penelope Cruz), who does what she must to carry on, to help her parents, even it means working as a discrete call girl and a secretary for a wealthy industrialist. Gradually she is pulled into a web of intrigue and duplicity and the film takes on a noirish tone as it moves from 2008 to 1994 in revealing flashbacks. The film is also completely taken with the transformative face of Elena/Cruz. She is shown in tight shots, pouting, smiling, making love, dressed in a variety of stylish clothes, at times looking like Audrey Hepburn or Marilyn Monroe. No doubt the camera loves Cruz and she loves it back. There are moments in the film when it feels like a Vogue layout so lovely is she photographed. But as a story, constructed around intense relationships, a story that is convoluted and multilayered, it feels strangely detached as if Almodovar cannot quite penetrate an abiding distance, perhaps because he is telling three stories simultaneously: one in 1994, another in 2008, and a third derived from the fact that there is a film within the film. Surprisingly, there are few if any moments in Broken Embraces when the characters reflect on the meaning of their actions. They are undisturbed by their choices and the narrative simply glides along in an undemanding way based on the assumption, presumably, that the filmgoer is not interested in knowing anything about the interior motivations of the characters. It is a missed opportunity by Almodovar to build intimacy with the audience. And so, though all is revealed, little is revealed. Even when the film is set, briefly, on two islands, Ibiza and Lanzarotte, Almodovar seems inclined only to use the lush scenery as a mere backdrop for Elena and her lover, Harry Cain (Luis Homar) and not as an extension of the heat of their relationship. Clearly Almodovar doesn’t believe in foreplay. If you love movies and have followed the career of Pedro Almodovar – or perhaps you saw Volver and were charmed by the power and intimacy of the women, or taken with a filmmaker who clearly loves to tell stories about wonderful women of all types – then Broken Embraces is a film not to be missed. Or if you simply love movies and are tempted to see a film by an artist like Almodovar who consistently struggles to convey the elusiveness inherent in exploring the human condition. Broken Embraces. Starring Penelope Cruz, Luis Homar, Lola Duenas, Blanca Portillo and Angela Molina. Written and directed by Pedro Almodovar. 2 hrs., 8 min. Rated R. Streaming on Fandango/prime/apple tv. Released in 2009. Penélope Cruz and José Luis Gómez in Broken Embraces

articles.text: A scene from Pixar’s Cars 3 To the delight of young audiences, Pixar’s wonderfully animated cars (the equivalent of Hot Wheels), are characters with large, expressive eyes (the windshield), a mouth/voice (cum grill) and are emotive in all the right ways (anthropomorphic). And so this brings us to Cars 3, and the return of Lightning McQueen (Owen Wilson), racecar extraordinaire. We quickly learn that McQ. has had a hard crash and the world of racing waits to hear whether the legendary winner of the Piston Cup will return to the track. But as the veteran racers quickly learn, things have changed: hard-core rookies have come onto the scene who aggressively feel the need for speed. As a result, some of the familiar denizens of the track have retired. Some of the car sponsors are taking a serious look at the new hotshots such as Jackson Storm (Armie Hammer), and they wonder if the newbies will take the lead in the up and coming racing teams. articles.text: Nearing the end of 2024, the Walking on Wednesdays group realized they hadn’t been to King Avenue this year, so that was last week’s destination. The walkers went up Highland to Sheridan Avenue and then up Lincoln to King Avenue, where ginkgo trees with striking yellow leaves lined both sides of the street. Native to East Asia, they are considered the oldest specie of tree in the world. The group went down King enjoying its lovely homes whose construction was spread out over the first half of the last century. The group stopped at 84 which was built in 1910. From Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi’s research, it was shared that Wallace Alexander, who has been called “Piedmont’s Philanthropist,” built a threestory mansion at Sea View and Hampton in the first years of the 1900s and a carriage house that is now the home at 84 King. Across the street from it is Crocker Park. The land for it was purchased by a group of neighbors headed by Alexander. ing improvements to make the land into a city park, but the Key System extended their #10 line to what is now the Hall Fenway and Crocker Park, and it acquired a right of way for its electric streetcars. From 1912 to 1956, this right of way ran on a straight diagonal path through the park from the Hall Fenway to the corner of King and Hampton. Two rows of Canary Island Pines were planted along the way, and what is left of them line up in a pair of lines through the park. A few years back, one of them fell on Hampton Road during a strong windstorm. The streetcars stopped operating in 1956 and AC Transit used the right of way briefly to park buses. When this stopped, Herbert Hall bought the right of way land. He built the Japanesque house at 90 Crocker in 1961 and gave the deed for the right of way to the City. In his deal with the City, Hall negotiated the right to keep his pool equipment garage on a small portion of the land. This garage has the same Japanesque design as the house. There was a strong turnout of 50 walkers and two K-9 best friends on last week’s walk. Pictured in Crocker Park wre Quincy Dong, Dottie Hutch, Chuck Oraftik, Sheila Leunig, Jim Kellogg, Margaret Leunig, Dave DeRoche, Nancy DeRoche, Edith Lee, Charlene Louie, Martin Levy, Aabha Kothari with K-9 best friend Ruby, Eric Behrens, Bob Wong, Matt Gerhardt, Sharona Fischrup, Joyce Hicks, Jack Fischrup, Phil Witte, Ken Hubbert, Peggy Shultz, Lao Xia, Lorek Haghnazarean, Kat Lang, Lao Wang, Adrienne Hamlin, Alan Goldhammer, Bill Ahern, Brenda Ferrero, Fangfang Lai, Sherry Jacobs, Leigh Sorensen, Renne Goldhammer, Bonnie Sherwood, Rick Eigenbrode, Lisa Euphrat, Claudine Bach, David Haecker, Judy Love, Lori Austen, Jim Kuo, Denny McGee, Karen Palmer, Nancy DeRoche, Irene Thompson, Helen Dong, Michele Yang, Vicki Trimbach, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome Regina O’Connor and Cathy Meyer with her K-9 best friend Roomy who were walking with them for the first time. pages.text: 28 Wednesday, November 20, 2024 Walking on Wednesday Wednesday Walkers visit Bear Park on King Ave. By Dick Carter Nearing the end of 2024, the Walking on Wednesdays group realized they hadn’t been to King Avenue this year, so that was last week’s destination. The walkers went up Highland to Sheridan Avenue and then up Lincoln to King Avenue, where ginkgo trees with striking yellow leaves lined both sides of the street. Native to East Asia, they are considered the oldest specie of tree in the world. The group went down King enjoying its lovely homes whose construction was spread out over the first half of the last century. The group stopped at 84 which was built in 1910. From Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi’s research, it was shared that Wallace Alexander, who has been called “Piedmont’s Philanthropist,” built a threestory mansion at Sea View and Hampton in the first years of the 1900s and a carriage house that is now the home at 84 King. Across the street from it is Crocker Park. The land for it was purchased by a group of neighbors headed by Alexander. By 1917, the City was making improvements to make the land into a city park, but the Key System extended their #10 line to what is now the Hall Fenway and Crocker Park, and it acquired a right of way for its electric streetcars. From 1912 to 1956, this right of way ran on a straight diagonal path through the park from the Hall Fenway to the corner of King and Hampton. Two rows of Canary Island Pines were planted along the way, and what is left of them line up in a pair of lines through the park. A few years back, one of them fell on Hampton Road during a strong windstorm. The streetcars stopped operating in 1956 and AC Transit used the right of way briefly to park buses. When this stopped, Herbert Hall bought the right of way land. He built the Japanesque house at 90 Crocker in 1961 and gave the deed for the right of way to the City. In his deal with the City, Hall negotiated the right to keep his pool equipment garage on a small portion of the land. This garage has the same Japanesque design as the house. Since 1972, the Piedmont Beautification Foundation has contributed to the landscaping, planting, and maintaining the iron benches in the park. A granite sculpture of a smoothly rounded bear and her two cubs by Beniamino “Benny” Bufano sits in the park’s center. Bufano was a California-based Italian American sculptor and known for his large-scale monuments representing peace. This Bufano Bear was installed by the Piedmont Beautification Foundation in 1978, and the cobblestone base is a memorial to Marie Veitch who lived nearby. The walkers continued down King to La Salle Avenue. Just before La Salle there is a wonderful, exotic front yard garden. On a past walk the group met the homeowner and he told them the story of the garden’s creation. It was originally a typical Piedmont grass front yard, but he had an inspiration. A neighbor was doing an excavation and had a truckload of dirt that he was willing to trade for a case of beer. The mound of dirt provided the base for this large tropical plant garden. Jim Kellogg and Mike Henn were on the Piedmont Planning Commission at the time and Jim told the walkers about the challenging approval process for the unusual landscape design. It started out with a 10’ hill but was reduced to 5’ after a “ballistic” neighborhood reaction to the plan. The walkers agreed the garden turned out to be wonderful. The group made their way to the end of King at La Salle and turned up it. A PG&E crew was replacing a 1954 AT&T power poll just before Crocker Avenue. The walkers navigated their way around the closed street and made their return to the Exedra. They passed the lower end of Crocker Park and went through the Hall Fenway with a new understanding of this beautiful part of Piedmont’s history. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 AM. Everyone is invited to join. There is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required and can be done at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu, or by calling 510 420-3070. There was a strong turnout of 50 walkers and two K-9 best friends on last week’s walk. During the applicant hearing, Shell advocated for 24 hours a day every day for business hours. The Shell representative argued that 24-hour fueling was necessary to offer a “world-class charging experience” as stated by Shell representative Matt Lions. The meeting opened to public comment, when six neighbors and community members publicly opposed approval of the Shell permit, pointing out Shell’s reluctance to provide a list of other Shell EV charging sites, as well as the difference between 29 Wildwood Ave and Shell’s EV stations on busy thoroughfares and commercial areas. Multiple speakers focused on Shell’s EV charging station on 19th Avenue in San Francisco, which Shell had described as being close to a residential area despite the location being along a six-lane highway. Comparing these two locations “is like comparing apples to oil drums,” said resident Rick Schiller. In their response time, Shell claimed that the charging equipment would be “virtually silent”, with noise only produced by cooling fans while equipment was drawing maximum energy in very hot weather. Shell also pushed back against requests for a bathroom, claiming that it would be a security risk with no regular on-site worker present. However, Shell did agree to include an air compressor for refilling tires with air. Concerns were raised about the security of the proposed EV charging station, specifically if Shell would be able to provide security footage quickly enough upon police request. Shell was open to having a detailed security plan, including quick footage access and posted emergency number signage, as one of their conditions for approval. articles.text: lution making November 14 Ruby Bridges Day. The annual tradition has expanded since then and now includes Piedmont. Ruby Bridges Walk to School Day honors the bravery of a sixyear-old girl who integrated her New Orleans elementary school in 1960. Bridges’ footstep, short in gate, but long in courage, were the first to desegregate any grade school in the South. Despite threats and with U.S. Marshals providing an escort for Bridges, she attended school. The U.S. Supreme Court case Brown vs. Board of Education opened the doors to allow African Americans at all-white public schools in 1954. At Piedmont’s event, giveaway purple “Walk” beanies were sported by participants out in the November cold. After walking to school, students were encouraged to further show their support by performing an act of kindness that day and offering visual support by wearing purple. “Seeing students, families, and Adhira Chokshi (left) and Zyah Varma in Piedmont Park on the morning of November 14. staff participate in such a meaningful event filled me with pride for our school community,” said Takazawa. “We witnessed the next generation learning about and honoring Ruby Bridges’ bravery, which strengthens our resolve to continue addressing issues of equity and representation.” • Turn your appliances back on one at a time. pages.text: Wednesday, November 20, 2024 31 Secret of NIMH Continued from page 22 that Farmer Fitzgibbons is going to start plowing early. Suddenly, time is of the essence, and she realizes that she needs help. With her friend Jeremy (Dom DeLuise), a clumsy but comical crow, she goes to consult the Great Owl (John Carradine) for advice. He wisely tells her to seek out the rats who live under a large rose bush near the Fitzgibbon farm house. It’s at this point that act two of The Secret of NIMH begins. Mrs. Frisby is increasingly frantic to find a way to move her home without risking the life of Timothy. She discovers, on her visit to the rose bush, that the rats possess a superior intelligence and have created a community that is beyond anything she has ever seen: it’s a warren of sophisticated technology and they even have electricity, which they steal from the Fitzgibbon house. It’s there that she meets the leader of the rats, Nicodemus (Derek Jacobi). He agrees to help her and gives her an amulet that will help her when she needs it most. Thus begins the adventure of Mrs. Frisby in earnest, and the secret of NIMH (the National Institute of Mental Health) is revealed. NIMH is simply great storytelling by a group of ex-pats from Disney who launched a new studio headed by Don Bluth, committed to sustaining animation as an art form and not one ruled by CGI. This feature film was their first effort, and it proved to be warm and filled with thrills. There is, however, a caveat for parents. ADVERTISE IN THE POST Walk to School Day Continued from page 8 lution making November 14 Ruby Bridges Day. The annual tradition has expanded since then and now includes Piedmont. Ruby Bridges Walk to School Day honors the bravery of a sixyear-old girl who integrated her New Orleans elementary school in 1960. Bridges’ footstep, short in gate, but long in courage, were the first to desegregate any grade school in the South. Despite threats and with U.S. Marshals providing an escort for Bridges, she attended school. The U.S. Supreme Court case Brown vs. Board of Education opened the doors to allow African Americans at all-white public schools in 1954. At Piedmont’s event, giveaway purple “Walk” beanies were sported by participants out in the November cold. After walking to school, students were encouraged to further show their support by performing an act of kindness that day and offering visual support by wearing purple. “Seeing students, families, and Adhira Chokshi (left) and Zyah Varma in Piedmont Park on the morning of November 14. staff participate in such a meaningful event filled me with pride for our school community,” said Takazawa. “We witnessed the next generation learning about and honoring Ruby Bridges’ bravery, which strengthens our resolve to continue addressing issues of equity and representation.” Heavy Rains Continued from page 1 • • Keep flashlights for every member of your household and spare batteries on hand. The pain of the Roman destruction of the temple would give rise both to synagogue-based Judaism and to house church-based Christianity. Neither of these expressions of faith are perfect, but I would not want to live in a community without both synagogues and churches. For many of us, the recent weeks have been a very low point. Can they be a turning point? The answer of faith is an emphatic yes. They can be a turning point if they cause us to turn anew to the only one who can tell us who we are, the only one who can teach us who we are born to be, the only one who holds us when the world breaks us, the only one who stills us when our foundations shake. Theologian Emilie Townes says it well. “Yes, we will be touched by awful destruction… but for those who live with a faith that seeks a deep relationship with God – one that does not rely on trite formulas or poorly developed doctrines – we find, in and through God’s grace the pathway through the devastation, salvation. For the time of destruction, which is an ending, is also a new beginning for people of deep faith.” Let us believe that low points can indeed be turning points. Rev. As the political landscape shifts, this historic tax policy faces renewed scrutiny. Capital Gains Tax Note Currently, there is a capital gains tax exclusion that enables homeowners who meet specific requirements to exclude up to $250,000 (or up to $500,000 for married couples filing jointly) of capital gains for their primary residence. After WWII, it became central to U.S. housing policy, helping millions buy homes and stabilizing real estate markets. articles.text: Current vote counts published by the Alameda County Registrar of Voters show Michael Malione, Max Roman, and Susy Struble have been elected to fouryear terms on Piedmont’s School Board. They were elected in the November General Election in a race not contested. All three candidates were on the ballot for the first time and enjoyed healthy leads over candidate Victoria Rosenbaum after she withdrew from the race and endorsed Malione, Roman and Struble. Approximately 5,500 Piedmont ballots have been counted of the 8,975 registered voters in the city. Many following school news may be surprised at how many votes Victoria Rosenbaum received even though she endorsed the other three candidates. The registrar’s office was unable to remove her name from the ballot prior to the election, and she has received 17% of the votes. The next round of results will be dropped on Friday, but regardless of tally finalities Malione, Roman and Struble will join the school board.
articles.title: Malione, Roman, Struble elected to School Board

articles.text: The political and religious circles I move in are generally center or left of center. Thus, I am in touch with a host of people who are very upset by many of the results of the 2024 elections. I hear their disappointment and feel their pain. I am also trying to find a way to remind myself, as well as my friends, that the purpose of our faith is not to win elections or gain political power. Our purpose is to love God with everything we have and to love our neighbors, even when we can think of many reasons not to. Winning elections and gaining political power may be a means by which we love our neighbors, but they are not, in and of themselves, our reason for being. In this vein, I find myself drawn to Psalm 146, verses 3-6 which read: 3 Do not put your trust in princes, in human beings, who cannot save. 4 When their spirit departs, they return to the ground; on that very day their plans come to nothing. 5 Blessed are those whose help is the God of Jacob, whose hope is in the Lord their God. Our purpose is to love God with everything we have and to love our neighbors, even when we can think of many reasons not to. Winning elections and gaining political power may be a means by which we love our neighbors, but they are not, in and of themselves, our reason for being. In this vein, I find myself drawn to Psalm 146, verses 3-6 which read: 3 Do not put your trust in princes, in human beings, who cannot save. 4 When their spirit departs, they return to the ground; on that very day their plans come to nothing. 5 Blessed are those whose help is the God of Jacob, whose hope is in the Lord their God. While the psalmist did not live in a democracy and thus did have the right to vote for political leaders, they were not a stranger to narratives that proclaimed the king to be divine or theologies that declared the king to be heaven sent. Thus, the words of the psalm are prophetic, “We refuse to entrust our ultimate well-being to any human ruler, as powerful as they may be. It is only the Creator of All to whom we turn for lasting help, enduring hope.” This is the prayer I offer in response to the prophetic theology of this enduring psalm. Creator of All: While, in these confusing days, we recognize the importance of government and those who govern, we also recognize that the well-being of our souls is in other hands, hands that are eternal, hands that embody steadfast love. Amen. I hope the prayer might be helpful to each of you in your work of loving God and neighbor. Rev. articles.text: The following letter was sent to Piedmont City Council on November 12. Editor: I live in the immediate vicinity of 29 Wildwood Avenue (site of the former Shell Station). I’m pleased about the overall direction of development; the EV hub is very promising. We appreciate the effort that Shell Oil and the Planning Commission have executed towards developing the plans. We are especially grateful for the Planning Commission resolution (not available yet, so relying on notes from the 10/28 meeting) which includes: Recommending the historical operating hours of 6am to 10pm • Requiring a written assessment of an underground vault for the electrical transformers (a one-time expense for the permanent benefit of reducing noise and EMF exposure) • Considering that the electrical transformers be at the furthest location from the residences rather than closest As a reminder to the Council, the consistent feedback from neighborhood residents has been very positive about the EV Hub itself but opposed to 24/7/365 operating hours as an attractive nuisance. Actual nuisance is when the site is used as intended, and it’s 3 am. Attractive nuisance is when the site is used for unintended purposes, again at 3 a.m. Shell has argued that CCTV and lighting will discourage the crime and nuisance elements. We agree, however 24/7 operation is not a prerequisite for CCTV and lighting. We are uneasy offering comments without the benefit of the resolutions from the October 28 Planning Commission meeting. We hope these will be faithfully represented by Staff recommendations and without any new information that has not yet been shared with the community. The immediate neighbors of this project, and the broader residents of Piedmont, rely on the Planning Commission and City Council for stewardship. You have the greatest influence and control over development at this site at this moment; there is no going back. Your active leadership and support for the above mitigations will make this project a success for everyone. –Miguel DeAvila For 25 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. articles.text: Piedmont is launching a Local Hazard Mitigation Plan update project to assess any changes to the hazards the city faces as well as recommend projects to reduce risk. This initiative, which formally kicks off next week, will study the specific ways Piedmont would likely be impacted by natural hazards like earthquakes, wildfires, and severe weather and develop a roadmap showing what can be done to reduce or avoid expected damages. Developing this plan and receiving approval from FEMA and Cal OES ensures Piedmont is eligible for state and federal disaster assistance and mitigation grants. Public participation is a key focus for the project, and there will be multiple opportunities for community members to help shape the plan over the next nine months. Subscribers to the project email list will be notified directly about upcoming meetings, events, and opportunities to provide input. Community members can learn more, offer comments, and connect with members of the project team at the following events: • Wednesday, November 13, 1-4 p.m. - Hazard Mitigation Planning Committee meeting at the Piedmont Veterans Memorial Building, 401 Highland Avenue • Sunday, November 17, 2-4:30 p.m. - Fire Department table at the Piedmont Adult Recreation Expo at the Piedmont Veterans Memorial Building, 401 Highland Avenue • Thursday, December 5, 5:30 p.m. - Public Safety Committee meeting at Piedmont City Hall, 120 Vista Avenue Residents can stay informed about the City’s Local Hazard Mitigation Plan update project by subscribing to project email updates at piedmont.ca.gov/ LHMPnews.
articles.title: Hazard Mitigation Plan seeks to identify ways to reduce damage from natural disasters

articles.text: The Piedmont Fire Department (PFD) held its second annual Family Day last week to celebrate the families of its firefighters and honor Firefighter-paramedic Niko Christ as the first winner of the department’s Firefighter of the Year Award. Family members and PFD retirees gathered at the fire station with current firefighters to celebrate together. The Fire Department hosted the event to thank and celebrate the people who support the fire department, and to recognize retired firefighters. The award presented to Christ was for his outstanding work at three separate fires this year, at which he demonstrated exceptional core skills in firefighting. On top of that, Christ has taken on extra projects such as helping with the emergency medical program. “Niko is an overall positive Piedmont Fire Department retirees arrived in large numbers for the first Family Day. Fire Chief Dave Brannigan (left) with award recipient Niko Christ. influence, helping train new firefighters and taking on whatever is asked, “ said Chief Brannigan. Candidates were nominated by a Command Staff consisting of three captains and three lieutenants in the department. “It was a nice day… The families, who we really enjoy seeing on this day, they’re home for days at a time, dealing with whatever is going on at home while their loved ones are here protecting Piedmont,” said Brannigan. “There can be an emotional toll from doing this job, so our friends and families really help us to overcome a lot of what we go through here… I think it’s important to help them understand that Piedmont benefits from what they go through also.” Attendees at the Fire Department Family Day gather for a group photo.

articles.text: The city of Piedmont has released a brief survey about two recent Red Flag Warnings – periods of heightened fire risk due to weather conditions. These were the first Red Flag Warnings declared for Piedmont since 2021. The first warning was on October 16, two days before the Keller Fire burned parts of the Oakland Hills. The most recent warning began at 11:00 a.m. on Tuesday, November 5th, and lasted until Thursday, November 7th, at 7:00 a.m. PG&E had issued plans for rolling blackouts in parts of the Bay Area following last Tuesday’s warning, although none were planned within Piedmont. These Public Safety Power Shutoffs (PSPS) were intended to reduce the likelihood of fires in high-risk areas. The survey will help the Piedmont Fire Department understand how well attempts to inform the community about these weather events worked, and what, if any, actions residents took in response. The survey is available at piedmont.ca.gov/RedFlagSurvey and will remain open through Sunday, November 24th. Responses will help the Fire Department refine notification procedures, public education, and preparedness programming to better support the needs of the community. articles.text: A brief power outage occurred on Blair Avenue last Wednesday, November 6, due to a tree branch falling on a live power line. PG&E sent a notice at 7:25 a.m. notifying residents of the outage. The fire department was swiftly mobilized to investigate the source of the disruption. On his way home to a nearby street neighbor Dana Schultz saw firefighters begin to close parts of the street with yellow “Do Not Enter” tape. A large branch had broken off a tree in the 600 block of Blair Avenue and landed on a live power line. Power was automatically shut off in the immediate neighborhood. Firefighters were able to remove the branch and power was restored to the neighborhood one hour later at 8:35 a.m. Piedmont fire department responded to a power outage to a branch falling on a power line. Piedmont firefighters survey the scene on Blair Avenue.
articles.title: Neighborhood power outage resolved quickly by PG&E
