articles.text: Piedmont Police received a call from Alameda County Behavior Health Department at 11:49 a.m. yesterday, Tuesday, November 12, advising that a gunman was in front of Piedmont High School. The county department said they received a text reporting a male subject dressed in black and armed with an AR-15 rifle was threatening to shoot people in the area. “Officers responded immediately, met with school staff and locked the schools down as a precaution. Upon the officers’ arrival, no subject was found with a rifle, but the school and adjacent areas were searched.” said Police Captain Chris Monahan. “A short time later, we were informed this same thing happened at many other schools.” In Palo Alto, Gunn High School and Palo Alto High School received similar “swatting” false threats, as did Cupertino High just before noon. A school in Colorado, Rifle High, received a similar warning, in what was also a hoax report. Piedmont police were immediately dispatched to Piedmont High School, Millennium High and Piedmont Middle school. The schools were in lockdown mode while a systematic search was conducted. An initial “Community Alert” appeared on the Police’s Instagram and Facebook pages by
articles.title: Fake threat of gunman locks down middle, high school

articles.text: 12:30 p.m.. In the Instagram Post, Police asked parents to stay away from the area while their investigation was in process. At 12:39 p.m. Piedmont Police sent out the following update: “We have information that several other schools in the Bay Area have received similar types of threats. It appears that this may be a widespread ‘Swatting’ incident. Out of an abundance of caution, we are continuing with our investigation and the clearing of all buildings,” stated their Instagram. articles.text: For many, the idea of speech therapy conjures images of children learning to pronounce sounds correctly or overcome stutters. However, speech therapy is not just for kids—it plays a crucial role in helping adults navigate communication challenges as well. Whether due to injury, illness, or long-standing speech difficulties, adults can benefit greatly from speech therapy. This vital healthcare service is often underutilized by adults who may not realize how much it can improve their quality of life. Speech therapy for adults is designed to help individuals improve their communication abilities. This may involve refining articulation, enhancing fluency, or strengthening the muscles used for speech. In adults, therapy is often necessary after medical events such as strokes, traumatic brain injuries or concussions, or surgeries. Speech-language pathologists (SLPs), or speech therapists, also work with adults experiencing conditions like Parkinson’s disease, multiple sclerosis, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), which can impact both speech and swallowing functions. Some adults may have dealt with speech issues throughout their lives, such as stuttering or voice disorders. Others may struggle newly acquired communication issues, such as aphasia, a condition that affects language comprehension and production, often following a stroke or brain injury. In these cases, speech therapy helps restore communication skills, empowering individuals to regain independence and confidence. Adults seek speech therapy for many reasons, but the primary goal is always the same: to improve communication and quality of life. For those recovering from strokes, speech therapy can help them regain the ability to speak clearly, which is critical for reestablishing social connections and functioning in everyday life. In some cases, therapy may involve relearning how to speak entirely. Similarly, individuals with degenerative neurological diseases, such as Parkinson’s, often face challenges with speech volume, clarity, and swallowing. Therapy can slow the progression of these issues, giving patients more control over their speech for longer periods. Voice disorders, caused by vocal strain, injury, or surgery, are another reason adults turn to speech therapists. Teachers, singers, and public speakers are especially prone to vocal damage and may require therapy to heal and retrain their vocal cords. Speech difficulties can be deeply frustrating, leading to feelings of isolation, embarrassment, and low self-esteem. Many adults find themselves withdrawing from social situations or avoiding conversations because they fear being misunderstood. The emotional toll can be as significant as the physical challenges. Speech therapy provides not only practical tools but emotional support. As patients make progress, their confidence grows. The ability to communicate effectively – whether in personal relationships, at work, or in public – can transform a person’s outlook on life. The therapeutic process is also about building a new identity around a stronger, more capable voice. For adults facing speech and communication challenges, speech therapy offers a lifeline. It’s more than just about words and sounds; it’s about reconnecting with the world. With the guidance of skilled speech-language pathologists, adults can overcome their speech limitations and rediscover the power of their voice. This journey may take time, but with persistence and expert help, the results can be life-changing. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of Speech, Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language, reading and writing. She can be reached at kathryn.pengilly@speechinc. com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com. S P E E C H , I N C .

pages.text: 6 Wednesday, November 13, 2024 SchOOLs Fake threat of gunman locks down middle, high school By Jay Russell Piedmont Police received a call from Alameda County Behavior Health Department at 11:49 a.m. yesterday, Tuesday, November 12, advising that a gunman was in front of Piedmont High School. The county department said they received a text reporting a male subject dressed in black and armed with an AR-15 rifle was threatening to shoot people in the area. “Officers responded immediately, met with school staff and locked the schools down as a precaution. Upon the officers’ arrival, no subject was found with a rifle, but the school and adjacent areas were searched.” said Police Captain Chris Monahan. “A short time later, we were informed this same thing happened at many other schools.” In Palo Alto, Gunn High School and Palo Alto High School received similar “swatting” false threats, as did Cupertino High just before noon. A school in Colorado, Rifle High, received a similar warning, in what was also a hoax report. Piedmont police were immediately dispatched to Piedmont High School, Millennium High and Piedmont Middle school. The schools were in lockdown mode while a systematic search was conducted. An initial “Community Alert” appeared on the Police’s Instagram and Facebook pages by 12:30 p.m.. In the Instagram Post, Police asked parents to stay away from the area while their investigation was in process. At 12:39 p.m. Piedmont Police sent out the following update: “We have information that several other schools in the Bay Area have received similar types of threats. It appears that this may be a widespread ‘Swatting’ incident. Out of an abundance of caution, we are continuing with our investigation and the clearing of all buildings,” stated their Instagram. At 12:46 p.m. Police advised the areas were clear and classes could resume. Piedmont High School’s Advanced Acting class will perform The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time this weekend at the Alan Harvey Theater from Thursday, November 14 through Saturday, November 16. Written by Simon Stephens and based on the best-selling novel by Mark Haddon, the play was winner of five Tony Awards. The play follows Christopher Boone (MHS junior Collin Cameron), a neurodivergent 15-year-old boy who embarks on an expedition after discovering a dead dog. Christopher loves math and science but struggles with everyday interactions and understanding people. The play transports viewers inside Christopher’s vivid inner world as he tries to uncover the mystery of the dog’s death. Along the way, he uncovers the mysteries within his own family. The show is directed by Kimberly Taylor with a cast that includes Sacha Andrews, Ali Atanasio, Collin Cameron, Caleb Canada, Jake Hanke, Dinar Kidane, Isabelle Myers, Ben Sachs, Friedie Schickedanz, and Danielle Zaroukian. Scenic Projection design is by Noah Bruggeman, Jerry Yu, and Clea Villaluz, with help from Nasreen Schulze and Ella Fleischer. Lighting design is by Sophie Hess, with sound design by Chaz Amit-Guite and Theo Ferguson. Advance tickets ($12 for Students, $18 for General Admission) may be purchased at phsacting.ludus.com or at the box office. For more information or questions contact director Kimberly Taylor at ktaylor@piedmont.k12. ca.us Due to strong language and themes, the play is intended for mature audiences. articles.text: Paul Nelson, a Piedmont resident of 36 years, published his first book on November 12, entitled Lost Grand Resorts of Old Lake Tahoe. The 224-page book is the culmination of several years of research uncovering the mostly-lost stories of the grand resorts of Lake Tahoe. Nelson unearths the histories of the unique uber-exclusive grand hotels that were built at Lake Tahoe beginning in the 1880s catering to the wealthy owners of California gold mines and Nevada silver mines, and San Francisco society. Most of the stories are not widely known and never have been told in book form. They are enhanced with more than 100 rare historical photos. After setting a contextual background and the resorts’ histories, the book focuses on the lives and exploits of the unique individuals who built and operated them. The central story begins in 1884 with ”Lucky” Baldwin’s fabulous Tallac House (“the world’s grandest hotel”) built on the South Shore of Lake Tahoe. Baldwin was a wealthy and eccentric San Franciscan who built San Francisco’s largest and finest hotel and first grand theater at Powell and Market. Tallac House at Lake Tahoe was operated to great acclaim by the Comstock and Lawrence families for 30 years, with elaborate activities, eight-course French dinners and music by a string quartet. They hired the Maître d’ from the Palace Hotel to give it status. The narrative also follows Tahoe timber baron Duane Bliss, who constructed his ultimate fantasy hotel, the Tahoe Tavern, in Tahoe City, with hundreds of rooms, a theater, bowling alley, restaurants. Later it would become the site of California’s first ski area. New highways built in the 1920s helped bring popularity to Brockway Hotel on Stateline Point with high-end customers including Hollywood celebrities, politicians, mobsters and some of Piedmont’s prominent families. The hotels’ stories are followed through the Depression and World War II up to their ultimate closing and demise in the Lost Grand Resorts of Old Lake Tahoe by Piedmont’s Paul Nelson was published by History Press. 1960s when the taste of tourists moved away from all-inclusive hotels to family cabins, motels and condominiums. Signed first editions of Lost Grand Resorts of Old Lake Tahoe are available by emailing PaulNelsonLaw@gmail.com. The first general release of copies became available online and in bookstores on November 12. Tallac House on Tahoe’s South Shore. Tahoe Tavern in Tahoe City

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, free compostable bags are available at City Hall to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. Compostable bags are also available from Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) for a fee. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. articles.text: Cory Johnson (right) stands with Dennis Page, owner of SLAM Magazine, which was recently inducted into the Basketball Hall of Fame. Piedmont resident Cory Johnson recently saw a distant dream become a reality. Over 30 years ago in the early 1990s, Johnson became the Founding Editor in Chief of the renowned SLAM Magazine alongside Dennis Page. Being a major piece of the foundation of journalism circling the NBA, SLAM Magazine was inducted into the Basketball Hall of Fame in August, forever holding a piece of professional basketball’s foundation. “It’s super exciting, it’s just so out of the left field bleachers. Dennis and I started the magazine 30 years ago; I went on to do many different things, but Dennis stayed at SLAM Magazine throughout. He told me about their 30th anniversary, then told me the magazine was being inducted and he wanted me to be at the ceremony,” Johnson said. Sitting in a room filled with NBA greatness, Johnson reflects on the night of SLAM’s induction. “Pat Reilly comes in with his wife. Vince Carter and Chauncey Billups were being inducted and were there. Michael Cooper was there and then I look and see James Worthy—then Magic Johnson comes in and says hello. Then Larry Bird comes in, then Dr. J [Julius Erving] comes in, and you’re like holy crap. Then there’s more commotion and in comes Michael Jordan. But the coolest moment of the thing was I was looking at Rick Barry and I notice Dr. J was looking at me and waves. I’m looking around like, do you mean me? Then he waves again and says, ’Yeah, you hi.’ I couldn’t believe he remembered me, it was so cool,” Johnson said. SLAM Magazine was a publication ahead of its time in the world of sports journalism. Instead of the Xs and Os behind sports, they focused on the lesser told story of basketball’s culture rising out of the playgrounds of New York City. It featured hip hop, fashion, and language on the zestier side than what you would find in Sports Illustrated. “The idea was how we would treat language, images, names of the sections, and the pace you’d go through as you read it. In the first issue, we devoted 2-3 pages to Letter to the Editor, and they were all fake letters. No one was reacting to SLAM Magazine yet because we didn’t exist; we just so much wanted to have a connection to the readers. I wanted the readers to be a part of the magazine, just like comic books were for me when I was a kid,” Johnson said. SLAM was a major part of a culture shift in sports in the 90s. They never wanted to act in the traditional sense, which is what Johnson thinks helped propel them to the top of NBA media. “The notion of journalism should be to tell the stories that aren’t being told and to connect with people through those stories. Our goal wasn’t to tell the story of Michael Jordan 50 different ways, the goal was to tell a story of people in the world through the lens of basketball. That meant the playground, high school, and college,” Johnson said. “It’s hard to imagine how racist was American institutions were in the 90s. Rolling Stone didn’t have hip hop coverage, MTV wasn’t playing hip hop… Back then, the league didn’t want anything to do with us. So when we started talking players about music instead of missing a layup, it was to tell the story of a culture. The result was us connecting to the players very quickly,” he added. The magazine became a trendsetter away from the court and journalism. Its cover art became a hallmark of its place in basketball culture; like Allen Iverson on the cover in June 1997 with his hair picked out, or the LA Clippers’ Elton Brand, Lamar Odom, and Darius Miles sporting their jerseys on backwards in February 2002.
articles.title: Cory Johnson elected to Basketball Hall of Fame

articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont players celebrate following their WACC Mission Division clinching win over Newark Memorial. Friday, November 8 marked mission accomplished for Piedmont High’s football team. It concluded its regular season with a resounding 31-7 win over Newark Memorial under the lights at Witter Field. The result solidified the Highlanders winning the Western Alameda County Conference’s Mission Division title, and winning its second consecutive banner after going undefeated in league. “It’s hard to complain about being 9-1,” said coach Jordan Seiden. “I can nitpick about certain things but, if you ask me, we were the second-best team in the entire WACC. Once our offense gets rolling, it’s pretty hard to stop. I’m excited to see where we go from here.” It was a big night for running back Tommy Ashton who recorded three touchdowns on 11 carries for 92 yards. “The offensive line did a helluva job. I can always count on them. They did all that work for me. Cheers to them,” Ashton said. On the defensive side, it marked the fifth time Piedmont allowed one score or less. “We knew Newark was going to run the ball a lot with their Wing-T. The defense knew we had to come to play, and oh my gosh, we started off so strong. We had multiple three-andouts,” linebacker Cash Elmquist said. Making a huge impact was defensive end Jordan Alemania, who had three QB sacks and another tackle for loss. He suffered an injury late in the game and was unable to return. “Jordan Alemania’s presence was felt immediately. He was everywhere. He’s a warrior and a trooper. People like that are the keystones to our defense,” Elmquist said. In the North Coast Section’s new ranking system, Piedmont was placed in the small school Division 7 bracket as the No. 3 seed. They will host No. 6 Fortuna this Friday night at Witter Field, and will face the winner of No. 2 Ferndale vs. No. 7 Vallejo on November 22 or 23. “I always tell our guys; it’s not about the other team, it’s about what we’re doing. If we’re doing our job, executing, and staying on point with the fundamentals, we’re not worried about anyone else. If we come out and execute, we’ll take care of business,” Seiden said. Game Recap After forcing a punt on Newark’s first possession, Piedmont scored in six plays, which included a long 50 yard carry by quarterback Markos Lagios to the Cougars’ 15-yard line on a 3rd-and-14 situation. Ashton capped off with a three-yard carry into the end zone with 7:30 left in the first quarter. Newark missed a 42-yard Staff Photos Tommy Ashton ran for three touchdowns against Newark Memorial. articles.text: Piedmont High’s cross country team returned to toe the line at Hayward High for the 2024 Western Alameda County Conference Championship on Saturday, November 9. The girls’ team came away with a third-place finish out of six schools, while the boys placed sixth. “We did not let up on the training for the varsity boys and girls teams leading up to this meet. We took the approach and opportunity to maximize the amount of days of training to prepare for the NCS meet,” coach Steve Zirkelbach said. The girls’ team continued to excel with a third place overall finish. “The great thing about this girls’ team is that they are very supportive of each other. There is a strong sense of “team” and the way they work together in training and competition keeps propelling them forward,” Zirkelbach said. It marked another fine performance by standout sophomore Leighton Mand, who as g fifth out of 40 runners with a time of 19:16.77 on the three-mile course. “Leighton continues to impress everyone with her fiercely focused competitiveness. She improved her time to 19:16, which is a 22 second improvement over the last time she ran this course,” Zirkelbach said. Behind Mand was junior Skylar Best finishing 11th with a time of 19:55.46, freshman Viviane Oesterer was behind her in 12th in 19:50.60, sophomore Amalia Gray was 16th in 20:16.90, and junior Cora Chun rounded out Piedmont’s top five in 17th at 20:24.40. “Skylar Best is another consistent performer that the team can count on. Viviane Oesterer showed everyone that she definitely wants to be on the varsity squad and is a runner who doesn’t hold back anything on the course. Photos by Jenni Tsoi Leighton Mand, a sophomore, led Piedmont with a fifth place finish. Freshman Viviane Oesterer was PHS’ third-best time, placing 12th overall. Amalia Gray produced another terrific effort,” Zirkelbach said. Over to the boys, there are still sign of improvement despite finishing last in the WACC’s Foothill Division. With Piedmont’s top three runners being sophomores, there is a lot of room for growth going into 2025. Boys results Leading the way was sophomore Sebastien Swain, who was Sebastien Swain led the PHS boys team at the league championships. eighth in a field of 41 runners with a time of 16:19.95. He was two seconds off his personal best time despite losing a shoe during the race. “Sebastien continued to lead the team,” said Zirkelbach, “He went out in 5:10 for the first mile, even though he lost a shoe in the process. One of his shoes got stuck in the mud, came off his foot, and he had to stop and pull it out of the much and put it back on his foot,” Zirkelbach said. Behind Swain was sophomore classmate Alex Schleuning in 16th clocking a 17:09.04, while classmate Tomas Ero was 28th in 17:43.49. Behind them was senior Oliver Horsley in 32nd in 18:04.26 while junior Devon Thai in 34th in 18:12.26. “Alex Schleuning is another runner who had a good day. Alex has been focused and consistent in his training all season, and his times have been coming down 5-10 seconds each time he races,” Zirkelbach said. The Highlanders look ahead to the North Coast Section Cross Country Championship at Hayward in 10 days on Saturday, November 23.

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ tennis team competed a Chabot College in Hayward in the Western Alameda County Conference Individual Tournament on Friday and Saturday, November 8-9. Juniors Kate Jumper and Arianna Kortum battled their way to the doubles final and finished second to top-seed Juliana Johnson and Sophie Featherstone of Alameda, 6-1, 6-3. Also competing well in the tournament was senior Carolina Romanczuk, who was fourth overall in the singles bracket. Faith Chin finished sixth in singles and Maddie Tran and Emma Chan won the consolation bracket. In doubles. “We had a good WACC League tournament. Carolina took fourth in the singles and Kate and Arianna won a silver in the doubles. Faith also played in the singles winning a round in the main draw and went all the way to the fifth-place finals of the playoffs,” coach Jim Landes said. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team is returning to Witter Field this month with a new coach at the helm, Ben Russell. Hired in September, Russell takes over for the most successful coach in Piedmont High history, Todd Sullivan. “It’s a new group with new coaches and players coming in. We have a wide array of talent and some good freshmen coming into the squad alongside some experienced seniors. It should be a good mix and it’ll be about piecing together the puzzle,” Russell said. Russell comes to Piedmont High with a wealth of experience. He’s been at 24-7 UK Soccer Academy for the past nine years, the same club program that Sullivan coaches. Russell was its technical director from 2015 to 2023, and oversaw Piedmont Soccer Club, giving him a unique familiarity with the school’s student-athletes. “A lot of the players I’ve coached within that nine-year time frame. I think I coached most of these players at some point in their lives. It’s been quite cool from my own personal perspective to touch base with players who I started my journey with 8-9 years ago,” Russell said. Russell, another native of England, began his coaching career in the UK’s professional leagues before coming to the U.S. In addition to coaching at 24-7 he was assistant to Oakland Soccer Club’s men’s and women’s teams which play in the National Premier Soccer League. “I was working out in the Pacific Northwest along with the Canadian region. I wanted to pursue a professional coaching Piedmont High’s boys’ soccer team returns with new head coach Ben Russell at the helm. pathway and did that in England with professional academies like Tottenham, Arsenal, Chelsea and West Ham. But it wasn’t the sustainable lifestyle that I was looking for. I got an opportunity out here with 24-7 and that allowed me to have different experiences with all ages and experiences,” Russell said. Piedmont finished last season with a 12-3-3 record and was the No. 2 seed in the Division 3 North Coast Section postseason. They defeated No. 15 Novato 6-1 in the first round but lost 3-1 to No. 7 Archie Williams in the second round. “The program has had a lot of success and a lot of good players have come through the program, so hopefully we can build from that. Hopefully there’s promise for this year and years to come with young talent coming in,” Russell said. They have some big shoes to fill with Enzo Bernales, who was The Posts’ 2023 Sophomore of the Year, departing to focus on his MLS Next club. But PHS will still have potent options, like Bosco Lorin, Gianluca Bini, Niko Bosco Lorin is expected to lead the Piedmont attack. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team saw its season come to an end in the Division 2 North Coast Section Quarterfinals on Saturday, November 9. Playing as the No. 4 seed, the Highlanders were upset by No. 5 Washington 14-11 at the Livermore HS pool. Piedmont compiled a 16-10 record this season. Piedmont cut their deficit to one goal several different times in the match, but couldn’t find a way to take the lead. “We struggled with that all night. A lot of it comes down to defense, we weren’t able to stop them on a couple of opportunities. But the boys fought hard, they’ve been awesome,” coach Rik Krumins said. Piedmont entered NCS with a top-four seeding despite losing eight players from the previous year’s D2 championship team. Krumins thinks not having a home pool played a factor in the result. “On offense, not having a pool just seemed to catch up to us. Not having a pool and traveling around stopped us from condiGoalie Luke McAuliffe reaches for one of his nine saves. Charlie Wright scored three goals against the Huskies. Elles Kreickhaus had seven goals against Washington. Staff Photos tioning properly,” Krumins said. Junior leaders Elles Kreickhaus and goalie Luke McAuliffe, who were members of the 2023 roster, shared their thoughts on how the school’s lack of a pool impacted tournament results. “We only have an hour-long practice sometimes and there was a point where we weren’t in the water at all; running around the Witter track for conditioning. That stuff kind of catches up to you,” Kreickhaus said. PHS was without its leading scorer, freshman Rylan Patty. “He picked up and injury and we decided not to push it. Not having a player like Rylan definitely has an impact, but all the other guys stepped up. I’m proud of them,” Krumins said. Looking ahead to next year, the Highlanders could be suited to reload instead of rebuilding. Of this year’s roster, Piedmont will lose four players to graduation and potentially welcome back five juniors, including Kreickhaus and McAuliffe, along with two freshmen, Patty and Henry Stein. “I think we’re going to come back with a vengeance and we’ll be able to go even further (into playoffs),” McAuliffe said. Match Recap Washington got out to a 2-0 lead midway through the first quarter, but the Highlanders answered with two goals when Nick Riordan assisted Charlie Wright with a man-advantage with 3:11 on the clock, then Zach Dupree assisted Kreickhaus with 2:26 remaining. However, Washington scored after gaining a kick-out 30 seconds later to gain a 3-2 lead. In the second quarter, Washington scored 53 seconds into the action, but Piedmont responded in the next possession when Stein assisted Kreickhaus for a goal at the 5:45 mark. Washington gave itself another two-goal buffer at 3:50, while Stein assisted Kreickhaus again just 14 seconds later— 5-4. Washington made it 6-4 on its next possession, which was the score to end the half. Washington scored 35 seconds into the third quarter, but PHS’ Wright scored with a man advantage at 5:57. Kreickhaus brought Piedmont within one goal at 4:21, but the Huskies responded with a 6-on-5 advantage at 2:34. Wright scored after gaining a kick-out at 2:08, but Washington quickly answered 20 seconds later. Hayden Jahn scored with 31 seconds left, but the Huskies got one back with eight seconds left—10-8. In the fourth, Stein assisted Kreickhaus once again two minutes into the final goal, but Washington scored three straight goals to lead 13-9 with 3:51 remaining. Riordan found Kreickhaus for a goal 25 seconds later, but Washington got the next goal two minutes later. Yotam Kariv assisted Kreickhaus for the Highlanders’ last goal with 1:06 left, while Piedmont couldn’t find a clear shot from there. Final stats: Kreickhaus had seven goals. Wright had three goals, while Jahn had one. Stein had three assists, Dupree and Kariv had one assist. McAuliffe had nine saves.

articles.text: The largest and most comprehensive exhibition of American portraitist Amy Sherald’s work to date opens at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) this Saturday, November 16. Georgia-born Sherald is wellknown for her portrayal of prominent African American figures in intimate portraits. The exhibition, entitled American Sublime, features nearly 50 paintings made from 2007 to present, including iconic portraits of Breonna Taylor and former first lady Michelle Obama. In 2018, the artist was selected by the Ms. Obama to paint her portrait as an official commission for the National Portrait Gallery in Washington, D.C. Another highlight of the exhibition is For Love, and for Country (2022), which SFMOMA recently acquired for its permanent collection. “Amy Sherald is one of the most important artists working today and we are honored to present her first mid-career survey at SFMOMA,” Museum Director Christopher Bedford said. “Sherald’s vision deeply resonates with the museum’s goals to share and Artist Amy Sherald to champion a more expansive art history in our galleries. Her unique and exquisite renderings of her subjects encourage close looking, curiosity, and awe.” American Sublime is curated by Sarah Roberts, SFMOMA’s Head of Painting and Sculpture. “Sherald has invented an entirely new form of figurative painting. Her approach goes beyond portraiture to enact new conditions for seeing, feeling, and understanding shared humanity,” Roberts said. “In the spirit of great American artists like Edward Hopper, Alice Neel and Kerry James Marshall, Sherald’s works reframe our understanding of American culture.” Roberts added that Sherald’s portraits “invite viewers to recognize and move beyond preconceived ideas and engage in more expansive thinking about race, representation and the wide-open possibilities and complexities of every individual.” The exhibition will be on display through March 9, 2025. SFMOMA member previews are this Thursday through Saturday, November 14 through 16. Visit https://www.sfmoma.org/ exhibition/amy-sherald-american-sublime/ to learn more.

Amy Sherald exhibit opens at SFMOMA on Saturday By Allyson Aleksey The largest and most comprehensive exhibition of American portraitist Amy Sherald’s work to date opens at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) this Saturday, November 16. Georgia-born Sherald is wellknown for her portrayal of prominent African American figures in intimate portraits. The exhibition, entitled American Sublime, features nearly 50 paintings made from 2007 to present, including iconic portraits of Breonna Taylor and former first lady Michelle Obama. In 2018, the artist was selected by the Ms. Obama to paint her portrait as an official commission for the National Portrait Gallery in Washington, D.C. Another highlight of the exhibition is For Love, and for Country (2022), which SFMOMA recently acquired for its permanent collection. “Amy Sherald is one of the most important artists working today and we are honored to present her first mid-career survey at SFMOMA,” Museum Director Christopher Bedford said. “Sherald’s vision deeply resonates with the museum’s goals to share and Artist Amy Sherald to champion a more expansive art history in our galleries. Her unique and exquisite renderings of her subjects encourage close looking, curiosity, and awe.” American Sublime is curated by Sarah Roberts, SFMOMA’s Head of Painting and Sculpture. “Sherald has invented an entirely new form of figurative painting. Her approach goes beyond portraiture to enact new conditions for seeing, feeling, and understanding shared humanity,” Roberts said. “In the spirit of great American artists like Edward Hopper, Alice Neel and Kerry James Marshall, Sherald’s works reframe our understanding of American culture.” Roberts added that Sherald’s portraits “invite viewers to recognize and move beyond preconceived ideas and engage in more expansive thinking about race, representation and the wide-open possibilities and complexities of every individual.” The exhibition will be on display through March 9, 2025. SFMOMA member previews are this Thursday through Saturday, November 14 through 16. Visit https://www.sfmoma.org/ exhibition/amy-sherald-american-sublime/ to learn more. articles.text: Dr. Suess’s greatest children’s stories come to life on the Berkeley Playhouse stage in the whimsical musical Seussical, performing through December 22. Directed by William Thomas Hodgson and choreographed by Leslie Waggoner, the musical is a collection of the writer’s most beloved stories including Cat in the Hat, The Lorax and Horton Hears a Who. “I have such a fondness for this show,” said Berkeley Playhouse Artistic Director Kimberly Dooley. “I directed William in our production of Seussical in 2011 when he performed as Cat in the Hat. It’s an absolute delight to see him come full circle and get to be in the director’s seat.” Dooley added that the characters and cast this year “are zany and vibrant, and there are some really heartfelt moments that leave you feeling inspired.” Some cast members have family members performing, making Suessical “an intergenerational musical,” she said. The cast includes Stephen Kanaski as Cat in the Hat, Christian Arteaga as Horton the Elephant, No’Eau Kahalekulu as Gertrude McFuzz and Andrea Rae as Mayzie La Bird. “This is a family show, it’s a holiday show, it’s a feel-good show, it is a raucous show,” said director Hodgson. Performances run Friday through Sunday and select weekday evenings. For tickets or more information, call the box office at (510) 845-8542 x351 or visit berkeleyplayhouse.org to purchase online. Keenan Moran (Jojo) and Stephen Kanaski (Cat in the Hat) perform in Berkeley Playhouse’s production of Seussical.

articles.text: American Conservatory Theatre (A.C.T) presents the world premiere of A Whynot Christmas Carol, a brand-new take on Charles Dickens’s famous holiday classic. It opens on Tuesday, November 26, with performances through Christmas Eve, December 24 at the Toni Rembi Theater, 415 Geary Street in San Francisco. Award-winning playwright Craig Lucas and Tony Award winner and A.C.T. Artistic Director Pam MacKinnon re envision Dickens’ beloved classic A Christmas Carol as a joyous and comedic new-age play. A Whynot Christmas Carol is about a small theater troupe in the town of Whynot who put on their own holiday play, from first rehearsal to opening night. “A Whynot Christmas Carol brings together everything we love about the season—ghosts, music, magic, humor, and a fresh take on a beloved story that speaks to our times,” said director Pam MacKinnon. “It’s a celebration of the common good and the importance of community that resonates with audiences of all ages in the heart of San Francisco.” The cast, led by Stacy Ross as Aubrei and Dan Hiatt as Phil, includes Catherine Castellanos (Fran), Devin A. Cunningham (Chima), Michelle Drexler (Fran/ Karen Understudy), Rosie Hallett (Karen), Patrick Kelly Jones (Holts), John R. Lewis (Jess/ Chima Understudy), Sarah Toby Moore (Swan), Jenny Nguyen Nelson (Simone), Carrie Paff (Aubrei/Swan Understudy), Gianna DiGregorio Rivera (Lark), Michael Shipley(Holts/ Phil Understudy), Alyssa Leanne So (Simone/Lark Understudy), and Jomar Tagatac (Jess). Set and costume design is by Tony Award winner David Zinn, the costume mastermind behind A.C.T.’s The Wizard of Oz. Choreography is by Erika Chong Shuch. Single tickets are available online at act-sf.org/a-whynotchristmas-carol or by calling the box office at 415-749-2228. All performances are at the 415 Geary Street in San Francisco. articles.text: The San Francisco Symphony will perform Handel’s Messiah, a musical meditation on Christ’s birth, life, and resurrection, on December 6 and 7. Conductor Stephen Stubbs leads the symphony and chorus in this classic holiday favorite. Stubbs is a lutenist and has been a leading figure in the American early music scene for nearly three decades. The performances will feature Amanda Forsy the soprano, John Holiday, countertenor, Aaron Sheehan, tenor, and Douglas Williams, baritone. Davies Symphony Hall will be decorated for the holidays during these performances, filled with lit evergreen trees, and wreaths and garlands. The hall’s lobby bar will feature festive winter cocktails, including a Gingerbread Old Fashioned, sparkling wine and holiday-themed desserts. Performances begin at 7:30 p.m. on Friday and Saturday. Tickets are on sale now. Visit https://www.sfsymphony.org/ Buy-Tickets/2024-25/messiah or call the box office at (415) 864- 6000 to purchase tickets. Soprano Amanda Forsythe
articles.title: SF Symphony to perform Handel’s Messiah in December

articles.text: The Old Man & the Gun is billed as Robert Redford’s farewell role. And what a wonderful tip of the hat it is. It’s an easygoing, amiable crime comedy of sorts, filled with moments that create a long-lasting smile because it’s so enjoyable. Redford portrays Forrest Tucker, a fedora-wearing oldster who happens to be a bank robber (and a prison escape artist). Set in the early 1980s every frame of the film has an old-time feel to it, most shot in soft sepia tones. The look of it is a perfect fit for Redford. The film opens in a small town inside a small bank. Forest walks up to the manager and with a smile explains that he’s not there for a loan or to make a deposit. He’s there to rob the bank. Flashing his gun in his waistband, he asks politely, still smiling, for the cash on hand. He is so pleasant, so gentlemanly that those he robs describe him in endearing terms. Getting what must be his second or third wind, Forrest cuts a crimespree bank-heist swath across the Southwest. Clearly, he feels more alive, more himself when strolling into and then out of a bank with an old, worn briefcase full of teller cash. On his way home from one “job” he stops to help a woman, Jewel (Sissy Spacek), who is having car trouble. Offering her a ride home, they make a stop for a cup of coffee. And, like everyone else that Forrest meets, she takes a liking Robert Redford stars in The Old Man & the Gun to him. Ditto detective John Hunt (Casey Affleck), who is determined to catch up with not only Forrest but with his two partners in crime (Danny Glover and Tom Waits). What makes this film exceptional is how it moves forward with the audience completely on Forrest’s side. As well, the small ember romance between Jewel and Forrest rings true – from their first coffee shop chat and then, later, when he tells her he’s a bank robber and she laughs and says something to the effect, “Yeah, right.” Perhaps she believes him; however, he is gently likable and good company. Redford is 82 and he aces Forrest Tucker like he’s slipping into a much-washed flannel shirt. It’s not a stretch for Redford to inhabit this sly old guy whose face is deeply lined and filled with good intentions. As Forrest, he exudes style and integrity. Clearly, it’s not about the money. As well, the movie is filled with small moments. One scene I found so very charming was when there was a quick cut from Forest being chased by the police to three kids with an old paint can, painting a fence, just around the corner from the bank. Then it was back to the cops and Forrest. Just great stuff and confident filmmaking. It’s Redford and Spacek who create the unadorned delight of this film. They react to one another with warmth and caring, leavened by years of life experience, conveying their characters’ hidden loss, absent even a hint of the maudlin. If this is truly Redford’s adios, then he has chosen a gem of a film to frame his exit. So nice. And I do hope he reconsiders. The Old Man & the Gun. Starring Robert Redford, Sissy Spacek and Casey Affleck. Directed by David Lowry, 1 hr., 33 min. Rated PG-13. Streaming on Fandango/ Prime/apple tv. Released in 2019.

articles.text: During the 1970s and 80s, Lee Israel was a celebrity biographer profiling such glitterati as Katherine Hepburn, Tallulah Bankhead and television panelist/journalist Dorothy Kilgallen. Israel’s success paid the rent for her West Side apartment, the vet bills for her aging cat, and granted her entry into New York City’s literary milieu, which she relished. The film is based on the autobiography of Israel, published in 2008. While at work on a bio of Fanny Brice, Israel (Melissa McCarthy) discovers that her nicely honed niche has become relegated to the remainder table in bookstores. She is told bluntly by her agent, Marjorie (Jane Curtain), that she’s lost touch with the market and no one is interested in reading about Fanny Brice. Lee doesn’t take this well, insisting that she is well into the book and makes it clear she is unwilling to change. Against Marjorie’s advice she continues to research Brice’s life in the New York Public Library. During one of those of leafing through an old tome, she discovers a typed letter signed by Brice. She reads it, examines the aged note and has a small revelation: it just might be worth a few bucks to the right collector. She slips the note into her book bag and later discovers later that indeed there is a market for such memorabilia and sells the letter. It’s at this point that Lee, broke, isolated, desperate, and perpetually corrosive launches a career as a literary forger. She takes a comment by one of the first collectors to heart: the writing of New Yorker fiction writer Dorothy Parker. The letter Lee is Melissa McCarthy and Richard E. articles.text: A scene from Pixar’s Cars 2 What has made Pixar animated feature films so extraordinary is that the Studio clearly understands its audience: kids. Hence the animators and storytellers can let their imaginations rip and the results have been award-winning. The Cars trilogy, beginning with Cars, followed by Cars 2, and Cars 3, are examples. Where the fist Cars is set in the small, sleepy town of Radiator Springs, Cars 2 changes and heads off to Europe where Lightning McQueen (Owen Wilson) intends to enter the World Grand Prix, intent on proving he’s the fastest of the fast. articles.text: Many Americans are crazy about Italian wines. Italian restaurants and wine shops here are full of examples from Piemonte, Tuscany and Veneto. It is well known how charming a Chianti or Barolo or Amarone can be with Italian food. There is one Italian region however where my own knowledge has until recently been lacking – the major wine producing region of Sicily. Recently I had the opportunity to study up and taste some outstanding examples of today’s Sicilian wine. Sicily, the largest island in the Mediterranean Sea, served as a crossroads for ancient civilizations. Today it boasts one of Europe’s most vibrant wine industries. Though a part of Italy, Sicily’s breadth of landscapes is like a small country itself. The Greeks, Phoenicians, Arabs and Italians have all held sway over Sicily. Though the Greeks brought their advanced viticulture techniques, Sicilians have been making wine since 4000 BC. The island’s dry, warm climate features regular sunshine and moderate rainfall that suits wine production. Arid conditions reduce the chance of rot and mildew, especially in areas kissed with coastal breezes. The three main red grapes are Nero d’Avola, Frappato and Nerello Mascalese. For white wines Catararratto is the most widely planted, followed by Grillo, Inzolia and Carricante. For purposes of this article we are focusing on the Sicilia DOC, a broad, island-wide appellation. It launched in 2011 by a consortium of wine producers who agreed to work in tandem to promote Sicily’s native grapes like Grillo, Nero d’Avola, Frappato and Catarratto as well as the lesser known Inzolia, Grecanico and Perricone. International varieties like Chardonnay and Cabernet Sauvignon are allowed. Since wines within this denomination can be made all over the island, the DOC is more a marketing tool to promote Sicily abroad and help familiarize consumers with the range of wines. To earn the designation, viticulture and winemaking must adhere to quality control practices laid out by the DOC’s regulations. I recently had the opportunity to taste some Sicily DOC wines and found them incredibly interesting and quite different from other Italian wines I have tasted. I highly recommend you search out some of the following wines.

articles.text: Photo by Deborah Quok Anytime Pumpkin Chocolate Snack Bars are easy to make and delicious to eat. Stay with me here, as we jump into the already crowded field of pumpkin-mania. This entry is a keeper though. I knew I was onto a winner when the batter tasted like my pumpkin pie filling, before it’s baked. With an intentional light hand on the spices, there’s plenty of pumpkin flavor. And when highlighted by chocolate chips, you have a classic favorite pairing. The sugar content is dialed down to a mere half cup. The addition of walnuts steer it toward a slightly healthy direction, hence I’ve dubbed these “snack bars” rather than a cookie or cake. The bars are plenty sweet enough to qualify for “treat” status, can be enjoyed anytime. I envision a future batch with a streusel topping to land it into breakfast territory; or a drizzle of melted chocolate to fancy it up a bit. P.S. An easy substitution of mashed, ripe bananas in place of the pumpkin puree is delicious. This idea came to me as I looked at some very speckled bananas on the kitchen counter. Of course then you’ll need to call them Banana Chocolate Snack Bars. Anytime Pumpkin Chocolate Snack Bars Makes one 9x9-inch pan Ingredients 3/4 cup pumpkin puree; canned is fine 1/2 cup granulated sugar 2 large eggs 4 tablespoons unsalted butter, melted and cooled slightly 1/2 teaspoon ground cinnamon 1/4 teaspoon ground ginger 1/4 teaspoon ground nutmeg 1 cup all-purpose flour 1 teaspoon baking powder 1/2 teaspoon salt 1 cup semi-sweet chocolate chips 1 cup walnuts, chopped (optional) Instructions Line a 9 x 9-inch pan with aluminum foil and butter lightly. The easiest way I’ve found to do this neatly is to invert the pan and cover it with a 12 x 12-inch sheet of foil. Carefully fold the corners as if wrapping a gift box. Gently lift the foil off of the pan, turn the pan right-side up, and then tuck the perfectly molded foil neatly into the pan. Place an oven rack in the center of the oven. Preheat the oven to 350° F. Measure the flour, baking powder and salt in a small bowl; stir or whisk to combine. Set aside. Combine the pumpkin and sugar into a large bowl and mix to blend. Either a sturdy hand whisk or electric mixer does the job. Add the eggs, one at a time, and mix well to incorporate into the batter. Add the spices, mixing until they are evenly distributed. Add the butter and mix until smooth. Slowly add the flour mixture and mix until fully incorporated. When the batter is smooth, but not over-mixed, add in the chocolate chips and nuts. Stir to combine well. Spread the batter evenly into the prepared pan. Bake for about 30 minutes, until a toothpick inserted into the center of the pan comes out clean. Cool on a wire rack for at least 20 minutes before cutting. Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on November 2, 2016

I knew I was onto a winner when the batter tasted like my pumpkin pie filling, before it’s baked. With an intentional light hand on the spices, there’s plenty of pumpkin flavor. And when highlighted by chocolate chips, you have a classic favorite pairing. The sugar content is dialed down to a mere half cup. The addition of walnuts steer it toward a slightly healthy direction, hence I’ve dubbed these “snack bars” rather than a cookie or cake. The bars are plenty sweet enough to qualify for “treat” status, can be enjoyed anytime. I envision a future batch with a streusel topping to land it into breakfast territory; or a drizzle of melted chocolate to fancy it up a bit. P.S. An easy substitution of mashed, ripe bananas in place of the pumpkin puree is delicious. This idea came to me as I looked at some very speckled bananas on the kitchen counter. Of course then you’ll need to call them Banana Chocolate Snack Bars. Anytime Pumpkin Chocolate Snack Bars Makes one 9x9-inch pan Ingredients 3/4 cup pumpkin puree; canned is fine 1/2 cup granulated sugar 2 large eggs 4 tablespoons unsalted butter, melted and cooled slightly 1/2 teaspoon ground cinnamon 1/4 teaspoon ground ginger 1/4 teaspoon ground nutmeg 1 cup all-purpose flour 1 teaspoon baking powder 1/2 teaspoon salt 1 cup semi-sweet chocolate chips 1 cup walnuts, chopped (optional) Instructions Line a 9 x 9-inch pan with aluminum foil and butter lightly. The easiest way I’ve found to do this neatly is to invert the pan and cover it with a 12 x 12-inch sheet of foil. Carefully fold the corners as if wrapping a gift box. Gently lift the foil off of the pan, turn the pan right-side up, and then tuck the perfectly molded foil neatly into the pan. Place an oven rack in the center of the oven. Preheat the oven to 350° F. Measure the flour, baking powder and salt in a small bowl; stir or whisk to combine. Set aside. Combine the pumpkin and sugar into a large bowl and mix to blend. Either a sturdy hand whisk or electric mixer does the job. Add the eggs, one at a time, and mix well to incorporate into the batter. Add the spices, mixing until they are evenly distributed. Add the butter and mix until smooth. Slowly add the flour mixture and mix until fully incorporated. When the batter is smooth, but not over-mixed, add in the chocolate chips and nuts. Stir to combine well. Spread the batter evenly into the prepared pan. Bake for about 30 minutes, until a toothpick inserted into the center of the pan comes out clean. Cool on a wire rack for at least 20 minutes before cutting. Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on November 2, 2016

The sizes, composition, and detailing of the openings are one of the most important design considerations in determining the style and quality of the architecture. Like so much in this field, this issue is a mixture and balance between aesthetics and function, heavily influenced by building code requirements. There are of course various types of window operations, such as casement, double hung, tilt and turn, as well as fixed windows (non-operable). But the choice is not only how they open, but also how well they are visually suited to the architectural style of the building – something that, as we Photos by Will Adams Good window fenestration requires detailing that coordinates operation, size, shape, and how the windows fit into the walls of the building, all the while making sure it looks good. Other openings in the building can also be considered fenestration. The trick is to give equal design consideration to all utilitarian components of a building -- such as this louver located in its own dormer. (Note the roof slope nomenclature discussed in the last column: 12:12 main roof & 6:12 dormer roof.) Fenestration includes the exterior composition of all the doors and windows together. The asymmetrical arrangement of the numerous openings in this Piedmont Mediterranean style home is interesting, rich in texture, and quite wonderful! The early high-rise buildings in the late 1800’s were equipped, for example, with residential style double hung windows. Some of these can still be seen in old downtown San Francisco office buildings but would be completely aesthetically and functionally unacceptable in a new high-rise building today. Glazing (the actual glass of the window) has itself evolved vastly over the last couple of centuries. In the old days, window sizes were limited by glass sizes. The invention of flat glass made large glass sheets possible and gave a new freedom to fenestration design. This used to be plate glass, which is characterized by imperfections and slight “wave” distortion as you look through it. Nowadays, pretty much all glazing is float glass. It is named for the manufacturing process which includes floating the glass over molten tin. Only developed in the 1950’s, it is of a uniform thickness and has the even, clear appearance we are most familiar with today. Since up to 70% of energy loss of a building is through the fenestration, high energy-efficient windows are required and used everywhere in our era. They include the familiar double (or even triple) glazing, and low E glass coatings. I have found that one of the most difficult parts of building design is to make the overall exterior composition of the fenestration jibe with the requirements of the interior rooms. In other words, the fenestration has to work both inside and out, visually and functionally. In addition to considering the proportions and light and ventilation of each interior room, certain windows (in bedrooms) have to be sized to meet emergency exit requirements to allow occupants escape and firefighters egress. Another important building code requirement that enters into fenestration design is the requirement for tempered glass. Tempered glass is stronger, but more importantly, breaks into small granular chunks instead of dangerous dagger-like shards, as does normal glass. All glass in doors, and windows adjacent to doors, is now required to be tempered glass. Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. He can be reached through Will@MakingDesignSense.com Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on July 14, 2021.

pages.text: Wednesday, November 13, 2024 23 Walking on Wednesday Wed Walkers learn history of Robert McNamara By Dick Carter Last Wednesday was the morning after the election and the results were in the thoughts of the members of the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group. They decided to clear their minds on this sunny, breezy day with a walk, and consider the connection of one of Piedmont High’s most prominent alumni to the Presidency. Robert McNamara was President Kennedy’s secretary of defense. Along the way to McNamara’s childhood home at 1036 Annerley the group could walk some less visited streets, a hidden path, a not hidden path, and a back alley. The group’s first destination was the hidden path between 216 and 220 Wildwood Avenue. It goes down to an alley between Winsor Avenue, Ranleigh Way, and Harvard Road. They found the path, went down some steps, and emerged at the top of a long alley behind the homes. The walkers stopped at a former garage that is now a wonderful ADU. Leigh Sorensen announced it was part of her house and invited everyone to look inside, which they enjoyed. After the home inspection, the group noticed their numbers were smaller. Some walkers at the back of the group’s long parade had missed the alley and were already on Annerley. A reunion at McNamara’s house was planned. The group took a short walk down Harvard before crossing into Oakland and coming to Lakeshore Avenue. They went up Lakeshore in search of Portsmouth Walk, a path that uniquely has its own Oakland street sign. Just beyond the path is Martin Levy’s garage door that has a mural of a stable with his then young son and a “black beauty” horse painted on it. The walkers climbed up the walk and at its top is Annerley Road where they saw Robert McNamara’s childhood home where a group photo was taken. McNamara graduated from Piedmont High School in 1933 He was one of the school’s brightest pupils, but the Depression left his family little money for his further education. However, he discovered tuition at the University of California in Berkeley, would cost only $52 a year, and he graduated in 1937 with a B.A. in economics with minors in mathematics and philosophy. He got a master’s degree from Harvard Business School and became an accountant with Price Waterhouse. He later joined Harvard’s faculty. Poor eyesight kept McNamara from military service during World War II, but he volunteered to train air force staff. After the war, he joined nine of his military colleagues as a team offering management expertise to companies. Henry Ford II hired them, and they successfully reorganized Ford Motor Co. McNamara rose steadily and became the first non-member of the Ford family to become the company’s president. After John F Kennedy was elected President, he offered McNamara his choice of being either Secretary of Treasury or Defense. He chose Defense. McNamara became increasingly embroiled in the Vietnam War. Kennedy believed that America’s reputation would be undermined if it seemed unwilling to protect a small Asian nation from communism. By the time of Kennedy’s assassination in 1963 there were 10,000 American “advisers” in South Vietnam, and America became mired deeply in the conflict. The anti-war movement swelled, and protesters began to dub the conflict “McNamara’s war.” However, McNamara became disenchanted with the war and in November 1967 he expressed his reservations in a confidential memorandum to President Johnson. Four weeks later Johnson announced McNamara’s election as president of the World Bank and his departure from the Defense Department. McNamara later acknowledged that his belief that a communist victory in Vietnam would lead to the successive collapse of all surrounding governments was “limited and shallow.” The McNamara experience gave the walkers hope that America can make a mistake, come to realize it, and still survive. The morning had passed quickly, and it was time to head back. The group reversed their steps, going up Annerley to Harvard Road and Prospect Avenue, and through Piedmont Park to the Exedra. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. There was a strong turnout of 47 walkers and four K-9 best friends for last week’s walk. On hand were Phil Chin with K-9 best friend Rocky, Adrienne Hamlin, Julia Chin, Dave DeRoche, Leigh Sorensen, Helen Dong, Alicia Rivera, Loren Haghnazarean, Irene Thompson, Bonnie Sherwood, Lori Austin, Sherry Jacobs, Lao Xia, Fangfang Lai, Ron Day, Eric Behrens with K-9 best friend Mocha, Jill Day, Joyce Hicks, Peggy Shultz, Lois Price, Bob Wong, Leilani Ching, Tina Shum, Judy Love, Stella Houston, Phil Witte, Abha Kothari with K-9 best friend Ruby, June Yee, Edith Lee, Denny McGee, Margaret Leunig, Sharona and Jack Fischrup, Claudine Bach, Alan Goldhammer, Shiela Leunig, Kat Lang, Michele Yang, Priscilla Wanerus, Bill Ahern, Quincy Dong, Lisa Euphrat, Jim Kuo, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome Mary and Brian Henderson who were walking with them for the first time. Williams, Willig, and White have formed what feels like the ultimate “dream team.” From page one, I was hooked — laughing out loud one minute and glued to the edge of my seat the next.” —Kate Seng, Poe & Company Bookstore, Milton, GA Every Valley: The Desperate Lives and Troubled Times That Made Handel’s Messiah By Charles King, Doubleday, History/Music “This story of Messiah has everything: war, a royal succession crisis, forbidden love, disgrace, and reinvention, all funded by the horrors of slavery. Thrilling stuff, no matter your religious beliefs or familiarity with classical music.” —Amy Woolsey, Bards Alley, Vienna, VA Forest of Noise: Poems By Mosab Abu Toha, Knopf, Poetry “Mosab Abu Toha, a poet from Gaza, here delves into the indignities, injustices, the utter cruelties he and his fellow Palestinians have been subjected to. In and through the sheer horror there is a most human spirit, a celebration of joy in the cracks where it might be found.” —Rick Simonson, The Elliott Bay Book Company, Seattle, WA Masquerade By Mike Fu, Tin House Books, Fiction “Past the layers of mirrors and doubles, peeling away history and memory, Masquerade is about resisting the inertia of remaining in life when and where it’s comfortable and instead (re)-writing the story as you would like to see it.” —Mikey LaFave, Avid Bookshop, Athens, GA Lowest Common Denominator By Pirkko Saisio, Mia Spangenberg (Transl.), Two Lines Press, Fiction “Lowest Common Denominator refuses to be neatly categorized. A surreal read full of linguistic magic that makes the world feel alive with possibility.” —David Vogel, Literati Bookstore, Ann Arbor, MI

articles.text: Nancy McDaniel, a former professional golfer and head coach of the Cal women’s golf team for 29 years, died in Oakland, California on October 23, 2024, her home for 30 years, after a courageous battle with breast cancer. Born Nancy Kessler in Portland, Oregon on November 9, 1966, she was the daughter of Donald and Marilyn Kessler and the youngest of five children. Nancy grew up in Portland, and sports were always in her life, starting early. She played basketball for LaSalle High School and in her senior year helped lead the team to a high school state championship. Nancy herself earned first-team all-state honors. Golf however was the sport that played the biggest part in Nancy’s life – she was a player, coach, a volunteer, and the wife of Jay McDaniel, a PGA head golf professional. Nancy started golf at a young age, playing and winning junior golf tournaments in Oregon. She competed for the University of Washington golf team from 1984 to 1988, and was the Husky women’s golf team captain, a collegiate All-American, and was chosen for the Pac- 10 All-Decade Team. After college, Nancy played professionally for five years, but left tour golf to create the University of California women’s golf team in Berkeley, where she was the head coach for 29 seasons. While there, she led the Golden Bears to 10 NCAA Championship appearances, 22 NCAA regional appearances, and two conference championships. Nancy’s contributions to the game of golf were recognized by her inductions into the National College Golf Coaches Hall of Fame and the Cal Athletics Hall of Fame. Nancy was also recently inducted into the Northern California Golf Association Hall of Fame. To those who knew her as “coach,” Nancy will be rememtaking a hike with friends. Being a mom and a wife were at the core of Nancy’s being, and she was devoted to her husband Jay and her children, Tyler and Molly. Nancy will be remembered as quick to laugh, always positive, direction-oriented, clear in what she thought, and full of energy and strength. Those who knew her will not forget the fun, light, warmth and humor she brought into every room. Her determination and courage in the face of adversity were an inspiration not only to her family but to everyone who knew her. Although she always projected strength, her capacity for love ran deep. Nancy will be greatly missed. Nancy is survived by her husband Jay McDaniel, and children Tyler and Molly of Oakland, as well as her siblings Ann Culhane, David Kessler, and Scott Kessler, and her uncle Kurt Kessler. She was preceded in death by her parents and brother, Thomas Kessler. articles.text: The First Mondays reading group met outside the Tea House in Piedmont Park on November 4 for a discussion of North Woods by Pulitzer Prize finalist Daniel Mason. It was a New York Times Book Review Editors’ Choice and a “Best Book of the Year” by Time magazine and others. The San Francisco Chronicle wrote the book has “the wicked creepiness of Edgar Allan Poe. Mason’s bone-deep knowledge of and appreciation for the natural world is on par with that of Thoreau.” Mason’s story tells how two young lovers flee from a Puritan colony, and their simple cabin in the New England woods becomes the home of an extraordinary succession of human and nonhuman characters across hundreds of years. Some of them come to violent ends, and the present is haunted by the past, both literally and figuratively. The book focuses on the characters’ lives, but it also encompasses American history, natural history, the march of time, and the cycle of the seasons. One of Mason’s characters sums up the novel’s theme, “The only way to understand the world as something other than a tale of loss is to see it as a tale of change.” Mason received a BA in biology from Harvard University, and later graduated from the UCSF School of Medicine. He is a psychiatrist affiliated with Stanford Hospital, and teaches literature at Stanford University. The depth of his intellect and knowledge of many different subjects was clear in North Woods. The readers’ reactions to the book ranged from “liked it” to “loved it.” They enjoyed Mason’s writing style and the book’s premise. Readers enjoyed how Mason intertwined lives and nature through the ages. His story is like a layered soil sedimentation of people. PAVING PROJECT NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that Bids shall be uploaded electronically to the BPX Printing & Graphics City of Piedmont planroom via the “Submit Bid Docs” tab on the Project page until the hour of 2:00 p.m., on the 5th day of December 2024 (no bids will be accepted after 2:00 p.m.) for the construction of the following project: Grand Avenue Paving and Pedestrian Safety Improvements Project Complete bid packages, including project plans, technical specifications, bid forms and contract documents may be secured from BPX Printing & Graphics by logging on to: www. piedmontplanroom.com or by calling 510-559-8299 or by email: Richmond@blueprinting.com There is a non-refundable fee of $100 per set for a printed or electronic package, plus shipping and handling. As the project is being bid through BPX Printing & Graphics, any changes via addenda will be available on the BPX website for this project. Bids shall be uploaded electronically to the BPX City of Piedmont planroom via the “Submit Bid Docs” tab on the Project page before 2:00 p.m., December 5th, 2024. Bids will be publicly opened via an online Zoom meeting at 2:30 p.m. on December 5th, 2024. The Zoom meeting login information can be found in the bid documents. Pursuant to the provisions of Section 1770 et seq. of the California Labor Code the Director of Industrial Relations for the State of California has ascertained the current general prevailing rate of wages for employer purposes, in Alameda County, State of California. Not less than the general prevailing rate of per diem wages for work of a similar character in Alameda County and not less than the general prevailing rate of per diem wages for holiday work fixed as provided in the California Labor Code shall be paid to all workers engaged in performing the project. The City of Piedmont has obtained from the Alameda County Housing and Community Development, the Federal Wage Decision listing the general prevailing wages and fringes in the County in which said work is to be performed for each craft and type of worker or mechanic needed to execute the contract. A copy of the Federal Wage Decision is included in the bid documents. The successful Contractor shall post said prevailing wage rates in a prominent place at the job site. If there is a discrepancy or difference between the state prevailing wage rate and the federal prevailing wage rate, the higher rate will apply. Pursuant to the provisions of Section 1771.1 of the California Labor Code, A contractor or subcontractor shall not be qualified to bid on, be listed in a bid proposal, subject to the requirements of Section 4104 of the Public Contract Code, or engage in the performance of any contract for public work, as defined in Chapter 1 of Part 7 of Division 2 of the California Labor Code, unless currently registered and qualified to perform public work pursuant to Civil Code Section 1725.5. Please note: It is not a violation of Section 1771.1 for an unregistered contractor to submit a bid that is authorized by Section 7029.1 of the Business and Professions Code or by Section 10164 or 20103.5 of the Public Contract Code, provided the contractor is registered to perform public work pursuant to Section 1725.5 at the time the contract is awarded. Any bids submitted without proof that Bidder and any listed subcontractor(s) are currently registered and qualified to perform public work, pursuant to Labor Code Section 1725.5, shall not be accepted by the City. In accordance with California Civil Code Section 1771.4, the project is subject to compliance monitoring and enforcement by the Department of Industrial Relations. In accordance with California Public Contract Code Section 3300, a valid class A California contractor’s license is required to bid on the project. The City of Piedmont reserves the right to postpone the date and time for the opening of proposals at any time prior to the date and time announced in the advertisement in accordance with applicable law. The City of Piedmont reserves the right to reject any and all bids or to waive any defects or irregularity in bidding in accordance with applicable law. In accordance with California Public Contract Code Section 20103.8, if the City elects to award a contract for performance of the project, the contract will be awarded in accordance with California Public Contract Code Section 20162 and other applicable law to the responsible bidder submitting a responsive bid with the lowest total bid price for the base bid without consideration of the bid price for any additive or deductive items. All bids will remain valid for 90 days after the bid opening. Except as permitted by law and subject to all applicable remedies, including forfeiture of bidder’s security, bidders may not withdraw their bid during the 90-day period after the bid opening. He shows up to practices with Halloween treats and finds a way to connect with each kid on the team. “Max has never given up on us,” said team member Zeke Stein. Sammy Sohn calls him “awesome and kind,” while Ramon Fierro appreciates that Max “is patient with us, even when we’re a little crazy.” Ben Callaway calls it “Max magic,” ically broke with a hint of living by his wits. He offers a wonderful contrast to Lee, whose heart is hidden behind revetments of hurt and rejection. Jack simply refuses to be less than upbeat, despite her sharptongued observations of a world she finds barely tolerable. They meet often in some of New York’s seediest bars and consume copious amounts of whiskey, Lee’s monologues are awash in cynicism, much to the delight of Jack whose smile triumphs. Ever curious, always in the hunt for a hook, Jack gets Lee to disclose her new gig. Following his own amoral compass he joins her in a life of crime and hustle, taking his charm and her finely crafted forgeries to rare book dealers as well. The Mangy Mutts are already planning their first road trip to visit Max in college next year, while parent-coaches lament the void he’ll leave behind. The Mutt Force has resolved to play on next season. Max is a hard act to follow, but they’ll welcome other high-energy high schoolers who can help keep the dream alive. Both McCarthy and Grant deliver exceptional performances. Hers is amazing, against type, and nuanced to perfection. McCarthy inhabits Lee Israel, her stocky shape hidden in a perpetual greybrown overcoat and a pageboy haircut. Every scene demonstrates that she is an exceptional actress who can embrace a role to perfection. Grant is equally perfect as he portrays Jack, the friendly foil who is undependable and self-indulgent, yet decidedly appealing. Can You Ever Forgive Me? will likely earn both McCarthy and Grant Oscar nods, they are that good. Can You Ever Forgive Me? Directed by Marielle Heller. Starring Melissa McCarthy, Richard E. articles.text: Earlier this year the Piedmont Beautification Foundation announced its Spring Campaign would focus on supporting the City of Piedmont’s project to reforest Piedmont neighborhood-by-neighborhood. The City had conducted a public tree inventory to catalog the many species of trees that comprise the City’s urban forest. That exercise identified dozens of trees that are either failing or have died This was a call to action for Thanks to generous donors, sufficient funds have already been received to plant 20 new trees in locations throughout the City. Coupled with its long-running Commemorative Tree Program, PBF is well on its way to strengthening Piedmont’s urban forest with culturally compatible trees that are more likely to thrive in harsher weather conditions. Under the Commemorative Tree Program, for a donation of $550 or more a donor may choose a tree and a specific location. A customized, permanent tag is affixed to the tree, providing long- term recognition to the honoree. Several such trees have been planted recently, including the beautiful new Island Oak planted at the Mountain-Bellevue circle thanks to generous neighbors. All these steps are building momentum for PBF’s reforestation efforts, and they are excited to see how many trees will ultimately be planted. Under the two programs, and the able guidance of Parks and Projects Manager Nancy Kent, PBF is preparing the City for a better future despite environmental changes ahead. PBF’s upcoming Lights Up brochure will offer prospective donors the opportunity to join the Reforestation Project to prepare for the future. Interested citizens need not wait for the brochure. They are encouraged to visit the PBF website: www.PiedmontBeautificationFoundation.org form, community members may indicate their preference for a specific location for a tree; the City will make every attempt to honor the request. The form may also be used for those interested in information about PBF’s Commemorative Tree Program or for any questions about the Reforestation Project. Those who prefer not to go online may mail contributions to the Piedmont Beautification Foundation, c/o Piedmont City Hall, 120 Vista Ave. Piedmont, CA 94611. Be sure to include a note if you wish to be contacted by a member of PBF. Despite difficulties of the current era, the Reforestation Project offers the opportunity to work for a greener future for the City. A Valley Oak, a California native species, is planted by Pedro Galvez of the Public Works Department. cuts just to make ends meet. The impact on our programs would have been devastating,” Marks said. pages.text: Wednesday, November 13, 2024 31 Update on reforestation of city By Cameron Wolfe Earlier this year the Piedmont Beautification Foundation announced its Spring Campaign would focus on supporting the City of Piedmont’s project to reforest Piedmont neighborhood-by-neighborhood. The City had conducted a public tree inventory to catalog the many species of trees that comprise the City’s urban forest. That exercise identified dozens of trees that are either failing or have died because of climate change. This was a call to action for PBF. Thanks to generous donors, sufficient funds have already been received to plant 20 new trees in locations throughout the City. Coupled with its long-running Commemorative Tree Program, PBF is well on its way to strengthening Piedmont’s urban forest with culturally compatible trees that are more likely to thrive in harsher weather conditions. Under the Commemorative Tree Program, for a donation of $550 or more a donor may choose a tree and a specific location. A customized, permanent tag is affixed to the tree, providing long- term recognition to the honoree. Several such trees have been planted recently, including the beautiful new Island Oak planted at the Mountain-Bellevue circle thanks to generous neighbors. All these steps are building momentum for PBF’s reforestation efforts, and they are excited to see how many trees will ultimately be planted. Under the two programs, and the able guidance of Parks and Projects Manager Nancy Kent, PBF is preparing the City for a better future despite environmental changes ahead. PBF’s upcoming Lights Up brochure will offer prospective donors the opportunity to join the Reforestation Project to prepare for the future. Interested citizens need not wait for the brochure. They are encouraged to visit the PBF website: www.PiedmontBeautificationFoundation.org By completing the “donate” form, community members may indicate their preference for a specific location for a tree; the City will make every attempt to honor the request. The form may also be used for those interested in information about PBF’s Commemorative Tree Program or for any questions about the Reforestation Project. Those who prefer not to go online may mail contributions to the Piedmont Beautification Foundation, c/o Piedmont City Hall, 120 Vista Ave. Piedmont, CA 94611. Be sure to include a note if you wish to be contacted by a member of PBF. Despite difficulties of the current era, the Reforestation Project offers the opportunity to work for a greener future for the City.
