pages.text: Wednesday, November 6, 2024 27 Piedmont Scout Council’s 40th annual Scouting for Food drive to support the Alameda County Community Food Bank was a resounding success this year. Approximately 10,000 pounds of food and more than $13,000 was collected, an increase of nearly 50% more food and 15% more Scouting for Food donations set new record donations than in 2023. One of every five Alameda County residents rely on ACCFB for assistance; two-thirds of those are children and the elderly. Every $1 donated through this virtual food drive becomes two meals for children, adults, and seniors in our community. Earlybirds from Troop 6 were the first to arrive at the collection site Saturday morning: Aidan Velasco (left), Lawrence Ly, and Adrian Lee. This was the 40th year for Piedmont’s Scouting for Food event and by far the most successful with more than 10,000 pounds of food items and more than $13,000 in monetary donations. Troop 11 Scouts Anna Benson and Adelaide Lopez empty food donations from a truck while Troop 11 Scouts get started unloading donations in their vehicle. Troop 1 Scouts wait for space to be created so they can drop off their collected items. All five Piedmont Troops and the Piedmont Community Service Crew pitched in to collect more than 10,000 pounds of food items. Thanks to the generosity of the Piedmont Community, Scouting for Food was so successful this year that the Food Bank had to bring extra bins and barrels to transport all of the food items collected. Tai March-Cunningham of the Piedmont Community Service Crew helps sort thousands of pounds of donated food items. Scouting for Food Chair Anne Hauss Davies has overseen the event for the last three years. She says she is humbled by the mission of ACCFB and how large the need is for food in this community. However, she says the best part of the job is the gratification in seeing the Scouts committed to gathering food and spreading joy in the process. “Every year I have a moment where I worry a little that no one will show up. But, this is Piedmont and Piedmont Scouting and they always show up in a big way,” she said. Approximately 100 Piedmont youth, grades K-12 representing Cub Scouts, Scouts and Venturing Crew, participated in this year’s Scouting for Food. Although this year’s in-person food collection has ended, there is still time for monetary donations to the Food Bank through the virtual food drive until November 30th. Ruth, on the other hand, says to Naomi Do not entreat me to forsake you, to turn back from you. For wherever you go, I will go. And wherever you lodge, I will lodge. Your people is my people, and your god is my god. Wherever you die, I will die, and there is I will be buried. So may the LORD do to me or even more, for only death will part you and me. (Robert Alter translation) Ruth encourages Naomi to remember – and to remember is a very important biblical work – what they had shared, what they had loved, what they had lost and what they held in hope. This is a time of year for remembering. With Naomi and Ruth let us travel together by remembering how we have lived, what we have love, what we have lost and what we hold in hope. Such remembering might keep us from giving up on each other. Ruth demonstrates true empathy for Naomi. She recognizes her struggle and responds accordingly. True empathy is essential for all who would travel together. True empathy is a must if we are to refrain from giving up on each other. There has been a quote from Captain G. M. Gilbert, an Army psychologist assigned to observing defendants at the Nuremberg trials, circulating on social media. The quote is this: In my work with the defendants (at the Nuremberg Trials 1945-1949) I was searching for the nature of evil, and I now thing I have come close to defining it: a lack of empathy. It’s the one characteristic that connects all the defendants, a genuine incapacity to feel with their fellow men…Evil, I think, is the absence of empathy. I don’t know if empathy can be created. I do believe it can be cultivated and certainly Ruth cultivates it. She cultivates it in herself, she cultivates it in Naomi and she calls it forth from us. As we feel for each other we are better able to travel together. As we show empathy one for the other we step back from giving up on each other. articles.text: A highly anticipated annual event for 37 years now, the Piedmont Avenue Halloween Parade is well-loved and consistently well attended by many in the community. It always proves to be great fun. Even families that have moved to cities a little further away will drive back out to participate in this tradition. As usual, droves of kids, parents, and even pets dressed in costume came. Some of the many activities this year were free cartoons at the Piedmont movie theater, pumpkin patches, story time for kids, a haunted house, a carnival at Piedmont Avenue Elementary School, face painting, live music at two locations, and of course trick-or-treating at all A group of pirates met up at the Halloween Celebration to discuss treasure maps. The Dental Touch put on quite a show for the celebration this year, giving out free grab bags for kids which included a toothbrush. businesses. Festivities kicked off in the morning with a bagpiper leading a decorated parade truck carrying this year’s Grand Marshal, Lexi Filipello, owner of The Lodge. Lexi and her entourage wore fun hot dog costumes and did a smashing job exciting all the parade goers and tossing candy to the kids. Nothing but good times were had by all, and that’s just what parade day is for. Lexi (front), owner of The Lodge, was the Grand Marshal to kick off the parade. articles.text: Final part in 7-part series The Post concludes its candidates’ questionnaire series with one final question posed to candidates for City Council. Each week a question was sent on Thursday to the four candidates with a request to limit answers to 200 words. Week 7 Question: Piedmont has very little commerce. Would you support encouraging some new business in the city? If so, please be specific on the location and type of businesses you would like to see? Lorrel Plimier, Candidate Yes, I support encouraging new business in Piedmont. I believe that businesses here should meet the needs of and foster community among our residents. I also believe it’s very important to continue to get community input when discussing changes to Piedmont’s by-right permitted commercial uses. I don’t support expanding our current commercial zoned area, without a vote of the residents to approve this change. We have 13 parcels zoned for commercial use along Grand Ave between Wildwood and Linda. Located on these lots are Ace Hardware, the Shell station that is under transition, a new beauty salon, medical and dental businesses, as well as five single family homes. Another six parcels are zoned for commercial use in the city center. This is where Mulberry’s, three banks, a real estate office, and the gas station are located. I think the commercial parcels could be more effectively used and I support thoughtful, strategic planning to evaluate the use. The city center is especially important for the vibrancy of our community. I personally favor uses like a cafe or other group gathering space, however, I don’t think my personal opinion is overly relevant here and would Lorrel Plimier Conna McCarthy James Green

articles.text: The following letter was sent to the Piedmont Planning Commission. Editor: I live at 1250 Grand Avenue, across the street from Ace Hardware and one house north of 29 Wildwood, on Grand Avenue. I’m pleased about the overall direction for 29 Wildwood; the EV hub is very promising. We appreciate the effort that Shell Oil and the Planning Commission have executed towards developing the plans. Unfortunately, I have not seen any discernible impact of the input from myself and affected residents on those plans. I will repeat the input here, and offer some solutions. The primary and consistent objection is the 24/7/365 operating hours, with attendant disturbances of noise and safety/security. 24/7/365 operating hours creates an actual and attractive nuisance. There is ample evidence of increased crime related to EV charging stations. 24/7/365 operating hours creates undue noise, invites loitering, and puts the burden of monitoring and supervision on neighbors and residents. 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmont-post.com Publisher & Editor: Gray Cathrall City Editor: Jay Russell PRODUCTION MANAGER Victor Cheng REPORTERS Sophie Hess, Intern Ed Gilligan SCHOOLS Jay Russell SPORTS Jonathan Comeaux B. pages.text: 2 Wednesday, October 30, 2024 Opinion By Jay Russell QUESTION: What candy do you hope to get while trick-ortreating on Halloween? Is there a candy you really don’t like? Originally printed on October 30, 2023. NOAH ADAMS, 5th grade My favorite candy is Skittles; Twizzlers are the worst. KAI CHILES, 4th grade I think the best candy bars are the full-size because they are super big and it takes a while to eat them. Plenty of problems with Shell Recharge proposal The following letter was sent to the Piedmont Planning Commission. Editor: I live at 1250 Grand Avenue, across the street from Ace Hardware and one house north of 29 Wildwood, on Grand Avenue. I’m pleased about the overall direction for 29 Wildwood; the EV hub is very promising. We appreciate the effort that Shell Oil and the Planning Commission have executed towards developing the plans. Unfortunately, I have not seen any discernible impact of the input from myself and affected residents on those plans. I will repeat the input here, and offer some solutions. The primary and consistent objection is the 24/7/365 operating hours, with attendant disturbances of noise and safety/security. 24/7/365 operating hours creates an actual and attractive nuisance. There is ample evidence of increased crime related to EV charging stations. 24/7/365 operating hours creates undue noise, invites loitering, and puts the burden of monitoring and supervision on neighbors and residents. The basis of Staff recommendations is the Initial Study prepared by LSA. The Initial Study is misleading regarding the change in site intensity, and Staff report repeats the misdirection. The Staff report quotes the Initial Study as to a reduction of 123 daily trips. This is based on an over-characterization of daily trips for the site as a gas station, and under-characterization of the intensity of usage as an EV hub. The table supposes there will be 468 EV average daily trips (gross). With a 30 minute charging time, this would allow for the 14 chargers to be in continuous use for 16.5 hours per day. articles.text: Thanks to the Piedmont Beautification Foundation’s Memorial Tree Program, a newly planted Valley Oak now stands 20 feet tall in Dracena Park to honor the memory of Piedmont native Victor Clifton Wykoff Jr., who passed away on September 16. The Tree Program makes it possible for family and friends to honor loved ones, living or deceased, in a manner which benefits Piedmont in several important ways. Vic Wykoff, as his family and friends called him, grew up on Scenic Avenue and attended Piedmont schools. He did not leave Piedmont until his graduation from U. C. Berkeley’s Boalt Hall (now Berkeley Law). Shortly after graduation Vic married Marilyn Brown, also a native of Piedmont. The pair met on a blind date arranged by Piedmonters Fran and Cameron Wolfe. The Wykoffs moved to Stockton when an opportunity to join Marilyn’s stepfather Parker Holt in managing his Caterpillar Tractor dealerships arose. Greatly expanding on the example of Holt, Wykoff soon began what would become a lifelong passion for planting trees. Often using seeds taken from fallen acorns, Vic planted Valley Oaks everywhere he went in the Central Valley. He planted them on his own property, in parks and on the property of farming clients. Following his retirement, Wykoff moved to Carmel Valley where he switched to planting Monterey Cypress trees. Before the wedding of his son Charles, Vic planted enough Cypress Trees to give one to every couple attending the wedding. The Wolfes raised theirs until it outgrew its container, at which point it was donated to the City of Piedmont where it now grows in Piedmont Park. Nothing could be more appropriate than to have Vic’s own Valley Oak growing in Dracena Park. In November the Wykoff family will be joined by the Wolfe family, which sponsored the tree through the PBF Program, to attach to the tree a tag honoring Wykoff. Now that the City and PBF have embarked upon a program to reforest the entire city, replacing trees that are suffering from climate change with new trees that will better survive current conditions, there are more reasons to donate a tree. For more information visit the PBF website: https://piedmontbeautificationfoundation.org/
articles.title: Valley Oak in Dracena Park to honor Victor Wykoff

articles.text: Meet Tuck, a gentle giant hoping to be adopted. Tuck is a striking young shepherd-mix who is at-risk due to Oakland Animal Services overcrowding. Shelter staff say he is social and loves people’s company, greeting visitors with a happy tail wag and a cute backside wiggle! Tuck has a big heart but is overwhelmed by the shelter and looking for a home where he can decompress and become his best self. As he is not yet confident around other dogs, he would prefer a low key dog companion, or to be the only dog in the family. This handsome guy is food-motivated, easy to handle, and working on his leash manners. A loyal, gentle soul with tons of potential, Tuck’s ready to be your buddy! Come Tuck is a gentle giant. meet Tuck at Oakland Animal Services Thursday from 12 - 7 p.m., or Friday, Saturday, or Sunday between 12 and 3 p.m. Potential adopters with a child younger than 12 or a dog that weighs 25 pounds more or less than Tuck must bring them to the shelter for the meeting. For more information, contact Piedmont resident Jessica McDevitt at jessicamcdev@ gmail.com. open every day 8:30 am – 3 pm
articles.title: Adoptable Dog of the Week

articles.text: Sunday November 3, from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., will be an Artist Open Studio at the Piedmont studio of Karen Stanton, teaching artist and children’s book author/ illustrator. As usual the studio has been busy with lots of fun art, but this year something a little different is being created. After the controversy over childless cat ladies erupted, a friend suggested we make cats in the style of Kamala Harris with Converse tennies and/or pearls, donating all proceeds to the campaign. Normally, I like to keep politics and controversy out of my art, but times are not normal. So, we set to work. The first litter was born on the opening day of the Democratic National Convention, selling out in a flash. The second litter was born on the eve of the Presidential debate, and most were quickly adopted too. Now the final litter has arrived and are available in my online shop and home studio at 140 Monticello Avenue. So far we have donated $3125 through ActBlue to the Harris/ Walz campaign. Please visit my online shop at www.karenstantonart.com/shop to support the project, or drop in on Sunday, November 3, between 11 a.m. and 5 p.m. to visit, meet the cats for Kamala and see the art for the holidays.
articles.title: Open Studio for the holidays

articles.text: The Piedmont Education Foundation and its Community Engagement Committee invites the public to a reception at Piedmont High School on Thursday, November 14, starting at 5:30 p.m. Piedmont’s highly regarded schools are a key draw for many residents. Even people without children in the district are attracted to the area because they align with a community that values education. Rich and Barbara Thompson were empty nesters drawn to Piedmont in part for its reputation for excellence in its public schools. They also realize that civic engagement is not only personally rewarding but critical to the success of the community. With this mindset, Rich joined the Piedmont Education Foundation Board in 2020 and this year is chairing the foundation’s Community Engagement Committee which includes Molly Lloyd and Sarah Pearson. “I want to make sure that other members of the community, who don’t currently have students in the district, have a chance to learn more about our schools firsthand,” said Rich. The first of several events planned for this year is the reception on November 14. School Superintendent Jennifer Hawn will provide an update on the district, and community members will have a chance to enjoy our beautiful school facilities and mingle with some current school leaders. “We are excited to reconnect with fellow empty nesters at the reception,” said Katherine Campbell. “We had three children graduate from PHS and are so thankful. Whether we were watching our children on stage, the football field or in the pool playing water polo, we are grateful for all of the great experiences.” To RSVP for the reception, click on: paperlesspost.com/ go/5BAe905hjLbyVahLwQd23. Following the reception, all are welcome to watch the PHS fall play, The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time, which begins at 7 p.m. in the Alan Harvey Theater. Tickets for the play are available at https://phsacting.ludus.com/ index.php and may be available at the door. The play is also being performed on Friday and Saturday, November 15 and 16.

articles.text: Final part in 7-part series Candidates for Piedmont’s school board received one final query from the Piedmont Post this past week. Candidates were asked to limit their answers to 200 words. School Board 3 open seats; 3 candidates. Question Traditionally, the top vote getter is on track for the role of school board president, after current board members. If Piedmonters only had one vote, instead of three, why should they vote for you to be on the school board? MICHAEL MALIONE, Candidate I’m running for school board to help deliver better outcomes for our students, staff, and community. As such, I’m not concerned about titles, but rather what we actually accomplish together. With that in mind, here’s what I hope to achieve over the next four years: As a member of the Board of Education, I will work tirelessly to ensure your student receives a solid education in a diverse, open, and welcoming environment. Every Piedmont student is unique – each has different interests, gifts, and goals, which often change as they grow. Consequently, I believe our district must meet each student where they are, and challenge them appropriately, as much and as soon as they’re ready. I support innovation in teaching and curriculum, but ultimately what matters is the quality of outcomes for our students. My position on curriculum calls for subject matter depth, with more direct exposure to and practice with foundational content, accessible to each and every student. I stand with Max and Susy on fiscal responsibility and getting us to a workable and sustainable budget. If this resonates with you, then I’d be honored to receive your vote, as a tangible affirmation of the vision I’ve expressed. SUSY STRUBLE, Candidate A key reason to vote for me for school board is because I bring a thoughtful, organized, and community-focused approach to problem-solving—an approach that’s essential for addressing important challenges and opportunities in our district. I frame problems clearly and collaborate effectively to find solutions that are both practical and impactful. However, I believe it’s a benefit to Piedmonters that they have more than one vote in this school board election. Over the past few weeks, Michael, Max, and I have dived more deeply into key district topics through community forums and district meetings. We’ve gotten to know each other better, and with each conversation, I’m even more excited about the value we will bring. Our knowledge, skills, and approaches differ but are complementary, and we each have connections in different Piedmont communities. This short time together has been incredibly productive, and I look forward to joining the existing board members to help serve the Piedmont community. MAX ROMAN, Candidate I truly believe that all five of us will make a great team, with varied experiences and expertise that we can use for the benefit of our kids. In my years on other boards, both corporate and nonprofit, I find there is often a disconnect between ideas and action; people often get stuck debating. Where I think I excel is in distilling ideas and feedback from multiple sources into actionable items that can make real change, and I look forward to doing that for our schools. Additionally I think my perspective as someone who grew up in Piedmont, attended and graduated from Piedmont schools, with a parent who worked in our district, is a valuable one. Michael Malione Max Roman Susy Struble

The play will come to life in three showings Thursday to Saturday, November 14-16, at 7:00 p.m. in the Alan Harvey Fifteen-year-old Christopher Boone lives in Swindon, a quiet working-class town on the outskirts of London with his single father. After Christopher’s neatly structured world is sent unraveling by the death of his neighbor’s beloved dog, he embarks on the adventure of a lifetime. This powerful drama weaves together the excitement of mystery and adventure as well as heartwarming and heartbreaking aspects of love, trust, and family as Christopher’s investigation alters the course of his life. This production of The Curious Incident is Simon Stephen’s abridged theatrical adaptation of Mark Haddon’s 2003 best-selling novel, which was translated into 44 languages and sold more than 5.5 million copies worldwide. The first production in 2012 in London’s West End, won seven Olivier awards including Best Play. articles.text: Beach School hosted its first Fall Colors celebration on Sunday, October 20. articles.text: On a blistering hot October day, seven Troop 1 Scouts and two adults set out to bike eight miles up 1,400 feet of vertical to reach Sibley Volcanic Regional Preserve in the Oakland hills. At the start of the trip they loaded camping gear into a car so that they only had to bike with a light day-pack with lunch, snacks, and water. The first four miles were easy, mostly downhill and flat; however it soon became steep. They stopped at Lake Temescal for snacks and soaked their shirts in the water to cool off The last four miles were a slow, steep climb up the winding hills. They stopped frequently to rest and rehydrate in the 93 degree heat. The climb was not without rewards though. There were breathtaking views of virtually the whole Bay stretching for miles. When they reached the apex of the climb they were rewarded with a short stretch of downhill riding to the entrance of the park. Their camping gear arrived shortly after by car taking only 15 minutes to do what took almost three hours by bike. After enjoying popsicles, they grabbed their gear and mustered some remaining energy for the short but steep hike to the campsite. After setting up the campsite, while the adults relaxed, most of the Scouts picked up their bikes to zoom around the dirt trails throughout the park. In late afternoon they went on a walk to explore one of the labyrinths in the park. After a hearty pasta dinner, everyone Zach Fisher (left), Adrien Messina, Theodore Cost, Ryan Morrison, Ciaran Gallagher, Ronin Price, and Jacob Keeney at an overlook A view of the campsite and surrounding hills Jacob Keeney (left), Adrien Messina, Felix Cost, Ciaran Gallagher, Ronin Price, Zach Fisher, Theodore Cost, and Ryan Morrison explore one of the labyrinths in Sibley Volcanic Regional Preserve. gathered around for a game of Mafia. Most people slept in tents, but a few decided to enjoy the warm night by sleeping under the stars. The downhill ride back home the next morning was exhilarating, fast and easy. Two Scouts decided to try to get all the way back to Piedmont. They almost did it until they encountered a hill on Linda Avenue. articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ water polo team glided through the first round of the Western Alameda County Conference playoffs with a 14-9 thrashing of Bishop O’Dowd on Monday, October 29 at the Encinal Pool in Alameda. The Highlanders face top seed Berkeley in the semifinals today, October 30. After ending the first quarter in a 2-2 tie with O’Dowd, PHS exploded for five goals in the second quarter while allowing two. Both teams added two goals in the third quarter, while the Highlanders poured on seven goals in the fourth. “Credit where it’s due, their goalie had a good game. We didn’t execute our 6-on-5, partly due to their defense. But in the third and fourth quarters, all the work we did drawing ejections paid dividends when we started getting mismatches,” explained John Savage, who has returned as head coach this fall. “We start a little slow sometimes and just have to come out with more intensity. We had a lot of opportunities in the first two quarters, but we improved as the game went on,” said junior Elles Kreickhaus. With a 13-8 overall record, Piedmont enters the WACC Tournament as the No. 4 seed. “We’re humming. We’re starting to see what we’ve been preaching – where to work the ball,” Savage said. “We’ve built a lot of chemistry as the season has gone on. The last two years we had George Stein and Declan Linnane really leading the way. Now, it’s more balanced. Everyone needs to do their part,” Kreickhaus said. Making an impact this year is freshman Rylan Patty, who was the Post’s Honorable Mention Athlete of the Month in September. “I love this team because everyone has been so welcoming,” Patty said. “No one has an ego, everyone is willing to pass and listen to input. We stick together and work together really well,” The Highlanders will have a tough task against Berkeley, which beat them 21-12 on October 15. A win will land Piedmont in its first WACC Final since winning the title in 2022. Match Recap In the first quarter, O’Dowd was on the board first after nearly half of the quarter ran out at 3:41, but Leo Hurwitz helped Piedmont respond on the next possession just 20 seconds later. BOD went up again with 42 seconds left, but Patty scored by way of a penalty shot with 24 seconds left. Piedmont got to the front with 5:07 left in the second quarter when Henry Stein assisted Kreickhaus for a goal. Kreickhaus then scored 45 seconds later, this time on an assist by Hurwitz. BOD got one back about a minute later, but PHS’ Kreickhaus scored with a man-advantage with 1:43 left on another assist by Stein. PHS then forced a quick turnover, leading to a counter-attack goal by Stein on an assist by Kreickhaus just 17 seconds later – 6-3. In the third period, goalie Luke McAuliffe opened with a save, which turned into a goal by Elles Kreickhaus scored six goals against Bishop O’Dowd. Staff Photos Freshman Rylan Patty scored two goals on Piedmont’s 14-9 victory against O’Dowd.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s football team continued its dominance atop the Western Alameda County Conference’s Mission Division. Last Friday, October 25, the Highlanders obliterated the visiting Washington Huskies of Fremont 56-20 at Witter Field. It wasn’t the best start after allowing the game’s opening touchdown and relinquishing a fumble on the first possession, but Piedmont jumped out to a 42-14 lead by halftime while forcing five turnovers on the night. The result improved Piedmont’s record to 7-1 overall and 3-0 against league opponents. a one-game lead over Hayward and Newark Memorial. PHS already defeated Hayward 35-14 on October 11. They will face Newark in the season-finale on November 8. “I was telling the coaches this was the most unsatisfying 50-point game. Yeah, we made plays, but we’re getting ready for playoffs and we have bigger aspirations than winning the Mission Division. We know that when we get to NCS, we can’t leave a team on the hook like we did in the first quarter tonight,” said coach Jordan Seiden. It was another big performance by Piedmont’s Xavier Henderson, who is a player that has a knack for filling the stat sheet on both offense and defense. On Saturday night, Henderson had one kickoff return for a touchdown, one twopoint reception, and had a forced fumble, fumble recovery and a tackle for loss all on one play. “I just relied on my blockers, let the play develop, and tried to turn nothing into something,” Henderson said of his long kickoff return. “On the fumble, it was one of my first blitzes of the game. I knew I had to execute and just show up when it mattered,” he added. Game Recap Piedmont led 28-7 by the end of a high-scoring first quarter and extended the gap to 42-14 by halftime. PHS added touchdowns in the third and fourth quarters, while allowing six points in the Staff Photos Xavier Henderson looks back on his way to a 95-yard kickoff return for a touchdown against Washington. Sam Shelby bursts into the end zone for one of his three touchdowns against Washington. final going. Washington opened up the game with a touchdown after three minutes of play and put itself in good position after recovering a fumble at its own 41. After driving down to Piedmont’s 20, linebacker Cash Elmquist blocked the Huskies’ field goal. On PHS ensuing drive, they drove down to the 13-yard line, leading to a quarterback keeper by Markos Lagios for the score. A missed extra point made it a 7-6 deficit with 4:21 left in the quarter. The following kickoff is where the wheels began to fall off for Washington. The Huskies poorly handled the kick, leading to Brandon Dicke recovering at the Washington 36. Piedmont scored after four plays on a 19-yard reception by Sam Shelby. Henderson then caught a pass in the flat for the two-point conversion, making it 14-7 with 2:22 left. Washington botched the next kickoff, where the returner let the ball roll thinking the ball was dead at the five-yard line. Tommy Ashton pounced on the recovery, leading to him scoring on a fiveyard carry on the next play—21-7 just nine after the last touchdown. The Huskies then fumbled on its first play of the next possession, leading to Faisal Malik recovering at the Washington 38. PHS scored in six plays, where Shelby had another touchdown reception, this time weaving around defenders on a 37-yard score with two seconds left, 28-7. Piedmont recovered another fumble at its own 27, where Henderson had a tackle for loss, forced fumble, and fumble recovery on the same play. Shelby then recorded his third receiving touchdown on a 21-yard catch and run, 35-7 with 8:24 left in the first half. Last Friday, October 25, the Highlanders obliterated the visiting Washington Huskies of Fremont 56-20 at Witter Field. It wasn’t the best start after allowing the game’s opening touchdown and relinquishing a fumble on the first possession, but Piedmont jumped out to a 42-14 lead by halftime while forcing five turnovers on the night. The result improved Piedmont’s record to 7-1 overall and 3-0 against league opponents. a one-game lead over Hayward and Newark Memorial. PHS already defeated Hayward 35-14 on October 11. They will face Newark in the season-finale on November 8. “I was telling the coaches this was the most unsatisfying 50-point game. Yeah, we made plays, but we’re getting ready for playoffs and we have bigger aspirations than winning the Mission Division. We know that when we get to NCS, we can’t leave a team on the hook like we did in the first quarter tonight,” said coach Jordan Seiden. It was another big performance by Piedmont’s Xavier Henderson, who is a player that has a knack for filling the stat sheet on both offense and defense. On Saturday night, Henderson had one kickoff return for a touchdown, one twopoint reception, and had a forced fumble, fumble recovery and a tackle for loss all on one play. “I just relied on my blockers, let the play develop, and tried to turn nothing into something,” Henderson said of his long kickoff return. “On the fumble, it was one of my first blitzes of the game. I knew I had to execute and just show up when it mattered,” he added. Game Recap Piedmont led 28-7 by the end of a high-scoring first quarter and extended the gap to 42-14 by halftime. PHS added touchdowns in the third and fourth quarters, while allowing six points in the Staff Photos Xavier Henderson looks back on his way to a 95-yard kickoff return for a touchdown against Washington. Highlanders bash Dragons in first-round of WACC Tournament By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High’s boys’ water polo team glided through the first round of the Western Alameda County Conference playoffs with a 14-9 thrashing of Bishop O’Dowd on Monday, October 29 at the Encinal Pool in Alameda. The Highlanders face top seed Berkeley in the semifinals today, October 30. After ending the first quarter in a 2-2 tie with O’Dowd, PHS exploded for five goals in the second quarter while allowing two. Both teams added two goals in the third quarter, while the Highlanders poured on seven goals in the fourth. “Credit where it’s due, their goalie had a good game. We didn’t execute our 6-on-5, partly due to their defense. But in the third and fourth quarters, all the work we did drawing ejections paid dividends when we started getting mismatches,” explained John Savage, who has returned as head coach this fall. “We start a little slow sometimes and just have to come out with more intensity. We had a lot of opportunities in the first two quarters, but we improved as the game went on,” said junior Elles Kreickhaus. With a 13-8 overall record, Piedmont enters the WACC Tournament as the No. 4 seed. “We’re humming. We’re starting to see what we’ve been preaching – where to work the ball,” Savage said. “We’ve built a lot of chemistry as the season has gone on. The last two years we had George Stein and Declan Linnane really leading the way. Now, it’s more balanced. Everyone needs to do their part,” Kreickhaus said. Making an impact this year is freshman Rylan Patty, who was the Post’s Honorable Mention Athlete of the Month in September. “I love this team because everyone has been so welcoming,” Patty said. “No one has an ego, everyone is willing to pass and listen to input. We stick together and work together really well,” The Highlanders will have a tough task against Berkeley, which beat them 21-12 on October 15. A win will land Piedmont in its first WACC Final since winning the title in 2022. Match Recap In the first quarter, O’Dowd was on the board first after nearly half of the quarter ran out at 3:41, but Leo Hurwitz helped Piedmont respond on the next possession just 20 seconds later. BOD went up again with 42 seconds left, but Patty scored by way of a penalty shot with 24 seconds left. Piedmont got to the front with 5:07 left in the second quarter when Henry Stein assisted Kreickhaus for a goal. Kreickhaus then scored 45 seconds later, this time on an assist by Hurwitz. BOD got one back about a minute later, but PHS’ Kreickhaus scored with a man-advantage with 1:43 left on another assist by Stein. PHS then forced a quick turnover, leading to a counter-attack goal by Stein on an assist by Kreickhaus just 17 seconds later – 6-3. In the third period, goalie Luke McAuliffe opened with a save, which turned into a goal by See Boys’ Water Polo on page 31 Sam Shelby bursts into the end zone for one of his three touchdowns against Washington. final going. Washington opened up the game with a touchdown after three minutes of play and put itself in good position after recovering a fumble at its own 41. After driving down to Piedmont’s 20, linebacker Cash Elmquist blocked the Huskies’ field goal. On PHS ensuing drive, they drove down to the 13-yard line, leading to a quarterback keeper by Markos Lagios for the score. A missed extra point made it a 7-6 deficit with 4:21 left in the quarter. The following kickoff is where the wheels began to fall off for Washington. The Huskies poorly handled the kick, leading to Brandon Dicke recovering at the Washington 36. Piedmont scored after four plays on a 19-yard reception by Sam Shelby. Henderson then caught a pass in the flat for the two-point conversion, making it 14-7 with 2:22 left. Washington botched the next kickoff, where the returner let the ball roll thinking the ball was dead at the five-yard line. Tommy Ashton pounced on the recovery, leading to him scoring on a fiveyard carry on the next play—21-7 just nine after the last touchdown. The Huskies then fumbled on its first play of the next possession, leading to Faisal Malik recovering at the Washington 38. PHS scored in six plays, where Shelby had another touchdown reception, this time weaving around defenders on a 37-yard score with two seconds left, 28-7. Piedmont recovered another fumble at its own 27, where Henderson had a tackle for loss, forced fumble, and fumble recovery on the same play. Shelby then recorded his third receiving touchdown on a 21-yard catch and run, 35-7 with 8:24 left in the first half. The Huskies scored with 4:51 left, but that’s when Henderson broke down the middle of the field for a 95-yard kickoff See Football on page 31 Elles Kreickhaus scored six goals against Bishop O’Dowd. Staff Photos Tommy Ashton scores a touchdown against Washington. Freshman Rylan Patty scored two goals on Piedmont’s 14-9 victory against O’Dowd.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ tennis team is wrapping up its regular season after defeating league rival Berkeley 4-3 at Berkeley Tennis Club on Thursday, October 24. The result brings their league record to 4-3, which clinches a berth in the Division 2 North Coast Section Team TourThe win reverses the outcome on October 3 when they lost by the same score to Berkeley. “We won two out of the three doubles matches and split the four singles matches today,” said coach Jim Landes. “Our first time against them we were only able to win one of the singles.” The team’s critical fourth match win came from the No. 3 doubles team of Abigail Call and Inara Mehtam who breezed to a “It’s exciting and rewarding. We were nervous about qualifyKate Jumper had a critical comefrom-behind win against Berkeley Faith Chin was Piedmont’s first win of the day against Berkeley. Staff Photos Abigail Call hits a forehand against Berkeley. Her No. 3 doubles match with Inara Mehta was the clinching victory for Piedmont’s tennis team. ing for NCS all season, but now that we’re won, it feels great,” Call said. “Last time against Berkeley, our match was really close, so we wanted to pull through with a win this time,” Mehta added. Kate Jumper was also a huge factor with a three-set win at No, 2 singles. After ;losing the first set 6-3, Jumper never lost a game in the second or third sets with a pair of 6-0 shutouts. “I strongly believe in the firstset curse. It feels like I lose every first set almost like a tradition now. I just always warm up in the first set. I just decided I couldn’t hit it to her forehand. Keeping it consistent is the best thing you can do when you’re down a set,” Jumper said. The Highlanders’ first win of the day came at No. 4 singles, where Faith Chin won 6-1, 6-2. Chin, a sophomore, has proven to be a mainstay in Landes’ singles order. “I just tried to stay consistent. She had a really good forehand; it’s very fast and has a lot of top spin. Her backhand was her weaker side, so I just kept hitting to that side,” Chin said. Piedmont now looks ahead to the Western Alameda County Conference Individual Tournament at Chabot College on Friday and Saturday, November 8-9. Match Recap Chin reeled in Piedmont’s opening win at No. 4 singles with a 6-1, 6-2 victory. PHS then went up 2-0 with a straight-set win by Emma Chan and Maddie Tran at No. 2 doubles, 6-4, 6-2. But Berkeley came back to tie the Match Day at 2-2 with a 6-3, 6-1 win at No. 3 singles over Arianna Kortum, followed by Berkeley’s No. 1 doubles team beating Emma Eisemon and Samantha Huynh 6-3, 6-2. Soon after, Jumper won her three-set match at No. 2 singles, 3-6, 6-0, 6-0. Call and Mehta then shut down their opponent 6-0, 6-1 for Piedmont’s clinching win. The last match on the court was a heated three-set match at No. 1 singles with Carolina Romanczuk against Sam Lopatin, but she lost a 6-3, 6-7 (7-5), 7-5 barnburner. articles.text: Photos by Jenni Tsoi Leighton Mand, a sophomore, was second overall in a field of 71 runners at a league meet at Oyster Bay. She achieved a big personal record time. The Highlanders’ cross country team competed in its third Western Alameda County Conference meet of the season at Oyster Bay in San Leandro on Wednesday, October 23. Piedmont’s girls’ team finished second of nine schools, and the boys’ team was fourth of 10 schools. Piedmont will next compete on Saturday, November 9 in the Western Alameda County Conference Championship at Hayward High. “We have about 15 days without racing to get ready for the WACC League Championship at Hayward High. It’s an important time for recovery and training,” coach Steve Zirkelbach said. For the girls’ team, it marked another strong performance by sophomore Leighton Mand, who was second overall in a field of 71 runners. Her time of 19:09.49t marked a personal record on a three-mile course, eclipsing her previous best by nearly 30 seconds after having her fastest time just four days earlier at the Wilder Mariner Invitational. Mand is having a breakout season. She was named Athlete of the Week by the Post on October 9 after leading Piedmont’s team to first place at the Artichoke Invitational in Half Moon Bay on October 5. Teammate Skylar Best, a junior, finished seventh with a time of 19:51.58 and classmate Cora Chun was 10th in 20:00.86. Freshman Viviane Oesterer was 11th in 20:07.37,and junior Cora Brozowski Schrader rounded out Piedmont’s top five with a 17th place finish in 20:37.06. Boys results Sophomore Sebastien Swain led the way once again, placing 10th of 91 runners with a time of 16:55.2. Behind Swain was junior Noah Sohn, clocking a time of 17:07.32 to finish 17th. Sophomore Alex Schleuning was 20th in 17:14.57, sophomore Thomas Ero was 27th in 17:29.58, and senior Oliver Horsley was 29th in 17:34.51. NEXT UP Piedmont goes to Hayward High for the 2024 WACC Cross Country Championship on Saturday, November 9. The varsity boys race starts at 12:00 p.m., and varsity girls at 12:30 p.m. Cora Chun finished her race in 10th place, helping Piedmont claim second place. Sebastien Swain placed 10th among 91 runners.

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ water polo team, the No. 6 seed, finished its regular season on Friday, October 25 with a 5-3 win on the road against San Rafael. They opened the league playoffs with a 10-3 loss to No. 3 Berkeley. Piedmont will compete in the WACC Consolation Bracket and will face No. 7 Lick-Wilmerding today, October 30, at San Leandro HS. With a win, PHS will face No. 5 Encinal on Friday, November 1 at the Jets’ home pool. PHS last defeated Lick-Wilmerding in a high-scoring 17-11 victory on October 3. The Highlanders also lost a 12-10 barnburner with Encinal on October 8. Against San Rafael, Piedmont scored the game’s first five goals before San Rafael got on the scoreboard. Coach Georgia Lewis praised junior Viviane Burke for her contributions, including setting up Abigail Jacoby, who finished with four goals. “Vivian Burke has become a pro at forcing multiple defenders to cover her. If three of their players need to defend her, that leaves our offense open, which creates scoring opportunities for the entire team. She takes a real beating doing it,” Lewis said. Senior Sonja ten Grotenhuis was also a big part of the win, recording seven steals on the night. Goalie Chloe Graham, meanwhile, had eight saves. “Sonja ten Grotenhuis has upped her defensive game to leap out and steal the ball before it ever gets to the offense. Tonight she had some beautiful interPhotos by Lynne Wright Abigail Jacoby scored four goals against San Rafael. ceptions leaping high out of the water. Chloe Graham was just on fire tonight. All in all, the team played a good, solid game,” Lewis said. 5-3 win vs. San Rafael Piedmont led 1-0 through the first quarter and 3-0 by halftime. articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ golf team wrapped up its season on Monday, October 28 at the Division 2 North Coast Section Championship at Rooster Run in Petaluma. PHS finished the 18-hole course with 436 strokes. They placed 9th among 14 teams, marking the first time in a considerable time for PHS to send a full team. Piedmont senior Mei Assalian led the way with a round of 82, finishing 13th of 144 athletes, qualifying for the Division 1 NCS tournament at Paradise Valley Golf Course in Fairfield on Monday, November 4. Behind Assalian was Peyton Watson with a round of 115, Mackenzie Seto-Ngyuen shot a 117, Gracey Ann Hatchell finished with a 122, while Jameson Sanford rounded things out with a 125. It marked the second time for Assalian to compete at Rooster Run after last qualifying for NCS in 2022 as a sophomore when we named her The Posts’ Honorable Mention for Sophomore of the Year. She finished the 2022 tournament with a round of 93 strokes, marking a nine stroke improvement. “I played that course two years ago, so it definitely helped. It was weirdly familiar. I remembered where to hit and to take certain angles on different holes to get a better view of the green,” Assalian said. The NCS tournament was played with individual rounds of 18 holes. articles.text: Happy Halloween! What better time to awaken some spooky history of around the area, including your very own town? Here’s a look into some locations with a spooky past. Hayward Plunge, Hayward Allegedly, a swimming instructor in the 1960s at the Hayward Plunge indoor pool led his entire class up the trail and left them in Ward Creek, telling them to wait until he returned. The children stayed there until the night; the coach returned and murdered them, leaving each of them in the creek. Many locals claim strange sightings, like voices of children around them, sometimes laughter or cries, sounds of footsteps, cold spots, and dark shadows. This writer even had a strange sighting of children in all-white garb from head-to-toe during a hike when he was a teenager. Starting at Memorial Park, the initial portion of the Hayward Plunge Trail starts in the back of the park past the bandstand. articles.text: The California Symphony will showcase the crowning achievements of a composer at the peak of his powers with “Brahms Odyssey” this Saturday, November 2 at 7:30 p.m. and Sunday, November 3 at 4 p.m. in Walnut Creek. The program, conducted by Donato Cabrera, will open with Benjamin Britten’s lively Young Person’s Guide to the Orchestra, which uses a memorable theme to introduce different instruments in the orchestra, taking listeners on a journey through the strings, woodwinds, percussion, brass and more. Former California Symphony Resident Composer Mason Bates will invoke the spirit of Disney’s classic Fantasia in his Grammy-winning concerto for orchestra and animated film, Philharmonia Fantastique: The Making of the Orchestra. The program will close with Johannes Brahms’ Symphony No. 4, a deeply emotional, poignant masterpiece from the eminent composer. It was the last symphony he wrote, and many consider it to be the pinnacle of his career. “In choosing Benjamin Britten’s Young Person’s Guide to the Donato Cabrera will conduct a California Symphony program this Saturday and Sunday featuring Brahms’ Symphony No. 4, preceded by two colorfully imaginative orchestral pieces for young listeners. Orchestra and Bates’s Philharmonia Fantastique, we will be performing two works that belong to a long tradition of works composed to showcase the incredibly powerful sounds that only the instruments of the orchestra can produce,” Cabrera added. Britten’s guide piece was commissioned in 1945 for a British documentary film, Instruments of the Orchestra with the London Symphony Orchestra. Philharmonia Fantastique is a multi-media concerto from Mason Bates and award-winning filmmakers Gary Rydstrom and Jim Capobianco. Fantastique, like Britten’s Guide, is a tour through the orchestra – this time paired with an animated film guided by a magical young character, Sprite, whose curiosity leads a vibrant dive into the makings of an orchestra and the inner workings of its instruments. This imaginative piece won a Grammy Award in 2023. Tickets ($25-$95) for the concerts at the Lesher Center for the Arts’ Hofmann Theatre (1601 Civic Drive, Walnut Creek) are available online at californiasymphony.org, or by phone at 925- 943-7469.

articles.text: The Young People’s Symphony Orchestra (YPSO) will open its 88th season with a magisterial Fall Concert this Saturday, November 2 at First Church Berkeley at 7:30 p.m. The program, conducted by YPSO Music Director David Ramadanoff, will feature Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov’s Russian Easter Festival Overture, Op. 36; Jeremy Cavaterra’s The Aquarium (Monterey Suite, Movement 3); and Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky’s Symphony No. 6 in B minor, Op. 74, more widely known as the Pathétique Symphony. Founded in 1936 in Berkeley, California by conductor Jessica Marcelli, Young People’s Symphony Orchestra (YPSO) is the oldest youth orchestra in California, and the oldest independent youth orchestra in the country. For 88 years and counting, YPSO has developed the musical talents of students throughout the San Francisco Bay Area; many alumni are internationally distinguished musicians. YPSO has performed in venues including Carnegie Hall in New York City; the War Memorial Opera House in San Francisco; Davies Symphony Hall in San Francisco; the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art; Memorial Hall at Harvard University; the Sydney Opera House; the Dvorak Hall in Prague; and the Golden Hall of the Musikverein in Vienna. Tickets ($20 regular, $30 premium early seating; free for children 13 and under, and students 14 and over with ID) for the performance at First Church Berkeley (2345 Channing Way) are available at ypsomusic.org/ events. articles.text: The Left Coast Chamber Ensemble presents Pierrot Lunaire, a concert of genre-breaking works from the 20th century, in two concerts this weekend. On Saturday, November 2, they will perform at 7:30 p.m. at Noe Valley Ministry in San Francisco, with a repeat concert on Sunday at 4 p.m. at the Hillside Club in Berkeley. The two concerts open the Ensemble’s 2024-25 season, and will feature Arnold Schoenberg’s melodrama opus Pierrot Lunaire. In honor of the late composer’s 150th birthday, conductor Nikki Einfeld will bring a theatrical flair to the role. Schoenberg has been long recognized not only for his invention of the twelve-tone technique but also for the extraordinary range of his compositional skill. Pierrot Lunaire is one of his most celebrated works, setting 21 selected poems from writer Albert Giraud’s cycle of the same name that explores the gamut of human emotion, from nostalgia to gallows humor. Listeners will enjoy a concert experience which combines theater, cabaret and avant-garde music. “This program exists in an atmosphere where melancholy and humor co-exist, The atmosphere is amplified by the intimacy of two of the Bay Area’s most enchanting small venues,” said Left Coast Chamber Ensemble Artistic Director Matilda Hofman. The performances will take place at Noe Valley Ministry (1021 Sanchez Street, San Francisco) and the Hillside Club (2286 Cedar Street, Berkeley). Tickets ($35 in advance, $38 at the door; $15 students in advance, $18 students at the door) may be bought online leftcoastensemble. org/pierrot, by phone at 415-617- 5223 or at the door. Enjoy a performance of Pierrot Lunaire spanning poetry, music and the human voice as the Left Coast Chamber Ensemble performs in San Francisco this Saturday and in Berkeley on Sunday.
articles.title: Left Coast Ensemble plays Pierrot Lunaire this weekend in Berkeley, SF

articles.text: Cal Performances will welcome the Dover Quartet this Sunday, November 3, for a 3 p.m. concert ar Hertz Hall exploring the cultural traditions that shape American concert music. The twice-Grammy-nominated ensemble will perform the West Coast premiere of Emmy-winning American Indian composer Jerod Tate’s new work Abokkoli’ Taloowa (“Woodland Songs”), co-commissioned by Cal Performances, om addition to Tate’s arrangement of Rattle Songs by Indigenous composer Pura Fé. Dvořák’s renowned American Quartet and composer Jessie Montgomery’s string piece Strum round out the program. The performance is part of Cal Performances’ “Illuminations: Fractured History” series of programs for the 2024–25 season. “The program illuminates and expands the robust connections between many American voices, including jazz, bluegrass, Indigenous American music and Western classical music. Dvořák’s most famous works were directly inspired by the music he heard and studied while living in Iowa, and included the music of Indigenous peoples and African Americans, explained Camden Shaw, the Dover Quartet cellist. Jerod Impichchaachaaha’ Tate, a member of the Chickasaw Nation in Oklahoma, has devoted Composer Jerod Tate The Dover Quartet his career to cultivating a distinctive language of Indigenous American classical composition. He was the 2021 Cultural Ambassador for the US Department of State, and the 2024 recipient of a USA Fellowship. His works have been performed by the National Symphony Orchestra, the San Francisco Symphony, Dallas Symphony, Detroit Symphony, Minnesota Orchestra, Buffalo Philharmonic and many others. “Abokkoli’ Taloowa’” is infused with the melodies, rhythms, and legends of Tate’s Chickasaw heritage. The work celebrates the woodland animals of his people’s Southeastern homelands, with movements named after the squirrel, the bird, the deer, the fish and the raccoon. “Each movement is a deep, dramatic, and rhapsodic expression of my feelings of being a Chickasaw man from a beautiful and robust culture… I allow myself to fluidly dance between cultural clarity and modern expressionism,” Tate said. Rattle Songs is a suite of compositions created by Tuscarora vocalist Pura Fé for her ensemble Ulali, a women’s a cappella trio that explores Native American song through innovative modern arrangements. Tate’s arrangement of this suite for a string quartet evokes the turtle shell shakers that are part of Native American stomp dancing and social songs. Jessie Montgomery’s ebullient work Strum is inspired by American folk and dance music, and features strumming pizzicato, layers of rhythmic ostinati, and interwoven melodies. Dvořák’s well-loved American Quartet. which the Czech composer wrote during a visit to Spillville, Iowa in 1893, serves as a backdrop for the more recent works on the program. This quartet, composed shortly after his New World Symphony, features prominent motifs from the African American spiritual songs that Dvořák heard during his time in Iowa. Tickets ($69-$74) for the performance at Hertz Hall pm the UC Berkeley campus (101 CrossSproul Path, Berkeley) are available online at secure.calperformances.org/23657/23772, or by phone at 642-9988.
articles.title: Grammy-nominated group to highlight American Indian songs, Dvorˇák

articles.text: Italians invented the scenario and the word. It entered the American vernacular. The story is fascinating. Giuseppe Tartini (1692-1770) was the most important violinist of his generation. He was also a great swordsman and a famous lover. Our story begins with love. Tartini was in love with the daughter of a wealthy man. The girl’s father not only objected to the marriage, he wanted to kill Tartini. Hearing of the plot to kill him, Tartini fled his city and took refuge in a monastery. Night after night, he had the same dream. It was his desire to become the greatest violinist in the world. In his dream, he makes a pact with the devil – a timeless story. Tartiini would become the greatest violinist, but he must relinquish his soul to the devil. At the last minute, Tartini questions, the honesty of the Lord of darkness. He challenges the devil to demonstrate his ability to play the violin…and the devil does just that! In the dream, the devil performs the most beautiful and difficult music on the violin. Tartini said afterward, that he was unable to breathe, so beautiful was the devil’s music. Night after night, he attempted to write on paper the music of his dream. The result was “The Devil’s Trill Sonata,” certainly Tartini’s most famous composition, and without a doubt his greatest. It begins with a dreamlike introduction. In the second movement, the music becomes more agitated with the violinist conversing with the devil. In the third movement, we hear the extraordinary devil’s trill. The Sonata comes to a dramatic conclusion with a florid cadenza for the solo violin played with continuous trills. And then the orchestra joins in a triumphant finale. This composition is certainly one of the monuments in all of music. Almost parallel to the story of Tartini is the story of another Baroque composer, Alessandro Stradella. He was in love with a mistress of a Venetian Senator. To save themselves, they fled to Rome. Stradella’s musical career flourished and his music was performed everywhere. Two assassins were engaged to murder Stradella. They attended a performance of one of Stradella’s compositions and intended to murder him afterwards. They were overcome by the beauty of the music and instead of murdering him they told him that his life was in danger and allowed him to escape unharmed. Once again, the young couple fled and came under the protection of the Duchess of Savoy. articles.text: Catch the Olivier Award-winning comedy The Play That Goes Wrong before it closes at the San Francisco Playhouse with a final performance this Saturday. This fast-paced farce filled with slapstick silliness finds the bumbling Cornley Polytechnic Drama Society on the opening night of its newest production, “The Murder of Haversham.” As the incompetent theatre troupe attempts to stage this 1920s murder mystery, their production devolves into madcap mayhem. Lost props, forgotten lines and poorly constructed scenery conspire against the clumsy cast, who fight for the show to go on as they struggle to survive until the final curtain call. Written by London’s Mischief Theatre co-founders Henry Lewis, Jonathan Sayer and Henry Shields, The Play That Goes Wrong was performed for nearly a decade in London’s West End, winning the Olivier Award for Best New Comedy before moving to Broadway. The New York Times deemed it a “gut-busting hit. One of those breakneck exercises in idiocy that make you laugh till you cry. It starts off punch-drunk and just keeps getting drunker.” San Francisco Playhouse co-founder Susi Damilano directs this hilarious whodunit. Tickets ($63-$135) and showtimes for performances at SF Playhouse (450 Post St.) are available at sfplayhouse.org/sfph/ get-tickets.

It begins with a dreamlike introduction. In the second movement, the music becomes more agitated with the violinist conversing with the devil. In the third movement, we hear the extraordinary devil’s trill. The Sonata comes to a dramatic conclusion with a florid cadenza for the solo violin played with continuous trills. And then the orchestra joins in a triumphant finale. This composition is certainly one of the monuments in all of music. Almost parallel to the story of Tartini is the story of another Baroque composer, Alessandro Stradella. He was in love with a mistress of a Venetian Senator. To save themselves, they fled to Rome. They attended a performance of one of Stradella’s compositions and intended to murder him afterwards. They were overcome by the beauty of the music and instead of murdering him they told him that his life was in danger and allowed him to escape unharmed. Once again, the young couple fled and came under the protection of the Duchess of Savoy. Violinist Giuseppe Tartini She arranged their marriage and made sure that Stradella achieved musical greatness. Unfortunately for Stradella, the Venetian Senator never forgot nor forgave, and Stradella ended up in the morgue. The story became so famous that it was made into an opera. What is so interesting is that the music of these star-crossed lovers lives on. In the triumph of music over evil, Tartini’s great composition “The Devil’s Trill” sonata remains one of the great pieces of the repertoire. Stradella’s most famous piece is “Pita Signore”. Tar tini was acclaimed throughout the world. Interestingly enough, he was a very simple man who had no need of the fortune that comes with fame. He refused “King‘s ransom’s” time after time - including an offer of 3000 pounds to come to England. He rode off into the sunset, a happy man. Stories like this crossed the ocean to America. Romance will always endure. But what about revenge? The word in Italian is…Vendetta. articles.text: Though the film Suffragette takes place more than 100 years ago (1912-1913), and though its core issue – a woman’s right to vote – has long ago been settled, the narrative still feels contemporary and relevant. A century has indeed passed, yet we know that women today still struggle for equal pay and job opportunities and, of course, the ongoing debate regarding the ultimate control of their bodies. What has been dimmed by the passage of time are the harrowing risks women took as they did battle with an iron-fisted, often misogynistic patriarchy that was committed to preventing them from acquiring the right to vote. The story is told through the eyes of Maud Watts (Carey Mulligan), an English working class woman, who works 12-hour days in a large factory-like laundry, washing and ironing other people’s clothes. In act one, Maud, who leads an insulated, narrow life – she’s married and has a son – is terrified when she finds herself on a London street and is unexpectedly swept up in a demonstration by suffragettes who are insisting on the right to vote. Suddenly Maud finds herself surrounded by women who are prepared to confront the police, feel the pain of their clubs, and endure arrest and weeks of incarceration for a cause in which they passionately believe. These courageous women are a revelation to Maud. She has long felt oppressed and treated as if she were mere property to be used and then disposed of by men. Abruptly the scales fall from her eyes and her consciousness is raised. Against all of her instincts, against everything she has been told about her place in the world (repeatedly by her husband), she rebels and joins what soon becomes a rising tide of civil disobedience, meaning destruction of property. In one moving moment in the film, Maud sits in front of government officials and describes her work and life and finally says quietly, “There might be another way of living this life.” That other way comes at great cost and personal pain. She discovers that the government is capable of remorseless harm: the suffragettes are beaten, jailed, and force-fed. As well, their neighbors (and society at large), voice their disapprobation by shunning and ridiculing them. Maud didn’t know that she would be asked to sacrifice all that she once held dear; but that is exactly the price that is exacted. Suffragette tells a powerful story. And Carey Mulligan gives “Strictly Business”, Acrylic on Canvas, 38x40”, 2024

articles.text: Reese Witherspoon, Oprah Winfrey, Zach Galifianakis, Mindy Kaling, Storm Reid, Levi Miller, and Deric McCabe in A Wrinkle in Time If you have some youngsters hanging around the house, well, find A Wrinkle in Time. It’s a gorgeous film, a solid adventure, and will easily touch their sense of wonder. As an adult I acknowledge that the most interesting part of the story for me was the beginning when Meg Murry (Storm Reid) is introduced. She’s a 13-year-old middle schooler who has developed an attitude that gets her either picked on by her school’s Mean Girls or results in a visit to the principle’s office. In truth Meg has been grieving since the baffling disappearance four years ago of her beloved father, Dr. Alex Murry (Chris Pine), a physicist. Meg is clearly gifted, though she suffers from a damaged self-image and sense of self-worth. Her mother (Gugu Mbatha-Raw), who’s also a physicist, is equally devastated by the loss of her husband, and is upset with Meg. It’s only Meg’s brother, Charles Wallace (Deric McCabe), who is convinced some new friends can assist them in finding their father. As it turns out, Calvin, from Meg’s school, shows up one day and is around when Charles’ new acquaintances reveal themselves: Mrs. Which (Oprah Winfrey), Mrs. Whatsit (Reese Witherspoon) and Mrs. Who (Mindy Kaling). They are celestial, ephemeral beings that agree to help Meg and Charles Wallace and Calvin find Dr. Murry. And so off they go, into the farthest parts of the universe. It’s quite a journey and one that first introduces the kids to a planet of light. It’s there that they confront the IT, which represents the dark side of life – a threatening essence that the three must face alone and likely has Meg’s father. Mrs. Which tells them that IT is spreading through the universe and to be careful. Remember, this is a kids’ movie and therefore has as its premise a complete suspension of disbelief. An example is the word “tessering,” meaning a wrinkle in time and the way that the three Mrs. and Meg, et al. travel across the universe. It proves to be a great trip (and back), filled with lessons for all of them. Older kids will enjoy A Wrinkle in Time, especially tweens and newbie teens. A Wrinkle in Time. Directed by Ava DuVernay. Starring Storm Reid, Oprah Winfrey, Reese Witherspoon. Walt Disney Films. 1 hr., 49 min. Rated PG. Released in 2018. articles.text: Gifted is a heartwarming, engaging family-friendly film (best for older kids) with outstanding performances by McKenna Grace, portraying a remarkably precocious first grader, and Chris Evans as her uncle, Frank, who has raised Mary since she was an infant. And not to forget Octavia Spencer as Roberta, who has helped Frank raise Mary since their arrival in Florida. Mary’s mother, Frank’s sister was a brilliant mathematician who took her own life, asked only that Frank raise Mary, no matter her possible gifts, and let her be simply a kid. Frank agreed. Set on the balmy coast, we soon learn that Mary is slated to begin first grade. She’s not happy, insisting that she simply wants to be home-schooled. As usual. Frank, who repairs private pleasure boats at the local marina, makes it clear that going to public school with kids her age is going to happen. And he has counseled Mary not to reveal her mathematical skills, something that has become evident in a few short years. The school bus arrives, and off she goes on the first day of school. What could go wrong? Cut to Mary sitting in class listening to her teacher, Ms. Stevenson (Jenny Slate), as she takes the class through a very elementary addition problem (e.g., 6+2). Mary, slumped in her chair, clearly bored, is growing impatient and finally blurts out, “eight.” Ms. Stevenson looks at Mary, intrigued, and poses a more difficult probMckenna Grace stars in Gifted

articles.text: Dear Abby: As Halloween looms closer, do you think there will be anything fun happening for dogs? We love those treats. Arf. –Chunk the English Bulldog dressing up as a toy poodle Dear Chunk: I suspect they’ll be an informal Weener Parade at the base of Piedmont Park, starting at 8:30 a.m. on Halloween. It usually has some of the best doggy treats you can find. Piedmonters love their dogs. So put on your toy poodle costume and head to the foot of Bushy Dell Creek by 8:30 a.m. and you’ll have some great sniffs and goodies. –Abby Dear Abby: I am confused. Near the entrance to the Parking Lot in front of Piedmont Park Community Center, there are three fancy new steel garbage cans, red, blue and green. But not far away sits an older garbage can with a large board nailed on top of it, so no one can toss garbage into it. However there’s garbage in it which can’t be taken out? Why would they leave garbage in there when nailing on a top? –Sparky the Doodle Dear Sparky: I’ve sniffed at that can myself a few times and I have no clue why they would leave old garbage in there before enclosing it. I was surprised they wouldn’t just keep it and use it as an extra spot for garbage on special fun days. I haven’t learned a thing but I’m still digging. If anyone out there’s knows anything please let me know. Woof. –Abby Dear Abby: We have just adopted a dog and wanted to let everyone know that there’s a surplus of dogs and puppies up for adoption. If you want a dog, this is a great time to adopt. Good dogs need good people. –Don A, Piedmont Community Church Dear Don: I wasn’t aware of that but it makes sense with these postCovid prices of dog supplies and medical needs. We will be howling at St. Francis to help all. Autumn is a good time for puppies to come into a home. Yelps for help. –Abby E-mail your comments, ideas and dog thoughts on any pet topic to Melanie Johnston at MSJ312@ aol.com.

articles.text: It was a beautiful fall morning last Wednesday for the Walking on Wednesdays group. Halloween was just a week away, so they decided to see some Halloween house decorations. A large turnout of 48 walkers and four K-9 best friends were on hand for the fun. Before last week’s walk, some history was shared. Halloween’s origins date back to the ancient Celtic festival of Samhain (pronounced sow-in) when people lit bonfires and wore costumes to ward off ghosts. The Celts, who lived 2,000 years ago mostly in what is now Ireland, the UK and northern France, celebrated their new year on November 1. This day marked the end of summer and the harvest, and the beginning of the dark, cold winter. It was a time of year often associated with death. Celts believed that on the night before the new year, the boundary between the worlds of the living and the dead became blurred. On the night of October 31, they celebrated Samhain, when they believed ghosts returned to earth. The people built huge, sacred bonfires to burn crops and animals as sacrifices to their Celtic gods. During the celebration, the Celts wore costumes, typically consisting of animal heads and skins. had conquered most of the Celtic territory. During the 400 years they ruled they combined their Roman festivals with the Samhain celebration. In the eighth century, Pope Gregory III designated November 1 as a time to honor all saints. Soon, All Saints Day also incorporated some Samhain traditions. The evening was known as All Hallows Eve, and later became known simply as Hallowe’en (Hallloween). Over time, Halloween evolved into a day of activities like trickor-treating, carving jack-o-lanterns, wearing costumes, and eating treats. However, it was not until after the mass Irish and Scottish immigrations in the 19th century that Halloween became a major American holiday. With this new understanding of Halloween, the walkers went down Magnolia Avenue in search of ghosts and goblins. Sherry Jacobs led them to a front yard she thought the group would enjoy. It had headstones for family cats with funny names, and a “Cat Crossing” sign attached to the back of a city street sign. The walkers went to Dracena Avenue, now famous for its annual tradition of transforming the block-long street into Sleepy Hallow, with small, white ghosts hanging from trees all along the street. On Park Way and on Blair the group found a two-story, inflatable, black cat. Them it was over to Sheridan and Lincoln and Crocker Avenue. The front yard of a house on Crocker had been transformed into a fully occupied graveyard with headstones, ghouls emerging from their graves, huge spiders, a ghost clown swinging from a tree. By chance, the notscary owner of the house, Peter Wagener, was unloading his car, so he stopped to tell the walkers how his family had bought the house three years ago. Each year they create a spooktacular show for trick or treaters. About 350 brave ones got full size candy bars last year. Peter said his dentist, a brother-in-law, voiced no objections. It proved to be a great spot for a group photo with Peter and his other-world friends. There were more yards to see on Sea View Avenue, but time had run out, so they returned to the Exedra after a good long walk with lots of Halloween fun. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. Among those participating on last week’s walk with the Wednesday group were Irene Thompson, Leigh Sorensen, Phil Chin, Julia Chin with K-9 best friend Rocky, Bob Wong, Jim Kellogg, Joanne Larson, Kathy Rolfson, Kat Lang, Albert Chen, Brenda Ferrero, June Yee, Sherry Jacobs, Adrienne Hamlin, Lois Price, Karin Fetherston, Judy Love, Elizabeth Richter, Bonnie Sherwood, David Haecker, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Dave DeRoche, Claudine Bach, Noemi Alvarado, Abha Kothari, Gloria DaSilva, Phil Witte, Lisa Euphrat, Michelle Yang, Quincy Dong, Helen Dong, Peggy Shultz, Mark Davis, Jack Fischrup, Matt Gerhardt, Sharona Fischrup, Nancy Henn, Renee Goldhammer, Alan Goldhammer, Lori Austin, Jim Kuo, Mike Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, Pat Keller, Priscilla Wanerus, Shirley Nakao, Eric Behrens with K-9 best friend Mocha, Fangfang Lai, Lao Xia, Lao Wang, and Dick Carter.

The front yard of a house on Crocker had been transformed into a fully occupied graveyard with headstones, ghouls emerging from their graves, huge spiders, a ghost clown swinging from a tree. By chance, the notscary owner of the house, Peter Wagener, was unloading his car, so he stopped to tell the walkers how his family had bought the house three years ago. Each year they create a spooktacular show for trick or treaters. About 350 brave ones got full size candy bars last year. Peter said his dentist, a brother-in-law, voiced no objections. It proved to be a great spot for a group photo with Peter and his other-world friends. There were more yards to see on Sea View Avenue, but time had run out, so they returned to the Exedra after a good long walk with lots of Halloween fun. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. It’s Halloween – time for the dogs to howl By Abby, a Bernese Mountain Dog Dear Abby: As Halloween looms closer, do you think there will be anything fun happening for dogs? We love those treats. Arf. –Chunk the English Bulldog dressing up as a toy poodle Dear Chunk: I suspect they’ll be an informal Weener Parade at the base of Piedmont Park, starting at 8:30 a.m. on Halloween. It usually has some of the best doggy treats you can find. Piedmonters love their dogs. So put on your toy poodle costume and head to the foot of Bushy Dell Creek by 8:30 a.m. and you’ll have some great sniffs and goodies. –Abby Dear Abby: I am confused. Near the entrance to the Parking Lot in front of Piedmont Park Community Center, there are three fancy new steel garbage cans, red, blue and green. But not far away sits an older garbage can with a large board nailed on top of it, so no one can toss garbage into it. However there’s garbage in it which can’t be taken out? Why would they leave garbage in there when nailing on a top? –Sparky the Doodle Dear Sparky: I’ve sniffed at that can myself a few times and I have no clue why they would leave old garbage in there before enclosing it. I was surprised they wouldn’t just keep it and use it as an extra spot for garbage on special fun days. I haven’t learned a thing but I’m still digging. If anyone out there’s knows anything please let me know. Woof. –Abby Dear Abby: We have just adopted a dog and wanted to let everyone know that there’s a surplus of dogs and puppies up for adoption. If you want a dog, this is a great time to adopt. Good dogs need good people. –Don A, Piedmont Community Church Dear Don: I wasn’t aware of that but it makes sense with these postCovid prices of dog supplies and medical needs. We will be howling at St. Francis to help all. Autumn is a good time for puppies to come into a home. Yelps for help. –Abby E-mail your comments, ideas and dog thoughts on any pet topic to Melanie Johnston at MSJ312@ aol.com. articles.text: Osh, Oakland Zoo’s male African elephant bull and the zoo’s last African elephant, successful moved cross country to settle into his new home on October 18 at The Elephant Sanctuary in Tennessee. Oakland Zoo Animal Care Team members and a Zoo Veterinarian accompanied Osh on the 46-hour road trip to Tennessee where he joins six female African elephants and a prospective male companion named Artie. With Osh’s move, the Oakland Zoo will be without elephants for the first time in 75 years. This provides the opportunity for the zoo to reimagine the future of the elephant habitat. The zoo will have to renovate the 35-year-old habitat, including the barn and behind-the-scenes areas. The zoo announced Osh’s departure in July and plans for him to relocate to The Elephant Sanctuary. This decision was made due to The Sanctuary’s unwavering commitment to animal care and wellbeing, and their ability to provide a suitable home catering to his companionship needs. Moving an elephant is challenging, and several things needed to be done before Osh was cleared to move across the country. Osh’s Animal Care Team worked with him several times a week through voluntary training to help him get used to his custom air-conditioned trailer, which was built to accommodate his 15,000 pound weight and 11’2” height. Osh’s keepers described him as highly adaptable, calm, and resilient. The Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital staff conducted foot and tusk radiographs, blood tests, and physical and visual exams. When loaded onto his trailer last Wednesday morning, he was prepared and healthy for his move to Tennessee. The journey to Tennessee was smooth, according to zoo officials, and Osh remained calm throughout. The team, consisting of two of Osh’s Oakland Zoo animal care keepers and an Oakland Zoo veterinarian, stopped every three hours to check on Osh and feed him. He ate celery, beet pulp, and watermelons – lots of watermelons – during the trip. The team also monitored him closely with cameras in his trailer. After the long journey he joyfully began clearing trees, eating, and roaming through his new habitat. “After only a few days at The Sanctuary, he continues to be a rambunctious and resilient being, joyfully exploring his new habitat. My heart is so full seeing Osh at his new forever home,” said Gina Kinzley, Zoological Manager at Oakland Zoo.
