Osh explores his new home in Tennessee. Elephant Sanctuary for Osh and his new companion, Artie, a 41-year-old male African elephant. Osh has begun interacting with Artie through fence lines. Osh also rejoins African Elephant Donna in Tennessee, the pair lived at Oakland Zoo together for 15 years. The dedicated care team at The Sanctuary visited Osh in Oakland in August this year to get to know him better, learn about Oakland Zoo’s elephant program, and deepen their understanding of the strong relationship they have built over 20 years. They also discussed and received a comprehensive background on Osh’s medical history from the Oakland Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital staff. “His arrival marks a significant moment for us as our second African male elephant. We are grateful for the ongoing collaboration with Oakland Zoo and for his safe travels,” said Janice Zeitlin, CEO of The Elephant Sanctuary. The Sanctuary staff have helped Osh settle into his new home and provided comprehensive support during his transition. Once he is fully settled, they will consistently update the public on his progress through social media. His community can continue to follow his journey online at Elephants.com/elecam. The elephants at Oakland Zoo, including Osh, have been beloved in the community for many years. They have served as animal ambassadors for their counterparts in the wild, leaving a lasting impression on the memories of Zoo guests and followers. “It is undeniable that Osh and the other African elephants who have lived at the Zoo have made a deep impact in Oakland. They have left a mark on our staff and zoo community, who love them. We know this is the right decision for Osh, and we are celebrating his future, his ability to be with other elephants, and the next chapter of his life,” said Nik Dehejia, CEO of Oakland Zoo To honor the special relationship between the elephants and the community, the Zoo began posting elephant memories online and hosting events to see Osh before he left, including a Farewell Party held last week. In 1991, Oakland Zoo was the first institution to broadly adopt the “protected contact” methodology with their male and female elephants. This methodology places barriers between zookeepers and elephants and incorporates cooperation through rewards rather than discipline. The standard at the time was to share space with elephants and use a tool called a bullhook to control and punish elephants. In recent years, the more humane approach of protected contact with elephants has become a standard method within AZA. In 2016, the Zoo raised awareness of circuses using bullhooks on elephants and helped ban bullhooks in California. This led to Ringling Bros. retiring its elephants and the passing of AB96, a law closing loopholes in the ivory trade. Through community donations, the Zoo raised $500,000 to fund Osh’s move and to fulfill its elephant conservation and welfare commitment. The Zoo will continue to maintain its commitment to ensuring the success of this species through advocacy, education, and programs such as the Wings Over Kenya eco-trips and its support of conservation partners like Amboseli Trust for Elephants. articles.text: Fifteen members of the Piedmont Seniors group attended a performance of the screwball comedy Arsenic and Old Lace at the Lesher Theatre of the Arts in downtown Walnut Creek on September 21. This enduring show is a wacky makeover by Matt Morrow making his Center REP directorial debut. Mortimer Brewster (Cody Sloan), who lives with his two elderly spinster aunts, Martha and Abby Brewster (humorously portrayed by Michael Patrick Gaffney and Danny Scheie), discovers that they are harboring some killer secrets, just as his estranged brother descends upon the family home, upending everything he thought to be true in his life. The two aunts had poisoned some boarders and then hid them in the basement of their lodging house. To save his family and his own sanity, Mortimer, who works as a theater critic and is dating Elaine, the daughter of the minister who lives next door, must learn to navigate a new world gone mad. What follows is funny and the audience tries to navigate how the sisters will manage to redeem themselves from these murders. Many of the other characters also play roles of the opposite sex, which is a hilarious take on this classic comedy. The laughs are too numerous to count, and the performances are strong from top to bottom. Center Rep’s version of this classic offers a new vision for one of theater’s most enduring comedies. After the show the Seniors headed to a nearby Thai restaurant, Andaman. Though some of the Seniors were a little reluctant to try a new style of Asian food, they enjoyed the flavors of this terrific restaurant. Several members commented that this restaurant served the best drinks they had ever tasted. The service was superb and the wait staff was very eager to please. articles.text: The Piedmont Seniors prepare to begin a guided tour of Safari West. Pictured are: Peggy Rourke (left), Nava Shaham, Mona Jamieson, Gloria Wilmer, Carole Jones, Nancy Hinsch, Lois Horwitz, Susan McCreary, Elizabeth Wierzbianska, Piedmont Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein, Tanya Hu, Jim Ayotte, and Larry Hu. The Piedmont Seniors group recently put on their collective safari hats and ventured north to Santa Rosa for a tour of Safari West, a 400-acre wildlife refuge preserve and home to over 800 animals representing the biodiversity of Africa. The Seniors hopped on a rugged safari truck as they made their way through the park. Animals seen on the tour included ostriches, monkeys, antelope, rhinos, cheetahs, steer, bulls, flamingos, and giraffes. Some of the animals were even on the endangered list. The Seniors learned that the taller giraffes’ tongues could extend to 17 inches and that they eat for up to 10 hours during the day. One of the highlights was seeing the Watusi cattle with large horns casually lounging together. After a tour on the Safari truck, the Seniors split into two groups and had a guided walking tour, allowing them to get close to many of the birds, including cranes, ducks, geese, guinea fowl, hornbills, and flamingos. Following the walking tour the group had lunch at Safari West’s Savannah Café, sharing an experience inspired by the legendary South African Braai (pronounced “bry”). This outdoor buffet, with an American barbecue tradition, featured a feast of culinary creations that appealed to everyone. Then it was time for the group to visit Safari West’s wonderful gift shop, which offers a number of interesting items for purchase including gemstones, jewelry, and apparel. They even sell huge ostrich eggs. The group was fortunate to be able to visit the park as the disastrous Tubbs fire in 2017 did enormous damage to the surrounding area. Safari West’s owner lost his home and vehicles while trying to save the animals. No animal was lost in the terrible fire. Safari West invites visitors to stay overnight in its comfortable tent cabins. Though the tents are comfortable with necessary amenities, be aware that the animals can get a little noisy during the nighttime hours. Binoculars and cameras are encouraged throughout the park. This park is suitable for people of all ages, and its purpose is to conserve the animals. Reservations are required to visit Safari West. It is the closest you can get to Africa without a passport! For more information about the Piedmont Seniors program, contact Janet Epstein, coordinator, at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov. The Seniors meet monthly on Wednesday mornings from 10 to noon at the Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue, in addition to monthly excursions throughout the Bay Area. Safari West tour guide Dena shows the Piedmont Seniors an ostrich egg.

articles.text: A list of fire alarm boxes was printed in The Piedmonter in 1955. Where was the fire alarm box in your neighborhood? In a photo from the 1960s, Piedmont’s Fire Chief is shown with the fire alarm box equipment. Ticker tape machines are shown in the background. to a ticker tape machine in the fire station and to a large panel (see photo). The location of the alarm box would quickly be identified, and the fire engines were off. In the Fall of 1955, there was a telephone strike, and phone service was undependable. On October 14, 1955, The Piedmonter published a list of fire alarm boxes and encouraged residents to use them in case of fire. The list shows 51 fire alarm boxes installed at street corners throughout Piedmont. Where was the fire alarm box in your neighborhood? The first call boxes were developed in Boston in 1852. San Francisco still maintains active fire alarm boxes within two blocks of any part of the city and considers the alarm boxes faster than calling 911 by phone to report a fire. These fire alarm boxes send a signal directly to the nearest fire station and are still considered crucial in the event of a power failure. The alarm boxes in San Francisco worked during the Loma Pieta earthquake in 1989 when electricity failed. In most parts of the state alarm boxes have been replaced by the calling 911 as an emergency phone number. In addition to San Francisco, Nevada City, Sacramento and Ventura continue to use fire alarm boxes in California. Fire alarm boxes were removed in Piedmont in 1978, and were offered for sale for $50 each. At that time the Fire Department said they were 50 years old. Before telephones were considered reliable, and before every house had a telephone, the fire alarm box was the main way to summon the fire department. Piedmont maintained more than 50 fire alarm boxes on street corners. To report a fire, you ran to the nearest fire alarm box, lifted the cover and pulled the handle. A blue light on top of the alarm box lit up when the alarm was activated. You were to stay at the alarm box to direct the firefighters to the fire. The boxes were connected directly to the Piedmont Fire Department through a low voltage wire which allowed them to work even in a power failure. The alarm box sent out a coded signal A photo of an early fire alarm box in Piedmont is in the Piedmont Historical Society collection. It originally had a blue light bulb on top that lit up when the alarm was activated. A ticker tape machine in the Piedmont Fire Station would receive the coded location of an activated fire alarm box. The ticker tape machine now is part of the collection of the Piedmont Historical Society – and still has ticker tape.

Conna McCarthy, Incumbent Piedmont’s Planning Department is working to streamline permitting processes for new businesses in commercial areas. Under the current system, any new business wanting to open in Piedmont must go through a public hearing process before the Planning Commission and City Council. Piedmonters were surveyed June-July 2024 seeking perspectives on the types of businesses that should be allowed “by right” without a public hearing, in the commercial mixed-use districts along Grand and Highland Avenues. Survey results were publicly discussed at the August 19th City Council meeting and revealed strong community support for businesses that directly serve community interests, including, but not limited to: restaurants or cafes, tutoring and lessons, retail or personal services, professional offices and fitness centers. Once again, Piedmonters have confirmed their consistent interest in social gathering spaces and amenities that improve quality of life. I support community sentiment and preferences. It is especially important that any desired new business integrates positively with existing neighborhoods by establishing clear standards on topics such as number of staff, floor area sizes, limits on the types of sales and service, hours of operation, loading zone. articles.text: Editor: I am writing to share how much of an impact Mr. Peters has had on my life. He was my P.E. and weight room teacher, and from the very beginning his friendly and positive attitude made the class a place I looked forward to every day. His encouragement helped me build confidence, both in the weight room and beyond. He was always cracking jokes and making his students smile. He was more than just a teacher to me; he was a trusted adult. His class was lively and gave everyone an opportunity to bond. Even though we no longer have Mr. Peters as a teacher and friend and I still visit him to check up on his new classes of students. He remains someone I trust and look up to. Mr. Peters has made a lasting difference in my life, and others feel the same way. Please support Measure P so we can keep dedicated and caring teachers like Mr. Peters in our schools. –Juliette Cabirol, Senior, Piedmont High School

articles.text: Editor: Several years ago, there was a proposal to build a soccer field at Moraga Canyon. At the time, many of us were opposed to the idea based on our research of 33 species of wildlife who lived in Moraga Canyon. Now again, there is a proposed idea to build nearly 200 housing units near the corporation yard and across the street as well. Once again we are opposed to this idea. The species of wildlife in the Canyon would be completely displaced by this project. I understand that this proposal also includes a traffic signal that will snarl traffic along Moraga Way. This also raises safety concerns for the children who play at Coaches Field and the Skate Park as well as the environmental impact on the area. –Karen and Ken Keller Pinehurst and Redwood Road, there is a former preschool with a gruesome history. Legend has it, a knife wielding murder in the early 80s slayed an entire class of preschoolers on the grounds. Other reports from the Gasden Times indicated a man, Alan Robert Baer, was shot by police on the preschool property in 1981. All that is left of the school is the foundation and a lone swing set. People have reported paranormal experiences of children’s laughter, voices, and swings in full-motion as if the school yard was bustling.

articles.text: Gary Ruvkun, PhD, has been named a co-recipient of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his role in the discovery of microRNA and its role in post-transcriptional gene regulation. Ruvkun graduated from Piedmont High School in 1969. “I received what seemed like an authentic call from the Nobel Committee,” Ruvkun said. “There’s always a chance it’s one of my friends,” he said with a smile. Ruvkun and Victor Ambros share the 2024 Nobel Prize in Medicine as announced by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences on October 7 in Stockholm. “Ambros, a professor at the University of Massachusetts Chan Medical School, and Ruvkun, a professor at Harvard Medical School and Massachusetts General Hospital, were honored for their discovery of microRNA, a class of tiny RNA molecules that play a critical role in gene control,” reported Anne Trafton of MIT News. “Their groundbreaking discovery revealed a completely new principle of gene regulation that turned out to be essential for multicellular organisms, including humans,” said the the Nobel committee. “MicroRNAs are proving to be fundamentally important for how organisms develop and Piedmont High School alum Dr. Gary Ruvkun received the 2024 Nobel Prize in Medicine for his work discovering microRNA.
articles.title: PHS Alum Gary Ruvkun wins Nobel Prize in medicine

articles.text: The 12th annual Artisanal Piedmont Beer Festival took place on Friday, October 18, on a perfect evening for tasting the 20 craft beers presented. Local brewers brought their finest concoctions for consumption, and a larger crowd enjoyed the event on the lawn of the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia. This year’s attendance matched last year’s crowd with many repeat Piedmont attendees as well as beer lovers throughout the Bay Area. While the event is a perennial crowd pleaser, its success as fundraiser owes much to the generosity of Dave Larson of Piedmont Grocery. This year’s Oktoberfest meal was donated – and served – by Piedmont GroPiedmont resident and brewer Jon Rhodin (left) won the Best Ale award for his beer “Ah Bitter, Dregs.” Judges deliberate in the Gray Cathrall board room at the PCA. cery’s staff. Apparently, brewers enjoy naming their beers as much as they do creating them. Some of this year’s names caused pause and quite often required drinkers to ask what style of beer it was. Some of the memorable names were Ah, Bitter Dregs; Box of Birds; Prime Ordinal; and Nipple Confusion. While most brewers presented a single beer, several spoiled the crowd by presenting two or three distinct offerings. The trio of Piedmont High musicians Deniz Radzik, Eric Venner and Maximo Miller, charmed the crowd with mellow jazz performed while guests enjoyed a German dinner on the front lawn at the Center. This year’s judges had their work cut out for them in awarding winners in the five award categories. Comprising the panel were Councilwomen Conna McCarthy and Jennifer Long, Recreation Commissioner Dick Carter, Public Works Supervisor Nick Millosovich, and Piedmont Grocery owner
articles.title: Artisanal Beer Festival brings happy hops to PCA

articles.text: The late Sandra Day O’Connor, the first woman to serve on the United States Supreme Court, once said “Those who would renegotiate the boundaries between church and state must therefore answer a difficult question: why would we trade a system that has served us so well for one that has served others so poorly.?” With these words Justice O’Connor states succinctly the challenge before us. Religious nationalisms, like other nationalisms, are not a new thing in human history. Their force and power have waxed, as they have waned, but the idea that the adherents of a particular theology, wrapped into the apparatus of a particular political philosophy, should have authority over all they come into contact with, has been tried repeatedly, and repeatedly found wanting. Why she asks, why would we trade something that has been proven to work, democracy, for something that has been proven not to work, religious nationalism? Look at what is going on in our world today. Is Islamic nationalism working? Is Buddhist nationalism working? Is Jewish nationalism working? Is white Christian nationalism working? Democracy is a system of governance in which power is vested in the people, who exercise that power directly through the vote and indirectly through elected representatives. It is characterized by principles such as political equality, free and fair elections, the rule of law, and the protection of individual rights and freedoms. In a democratic society, citizens have the right to participate in decision-making processes and to hold their leaders accountable. So defined, democracy works, albeit imperfectly, much better than any system of religious nationalism has ever worked. Thus, my main point, Christian nationalism threatens democracy by trying to replace something that has been proven to work, democracy, with something that has been proven not to work, Christian nationalism; something superior with something inferior. articles.text: The Piedmont League of Women Voters hosted a virtual candidates forum for the East Bay Regional Park District Ward 2 election. articles.text: Editor: As a Piedmont graduate who returned to raise my family here, I know how important our schools are – not only for students, but for our pocketbooks, too. Whether or not you have children enrolled, our schools are working for you by keeping demand for homes high and protecting property values. This commitment to excellence will continue to draw families to Piedmont, ensuring a vibrant housing market that benefits all homeowners. Voting Yes on Measure P is necessary for our teachers, the long-term health of our community, and our home values. Our community stands out for its willingness to support our schools through a long tradition of parcel taxes and private donations. articles.text: Editor: In response to a letter by Michael Gallagher regarding plans to convert the Shell Station to an electric vehicle charging center. I had no idea that the proposed equipment would generate such a powerful electromagnetic field and that it would be a health risk to humans. Your attachments and references certainly provide corroboration for your statements about the risk. Putting this equipment in an underground vault near the intersection of Grand and Wildwood Avenues would certainly seem to be the safest location for this equipment on the site, that is if it is safe to even have it there. It is very disappointing that the consultants from LSA who prepared the IS/ MND were seemingly unaware of this significant environmental impact. I’m glad that you made your comments on the IS/MND and I look forward to reading the next draft of the IS/MND to see how they address this issue. –Malcolm Talcott
articles.title: Concerns about removal of Shell Station

articles.text: The public is invited to St, Paul’s Episcopal Church in Oakland for a special viewing of the film A Case for Love on Saturday, November 2, at 2:00 p.m. The heartfelt, personally challenging movie inspired by the teachings and writings of Presiding Bishop Michael Curry, most well-known for his passionate sermon about “The Power of Love” at the royal wedding of Prince Harry and Meghan Markle. This film examines whether or not love – specifically unselfish love – is the solution to the extreme societal and political divide facing the U.S. In the documentary, the cinematographers travel across the country interviewing everyday people from various walks of life and ethnicities. Stories include racial justice, the military, foster care, sexual trafficking, love and loss and others as well-known figures including Pete Buttigieg, Al Roker, Sam Waterston, Becca Stevens, Russell Moore, John Danforth, John Clyburn, Kelly Brown Douglas, and Jon Meacham weigh in on the issue. Ultimately, Bishop Michael Curry puts what we’ve seen into context. What’s the verdict on “ A Case for Love?” Come watch and decide for yourself. A Q&A led by film director Brian Ide and the Rev. Dr. Mauricio Wilson, St. Paul’s rector will follow the screening. For a preview, watch the film’s trailer at https://www.youtube. com/watch?v=jLTxUBCbLiQ. St. Paul’s Episcopal Church is located at 114 Montecito Avenue in Oakland.
articles.title: St. Paul’s Episcopal Church presents film A Case for Love

articles.text: On September 21, local poet John Fang (Chinese name Fang Xin 方莘) presented his poetry at the Piedmont home of Deede Liu and Dan Aires. As a student in Taiwan 55 years ago, Fang had already been recognized and received awards as a leading poet. More recently, with the encouragement of his daughter Etienne Fang, and assistance from Berkeley poet David Roderick, John began translating his original Chinese work into English. He is a rare poet who is able to compose in both his native language and his adopted language. The assembled friends, family, and admirers were treated to a reading of 11 poems including his “Horsehead Nebula,” which refers to the classic characters of Homer’s Iliad. It includes recent WWII history and a contemporary tragedy in America, to draw connections and reveal historical patterns. Sprinkled throughout the poem are allusions to astronomical objects which John is fond of tracking at the Chabot Observatory, where he serves as Archivist. He is also a member of the Eastbay Astronomical Society, hence his “Astropoet” moniker. Fang Xin derives inspiration from music, especially the sounds of Chopin from which he composed four poetic Études. He has been collaborating with Holly Mead, a pianist, composer, and Bilingual poet, translator, star-gazer, and Piedmont resident, Fang Xin, reading his most recent poem, “Horsehead Nebula” David Roderick (left) of Left Margin Lit in Berkeley, the writing adviser to Fang Xin Holly Mead and artist Onikho describing the unique arrangement of “Night falls so impatiently” recording artist, who composed melodies to accompany the spoken words. Holly was joined by singer and composer Carina Ho (Onikho). Together, they took the combination of music and poetry to new experiences as their two voices echoed and re-echoed words and phrases while the poet’s voice slowly unfurled the stanzas. The stanzas are laid out on the page in a way that suggests a musical score. Usually shy and self-effacing, John’s personal presentation of his poetry was warmly appreciated. “I exposed myself to the Universe,” Fang confessed, as the Universe who heard him applauded. Fang Xin’s poems were recently published in the New England Review (volume 44.3, 2023) and the Georgia Review (Summer 2023). Fang Xin will be having a Chinese rendition of this event in Taipei, Taiwan, on October 30th, at National Taiwan University with Holly Mead, performing his own poetry in Chinese. Renowned contemporary artist, Han Hsiang Ning has arranged the event. For more information see: Holly Mead’s music: https://hollymeadmusic.com/. Fang Xin’s poetry: https://www.fangxinpoet. me/ Etienne Fang (left), poet Fang Xin, with musical composer Holly Mead, and artist Onikho after the performance Long-time Piedmonters Theresa Hau (left), Karen Joffe, with Deede Liu in her home where the intimate event was held.
articles.title: Astropoet John Fang presents his work publicly

articles.text: Fall is back and it’s time to talk turkey. Preparations for the 23rd Annual Piedmont Turkey Trot are underway. The 5K run on Piedmont streets will take place on Thanksgiving morning, November 28. The 2024 race shirts are produced with a wicking tech fabric, utilizing secondary consumer plastics, specifically water bottles. This year’s color is Piedmont Purple, a shade not seen for a decade on its race gear. The 2024 race will be held on Thursday, November 28th, at 8:30 am with the start and finish line at the Exedra on Highland Avenue. The pickup for race bibs will be at the Veterans Hall on Wednesday, the day before Thanksgiving, from 3:00-5:30 p.m. The inaugural Tiny Tot Trot for 3-6 year olds will be at Witter Field at 4:15 pm on Wednesday, November 27th. It will be a 1-2 lap race around the track. This year’s race proceeds will be donated to the Piedmont High School track & field and cross-country programs, and the PHS Athletic Boosters. articles.text: A long-standing Halloween tradition continues this Saturday, October 26, from 12 p.m. to 3 p.m., with Mountain View Cemetery’s 16th annual Pumpkin Festival. The free event follows the Piedmont Avenue Merchants Association’s annual Halloween Parade, which is part of a daylong celebration that includes trick-ortreating at businesses all along the avenue. “The parade is a much longer tradition, but we decided to put on this festival at the coattails of the event 16 years ago so the tricks and treats would continue through the day,” said Kristie Ly, special events coordinator for the cemetery. At the festival, parent- or guardian-accompanied children can choose a free pumpkin from a broad, festive patch and enjoy activities including several inflatable bounce houses; a hay bale tunnel; treat tents with free candy bags; a clown balloon artist; face painters; an area with arts and crafts tents to decorate pumpkins, masks and treat bags; and food truck vendors selling tacos, empanadas, Chinese bao burgers, cupcakes, smoothies and shaved ice. The event will also feature live jazz, blues and swing music by Pumpkins and hay bales will await Pumpkin Festival-goers at Mountain View Cemetery this Saturday following the Piedmont Avenue Halloween Parade. the locally based Donna Spitzer Jazz Group. “Other than the food trucks, the event is completely free,” said Ly, adding that the festival will also feature a live animal show with a trained handler displaying turtles, rabbits, insects, and reptiles including a large albino python. “The animals are all very docile, the kids get to pet them if they want, and it’s always a hit.” “This is our second year back from the pandemic, so the turnout is hard to predict, but usually we have more than 1,000 people,” she continued. “My favorite part is seeing all of the costumes that the parents and children come dressed up in.” “A few years ago we had someone come in a blow-up dinosaur costume that looked like it was eight feet tall but with a real person inside,” Ly added. “That’s the best part. I can’t wait to see the creativity that people will bring this year.”

articles.text: Part 6 in a series School board candidates answered one more question in week six for Piedmont voters. Each candidate was asked to describe the role they intend to perform upon being elected. School Board 3 open seats; 3 candidates. Week 6 Question What do you see as a school board member’s primary role and responsibility? MICHAEL MALIONE, Candidate I see the board’s primary role and responsibility falling into three areas: Support, Governance, and Guidance. Support - Operating a school district such as ours is challenging. Our district leaders (administration and staff) benefit from having access to board members who care, who are knowledgeable and listen well, and who reflect as they navigate tough decisions and make difficult tradeoffs. Governance - The school board also provides oversight of the Superintendent on behalf of our constituents, to ensure that the district continues to deliver excellent educational outcomes for all of our students and is accountable for doing so in a sustainable and fiscally responsible manner. Guidance - Last but certainly not least, the school board serves to maintain the district’s focus on its primary responsibility – providing the best academic experience for all of our kids – by applying current best practices for pedagogy and curriculum and ultimately codifying all of the above in policies and procedures to guide the administration and staff. SUSY STRUBLE, Candidate The roles and responsibilities of school board members are defined in the Board Bylaws (Section 9000) and guided by governance standards (Section 9005) – see Piedmont.k12.ca.us/ about/policies. I encourage anyone interested to read them. According to these guidelines, no single role or responsibility is prioritized above the others. I cite these policies not to avoid the question, but to affirm that those policies are the answer – and that I will uphold them equally, as previous school board members have done. While I believe Section 9000 blurs the distinction between roles and responsibilities (just my opinion as a bit of a policy nerd), the bylaws are clear and well-defined. MAX ROMAN, Candidate No response received.

articles.text: The following is a letter to the school community from Piedmont School Superintendent Jennifer Hawn via her Piedmont Pulse newsletter on Monday, October 21. Dear PUSD Families & Staff: It was wonderful seeing so many of you this weekend at Legally Blonde Jr., a fun production for our middle school students. Thank you to Amy Moorhead for her dedication to musical theater in our district! Thanks also to the Havens Parent Club for inviting me to speak to our Havens parents, including my partner in presentation, a future Havens student. Presentations are always better with our kids. And finally, a very special thank you to the Wildwood staff and families during this time of leadership transition. Ariel Dolowich and I have provided administrative support during the last several weeks, and we have loved every minute of it. Later this week, we are recommending the appointment of an Interim Principal for Wildwood, and we are grateful to the Wildwood community for their support during this time of change. In partnership. Jennifer Hawn, Ed.D. Superintendent • Affinity Mentors - The Power of Words Thank you to Jean Chen Takazawa and our Affinity Mentors for an outstanding program that engaged our middle school students in a lesson on the power of words, including racial slurs, discriminatory comments, and other actions that create harm in our community and prevent our ability to create an environment for students to thrive. I observed our high school affinity mentors facilitate a lesson, and I was impressed by the overall empathy and sophistication of our students, both our high school mentors and our middle school students. Educating our students on the meaning, historical context, and impact of words reinforces knowledge that eliminates the idea that “we just did not know.” When we know more, we can do better. And, I have no doubt we will. • WW Author Presentation: Barry Fischer: Thinking Through Planet Earth Thanks to Barry Fischer, a Wildwood Kindergarten dad and an author/illustrator of his book, Thinking Through Planet Earth, for his book presentation. He demonstrated for Ms. Beary’s students what an antipode is (...i.e. Piedmont’s antipode is a spot in the Indian Ocean ) using a plastic globe. Barry has a website that includes a tool with which you can explore the concept of antipode with your children. Thank you, Barry Fischer! • The Book Fair...is HERE This week is the book fair at all of our elementary sites, and it’s going to be great! Thank you to our librarians and volunteers who hold this wonderful event. What a wonderful event! The collection of Hawn’s Piedmont Pulse updates can be found at: https://www.piedmont.k12. ca.us/ref/superintendent Superintendent Hawn speaks to Havens Parent Club members in the Havens School Library.

articles.text: Have you ever seen a dog shake someone’s hand or sit on command? Believe it or not, keepers at Oakland Zoo work with our animals to train them to behave similarly. If you are at the Zoo at the right time, you might see a bear standing up with front paws on the fence, a macaw being asked to put its wing out, or other interesting behaviors from the Zoo animal residents. Our animals are trained to exhibit different behaviors to help us better care for them. For example, a bear standing up with paws on the fence allows Keepers to check their belly and feet for injuries. This helps ensure the animals are happy and healthy in a safer, more frequent, and less stressful manner. Animal Training Game Using a “bridge” signal during training helps animals understand what action is rewarded, reducing confusion. This signal, such as a whistle or clicker, bridges the gap between the desired action and the reward, which is usually a yummy treat. For this game you will “train” another person to act. First, send the person who will be the trainee into another room, so the person guiding them can decide on a task. Once the trainer chooses the action, the trainee re-enters the room, and the people guiding use claps to direct the trainee. The claps are slow at first and then speed up as the person gets closer and closer to the correct action. The clapping acts as your “bridge” guiding the person to the proper action. Keeper Jessie Sayre asks one of Oakland Zoo’s resident brown bears for a “focus behavior” to steady himself during training. Nathaniel Landers is Manager of Teen Outreach at Oakland Zoo. Got a burning question for an animal expert? Submit questions to education@oaklandzoo.org with “Piedmont Post” as the subject for a chance to be featured.

pages.text: Wednesday, October 23, 2024 9 Troop 15 Continued from page 8 Cathedral Lake before setting up camp at Upper Sunrise Lake where temperatures plummeted into the 20s overnight. On Sunday, the backpackers ascended the knife’s edge ridgeline of Cloud’s Rest to 9,900 feet with a stunning view of Half Dome and Yosemite Valley below before descending to the John Muir Trail and the foot of Half Dome. On Monday the Scouts group broke camp early to ascend Half Dome and complete the 30-mile journey all the way back to the Yosemite Valley floor. A second group of Scouts and adult leaders left Piedmont Friday afternoon, camped in Yosemite Valley, and awoke before dawn on Saturday morning for an ascent to Half Dome and back to the Valley on an 18-mile hike. Troop 15 Scouts ascend the knifes-edge ridgeline of Cloud’s Rest at 9,900 feet in Yosemite The third (and largest) group of Scouts left Piedmont Saturday morning for Wawona campground in Yosemite Park, enjoying Mariposa Grove on Saturday afternoon. A total of 19 Scouts and nine adults hiked among the Giant Sequoias. On their way Rory Hull, Regina O’Connor, and Victoria Mbise enjoy the view from the top of Half Dome in Yosemite National Park. to the Grove they bumped into friends from Piedmont’s Troop 6, who were staying at the same campground. On Sunday, both troops took on a 7-mile hike for views of Chilnualna Falls and the Wawona Valley below. Back at camp many spent some well earned time rock hopping and wading in the river or fishing from the river’s edge. A smaller caravan of Scouts and parents left the park on Monday via Tunnel view to share the splendor of Half Dome and El Capitan in the distance. articles.text: On a beautiful summer weekend August 9-11, Piedmont High School’s Class of 1974 celebrated its 50th reunion with various parties, tours and activities. Fifty years after graduation, the class had a wonderful time reflecting on its journeys to “Achieve the Honorable” over the decades. The weekend began with a Friday tour of the current PHS campus, which simply stunned classmates with its world-class STEAM building, the new Alan Harvey Theater, and even a visit to our previous outdoor “quad,” which is now encompassed by the current library. Thanks to current PHS Superintendent Jennifer Hawn for joining us for the tour, and for classmate Ron Mockel for leading the tour. Friday evening found classmates in downtown Oakland at Drakes Dealership beer garden for an informal, no-host pizza party…a great way to start more in-depth visits with one another. The capstone event of the Committee members Jeanine Loughran Odell and David Bowman, with spouses Ted Odell and Gloria Miller Mike and Julie Bartlett’s Piedmont home was the reunion location on Saturday night. Classmates Kathy Wells, Mary McDevitt, Cheri and Mike Betts Classmate and PHS Tour Guide Ron Mockel, with Committee member Lisa Brickell Christensen Committee member Kathleen Galloway Di Stefano with husband Al Di Stefano Open Wednesday to Sunday • 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. articles.text: Photo by Jacque Jumper Piedmont celebrated its four seniors on Senior Night on October 17: Alina Shahid (left), Carolina Romanczuk, Abigail Call, and Emma Eisemon. Piedmont’s girls’ tennis team played its final home match of the regular season on Thursday, October 17 at the Corey Reich Tennis Center, shutting out the visiting Castro Valley Trojans 7-0. The Highlanders honored its four seniors on the roster om Senior Day, Carolina Romanczuk, Emma Eisemon, Alina Shahid, and Abigail Call. “We played too well; there weren’t any close matches. The highlight of the day was our senior celebration. We’re going to miss them a lot next year,” coach Jim Landes said. Of the group, Eisemon is a four-year starter in doubles and Romanczuk is a three-year starter in singles. Eisemon played alongside Call’s older sister, Audrey, as a freshman. Piedmont’s win improves their record to 8-9 overall and 3-2 against Western Alameda County Conference opponents. To qualify for the Division 2 North Coast Section Team Tournament, schools must achieve a .500 winning percentage on its overall record or league record—making their win over Castro Valley a bit more important. “We need to stay at least even (.500) to qualify for NCS, so we have to keep playing well. We have some good teams ahead,” Landes said. The Highlanders have three away matches remaining on the schedule before the Western Alameda County Conference Individual Tournament on November 8-9 at Chabot College in Hayward. Before that, they’ll face Alameda today, October 23, Berkeley the following day, and Bishop O’Dowd on October 29. All PHS needs is one win over its last three to achieve an even league record. They last lost to Alameda 5-2 on September 26 and had a heated 4-3 loss to Berkeley on October 3. Piedmont bashed Bishop O’Dowd 6-1 on October 10. Match Recap At singles, Romanczuk beat Castro Valley’s top starter 6-3, 6-1 at the No. 1 spot. Kate Jumper nearly double-bageled her opponent at No. 2 in a 6-0, 6-1 win. Arianna Kortum won her No. 3 match 6-2, 6-1, while Lila Rosen Photo by Sophie Hess Emma Eisemon is in her fourth year as a starter on the tennis team. won 6-3, 6-3 at No. 4. At doubles, Eisemon and Samantha Huynh won their No. 1 match in straight sets, 6-1, 6-3. Seniors Shahid and Call paired at No. 2, winning in straight sets 6-4, 6-1. Ella Thomasson and Chiara Silvia made their varsity debuts at the No. 3 spot, winning 6-4, 6-3. NEXT UP Piedmont (8-9 overall, (3-2 league) travels to Washington Park in Alameda to face the Alameda Hornets today, October 23, at 3:30 p.m. They also travel to the Berkeley Tennis Club to face Berkeley High on Thursday, October 24 at the same time. Their regular-season finale against Bishop O’Dowd on Tuesday, October 29 will be played at Merritt College. Photo by Sophie Hess Senior Alina Shahid, playing at No. 2 doubles, wins a point on a forehand.
articles.title: Piedmont slays Trojans 7-0 on Senior Night

articles.text: October 17 was a big night for Piedmont’s football team. Playing a rare game on a Thursday, it demolished Irvington 49-7 on the road in what was perhaps the season’s marquee game for the Mission Division of the Western Alameda County Conference. Piedmont entered at 5-1 and Irvington’s record was 6-0. It was also Irvington’s Homecoming Night. But Piedmont spoiled their party in a dominant blowout. The game was never close. All drama expired long before halftime when Piedmont led 35-0, with 28 points coming in the second quarter. “It was totally a statement win. They thought they could schedule us on their homecoming game to get a league win. We showed them why that was a huge mistake,” said linebacker Brandon Dicke. Piedmont’s defense was a big part of the beating with three interceptions, including 50-yard interception returns for touchdowns in the second quarter by Miguel Long and Dicke. “I saw the QB underthrew it. It was like my interception against Encinal, I knew I had to keep my legs churning,” Long said. Dicke extended Piedmont’s lead to 35-0 with an interception return as time expired in the second quarter. Instead of playing it safe at their own 16 with the clock ticking away, Irvington attempted a long pass, leading to Dicke’s interception. Staff Photos Brandon Dicke follows lead blocker, Xavier Henderson, on a 50-yard interception return for a touchdown. With three games left in the regular season, it was an important win for the Highlanders in a battle between the top two teams in the division. Piedmont’s remaining games are with Washington and Kennedy of Fremont, which are both 2-4. The season-finale is against Newark Memorial, currently at 4-3. “No one is close to us in this league, we realized that last week against Hayward. We’re sitting good right now. We have momentum right now. This was a full, complete game,” Lagios said. Game Recap Irvington started with possession, but committed a turnover on downs after Jordan Alemania made a tackle for loss on a 3rd down, Miguel Long sprints down the sideline on a 50-yard interception return. followed by Tommy Ashton sacking the quarterback on 4th down. PHS then scored on 10 plays on an 11-yard touchdown run by Lagios with 3:43 left in the first quarter. During the drive, PHS converted a 4th-and-12 on a fake punt and had a 21-yard pass to Rehan Mumtaz. On Irvington’s next drive, Xavier Henderson had a forced fumble and recovery at the 50. Henderson wound up scoring on a 14-yard touchdown reception at the end of an 11-play drive with 9:41 left in the second quarter. Then with eight minutes left in the second, Long grabbed his interception at the 50, leading to him sprinting down the sideline for the touchdown after manipulating the opposing team by hesitating toward the inside. Piedmont led 28-0 on a fourplay drive after assuming possession at its own 21 with 1:14 left. On 3rd-and-2, tight end Cash Elmquist took a reception 55 yards to the Irvington 16 with 30 seconds left, followed by Elmquist taking the next pass into the end zone four seconds later. The Vikings then made the costly error of tossing an interception as time expired on its next series, resulting in Dicke’s 50-yard touchdown return—35-0. In the third quarter, Ashton scored on a one-yard punch into the end zone with 8:18 left, while Jack Meyjes scored on a 15-yard touchdown reception with 2:00 minutes remaining. Irvington scored its only touchdown with 7:10 left in the fourth. Final stats: Lagios completed 12-18 passes for 272 yards and three touchdowns, to go along with nine rushing attempts for 39 yards and one touchdown. Ashton had 21 rushing yards and one touchdown. Henderson had four receptions for 85 yards and a touchdown. Elmquist had two receptions for 71 yards and a touchdown. Defensively, interceptions were recorded by Long, Dicke, and Miles Silver. Alemania had two tackles for loss. Ashton and Faisal Malik had one sack. Henderson had two tackles for loss, one fumble recovery, and one forced fumble. NEXT UP Piedmont (6-1 overall, 2-0 league) hosts Washington for a league game this Friday, October 25 at Witter Field at 7:00 p.m.

Then with eight minutes left in the second, Long grabbed his interception at the 50, leading to him sprinting down the sideline for the touchdown after manipulating the opposing team by hesitating toward the inside. Piedmont led 28-0 on a fourplay drive after assuming possession at its own 21 with 1:14 left. On 3rd-and-2, tight end Cash Elmquist took a reception 55 yards to the Irvington 16 with 30 seconds left, followed by Elmquist taking the next pass into the end zone four seconds later. The Vikings then made the costly error of tossing an interception as time expired on its next series, resulting in Dicke’s 50-yard touchdown return—35-0. In the third quarter, Ashton scored on a one-yard punch into the end zone with 8:18 left, while Jack Meyjes scored on a 15-yard touchdown reception with 2:00 minutes remaining. Irvington scored its only touchdown with 7:10 left in the fourth. Final stats: Lagios completed 12-18 passes for 272 yards and three touchdowns, to go along with nine rushing attempts for 39 yards and one touchdown. Ashton had 21 rushing yards and one touchdown. Henderson had four receptions for 85 yards and a touchdown. Elmquist had two receptions for 71 yards and a touchdown. Defensively, interceptions were recorded by Long, Dicke, and Miles Silver. Alemania had two tackles for loss. Ashton and Faisal Malik had one sack. Henderson had two tackles for loss, one fumble recovery, and one forced fumble. The highlight of the day was our senior celebration. We’re going to miss them a lot next year,” coach Jim Landes said. Of the group, Eisemon is a four-year starter in doubles and Romanczuk is a three-year starter in singles. Eisemon played alongside Call’s older sister, Audrey, as a freshman. Piedmont’s win improves their record to 8-9 overall and 3-2 against Western Alameda County Conference opponents. To qualify for the Division 2 North Coast Section Team Tournament, schools must achieve a .500 winning percentage on its overall record or league record—making their win over Castro Valley a bit more important. “We need to stay at least even (.500) to qualify for NCS, so we have to keep playing well. We have some good teams ahead,” Landes said. The Highlanders have three away matches remaining on the schedule before the Western Alameda County Conference Individual Tournament on November 8-9 at Chabot College in Hayward. Before that, they’ll face Alameda today, October 23, Berkeley the following day, and Bishop O’Dowd on October 29. All PHS needs is one win over its last three to achieve an even league record. They last lost to Alameda 5-2 on September 26 and had a heated 4-3 loss to Berkeley on October 3. Piedmont bashed Bishop O’Dowd 6-1 on October 10. Their regular-season finale against Bishop O’Dowd on Tuesday, October 29 will be played at Merritt College. articles.text: Photos by Karen Tsoi Leighton Mand (3193) led the girls’ cross-country team at the Wilder Invitational, finishing 43rd of 188 runners. Piedmont High’s cross country team wrapped up a busy week with a pair of meets. They recently completed its second Western Alameda County Conference meet of the season on Wednesday, October 16, while they took to Hayward High for the Wilder Mariner Invitational hosted by Moreau Catholic on Saturday, October 19. At the WACC meet, Piedmont’s girls’ team placed fourth of nine schools while the boys’ were fifth of nine. At the P. Wilder Invitational, PHS’ girls finished 11th of 26 teams in The Championship division; the boys’ were 12th of 33 in the Varsity Open division. “With so much racing on the calendar this month and with little time to rest in between the meets, the athletes are feeling the fatigue in their legs. Unfortunately, many runners have also been or are currently sick and that’s been tough on their training and racing performances,” said coach Steve Zirkelbach. Piedmont has its final league meet of the season today, October 23, before returning to Hayward High for the WACC Championship on Saturday, November 9. “We have another meet on Wednesday and then will have about 15 days without racing to rest up and get ready for the WACC League Championship on November 9th,” Zirkelbach said. Wilder Invitational Sophomore Leighton Mand led the way for the girls’ team, placing 43rd in a field of 188 runners with a time of 19:38.07 on the three-mile course. It eclipsed her previous best three-mile time by 48 seconds. It was also an impressive display from standout freshman Viviane Oesterer, who was 53rd in 19:53.33. “Viviane Oesterer and Leighton Mand both started out conservatively and moved their way up toward the front, completing the three-mile course in under 20 minutes—a first for both of them. Mand notched a 48 second PR and Oesterer a 37 second PR,” Zirkelbach said. Behind them was junior Cora Chun in 69th in 20:18.79, while junior Skylar Best and senior Caroline Taylor finished backto-back in 81st and 82nd with respective times of 20:38.06 and 20:39.67. Sophomore Sebastien Swain had a strong day, leading the boys’ team with a sixth place finish in a field of 244 runners and a time of 16:26.25. “Sebastien Swain showed up to the race feeling a little sick, but was still able to keep up with the competition in the Varsity Open race,” Zirkelbach said. Behind him was junior Noah Sohn finishing 38th in 17:16.16. Sophomore Thomas Ero placed 45th in 17:25.61, junior Devon Thai was 93rd in 18:16.23, while senior Oliver Horsley was 145th in 19:14.07. WACC Meet Oesterer was Piedmont’s lead-runner in 22nd of 71 runners with a time of 20:30.55. From there, PHS’ next five runners finished in order with four qualifying toward the Highlanders’ point total, including sophomore Cora Brozowski Schrader in 25th in 20:33.78, Best in 20:35.51, Mand in 20:35.36, and Amalia Gray in 20:38.40. Taylor also finished 29th in 20:39.27. For the boys’ squad, Sohn led and was 18th overall of 79 runners in 17:10.75. Swain was 22nd in 17:24.01, sophomore Alex Schleuning was behind him in 23rd in 17:25.45, Ero was 42nd in 17:54.29, while Horsley rounded things out in 44th, 17:55. NEXT UP Piedmont competes in its third WACC meet of the season today, October 23, at Oyster Bay Regional Park in San Leandro at 3:30 p.m.

articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont looks ahead to its final match of the season on October 24. Piedmont’s girls’ volleyball team is wrapping up its season after recently suffering three straight losses against Western Alameda County Conference teams. It has one remaining match. The Highlanders lost by scores of 3-0 to Berkeley on October 15, ng Encinal on October 16, and Castro Valley on October 18. “We are low on numbers at this point and teams are attacking our weak points,” coach Mariah Cardenas said. Despite taking the losses, Piedmont had some closely contested sets against all three teams. They went to an extra point in their third-set loss against Berkeley, which finished 26-24. They finished within four of Encinal in the third set, a 25-21 loss, while they finished within six points in all three sets versus Castro Valley, including a close 26-24 loss in the second set. With a team of one junior, six sophomores, and two freshmen, Cardenas knew this would be a rebuilding year. Piedmont has shown glimpses of brilliance, including its 3-0 win over Alameda on October 11, but they are still working on building a fluid attack. With time, the goal is for players to continue molding together in time for 2025 and 2026 campaigns. “I want us to swing and go crazy instead of tipping it and being tentative. You’ll see spurts of greatness where we are getting a hand on the ball, but then we’ll commit and error and get in our own heads a bit,” Cardenas said. 3-0 shutout by Berkeley Piedmont fell by scores of 25-10, 25-18, 26-24. In the first set, PHS’ Jules DeYoung gained two kills while Fiona Olsen and Stella Wilks had one. Olsen added two more in the second set, while Charli Panico had a pair as well. Wilks and Mira Sachs had individual kills in the second set. In the third set, Wilks led the way with four spikes while Olsen had three. DeYoung and Sachs added individual kills. Final stats: DeYoung had four kills and two blocks, Olsen had six kills and one block, Panico had two, Wilks had six, and Sachs had two. 3-0 loss to Encinal Piedmont lost 3-0 by scores of 25-12, 25-17, 25-21. PHS kept things competitive in the first set until about midway through, then struggled to find consistency. They trailed 11-9 at one point, but only scored three more points from that point. Piedmont scored kills in the first set by Panico, Sachs, and Wilks, while Kalindi Kim scored an ace. In the second set, Piedmont opened strongly and held a 5-1 lead before extending to 10-5. However, the Jets took the lead at 12-11 and never relinquished their advantage with PHS only scoring six more from that point. PHS’ Olsen scored three kills in the set and two aces, while DeYoung had one, Wilks had one, and freshman Julia Stokes had one. In the third, Piedmont opened with a 6-3 lead but Encinal got to the front at 7-6 and never gave it away despite PHS pulling within a couple of points on several occasions. Piedmont got to onepoint deficits at 12-11, 13-12, 18-17, and 20-19, but couldn’t find the equalizer. PHS got close at 23-21, but Encinal got its final two points on a kill and an ace. Final stats: DeYoung had three kills and three blocks. Panico had two kills and one ace. Sachs had four kills. Wilks had tree kills. Olsen had three kills and two aces. 3-0 loss to Castro Valley Piedmont lost 3-0 by scores of 25-18, 26-24, 25-19. Official stats were not provided. NEXT UP Piedmont (3-17 overall, 1-7 league) host Bishop O’Dowd for the season-finale on Thursday, October 24 at 6:30 p.m. Fiona Olsen notched six kills against Berkeley and three in the match with Encinal.

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ golf team came away with an impressive second-place finish out of seven schools at the Antioch Invitational on Monday, October 14 at Lone Tree Golf Course. Playing a full round of 18 holes, Piedmont finished with a score of 393 strokes, well back of first-place Dublin and three strokes ahead of third-place Liberty High of Brentwood. Mei Assalian shot an 81 and was third among 37 golfers. She was four shy of second-place Chloe Giang of Dublin and nine behind first-place Callie McLoughlin of Dublin. Other golfers scoring for Piedmont were Mackenzie SetoNguyen, 12th (97), Gracey Ann Hatchell 17th (105), Peyton Watson, 21st (110) . Monday at WACC Tournament Piedmont traveled to Monarch Bay on Monday this week in San Leandro for the Western Alameda County Conference Tournament. See next week’s Post for match results.

articles.text: After coming off of a tough loss at Hayward the previous week, Piedmont’s Junior Varsity football team looked to bounce back against the Irvington Vikings. They did just that in a dominant 48-6 blowout win over Irvington at Tak Fudenna Stadium in Fremont. The result was similar to the varsity’s 49-7 win. Irvington had the first possession of the game and was immediately forced into a turnover on downs. Although the offense suffered a fumble on its first play, the defense forced a punt. The Highlanders marched down the field on the ensuing drive and capped it off with a 30-yard touchdown reception by Diego Hurwitz. Piedmont’s defense continued to dominate and quickly get the ball back. On its next drive PHS converted a 3rd-and-long situation with a 35-yard screen pass to Jonah Cha-Foster, who reversed field for a big run. After big carries by Noah Hussain and Eric Venner, Cha-Foster took a quarterback keeper into the end zone. Irvington ended its next drive quickly after ta pass was intercepted by Mateo Long, his first of the season, returning the ball to the five-yard line. The Highlanders took advantage on an end-around to Hurwitz for the touchdown. Piedmont’s defense didn’t turn down the heat, recording another interception on Irvington’s next drive, this time with linebacker George Saunders returning the ball to he Irvington’s one-yard line. Quarterback Jimmy Lagios then connected with Xavier Laroche for a touchdown and his first reception of the season. With one minute left in the half, Hussain ran in for a touchdown to make it 35-0, the same halftime score as the varsity. The Highlanders came out of halftime excited to continue their dominance. Hurwitz returned the opening kickoff for a touchdown for his 14th touchdown of the year. Irvington scored its only touchdown late in the third. Cha-Foster came into the game at quarterback in the 4th quarter to end the game and Eric Venner put the cherry on top by rushing for a touchdown for the one-sided 48-6 victory. NEXT UP Piedmont (4-2-1 overall, 1-1 league) hosts Washington for a league game at Witter Field this on Friday, October 25, at 4:00 p.m.
articles.title: JV football team thumps Irvington

JV football team thumps Irvington By Jonah Cha-Foster After coming off of a tough loss at Hayward the previous week, Piedmont’s Junior Varsity football team looked to bounce back against the Irvington Vikings. They did just that in a dominant 48-6 blowout win over Irvington at Tak Fudenna Stadium in Fremont. The result was similar to the varsity’s 49-7 win. Irvington had the first possession of the game and was immediately forced into a turnover on downs. Although the offense suffered a fumble on its first play, the defense forced a punt. The Highlanders marched down the field on the ensuing drive and capped it off with a 30-yard touchdown reception by Diego Hurwitz. Piedmont’s defense continued to dominate and quickly get the ball back. On its next drive PHS converted a 3rd-and-long situation with a 35-yard screen pass to Jonah Cha-Foster, who reversed field for a big run. After big carries by Noah Hussain and Eric Venner, Cha-Foster took a quarterback keeper into the end zone. Irvington ended its next drive quickly after ta pass was intercepted by Mateo Long, his first of the season, returning the ball to the five-yard line. The Highlanders took advantage on an end-around to Hurwitz for the touchdown. Piedmont’s defense didn’t turn down the heat, recording another interception on Irvington’s next drive, this time with linebacker George Saunders returning the ball to he Irvington’s one-yard line. Quarterback Jimmy Lagios then connected with Xavier Laroche for a touchdown and his first reception of the season. With one minute left in the half, Hussain ran in for a touchdown to make it 35-0, the same halftime score as the varsity. The Highlanders came out of halftime excited to continue their dominance. Hurwitz returned the opening kickoff for a touchdown for his 14th touchdown of the year. Irvington scored its only touchdown late in the third. Cha-Foster came into the game at quarterback in the 4th quarter to end the game and Eric Venner put the cherry on top by rushing for a touchdown for the one-sided 48-6 victory. By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont’s girls’ volleyball team is wrapping up its season after recently suffering three straight losses against Western Alameda County Conference teams. It has one remaining match. The Highlanders lost by scores of 3-0 to Berkeley on October 15, ng Encinal on October 16, and Castro Valley on October 18. “We are low on numbers at this point and teams are attacking our weak points,” coach Mariah Cardenas said. Despite taking the losses, Piedmont had some closely contested sets against all three teams. They went to an extra point in their third-set loss against Berkeley, which finished 26-24. They finished within four of Encinal in the third set, a 25-21 loss, while they finished within six points in all three sets versus Castro Valley, including a close 26-24 loss in the second set. With a team of one junior, six sophomores, and two freshmen, Cardenas knew this would be a rebuilding year. Piedmont has shown glimpses of brilliance, including its 3-0 win over Alameda on October 11, but they are still working on building a fluid attack. With time, the goal is for players to continue molding together in time for 2025 and 2026 campaigns. “I want us to swing and go crazy instead of tipping it and being tentative. You’ll see spurts of greatness where we are getting a hand on the ball, but then we’ll commit and error and get in our own heads a bit,” Cardenas said. 3-0 shutout by Berkeley Piedmont fell by scores of 25-10, 25-18, 26-24. In the first set, PHS’ Jules DeYoung gained two kills while Fiona Olsen and Stella Wilks had one. Olsen added two more in the second set, while Charli Panico had a pair as well. Wilks and Mira Sachs had individual kills in the second set. In the third set, Wilks led the way with four spikes while Olsen had three. DeYoung and Sachs added individual kills. Final stats: DeYoung had four kills and two blocks, Olsen had six kills and one block, Panico had two, Wilks had six, and Sachs had two. 3-0 loss to Encinal Piedmont lost 3-0 by scores of 25-12, 25-17, 25-21. PHS kept things competitive in the first set until about midway through, then struggled to find consistency. They trailed 11-9 at one point, but only scored three more points from that point. Piedmont scored kills in the first set by Panico, Sachs, and Wilks, while Kalindi Kim scored an ace. In the second set, Piedmont opened strongly and held a 5-1 lead before extending to 10-5. However, the Jets took the lead at 12-11 and never relinquished their advantage with PHS only scoring six more from that point. PHS’ Olsen scored three kills in the set and two aces, while DeYoung had one, Wilks had one, and freshman Julia Stokes had one. In the third, Piedmont opened with a 6-3 lead but Encinal got to the front at 7-6 and never gave it away despite PHS pulling within a couple of points on several occasions. Piedmont got to onepoint deficits at 12-11, 13-12, 18-17, and 20-19, but couldn’t find the equalizer. PHS got close at 23-21, but Encinal got its final two points on a kill and an ace. Final stats: DeYoung had three kills and three blocks. Panico had two kills and one ace. Sachs had four kills. Wilks had tree kills. Olsen had three kills and two aces. 3-0 loss to Castro Valley Piedmont lost 3-0 by scores of 25-18, 26-24, 25-19. Official stats were not provided. articles.text: Piedmont High played its last flag football game at Witter Field for its regular season on Monday, October 21, falling to 6-2 to Berkeley in a strong defensive showing. The Highlanders honored its eight seniors for Senior Night: Dorothy Nemeth, Miya Fujimoto, Ella Yasar, Mary Schickedanz, Alma Ruberto, Lucy Barton, and Eunice and Cyntiche Kouadio. “The seniors had a good night tonight, which is great to see. It’s going to be hard replacing them because they are the original players,” said coach Beth Black. Piedmont’s only points came on a safety where rusher Elspeth Grippando locked down Berkeley’s running back in her own end zone. “I knew they did a lot of handoffs and it tricked me a few times, but adjusting paid off,” Grippando said of the play. Grippando has been a bright spot this season as a rushing defender on every single play. She’s recording sacks in every game since moving into the role and poses problems for quarterbacks, forcing them into quick decisions. Grippando, who also plays soccer, found the ability to translate her pressing on the pitch into pressure on the gridiron. “I was put on rush and something clicked. I like rushing, I feel like I can change the game there. It’s perfect because I can just chase people. I play soccer and that’s a lot of running,” Grippando said. The result brought their record to 5-10, now suffering their fifth loss in a row. The Highlanders’ offense has scored one touchElspeth Grippando sacks the Berkeley quarterback. Staff Photos Piedmont honored its eight seniors on the flag football roster. Pictured on Senior Day are coach Beth Black (back left), assistant coach Hayley Adams, Ella Yasar, Alma Ruberto, Miya Fujimoto, Cyntiche Kouadio, assistant coach Reggie Smith, Dorothy Nemeth (front left), Mary Schickedanz, Lucy Barton, and Eunice Kouadio. down or less in every game during the span. Black knows their offense needs to get into the end zone to win games. “Our defense is holding people down and once we connect all the pieces, we’re going to be amazing. We need to score touchdowns, that’s really it, that’s what I’m looking for in these last games,” Black said. Piedmont travels to Arroyo in San Lorenzo for its final regular season game on October 23 before the Western Alameda County Conference tournament with the first round next week on Monday, October 28. To qualify for the tournament, PHS must be among the best four teams in the WACC’s North Division. Game Recap Both teams traded possession until Berkeley broke the deadlock with 8:08 left in the first half. Piedmont’s defense forced a Yellowjackets punt in its first possession, including a pass defense from Yasar, while they forced a turnover on downs at its own 23 on Berkeley next drive. Dahlia Osman had a pass defense on Berkeley’s third series, helping toward a punt. Berkeley scored after taking an interception to Piedmont’s 14-yard line, hurling a 14-yard touchdown to the back corner of the end zone. A failed two-point conversion kept the game at 6-0 with 7:25 left in the first half. But Piedmont’s offense just couldn’t find the finishing touch despite putting together long drives. They had a 10-play series stall out at the Berkeley 27 with 15:40 remaining in the game. After forcing a punt thanks to a sack by Grippando, another _-play drive die after getting into the red zone. During the series, Nemeth was found for gains of 12 and 21. However, PHS committed another interception on 3rd-andGoal with 8:30 left. Keeping PHS in the game was Osman grabbing an interception with 4:40 on the clock, taking it to the 33. Piedmont drove down to the Berkeley 3-yard line, but an incomplete pass in the back of the end zone on 4th down caused a turnover on downs. Shortly after, Grippando tackled Berkeley’s running back in the end zone for a safety with 43 seconds left. On 3rd-and-17, Berkeley grabbed another interception. Final stats: Grippando had seven tackles, two sacks and two tackles for loss. Osman had one interception, one pass defense, and four tackles. Nemeth had five receptions. Yasar had three pass defenses. Fujimoto had seven carries and two receptions. articles.text: The Piedmont Avenue Halloween Parade was started in 1987 by a number of Piedmont Avenue merchants who “wanted to give kids a safe place to trick-or-treat,” recalled the late Richard Stone, owner of Continental Hearing. In its early years, Stone said just two or three blocks of the street were closed to traffic for an afternoon and kids were invited to wear their costumes and trickor-treat at various participating merchants. Stone, who was a member of the Lions Club, used the opportunity to raise money for Children’s Hospital and the Lions Center for the Blind in Oakland. “We sold all-beef hot dogs for a dollar and gave the proceeds to those charities,” he said. The Lions Club also gave big, carving pumpkins to children, but after a few years, they found that they were giving out thousands of pumpkins. “It’s been exciting to see the Halloween Celebration grow from this tiny thing into something huge,” said Stone, who was in business on Piedmont Avenue for more than 40 years. “Now you see not just kids, but moms and dads and dogs, with everyone all dressed up. It is a lot of fun,” he said. Another fan of the event is Piedmont Grocery’s Dave Larson, a longtime merchant on Piedmont Avenue and Grand Marshal of the Parade a couple times in recent years. “I had a wonderful time, mostly scaring children,” joked Larson, who one year dressed in tails, a top hat, a sash and a monster mask to lead the parade. “I think this is a great thing for Piedmont Avenue and a great way to connect with the community,” said Larson. Larson seemed a natural choice for the honor of Grand Marshal. In addition to his wonderful sense of humor, one would be hard pressed Halloween is for the young and old. This parade goer enjoyed the festivities of last year’s Piedmont Ave. Halloween Parade at the West Wind Martial Arts’ Haunted House. to find someone with stronger ties to Piedmont Avenue than he has. In fact, in one way or another, Larson has spent the better part of his life making sure Piedmont Avenue is a vital, vibrant destination for Piedmont and Oakland residents. He is a second-generation owner of the store, a veritable institution in the area. This year the Grand Marshal is Lexi Filipello, a newer fixture on Piedmont Avenue. articles.text: Thomas Wilkins will conduct Gershwin’s Rhapsody in Blue and music from Porgy and Bess at the San Francisco Symphony this Friday and Saturday evening, October 25-26. Guest conductor Thomas Wilkins will lead San Francisco Symphony in two performances this weekend of verve and vigor of 20th century American music, showcasing George Gershwin’s Rhapsody in Blue and music from his opera Porgy and Bess. Performances are on Friday and Saturday evening, October 25-26 at 7:30 p.m. The double-night program will include Leonard Bernstein’s operetta Candide. Fol low i n g B e r n s t e i n’s renowned work, Wilkins will conduct the first SF Symphony performance of William Grant Still’s Wood Notes, a suite inspired by the landscapes of the American South and the poetry of Joseph Mitchell Pilcher, a poet, social worker and clergyman who lived in Alabama from the late 19th through the mid-20th century. Before and after the concert Davies Symphony Hall will have a photography exhibit on the First Tier lobby showing the intersection of nature and art. Tickets ($30-$199) for the concerts are available online at sfsymphony.org/Buy-Tickets/2024-25/rhapsody-in-blue, or by phone at 415-864-6000.
articles.title: Rhapsody in Blue at SF Symphony Oct. 25-26

articles.text: Marin Theatre’s 2024-2025 season opened with the U.S. premiere of award-winning Canadian playwright Kat Sandler’s hit Yaga, playing in Mill Valley through Sunday, November 3. Coming directly from Toronto where it captured critical raves, Yaga follows a detective who finds himself in a small, isolated town, wondering what the disappearance of the young heir to a yogurt fortune has to do with lore about an old witch in the community. Joining forces with the local female sheriff, the detective zeroes in on a cast of curious characters, including a whip-smart forensic bone expert whose shadowy past includes her knack for leading young men astray. What begins as a classic whodunit tale veers into the supernatural as the mythic Baba Yaga, rumored to keep a magic hut in the woods where she grinds the bones of the wicked, becomes an unexpected character in this crime tale. Yaga premiered at Toronto’s Tarragon Theatre, where The Globe and Mail reported that it Yaga, a detective noir play-turned-folk-tale, opens Marin Theatre’s 2024-2025 season with performances through November 3. “triumphantly reclaimed the evilwoman myth. Move over, Wicked and Maleficent, and welcome Yaga to the sisterhood.” The production will be directed by noted theater director Barbara Damashek, who has helmed local productions at Berkeley Rep, Aurora Theatre and the Magic Theatre as well as the multi-Tony Award-nominated Broadway production of Quilters. Tickets ($35-$47) and showtimes for performances at Marin Theatre (397 Miller Ave., Mill Valley) are available online at marintheatre.org/tickets, or by phone at 415-388-5200.

articles.text: TheatreWorks’ 54th season is opening with the regional premiere of Pulitzer Prize finalist Rajiv Joseph’s play King James, with performances through Sunday, November 3 in Mountain View. This brilliant buddy comedy brings basketball to the center stage as superfans Matt and Shawn forge a friendship through their shared love of the Cleveland Cavaliers and the team’s star player, LeBron James. Spanning 12 years from James’ rookie season to his NBA championship game, tensions mount both on and off the court for the duo of friends in this honest exploration of love, redemption and the power of a good game to bring people together. King James first premiered Off-Broadway at the Manhattan Theatre Club, in a co-production with Steppenwolf Theatre Company and Center Theatre Group. The New York Times lauded the play as “a touching examination of male friendship and the powerful social currents beneath it.” The San Diego Union-Tribune hailed it as “enormously entertaining. A touching and funny story on the game of life and the audience wins every night.” Giovanna Sardelli directs the production, continuing a long tenure at TheatreWorks where, as its Artistic Director, she has directed Archduke, The Lake Effect, and The North Pool. She also directed Rajiv Joseph’s previous play, the Obie Award-winning Describe the Night, at Atlantic Theatre Company. Tickets ($49-$89) and showtimes for performances are available at theatreworks.org/mainstage/king-james. TheatreWorks is located at 500 Castro Street in Mountain View. The regional premiere of King James is now being performed at TheatreWorks in Mountain View through Sunday, November 3. articles.text: Award-winning actor and playwright Dan Hoyle’s latest work, Takes All Kinds, closes its first official run at The Marsh in San Francisco this Saturday, October 26. Directed by Aldo Billingslea and Michael Moran and developed with Charlie Varon, the play follows Hoyle as he travels across what he finds to be a polarized United States in an explosive election year. As Hoyle discovers a country full of rage and fear, he also encounters citizens who are joyfully and creatively attempting to unite the country against divisive odds. Continuing his brand of journalistic theater that has been called “riveting, funny and poignant” by The New York Times, Hoyle showcases the front lines of the biggest political battles in the country — including school board showdowns in Florida; organizers in the streets of Atlanta; churches in Charleston, South Carolina; and even a former violent extremist in Missouri who has since deradicalized hundreds of other violent extremists. Dan Hoyle becomes a panoply of different characters in his new solo show, Takes All Kinds, running at The Marsh San Francisco through this Saturday. In Takes All Kinds, audiences will see Hoyle bring to life the moving, funny, raw and surprising true stories of unlikely changemakers in this fresh exploration of America’s conflicting and collective psyche in 2024. Tickets ($20-$35 sliding scale, $50 and $100 reserved) and showtimes for performances at The Marsh (1062 Valencia Street in San Francisco) are available at themarsh.org.

pages.text: 18 Wednesday, October 23, 2024 Arts & Entertainment Rhapsody in Blue at SF Symphony Oct. 25-26 Marin Theatre premieres detective play Yaga through Nov. 3 By Selen Ozturk Marin Theatre’s 2024-2025 season opened with the U.S. premiere of award-winning Canadian playwright Kat Sandler’s hit Yaga, playing in Mill Valley through Sunday, November 3. Coming directly from Toronto where it captured critical raves, Yaga follows a detective who finds himself in a small, isolated town, wondering what the disappearance of the young heir to a yogurt fortune has to do with lore about an old witch in the community. Joining forces with the local female sheriff, the detective zeroes in on a cast of curious characters, including a whip-smart forensic bone expert whose shadowy past includes her knack for leading young men astray. What begins as a classic whodunit tale veers into the supernatural as the mythic Baba Yaga, rumored to keep a magic hut in the woods where she grinds the bones of the wicked, becomes an unexpected character in this crime tale.
