articles.text: “We Have a History” – visual artist Leilah Babirye’s first solo U.S. museum exhibition – is closing at the de Young Museum in San Francisco after this Saturday. Born in Kampala, Uganda and based in New York, Babirye transforms natural clay, wood, ceramic and found materials into modern objects that reclaim sculptural and carving traditions from West and Central Africa. With 12 new sculptures exhibited alongside works from the de Young’s historical African Art collection, Babirye illuminates the connections between past and present folk art, and the evolving nature of both Western and African art. Babirye whittles, scorches, and burnishes her wood sculptures and hand-builds her ceramics, firing them with expressive glazes. As a final touch, she adorns these works with wire, bicycle chains, inner tubes, scrap metal and other found materials collected from the streets of New York. Her choice to use discarded materials in her work is an intentional nod to the historical status of gay individuals in Uganda. The pejorative term for the gay community in the Ugandan language of Ganda is “abasiyazi,” meaning “sugarcane husk.” In other words, Babirye has said, “It means rubbish – the part of the sugarcane you throw out.” Babirye reclaims this term for discarded debris as a gesture of liberation in her work. Her sculptures range in scale from towering totemic forms to busts, talismans, and masks that form metal- and nail-adorned portraits of the LGBT community. This portrayed community includes princes and princesses within Buganda’s royal family who flouted homophobic cultural attitudes then and now. One of the largest of the medieval kingdoms in present-day Uganda, Buganda was established in the late 14th century along the shore of Lake Victoria and evolved to become an important and powerful state during the nineteenth century. “Leilah Babirye represents a new generation of sculptors transcending traditional boundaries while maintaining a deep connection to its roots. Her monumental sculptures have become recognized symbols celebrating the resilience and ingenuity of African people while also preserving their rich cultural heritage,” said Natasha Becker, curator of African Art at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. “Babirye has pushed sculpture forward by creating some of the most interesting, challenging, and ambitious forms—freely transforming the body, prodding social taboos, and redefining beauty,“ added Becker. The de Young Museum, 50 Hagiwara Tea Garden Drive in Golden Gate Park, is open from 9:30 a.m. to 5:15 p.m., Tuesday through Sunday. Tickets ($20 adult, $17 senior, $11 student, free under 18) are available at ticketing.famsf.org/events. Installation view of artist Leilah Babirye’s solo exhibit “We Have a History,” on view at the de Young through this Saturday.

articles.text: “Mary Cassatt at Work,” a major exhibition focused on the great woman Impressionist, is now on view at San Francisco’s Legion of Honor through January 26. The exhibition presents Cassatt (1844–1926), the most celebrated woman artist of her era, as a fiercely professional artist and an aesthetically radical painter and printmaker who helped shape the French Impressionist movement and transform the course of modern art. Cassatt produced images of “women’s work”— knitting, needlepoint, bathing children, and nursing infants — that also testify to the artistic work of the woman who made them. Juxtaposing paintings, pastels and prints, Mary Cassatt at Work explores the artist’s activity across media, revealing the daring methods she used to give form to her ideas. In the first North American retrospective exhibit of Cassatt’s works in 25 years, the Legion of Honor is this exhibition’s sole West Coast venue, featuring approximately 100 works. “‘Mary Cassatt at Work’ disrupts any preconceived notion that Cassatt was a sentimental painter and sheds fresh light on her groundbreaking practice,” said Thomas P. Campbell, director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. The exhibition shows Cassatt’s multifaceted exploration of modern life, particularly focusing on the roles of women and children during the late 19th century. It begins with groundbreaking early Mary Cassatt, “Little Girl in a Blue Armchair,” 1877–1878. The Impressionist painter’s work is now on view through January in a major new exhibit at the Legion of Honor. Impressionist works portraying women in the audience at the Paris Opera. Moving through Cassatt’s career, the exhibition includes depictions of bourgeois women engaged in various tasks, acute portrayals of children and revolutionary color etchings inspired by Japanese woodblock prints. The show delves into Cassatt’s process, challenging conventional notions of finish in both women’s work and artistic work, emphasizing experimentation and revision in her printmaking and painting. “Mary Cassatt at Work” concludes with the artist’s persistent return to the theme of women and children in the “modern Madonnas” of her final decade. Often stereotyped as sentimental, these pictures reveal Cassatt’s ability to extract infinite variation from a single motif of mother and child “In a sense, the mother-andchild theme was to Cassatt’s final decades what water lilies were to Monet’s or apples to Cézanne’s. Because this motif is and was so freighted with gendered meaning, it’s been too easy to write these pictures off as sentimental, when in fact they’re formally rigorous, engaged in an ever-deepening conversation with tradition and an ever-more experimental handling of paint,” said organizing curator Emily A. Beeny. “Given the social realities of Cassatt’s time, it’s perhaps useful to reflect on the fact that these works are all, in some sense, brought to us by Cassatt’s own childless state,” she added. “The ambitions of her career were, alas, often incompatible in the late 19th century with childbearing, even for a woman of her elevated social class.” The Legion of Honor, located in Lincoln Park, 100 34th Avenue in San Francisco, is open 9:30 a.m. to 5:15 p.m., Tuesday through Sunday. Tickets ($20 adult, $17 senior, $11 student, free under 18) are available at ticketing.famsf.org, or at the front desk.
articles.title: Major exhibition through January shows role of “women’s work”

articles.text: Visual artist Jessica Monette’s first solo exhibition, “Unveiling Histories: A Fabricated Archive,” is now on view at Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) in San Francisco through December 15. The show features mixed-media works that Monette crafted as a vehicle to navigate the profound loss and personal trauma left in the wake of Hurricane Katrina. Her research for the exhibition included DNA testing, collecting oral histories and photographic documentation, examining how the impact of natural ruin is historically accumulated. The New Orleans-born artist’s work is deeply rooted in familial history and heritage. Each work in “Unveiling Histories,” the fourth exhibition in MoAd’s 2024-2025 Emerging Artist Program, is a material expression of recovery from personal harm on the one hand, and a broader critique of marginalization of the social underclasses most vulnerable to disasters like Katrina on the other. Monette joins this program as a Jessica Monette, “Untitled (Decimation),” 2024, is among the works on view in “Unveiling Histories: A Fabricated Archive,” at Museum of the African Diaspora this month through December 15. 2024 Stanford MFA graduate. In her first exhibit since graduating, she uses visual motifs borrowed from aerial surveys of Hurricane Katrina’s impact. Additional materials used include commercial building materials such as house paint, plaster and thin-set mortar. The works’ archival look is amplified by the inclusion of site-specific soils and waters, as well as protective and healing ingredients like brick dust, Agua de Florida and cascarilla. Soil from both Georgia and California represent the physical patterns of forced and voluntary migration in the artist’s family, while water from the Mississippi River and Lake Pontchartrain signals a layered narrative that links past, present and future. Rope used in the works is a symbolic bridge between the weight of a violent past and the preserving ancestral bonds of DNA, expressing what Monette has called “integral fibers that resist erasure.” The Museum of the African Diaspora (685 Mission St., San Francisco) is open 11 a.m. through 6 p.m. Wednesday through Saturday, and 12 p.m. through 5 p.m. on Sundays. Tickets ($15 general, $7 seniors, students, educators) are available at moadsf.org/tickets, or at the front desk.

articles.text: Through November 11 “It’s All Relative” Art Exhibition Bill Prochnow presents a show of figurative abstractions. He is the former Design Director for the Golden Gate National Parks Conservancy. His paintings and drawings center on human relationships and connections. Open gallery hours are Saturdays and Sundays from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. Friday, October 25, 7:30 p.m. Mira Trio Chamber Concert Pianist Miles Graber brings to PCA the Mira Trio with violinist Lev Polyakin and flautist Martha Aarons performing J.S. Bach‘s Trio Sonata in G major BWV 1038; Five Pieces, Op. 56, by the Russian Cesar Cuil; Siete Canciones Populares Españolas by Manuel de Falla; Tchaikovsky’s Meditation for violin and piano; and a piece for flute solo and piano by Francis Poulenc, written in 1957. Advance tickets at https://bpt.me/6465993. Sunday, October 27, 4:00 p.m. Festival Opera Vocal Recital The second in a series of three recitals, Festival Opera presents contralto Sarah Couden accompanied by Derek Tam on the piano, with a program of art songs entitled Nothing to Fear. The world of classical music is rife with horrors, and Couden will introduce some of them as possible to the audience. The program includes works by Schubert, Strauss, Wieck, and Weill. Tickets at www.eventbrite. com/e/913718355197. Friday, November 1, 6:30 p.m. Big Harp George Band Concert George Bisharat (Big Harp George) is a Piedmont singer, songwriter, and chromatic harmonica player. He has released seven albums to critical acclaim since 2014. His current release, Cooking with Gas, has just been nominated for a Grammy. George’s current band, The Hung Jury, includes six renowned Bay Area musicians, including Piedmont blues guitarist Jules Leyhe. Advance tickets ($35) are available at https://bpt.me/6471243; $40 cash/check only at the door. Saturday, November 2, 7:00 p.m. Japanese-American Internment Camps WWII Part 2 in a 3-part series. The second event will include a performance by Piedmont Choirs singing Nagasaki, composed by Piedmont Choirs Artistic Director Eric Tuan. A devastating piece of choral storytelling, it depicts the dropping of the atomic bomb in 1945, when Tuan’s grandmother survived the blast. Former Piedmont resident Wendy Tokuda, the longtime News Anchor at KPIX, and Kimi Hill, the granddaughter of Chiura Obata, an artist and UC Berkeley art professor who continued to paint in the camps, will discuss their families’ stories from the camp years. Single event tickets available at https://bpt. me/6449591. Sunday, November 3, 4:30 p.m. Duo SaBu in Concert Songs and solo piano works by American and Nordic composers performed by Heidi Saario, piano, and tenor Erich Buchholz. They have performed at the Finnish Hall in Berkeley and at private house concerts. Heidi is a native of Helsinki who has performed piano in Finland, Canada and the USA. Tickets $25 general, $15 student/senior in advance at https://bpt.me/6466641 or $30 / $20 at the door, cash/check only. Sunday, November 9, 4:00 p.m. Achille Bocus and Friends mandolin concert Achille Bocus and an orchestra will perform a mandolin concert featuring e a wide variety of surprising and engaging pieces, including music by Prokofiev, Martucci, Sibelius, Gershwin, Ballerini, and three pieces written by Bocus. Tickets $30 at the door or $25 in advance at www. bpt.me/6475287.

articles.text: If you check your dates, you might be interested in coming to the new jazz club in Piedmont. When In the Tradition Jazz Trio plays in the Piedmont Center for the Arts, that elegant space becomes a sophisticated jazz nightclub. That’s the way it was on Sunday afternoon and the music was inspiring. Maybe you’d like to hear some secrets about jazz and improvised music. Jazz as a musical form is one of the miracles of multicultural assimilation. It blends African tradition and rhythms with European musical instruments and musical form. Almost all cultures have gotten into the act. The hey-day of jazz started at the end of the 19th century and blossomed, declined for a while, and then blossomed again. Virtually all of the early jazz players had classical music training. To this classical training, they added improvisation and jazz chords. Good jazz should always sound improvised even when it isn’t. That is one of the secrets of this musical idiom. Virtually all jazz players have an idea what they’re going to do in advance. In the Tradition Jazz Trio knows all of these things and what they produce is an inspiration. Perhaps you know them as Bill Jackman and his Trio – Bill Jackman, piano, Michael Jones, string bass, and Albert Brooks drums. Their program on Sunday was a tribute to American composer Jimmy van Heusen. Jackman told me that he prepares at least 20 pieces for his programs. They rehearse but everything sounds improvised as if they’re making the music up on the spot. That’s how jazz should be. Jazz can be many things. The Trio specializes in playing the “standards“ but they always strive for a fresh approach. Jazz must be that way. In my opinion, classical music could be that way also. We strive for perfection, but perfection should not come with a loss of humanity. Jackman sings some of the songs with an improvised feeling. There is always a sense of subtlety of tone and rhythm combined with rich harmonies. His spoken commentary is brief. Fortunately, they have dispensed with amplification. Acoustics are really good in the Center for the Arts. Ttruth be told, amplification is never needed unless you are in the Hollywood Bowl. The setting was about as good as it can be. A few tables were set out for the audience. Liquid refreshment and some munchables were available for the audience. It was a delightful late afternoon, both musically and socially. It would be nice if more people attended these types of concerts. Do we really need ear-deafening amplification, boring thump, thump, thump, thump of the percussion, the same rhythm, song after song? That’s the way it was on Sunday afternoon and the music was inspiring. Maybe you’d like to hear some secrets about jazz and improvised music. Jazz as a musical form is one of the miracles of multicultural assimilation. It blends African tradition and rhythms with European musical instruments and musical form. Almost all cultures have gotten into the act. The hey-day of jazz started at the end of the 19th century and blossomed, declined for a while, and then blossomed again. Virtually all of the early jazz players had classical music training. To this classical training, they added improvisation and jazz chords. Good jazz should always sound improvised even when it isn’t. That is one of the secrets of this musical idiom. Virtually all jazz players have an idea what they’re going to do in advance. In the Tradition Jazz Trio knows all of these things and what they produce is an inspiration. Perhaps you know them as Bill Jackman and his Trio – Bill Jackman, piano, Michael Jones, string bass, and Albert Brooks drums. Their program on Sunday was a tribute to American composer Jimmy van Heusen. Jackman told me that he prepares at least 20 pieces for his programs. They rehearse but everything sounds improvised as if they’re making the music up on the spot. That’s how jazz should be. Jazz can be many things. articles.text: A scene from The Red Turtle The Red Turtle is a breathtaking fable, written and animated by Oscar-winning Dutch filmmaker Michael Dudok de Wit, working in collaboration with Studio Ghibli, the renowned Japanese house of animation co-founded by Hayao Miyazaki and Isao Takahata. Though The Red Turtle has a PG rating and is only 80 minutes long, it is not simply kidfriendly. What gives this film its emotional power is that not a single word is spoken, nor is a single word needed. The silence of the film falls away as the audience, both young and old, is transported into a captivating story that is completely unexpected/ It is a story that gives the illusion of being slight but is instead deeply complex. The film opens with a raging, storm-tossed sea. Abruptly the head of a man appears floating just above the surface, struggling to survive. He spots a capsized lifeboat and clings to it as the wind howls and the water churns. When the sun rises, the sky now clear, the man is lying on a wide sandy beach. He doesn’t stir until a small sand crab crawls up the leg of his pants and bites him. It’s then that he wakes, slowly stands, and looks around. He is alone. All he sees is ocean and a necklace of sand, finally noticing that just beyond the beach is a forest of lush green bamboo that covers the island. articles.text: Last week I wrote about the wines of K Vintners and L’Ecole No. 41. If you read that article you can skip the first two paragraphs of this one.) In my 23 years of being a wine journalist I have traveled to many countries and several continents to visit the major wine regions of the world. One region I had missed was the wine growing region of Washington state. I have had many fine wines from Walla Walla and knew their reputation was soaring, but I had yet to visit. This past month that omission was corrected as I journeyed there with my good friends Wine.com founder Mike Osborn and winemaker Kent Rasmussen. Flying into Pasco and the Tri-Cities area and driving east one hour to Walla Walla you pass through vast open spaces of scrubland interlaced with wheat fields. Part of the journey we followed along the Columbia River with its dramatic gorges and beautiful scenery. Walla Walla itself (“place of many waters” in the Nez Pearce language)) is a green oasis of tree-lined streets, verdant parks and tidy little wooden houses. With a population of around 34,000 it seems like a charming livable city that would be a great place to raise a family. In the last 20 years an amazing thing has happened to Walla Walla. It has morphed from quiet, overlooked wheat town to a vibrant wine capital of Washington state. Leonetti, the area’s first winery, was started in 1973 and for years there were just a handful of wineries in the area. There are now over 120 wineries, and the main street is packed with tasting rooms promoting their wines. There are charming B and B’s, air BnB’s and trendy restaurants galore. In the early days of the wine industry most of the attention was focused on growing Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon. While those wines continue to thrive, the rising star is the Syrah grape and the region has been winning major accolades for those wines. Greg Harrington is the founder of Gramercy Cellars. Gramercy Cellars specializes in Syrah and Cabernet Sauvignon.
articles.title: Walla Walla a wine wonderland

The medium bodied palate is expressive and savory, with a fine balance of warm fruit and tones of maturity. It has supple powdery tannins, fresh acidity and a long, detailed finish. • 2020 Gramercy Cellars Syrah Forgotten Hills, $65 This Syrah gives up plenty of black pepper, black and blue fruit with some meat and herbs de Provence aromas. Medium bodied firm and chewy with plenty of freshness to support the earthy fruit. It is drinking beautifully now but will last for two decades in the cellar. • 2020 Gramercy Cellars Syrah John Lewis, $95 This is the flagship Syrah of the winery and it’s a massive powerful wine. It offers a fresh, lively bouquet of blackberries, cracked pepper, Asian spices and spring flowers. Gorgeous on the palate as well, with full-bodied richness punchy acidity and big firm tannins with good framing structure. This wine needs some time to show its best and will last for decades in the cellar. • 2020 Gramercy Cellars Cabernet Sauvignon, $60 This wine is sourced from three or four different vineyards and is a blend of 87% Cabernet Sauvignon and 13% Merlot. The palate is dark and powerful yet graceful and refined, finishing with fine-grained tannins. articles.text: Lester Isenstadt, born to Abraham and Charlotte Isenstadt, passed away on September 29, 2024, aged 82. He was surrounded by his family, to whom he was devoted. He is survived by his wife of 42 years, Catherine, and his sons Alex and Joseph. Lester grew up in Cambridge, MA. He suffered illness as a child and was determined to become a doctor in order to provide the same deep care and dedication that he received from his own doctors. He attended Boston University and then enrolled at the University of Arkansas Medical School to train to be a psychiatrist. He told colorful stories of the culture shock of being one of the few Jewish people in Little Rock. After medical school he moved to San Francisco for his psychiatric residency, and when that was completed trained as a child and adult psychoanalyst. He found deep purpose in his work and in helping his patients. He became passionate about neuroscience as the field of psychology became increasingly informed by it. He loved to spend his time studying neurobiological literature to better help his patients. He was particularly interested in how people react to mistakes and showing his patients that mistakes are a gift and a gateway to learning. He was devoted to learning, and used to say that a day was wasted if he hadn’t learned something. Even in his final weeks, he continued to study and remained devoted to his patients and their emotional wellbeing. Memorial donations in the name of Lester Isenstadt may be made to the Pancreatic Cancer Action Network.

articles.text: It was a mild day for the Walking on Wednesdays group last Wednesday with 45 walkers with one K-9 best friend on hand for their weekly walk. The group had not gone to Littlewood Drive this year, so it was the morning’s destination. The group walked on Highland, Sheridan, and Lakeview Avenue to Poplar Way, and stopped at Mountain and Bellevue to catch their breath. The walkers noted the small Island Oak that replaced the iconic Sequoia in the traffic circle there. The original tree stood in this intersection for generations. It served as Piedmont’s first holiday tree during the 1920s and 30s. However, the Sequoia was dying and needed to be removed last fall. Park commissioner Jack Fischrup, a regular Wednesday walker, noted that the small traffic island has no source of water, and a gator water bag has been put around the oak’s trunk. It will be supplied with water by the City for two years to help the tree thrive. The group then headed to Dudley Avenue and a climb to the top of the long Littlewood cul de sac. A group photo was taken, and the surprising history of Piedmont’s Silk Farm from a past Piedmont Post article by Gail Lombardi of the Piedmont Historical Society was shared. At the end of the 19th century there were only three types of cloth - cotton, wool and silk. The U.S. government thought silk could be produced in America, and funded groups to create experimental silk producing stations. It was believed silk production could provide employment for women, reduce unemployment, and increase family income. In the early 1880s the Ladies’ Silk Culture Society purchased 15 acres of land at the top of Mountain Avenue, where Dudley and Littlewood Avenues are today. The society planted mulberry trees, whose leaves are silkworms’ food, and built a twostory, eight-room cocoonery. The locals called it the “Silk Farm.” an additional seven acres were obtained, and about 100 women were employed. During their lives, silkworms consume 50 times their weight in mulberry leaves, which the women harvested, chopped, and fed to the worms in trays four times a day. The worms reached maturity in 35 days and spun their cocoons. The Silk Farm’s cocoons were fumigated to kill the pupa, softened in hot water, unreeled as separate silken fibers. One cocoon could produce a continuous silk filament 200 to 300 feet long. Several filaments were spun together to form one silk thread. Unfortunately, the Silk Farm didn’t prosper. The canyon was not warm enough for the worms and the women would not work for less than a dollar a day, while Chinese workers were only paid six cents a day. In 1895 the farm closed. The walkers descended the Littlewood canyon where the Silk Farm’s mulberry trees once were. Sadly, there are no Littlewood mulberry trees today to give witness to the street’s history. Some walkers remembered two years ago they got a surprise invitation to visit the home at the end of Littlewood with a unique yard by its then owners. Albert and Swee Ling Chen are neighbors and recounted that the owners bought the house in 2014 and wanted to build their version of Bali. They transformed the area at the front into a tropical garden with a swimming pool, water slide, and pool house. Jungle sound effects enhanced this imaginary. However, they later realized that maintaining this tropical paradise was very expensive and they sold the house. The walkers also remembered that in front of the home’s large front gate was an original red London telephone booth. However, like the Sequoia and the mulberries, it was gone. All this history was fun, but the walkers decided they didn’t want to do any more climbing on Dudley, so they retraced their steps back to the Exedra. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. Among those participating with the Walking on Wednesdays group last week were Abha Kothari, Melba Yee, Elizabeth Richter, Liana Wu, Noemi Alvarado, Judy Sokolof, Michelle Yang, Ken Moy, Peggy Shultz, Sherry Jacobs, Karin Fetherston, Alissa Quan, Gloria DaSilva, Leigh Sorensen, Claudine Bach, David Haecker, Alicia Rivera, Lori Austin, Bonnie Sherwood, Karen Palmer, Phil Witte, Albert Chen, Fangfang Lai, Sharona Fischrup, Pat Keller, Jasmine Cai, Jack Fischrup, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Bob Wong, Mark Davis, Jim Kuo, Judy Love, Chuck Oraftik, Dave DeRoche, Jim Kellogg, Denny McGee, Mike Gallant, Rick Eigenbrode, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome back Jill and Ron Day, who were again visiting from Great Britian. Additionally, two of Fangfang Lai’s friends from China were there, and Piedmont resident Vicki Trimbach was walking with them for the first time.

articles.text: Virginia Joan Foley Tornlof, known to friends and family as Joan, passed away peacefully at the age of 93 on March 2, 2024, in Oakland, California. Born to Edwin R. and Virginia M. Foley, on July 2, 1930, in Alameda, California, Joan lived a full and vibrant life marked by love, service, and adventure. Joan met and fell in love with Al Tornlof while both worked at the same bank in San Francisco. Al proposed to Joan at Coit Tower and they were married in Orinda. Together they enjoyed camping, hiking, fishing, dancing at the Treasure Island Officers Club, travel and raising their family in both Piedmont and Claremont, California. After the passing of her husband, she found joy and companionship with Dr. Philip Van Horn. Both widowed, Joan and “Dr. Phil” shared 25 wonderful years filled with summers at Clear Lake, cruises and visiting new places, and time with their combined families. An alumna of Piedmont High School and Stanford University, Joan had a lifelong passion for learning and community involvement. Her commitment to community service was evident in her 40-year volunteer work with the Oakland Museum and White Elephant Sale, where she served for two years as the Women’s Board President. While raising a family in Piedmont she held leadership roles in the Piedmont Schools Parent Clubs and the Samuel Merritt Hospital Volunteer Board. She also served on the Alameda County Grand Jury. Joan embarked midlife on a new career as a tax preparer with her longtime business partner, Luise Roke, in Alameda. She loved helping her clients and often visited their homes to assist in completing their taxes. An avid bridge player, Joan was highly regarded in her many bridge groups, including those at the Claremont Country Club, where she was a longtime member and also enjoyed playing golf. She remained active in her alumni associations, contributing to her Piedmont High School reunion committee and particJoan Tornloff passed away at age 93. ipating in numerous Stanford alumni events. Joan could always be found wearing red and white while cheering her team on Big Game day. She loved traveling with her many groups of friends to Mendocino’s Little River Inn, Oregon Shakespeare Festival, Lake Tahoe, and Carmel. At age 80, Joan was featured in a Junior League Sustainer publication. The article concluded with Joan’s own words of wisdom: “It really is true when one volunteers they receive more than they give. A woman truly misses a great part of life if she does not reach out and participate in everything interesting that comes her way. The experience has been great.” Joan is predeceased by her husband of 28 years, Albert Tornlof, and son-in-law, Dr. Carlos Sanseau. She is survived by her daughters, Virginia Sanseau and Susan Tornlof (Matt Gerhardt), as well as her grandchildren, Dr. Elizabeth Sanseau (Zeus Antonello) and Louise Sanseau. Joan was also a proud great-grandmother to Carlos, Alberto, and Tulio Antonello-Sanseau. As an only child Joan counted her many cousins as close siblings. Joan’s life was a testament to family, the joy of service, the importance of community, and the endless possibilities that come with embracing life’s adventures. She will be deeply missed by all who knew and loved her. A service will be planned at a later date and details will be shared with family and friends. In lieu of flowers, the family suggests donations be made in Joan’s name to the Oakland Museum or a charity of your choice.
articles.title: Super volunteer Joan Tornlof dies at 93

At age 80, Joan was featured in a Junior League Sustainer publication. The article concluded with Joan’s own words of wisdom: “It really is true when one volunteers they receive more than they give. A woman truly misses a great part of life if she does not reach out and participate in everything interesting that comes her way. The experience has been great.” Joan is predeceased by her husband of 28 years, Albert Tornlof, and son-in-law, Dr. Carlos Sanseau. She is survived by her daughters, Virginia Sanseau and Susan Tornlof (Matt Gerhardt), as well as her grandchildren, Dr. Elizabeth Sanseau (Zeus Antonello) and Louise Sanseau. Joan was also a proud great-grandmother to Carlos, Alberto, and Tulio Antonello-Sanseau. As an only child Joan counted her many cousins as close siblings. Joan’s life was a testament to family, the joy of service, the importance of community, and the endless possibilities that come with embracing life’s adventures. She will be deeply missed by all who knew and loved her. A service will be planned at a later date and details will be shared with family and friends. In lieu of flowers, the family suggests donations be made in Joan’s name to the Oakland Museum or a charity of your choice.

Lynda’s extensive background as a conservationist, scientist, public servant, employee of the EPA and someone who clearly understands the dynamics and needs of our ecosystems during this challenging time, make her an excellent person to fill this important role. Of the three candidates running for this position, Lynda’s rich background and serious commitment to the sustainability of our park system make her the best candidate. Vote Lynda for Ward 2. –Janet Thomas Lafayette

Democracy is about honest debate, respectful dialogue and shared decision making. Christian nationalism advances false narratives of the history of the United States, the cause of the problems faced by our nation and the rightful interpretation of our sacred texts. For example, Christian nationalism teaches that the United States was founded as a Christian nation when, in fact, it was founded as a nation that, while respecting religion, was careful not to give any single religion elevated status. Christian nationalism teaches that because the beliefs and practices of conservative Christianity have not been given precedence, the nation has been significantly weakened, when, in fact, the policies and practices advocated by Christian nationalism would, themselves, cause much pain and suffering. Christian nationalism teaches that Jesus sought to be a political leader when, in fact, he viewed that role as a temptation to be rejected. To be very clear. Jesus taught that the truth will make us free. Christian nationalism teaches that its own dogma will make us free. In that insistence, there is a clear threat to democracy. White Christian nationalism, is, at its heart, exclusionary. It seeks to marginalize those who do not embrace it. In this, we have another example, of the way it threatens democracy. Democracy, to be vibrant, needs the full and free participation of the citizenry. It needs the full and free participation of those whose party is in power. It needs the full and free participation of those whose party is not in power. It needs the full and free participation of those who belong to no political party. It is then that an enormous turtle with a bright red shell emerges from the deep. This time when he swims back the turtle follows, crawling awkwardly up onto the sandy beach. Angry and wracked by loneliness, the man’s plan to escape once again is ruined. He turns the massive turtle upside down and leaves it in the hot sun. What happens next is magical and I am reluctant to explain more. Suffice it to say that it is then that the narrative arc of the film is revealed and it beckons the audience to step into a reverie that is so quietly offered up it can only be called a meditation on life. Using a palette of vibrant and muted colors, it is all but impossible not to be drawn in, pulled, like a gentle out-going tide swirling around your ankles, the sand quering ones’ opponent so thoroughly that they are forced out of the political process entirely. White Christian nationalism threatens democracy by demanding that Congress pass laws which establish one narrow set of religious practices as supreme while expecting it, at the same time, to impede, if not prohibit, the free exercise of other faiths. Of course, this is antithetical to the way of Jesus. Jesus taught us to love our neighbors, to make their well-being central to our own existence. White Christian nationalism asks that instead of making the love of neighbor central to our faith, we make dictating to our neighbors central to our faith. I fail to see how this is good for us, good for our neighbors or good for democracy. The Reverend Benjamin Creamer puts it this way: Nationalism keeps telling us Christians to take up our swords and make our nation “Christian” by any means necessary. Jesus keeps calling us Christians to take up our crosses and be like him, serving the world through grace, humility, compassion, and self-sacrificial love. Doesn’t it seem that taking up our crosses, rather than taking up our swords, is much better for democracy? James Hopkins is Senior Pastor at Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church in Oakland. Robert Horvitz, who was awarded the Nobel Prize in 2002. While in Horvitz’s lab, the pair began studying gene control in the roundworm C. elegans – an effort that laid the groundwork for their Nobel discoveries. They studied two mutant forms of the worm, known as lin-4 and lin-14, that showed defects in the timing of the activation of genetic programs that control development. In 2000 Ruvk un published the discovery of another microRNA molecule, encoded by a gene called let-7, which is found throughout the animal kingdom. Since then, more than 1,000 microRNA genes have been found in humans. “Ambros and Ruvkun’s seminal discovery in the small worm C. elegans was unexpected, and revealed a new dimension to gene regulation, essential for all complex life forms,” the Nobel citation declared. After Ruvkun matriculated from Piedmont in 1969 he attended the University of California at Berkeley and then earned his PhD at Harvard University before joining Horvitz’s lab at MIT for postdoctoral training. Ruvkun is believed to be the first Piedmont alumni to win a Nobel Prize. articles.text: Piedmont Post sports reporter Jon Comeaux was evacuated from his home on Friday, October 18 due to the encroaching Keller Fire, which burned parts of 15 acres in the Oakland Hills. The incendiary action was first reported at 2:25 that afternoon. Comeaux was told to evacuate from the area later that afternoon, but captured some images on his camera before leaving. “The fire started right by the Keller Ave. on-ramp to 580 that I use every day. It burned a couple of houses on the bottom of Mountain Blvd., said Comeaux. The blaze occurred north of the Oakland Zoo, at the “end of Sanford Street in the area of Maynard in Oakland, according to CalFire. Comeaux’s home and 43 others were saved due to quick work and a large response of firefighters. The fire was active for two days and was declared to be contained at 12:37 p.m. on Sunday. The cause of the blaze is still under investigation. For a timeline of events and updates visit Fire.ca.gov/incidents/2024/10/18/ keller-fire/updates Photos by Jon Comeaux A helicopter aids in extinguishing the Keller Fire last weekend. Piedmont Real Estate Update October 2024 The House Price Super-Cycle “Housing seems to have a remarkable ability to keep appreciating, whatever the weather.” The Economist, October 2024 In a recent issue of The Economist, the paper outlined three drivers that they believe will ensure that, for decades to come, the housing market will continue on an upward trend. They are: Demographic Shifts Across the globe, the foreign-born population is rising at an annual rate of 4%, the fastest growth on record. Immigration increases the demand for housing, pushing both rents and home prices higher. Research has shown that even a small uptick in the immigration rate can significantly increase average house prices. 1 The Appeal of Urban Living When the pandemic began, many assumed that the rise of remote work would reduce the allure of living in cities. According to The Economist, this has not been the case. They found that, while remote work is more prevalent, 37% of businesses are still located in larger cities. Interestingly, the same share as in 2019. Consequently, urban centers like Oakland, Berkeley, and Walnut Creek retain their appeal due to the availability of jobs, amenities, and social opportunities. The competition for housing in these cities has remained intense, driving prices upward, particularly in desirable neighborhoods where housing supply is limited. 1 “The use price-supercyle is just getting going” October 1, 2024, The Economist 2 Study by CSU Sacramento and the Sacramento Regional Research Institute Infrastructure and Housing Supply Constraints Infrastructure challenges, limited land, and regulatory constraints have limited housing supply growth. The lack of supply is most notable in cities where restrictions against building new housing are the strictest. Further, recent studies have found that areas with rent-control actually see a decrease in the supply of rental housing. They found that, for instance, rental housing supply in Berkeley decreased 7.5% after two decades of rent control. Given that these three factors are relevant in the Bay Area, we expect that housing prices will continue their upward cycle. This is also supported by the trend in our local market chart shown below. articles.text: The 12th annual gathering of the Piedmont Artisanal Brewing Competition will be held at the Piedmont Center for the Arts this Friday evening. It offers a wide array of handcrafted creations by local craft brewers and an authentic Oktoberfest spread – is only a couple days away. The event will be held this Friday, October 18, from 5:30 to 7:30 p.m., offering residents the chance to sample beer from home brewers, and enjoy an authentic Oktoberfest meal complete with grilled bratwurst, potato salad and red cabbage. The cost for unlimited beer tasting is $15, which also provides participants with a custom Piedmont Center for the Arts beer glass. Attendants can also pay an additional $15 to partake in the Oktoberfest feast on the lawn, with all food donated by Piedmont Grocery owner Dave Larson. A three-piece band from Piedmont High School – composed of students Deniz Radzik, Eric Verner and Maxim Miller – will also play music outside while guests enjoy their German meal on the lawn in front of the Center. Brewers from Piedmont and the Bay Area will sling their suds at the event, a sizable increase from the past two years. articles.text: Wildwood Elementary School principal, Melissa Daymond suddenly resigned and departed from the school on Friday, October 11. Superintendent Jennifer Hawn and Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich are filling in temporarily until a new principal can be hired. On Tuesday, October 1, Daymond notified the district of her intent to resign from her post at the school. At that time, she indicated she could stay until November 1. Even with a one-month notice Hawn was optimistic that the district could replace her without any lapse in staffing. “Because Ms. Daymond has provided a month’s notice before her departure, we are able to post for a new Principal immediately with time to hire a replacement on or before Ms. Daymond’s departure,” Hawn told Wildwood parents on October 4. However, last week Daymond moved up her departure to Friday, October 11, and has since left the district. Daymond recently completed her first year as principal at Wildwood after replacing long-time Wildwood Principal Carol Cramer, a Piedmont resident, on July 1, 2023. Cramer, who worked for 35 years at Beach and Wildwood schools, said she is not available to fill in at the moment. In her brief time with the district, Daymond supported initiatives including the reorganization of a safer lunch location for students and adding an additional outdoor space for Kindergarteners. “I express my gratitude to the Wildwood staff and families for their support during this pivotal transition. By supporting one another, we can ensure that Wildwood continues to deliver an exemplary education to our students,” said Hawn. Daymond did not indicate a reason for her mid-year departure or why she did not provide the district with more than a oneweek notice. The job opening was posted October 1, and the application deadline has since passed. The now-closed job posting, with an annual salary range of $156,918- $172,928, can still be seen at Edjoin.org/Home/JobPosting/ 2003952 Wildwood parents installed a balloon wreath on campus principal Melissa Daymond’s last day. October 11.

articles.text: The Piedmont League of Women Voters held a virtual forum on October 1 with three of the four candidates vying for two spots on the city council. Participating were incumbent Conna McCarthy, James Green, and Lorrel Plimier. Candidate Nancy Bostrom did not participate. The forum, designed as educational and not a debate, provided the candidates with a platform to provide opening statements and answer a series of seven questions posed by moderator Kathleen Cha, president of the Bay Area League of Women Voters. “You are here today to make smart choices when you vote,” Cha said to viewers of the virtual forum. “It’s important for the League to give the community a voice, and that is why we invited the community to send these questions for the candidates in advance.” The questions included: What measures could the city of Piedmont take to combat crime? How will the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan affect evacuation plans in areas impacted by construction? What incentives could the city consider to improve conservation efforts? What are your opinions on expanding commercial businesses in the city? What lessons can be learned from Piedmont’s ongoing project to build a new community pool? Candidates were each given 90 seconds to deliver their positions on the questions posed by the moderator, and a recording of the League’s forum with the City Council candidates can be found at youtube.com/watch?v=D7XPX9mh64E. “The next step is up to you,” Cha said. “If you haven’t registered yet, you can still register to vote online through October 24. Remember same-day registration is available in person through election day on November 5.” The League of Women Voters of Piedmont is a women-led political grassroots network and membership organization. Members of the Piedmont City Council are volunteers who serve without compensation. The term office is four years, and may be extended through re-election to one additional term of four years.
articles.title: LWV hosts virtual forum with city, school candidates

articles.text: On October 1, the Piedmont League of Women Voters hosted a one hour virtual forum for the three school board candidates vying for three open seats on the Piedmont School Board in the November 5 election. For decades the League has hosted in-person forums for city and school elections. Due to concerns of recent outbreaks of Covid cases, the League chose to have a virtual candidates forum. Piedmont School Board candidates Michael Malione, Susy Struble and Max Roman were joined by moderator Jennifer Nixon, a member of the LWV. Nixon asked pre-selected questions from the community to each candidate, and candidates were given 90 seconds to answer. One question was “Piedmont students face myriad social pressures. How do you think the Board of Education can best address student mental and physical wellness while providing a rigorous education?” Struble answered the question by stating the topic of a “toxic achievement culture,” in Piedmont is well documented. She referenced last year’s PHS Valedictorian, Jasper Zietlow’s speech at graduation. “Basically he said ‘I lost a lot by working so hard just to get, what? Just so I could stand up here and be Valedictorian?’ Our students know that, but they work in a world that functions differently, that puts a lot of pressure on them,” said Struble. Another question was, “If measure P passes, how do you think the funds should be allocated? For example what percentage should be dedicated to teacher salaries?” and why what other items, if any, should Measure P fund?” Nixon also asked, “How can the board of education help make Piedmont schools safe and supportive places for members of the LGBTQ community as students teachers and staff?” Candidate Max Roman began his reply with the following. “I think that sometimes what people want is grand gestures and I think that those are fine and good sometimes, but I think that what really makes people feel included is when everyone includes people every day on a day-to-day basis,” said Roman. “I think that there need to be clear policies around behavior, that are fairly applied and clear to everyone, so that people are encouraged to be themselves and to bring themselves to school,” Roman added. The three candidates, all Piedmont parents, have clear paths onto the board. pages.text: Wednesday, October 16, 2024 3 LWV hosts virtual forum with city, school candidates By Andrew Fortin-Caldera The Piedmont League of Women Voters held a virtual forum on October 1 with three of the four candidates vying for two spots on the city council. Participating were incumbent Conna McCarthy, James Green, and Lorrel Plimier. Candidate Nancy Bostrom did not participate. The forum, designed as educational and not a debate, provided the candidates with a platform to provide opening statements and answer a series of seven questions posed by moderator Kathleen Cha, president of the Bay Area League of Women Voters. “You are here today to make smart choices when you vote,” Cha said to viewers of the virtual forum. “It’s important for the League to give the community a voice, and that is why we invited the community to send these questions for the candidates in advance.” The questions included: What measures could the city of Piedmont take to combat crime? How will the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan affect evacuation plans in areas impacted by construction? What incentives could the city consider to improve conservation efforts? What are your opinions on expanding commercial businesses in the city? What lessons can be learned from Piedmont’s ongoing project to build a new community pool? Candidates were each given 90 seconds to deliver their positions on the questions posed by the moderator, and a recording of the League’s forum with the City Council candidates can be found at youtube.com/watch?v=D7XPX9mh64E. “The next step is up to you,” Cha said. “If you haven’t registered yet, you can still register to vote online through October 24. Remember same-day registration is available in person through election day on November 5.” The League of Women Voters of Piedmont is a women-led political grassroots network and membership organization. Members of the Piedmont City Council are volunteers who serve without compensation. The term office is four years, and may be extended through re-election to one additional term of four years. LWV forum for School Board candidates By Jay Russell On October 1, the Piedmont League of Women Voters hosted a one hour virtual forum for the three school board candidates vying for three open seats on the Piedmont School Board in the November 5 election. For decades the League has hosted in-person forums for city and school elections. Due to concerns of recent outbreaks of Covid cases, the League chose to have a virtual candidates forum. Piedmont School Board candidates Michael Malione, Susy Struble and Max Roman were joined by moderator Jennifer Nixon, a member of the LWV. Nixon asked pre-selected questions from the community to each candidate, and candidates were given 90 seconds to answer. One question was “Piedmont students face myriad social pressures. How do you think the Board of Education can best address student mental and physical wellness while providing a rigorous education?” Struble answered the question by stating the topic of a “toxic achievement culture,” in Piedmont is well documented. She referenced last year’s PHS Valedictorian, Jasper Zietlow’s speech at graduation. “Basically he said ‘I lost a lot by working so hard just to get, what? Just so I could stand up here and be Valedictorian?’ Our students know that, but they work in a world that functions differently, that puts a lot of pressure on them,” said Struble. Another question was, “If measure P passes, how do you think the funds should be allocated? For example what percentage should be dedicated to teacher salaries?” and why what other items, if any, should Measure P fund?” Nixon also asked, “How can the board of education help make Piedmont schools safe and supportive places for members of the LGBTQ community as students teachers and staff?” Candidate Max Roman began his reply with the following. “I think that sometimes what people want is grand gestures and I think that those are fine and good sometimes, but I think that what really makes people feel included is when everyone includes people every day on a day-to-day basis,” said Roman. “I think that there need to be clear policies around behavior, that are fairly applied and clear to everyone, so that people are encouraged to be themselves and to bring themselves to school,” Roman added. The three candidates, all Piedmont parents, have clear paths onto the board. Despite the lack of urgency to win a seat, each candidate respected the opportunity presented by the League to express their views, not for gaining votes, but for educated voting and for the sake of healthy discussion. articles.text: Piedmont resident Les Ellis wasn’t born here. Over coffee recently at La Farine on Piedmont Avenue, the 87-year-old founder of the Strive for Change Foundation talked about his childhood growing up near the Richmond shipyards. “I grew up in a low-income family. When we arrived in the Bay Area, we qualified for an apartment in ‘war housing’. We eventually moved out because the buildings were being demolished.” Despite what some might call a disadvantaged beginning, Les received encouragement and support from his parents, family friends, church members and teachers. Later he was helped by mentors and colleagues. “Today I enjoy a level of success that neither my mom and dad, nor I, could have imagined in our war housing days.” In 2006, at a time when most of his contemporaries were planning to retire, Les made up his mind to create an organization that could help people like him. David K. Shipler’s award winning book from 2004, “The Working Poor: Invisible in America” was an inspiration. As Shipler made clear in this powerful study, the working poor are engaged in the activity most respected in American tradition – hard, honest work. But their version of the American Dream is no dream: low-paying, deadend jobs, the profound failure of government to improve on decaying housing, health care, and education; and the inability of families to break the patterns of social failure. These are the folks we encounter every day, for they do jobs that are essential to the American economy. Says Les, “Reading this book, I was struck by my conscience. That could have been my life too, but instead I was so extraordinarily lucky.” Unsure of the reasonableness of creating a charitable organization that would exclusively support non-profit job training programs in the East Bay, Les turned to the East Bay Community Foundation for advice. EBCF, founded in 1928, with over $590 million in assets under management and vast experience, said the program was not only viable but it was unique and they would help him get it launched. Les then sent a letter to 80 friends inviting them to join him. Their positive response and subsequent donations meant it was just a short time before the first two training programs were identified and $5,000 grants were made. In the eighteen years since its creation, the Strive for Change Foundation has given more than $1,420,000 to over twenty-five charitable organizations that help low-income East Bay residents improve their work and personal skills so they can move toward economic self-sufficiency. The organizations Strive supports are chosen carefully. The all-volunteer Board of Directors meets with program managers and Executive Directors annually to ask hard questions about budgets, and important outcomes such as graduation, job placements and retention rates. If the non-profit has achieved its goals, their grants are renewed for another year. And when an organization exceeds expectations by overIn 2006, Piedmont resident Les Ellis started the Strive For Change Foundation. Since then the organization has raised almost $1.5 million to help low-income East Bay residents improve their job skills. coming substantial challenges, their grant is increased. Today the Strive for Change Foundation supports nine local job-training organizations that change people’s lives. Les recalls, “I once read about a man who started with very little but through hard work, he became very successful. Upon his death, a friend observed that even when he reached the pinnacle of success, he ‘didn’t pull up the ladder.’ He remembered where he started and was generous in his encouragement and help to those who had not yet found success.” The Strive for Change Foundation extends that ladder to the people of this community who need and deserve a chance to achieve the dignity of a living wage. If you are interested in learning more about their work, please check their website, striveforchangefoundation.org.

articles.text: Staff photo A sign at Dracena Park advising area where dogs must be on leash. A reported uptick in unleashed dogs at Piedmont parks and public areas has prompted city police to remind residents and visitors to abide by ordinances mandated in the city code. Piedmont Police Capt. Chris Monahan said the department received a letter from a concerned citizen detailing what was described as “a notable increase” in the amount of dogs in the Piedmont parks for “offleash activities.” The report to police listed two separate incidents near the Piedmont Community Hall and at Coaches Field where the citizen came across unleashed, menacing dogs. No one was hurt in the interactions. Monahan said that the city of Piedmont includes codes that prohibit dogs being “at-large,” which the city defines as “not under restraint by leash, rope or chain. The City Code states “no owner or keeper of any dog shall cause or permit such dog to be or run at large upon any public place… unless such dog is securely restrained by a substantial leash not to exceed six feet in length and is under the charge and control of a person competent to keep such dog under effective charge and control.” The city code also notes that it is the duty of the police to impound and safely keep any animals that are found to be violating Piedmont’s leash laws.

articles.text: The annual Artisanal Beer Festival at the Piedmont Center for the Arts will include music on the front lawn while guests enjoy their freshly made German dinner. A trio of high school musicians – Deniz Radzik, Eric Verner and Maxim Miller – will perform jazz standards during the early part of the evening. Deniz Radzik’s father was a musician, and Deniz started playing violin in 4th grade, and ended up playing percussion and drums in the middle school concert and jazz band. As he entered high school he played with several California jazz conservatory bands. Eric Venner also comes from a musical family. His mother sang in the choir at Boston University where she met Eric’s father, who sang in the Stanford A Capela group. Eric started playing classical guitar at age eight. He switched to blues, jazz, and funk guitar at age 12 in middle school, and now is part of the PHS jazz combo. Maximo Miller started playing piano at age seven with the encouragement of his parents, and switched to jazz when he was 12. He plays in the high school jazz band, and gigs around the area with the sophomore combo. Guests will not hear traditional Bavarian music at the beer festival, but will be serenaded with the sounds of the high school jazz trio. This year’s Beer Festival takes place this Friday from 5:30-7:30 p.m. Tickets can be purchased in advance at pcabeerfestival. eventbrite.com, and are available at the door.

articles.text: Part 5 in a series future success, such as the way we cover math throughout all the grades, starting in elementary. Our weekly questionnaire series for local election candidates enters the fifth week. This week, one question was sent out on Thursday and candidates were asked to limit their answers to 200 words. School Board 3 open seats; 3 candidates Week 5 Question Do you think the rigor of the curriculum in Piedmont schools is consistent with parent expectations? Please explain, with specific examples. MICHAEL MALIONE, Candidate Piedmont schools do an excellent job providing a well-rounded, comprehensive education, with our standardized testing outcomes placing us in the top three statewide. That said, we must always evaluate the efficacy of the educational experience we offer in terms of 1) how well it lines up with the needs and interests of our students, and 2) how well it prepares our students to succeed in their next level of instruction, which for 94% of them is college. Where parents have expressed dissatisfaction, there’s a perception that PUSD has focused on merely achieving state standards, without enough differentiation for learners at different levels. With over 80% of our students meeting or exceeding the standards, there is going to be a fairly wide variation among them. To address prior practices that have proven to be inadequate, the district has focused on literacy. Elementary teachers are now receiving advanced training and will soon implement a new curriculum. This is a great example of how we can improve curriculum rigor. Time and money are limited, so it’s crucial to focus on the areas most important to students’ SUSY STRUBLE, Candidate Ideally, I could answer based on high-quality survey data. Even more insightful would be coupling parent input with survey data from teachers – the professionals who directly engage with students – and recent PHS graduates, whose feedback would be invaluable, as I mentioned in last week’s Q&A. However, based on informal conversations with a small, non-representative sample of Piedmont parents, it seems most are generally satisfied with the rigor of PUSD’s curriculum. Many parents also appear pleased with PUSD teaching practices, which are critical in bringing curriculum to life. That said, I have heard concerns. Some relate to the curriculum, but some go beyond to other aspects of learning. For example: K-12: Parents have expressed a desire for more developmentally appropriate, genuinely engaging learning opportunities focused on anti-bigotry and anti-racism. Middle School (and beyond): There have been questions about the effectiveness of the CPM curriculum, which teaches Common Core math standards, and a desire for stronger Arts programming High School: Some parents would like to see more hands-on engineering experiences, a greater emphasis on academic writing, and more AP Courses (e.g. AP Capstone Diploma Program). MAX ROMAN, Candidate I think by and large our schools do a great job preparing students for the requirements of college and the world beyond. I think that in certain cases, due to the smaller size of our district, there will be students who want to take classes that don’t make sense for Piedmont to offer, and in those cases I am in favor of those students being able to take them at community colleges for PHS credit.

articles.text: While the pursuit of meaning is often associated with adulthood, research suggests that the foundation for a meaningful life is laid much earlier—during childhood and adolescence. A sense of meaning in life is linked to numerous positive outcomes. • 52% higher levels of life satisfaction • Twice as likely to report psychological well-being in young adulthood • 31% higher GPAs on average • 45% more resilient in the face of challenges • 47% demonstrated better social relationships with peers and family members • 30% less likely to experience depression in adulthood • 28% reduction in risky sexual behaviors among teens with high meaning in life • 72% of young adults with high meaning scores chose careers aligned with their core values • 42% higher levels of compassion and 37% higher levels of gratitude • 155% less likely to engage in substance abuse Developing a sense of meaning helps young people navigate the complexities of growing up; it provides them with a compass, guiding their decisions and actions in a way that promotes well-being and fulfillment. The Peril of a Life Without Meaning Dr. Bill Damon, a leading researcher on purpose and adolescence at Stanford, succinctly states, “The biggest problem growing up today is not actually stress, it’s meaninglessness.” Without a sense of purpose, young people may struggle with decision-making, goal-setting, and navigating the challenges of transitioning to adulthood. This can have both long-lasting effects on their personal and professional lives, as well as presently: • Teens with low meaning in life were 2.1 times more likely to report feelings of social isolation • Adolescents reporting low meaning in life were 40% more likely to experience sleep disturbances • Adolescents with low meaning in life were 2.3 times more likely to develop internet addiction • Teens reporting low meaning in life had 55% higher levels of chronic stress as measured by cortisol levels • Adolescents with low meaning in life scores were 2.8 times more likely to develop disordered eating patterns • Adolescents reporting low meaning in life were 3.1 times more likely to engage in non-suicidal self-injury • Teens with low meaning in life were 2.5 times more likely to engage in regular binge drinking The Path for a Life with Meaning cultivate meaning, we can significantly improve their mental health and overall well-being. So, how can parents, educators, and communities help young people cultivate a meaningful life? Research points to four critical components: agency, hope, self-esteem, and openness to experience. Agency Agency empowers children to see themselves as active participants in their own lives; it builds confidence and a sense of ownership over their journey. Allow children to make age-appropriate decisions, emphasize the power of choice in difficult situations, and allow them to take responsibility for the outcomes • Broaden Choices: when there are seemingly only a couple or few, work to come up with a dozen instead • Respect Their Opinions: Actively listen to their thoughts and feelings without immediate judgment or correction. This validates their ability to think independently. • Offer Choices Daily: Allow your child to make decisions in everyday situations. For example, let them choose what to have for dinner from a selection of healthy options or decide how to organize their study schedule.
articles.title: A meaningful life starts in childhood

articles.text: Photo by Carolyn Pan The Freeman family visits with Giant Jack. Dad Crosby, with three year old son Spencer and mom Jessica with seven-week old Sophia. The Wildwood Dads Club Pumpkin Patch has been kept busy with pre-Halloween sales. So far they have sold 2,500 pumpkins and earned $20,000 in sales after two weeks, $3,000 ahead of last year’s pace. In addition to the classic orange carving pumpkins, this year’s top sellers include the Sparkler Long Stem pumpkin, French pumpkins, and Decorative Mini Pumpkins. “We’ve also introduced a new edible row, and the cheese pumpkin (aka Libby) is flying off the shelves! It’s absolutely delicious,” said Patch Papa Matt Derrigo. “Russ Griffith roasted one and let me try it. It’s hands down better than any pumpkin puree I’ve ever tasted. It would be amazing in ravioli, bread, or pumpkin pie,” he said. Visitors to the patch have continued to guess the weight of Giant Jack, the huge pumpkin in the middle of the patch. They have received around 170 guesses so far, with weights ranging wildly from 168 lbs to a whopping 4,385 pounds. “Without a doubt, Giant Jack remains a major attraction. Families are flocking in for photos with the big guy,” confirmed Derrigo. artwork from local kids who have traded a coloring sheet, of their own versions of Jack, for a free pumpkin. Kids received coloring sheets in Piedmont schools, and can also print out their own at Tinyurl.com/WWDC pumpkin The patch has also received Vera from Wildwood School made a pumpkin drawing and turned it into the patch to earn a free personal Wee-B-Little pumpkin.
articles.title: Wildwood Dads continue to dish out pumpkins

articles.text: St. Paul’s Episcopal Church in Oakland will have a Requiem Mass for All Souls’ Day on Friday, November 1, at 6:30 p.m. The choir will perform Maurice Duruflé’s Requiem, Op. 9 with organ and orchestra under the direction of Music Director Benjamin Bachmann. Everyone is invited to the Requiem Mass at which we will celebrate the lives of all the beloved departed. Maurice Duruflé’s Requiem Mass is one of the 20th century’s most outstanding compositions and his most acclaimed work. It is based on the chant of the Latin Requiem Mass, a compositional practice which Duruflé helped to revive in modern times. The church will be illuminated with candles, and votive candles will be available for individuals to light. You are invited to submit the names of loved ones to be held in remembrance and listed in the service sheet. Send to admin@ stpaulsoakland.org. You may bring photographs or mementoes of loved ones to place on a table near the altar rail before the service begins. For more information go to stpaulsoakland.org. St. Paul’s Episcopal Church is located at 114 Montecito Avenue by Lake Merritt.
articles.title: All Souls’ Day Requiem Mass

articles.text: Piedmont Community Church will host a free showing on October 25 of the documentary film, Join or Die. Directed by Pete and Rebecca Davis, the film explains to viewers the benefits of joining a club or being part of an organization. The movie will be shown in the Church sanctuary at 400 Highland Ave. at 7 p.m. on Friday, October 25. “At a time when American society is more and more fractured – and our politics are increasingly fractious – the need for people to get together with others in face-toface groups has never been stronger,” said Rev. Don Ashburn. The film follows the journey of social scientist Robert Putnam, whose groundbreaking research, titled Bowling Alone: The Collapse and Revival of American Community, examines America’s decades-long decline in community connections. For more information contact Don Ashburn at Don@Piedmont Church.org.
articles.title: Community Church to host free film screening on Oct. 25

The centerpieces of Havens’ collection were 162 large Russian pieces featured at the 1904 St. Louis Exposition. After the St. Louis Exposition the paintings were appraised at low value to dodge custom fees for storing in Canada. Havens purchased them from Canada at a fraction of their full value. The gallery had curators who gave visitors the feel of a proper museum. Havens’ son, Syed Havens, and sister-in-law Carrie Sterling curated the Piedmont vault along with artist Richard Partington. In addition to the Russian pieces the curators began highlighting the emerging Californian impressionist. William Keith’s massive oil painting “The California Alps” was located in the main gallery. John Muir, a lifelong friend of Keith, referred to this piece as “The bible of the Sierras. Painting by the notable R.D. Yelland, Thaddeus Welch, James Gamble and Charles Rollo Peters were also included. Xavier Martinez and Gordon Courts, both Piedmont residents, also had paintings in the gallery. In 1907 Laura Prather Waterbury said of the gallery, “I doubted the ability of one man, unaided as far as I knew, to collect enough art and the kind of art that would hold the attention of both the public and connoisseurs. The exhibit seen in Piedmont is undoubtedly the best permanent display of paintings ever seen on the Pacific Coast.” When Frank Havens died in 1918, the gallery was closed and the paintings were auctioned off. Some went to private collectors, and the new Oakland Art museum. Many were purchased for the deYoung Museum, just being built in San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park. Yelland, Thaddeus Welch, James Gamble and Charles Rollo Peters were also included. Xavier Martinez and Gordon Courts, both Piedmont residents, also had paintings in the gallery. In 1907 Laura Prather Waterbury said of the gallery, “I doubted the ability of one man, unaided as far as I knew, to collect enough art and the kind of art that would hold the attention of both the public and connoisseurs. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. articles.text: Photo by Karen Tsoi Piedmont cross-country runners stand proudly with their first-place medals and plaque. Pictured are Mara Kemp-Malone (left), Amalia Gray, Cora Chun, Caroline Taylor, Leighton Mand, Gladwin Horsley, and Skylar Best Piedmont High’s girls’ team continued its strong season, claiming the top spot in the 45th annual Clovis Invitational at Woodward Park in the small school division. With a score of 44, the Highlanders topped St. Mary’s of Berkeley, Colfax, Marin Catholic, and Nipomo. “The girls’ team had a successful day, claiming first place as a team in the small school race. Despite a few of the girls being sick or not feeling well, they persevered and worked together as a team, running in a close pack and finishing strong,” said coach Steve Zirkelbach. Skylar Best, who was named the Post’s’ honorable mention for Athlete of Month in September, continued her strong pace. She led the way for Piedmont on the 5K course, clocking a time of 20:47.6 to finish fifth of 117 runners. Trailing Best was sophomore Amalia Gray in seventh with a time of 21:06.5. Her time was a personal record by one minute, 41 seconds. Rounding out Piedmont’s top five runners was junior Cora Chun placing ninth in 21.28.4, sophomore Leighton Mand 11th in 21:34.5, and senior Carolina Taylor close behind in 12th, 21:36.9. Mand, notably, was dealing with a cold on race-day. We named her our Athlete of the Week last week. Staff photos Skylar Best led Piedmont’s harriers with a fifth place finish at the Clovis Invitational. “Leighton Mand was sick but was still able to pull through for an 11th place finish. She is a fierce competitor and not even a little sickness can keep her from finding a way to excel,” Zirkelbach said. Boys’ team The. PHS boys’ team finished 27th in the small-school blue division. Sophomore Sebastien Swain was the top runner for PHS, placing 74th of 200 runners in 16:57.9. Next in was junior Noah Sohn in 120th in 17:38, sophomore Thomas Ero placing 159th in 18:19.5, while Oliver Horsley rounded things out in 175th, 18:54.8. “Sebastien Swain led the way and sophomore Noah Sohn also had a strong performance. Thomas Ero and Alex Schleuning were not far behind as well,” Zirkelbach said. Piedmont has a busy week ahead with two meets in a few days. They’ll run at Hayward High for its second Western Alameda County Conference meet of the season tomorrow, October 16, before returning to Hayward three days later on Saturday, October 19 for the 41st P. Wilder Mariner Invitational. NEXT UP Piedmont’s WACC meet is tomorrow at 3:30 p.m., while the Wilder Mariner Invitational is Saturday, October 19 at 8:30 a.m. Staff photos Leighton Mand (3375), Caroline Taylor (left) and Gladwin Horsley run in a tight pack at the Clovis Invitational.
articles.title: Girls’ cross-country team wins Clovis Invitational
