articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team High continued its dominance over Encinal, beating the Jets 20-12 in Alameda on Tuesday, October 8. It improves Piedmont’s record to 12-6 and 3-1 in the Western Alameda County Conference with just two matches left in the regular season. PHS has now defeated Encinal in its last 11 meetings going back to 2015. In another big performance Rylan Patty, the freshman scored seven goals. The Highlanders look ahead to facing Alameda on tomorrow, October 17, and Bishop O’Dowd on October 22. Piedmont notably defeated Alameda in last year’s D2 NCS Championship, but lost to the Hornets 12-8 in an early-season tournament on August 31. Following the regular season, Piedmont will compete in the WACC Tournament starting on Monday, October 28. Match Recap Piedmont led 7-3 by the end of the first quarter and took a commanding 13-4 advantage by halftime. PHS put up five more goals in the third quarter and only allowed three to lead 18-7 going into the fourth, where they sent in four more. In the first quarter, Piedmont scored the first three goals of the game to lead 3-0 by the 4:14 mark with a goal by Zach Dupree and a pair of scores by Henry Stein, including the game’s opening goal in just 12 seconds. Leo Hurwitz then made it 4-1 with 3:23 on the clock to make it 4-1, then he scored again with 1:47 left. PHS had two goals in the final minute with Stein with 46 seconds, followed by Hurwitz after forcing a turnover with five Photos by Lynne Wright Freshman Rylan Patty led the way with seven goals against Encinal. Leo Hurwitz scored four goals on Encinal. seconds left, 7-3. Piedmont continuously scored in the second quarter with five straight until allowing one in the final seconds. Rylan Patty scored by way of a penalty after 44 seconds, then he scored again with 4:07 on the clock. Charlie Wright scored just 30 seconds later, followed by Patty’s next goal with 2:05 before halftime. Hurwitz then scored with 40 seconds left. Patty made it 13-4 with nine seconds left. Henry Stein also scored four goals against the Jets. PHS put up three more to start the third quarter to lead 16-4 at the five-minute mark with two goals by Patty and one by Wright. After three goals by Encinal, Dupree made it 17-7 at 2:26. Patty made it 18-7 with 21 seconds left. Nicholas Riordan scored for Piedmont to open the fourth quarter at 5:23, while Stein scored their final goal with 1:41 remaining. Final scorers: Patty had seven goals. Hurwitz and Stein had four goals. Wright and Dupree scored twice. Riordan scored once. Tuesday vs. Berkeley Piedmont traveled to Berkeley on Tuesday, October 15. See next week’s Post for match details. NEXT UP Piedmont (12-6 overall, 3-1 league) takes on Alameda at the Encinal pool on Thursday, October 17 at 5:00 p.m. They also play Bishop O’Dowd at the Trefethen Aquatic Center at of Northeastern University, formerly Mills College, on Tuesday, October 22 at 5:00 p.m.
articles.title: Highlanders fly past Jets, 20-12

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ tennis team came away with a big win over rival Bishop O’Dowd on Thursday, October 10. They dominated their Western Alameda County Conference foes 6-1 at the Corey Reich Tennis Center in Piedmont. Piedmont has four matches remaining in its regular season as it looks to secure a berth in the North Coast Section postseason. “That brings our Foothill record up to .500. We need to stay at least even to qualify for NCS, so we need to keep up the good play,” coach Jim Landes said. At 2-2, PHS’ final matches include their second meetings against Castro Valley, Alameda, Berkeley, and O’Dowd. Of the group, Piedmont had narrow losses to Berkeley and Alameda. PHS will host Castro Valley this Thursday, October 17 at 3:30 p.m. when it honors the four seniors on the roster for Senior Night: Emma Eisemon, Carolina Romanczuk, Emma Eisemon, and Alina Shahid. Match Day Recap Piedmont won three of four singles matches and swept all three at doubles. At singles, Kate Jumper won a three-set match at the No. 2 spot after dropping the first set and battling back to a strong final two sets, 4-6, 6-3, 6-2. Arianna Kortum won 6-3, 6-2 at No. 3, while Faith Chin played to a clean 6-4, 6-2 win at No. 4. Piedmont’s only loss on the afternoon was Carolina Romanczuk who lost at No. 1 against Ashley Carroll, 6-3, 6-2. “Kate lost her first set against but rebounded with very steady play to take the next two sets handily. Arianna recovered from her illness and played a great match. Carolina had had a rough day at number one against Ashley, who played like a backboard by how she was returning Carolina’s shots,” Landes said. At doubles, Samantha Huynh and Emma Eisemon won at the top spot in straight sets, 7-5, 6-3. Emma Chan and Maddie Tran won a three-set battle at No. 2, winning by scores of 4-6, 6-3, 6-2. Inara Mehta and Abigail Call also won in straight sets after a narrow first-set battle, 7-5, 6-3. “Sam and Emma E continued their strong play. After warming up in the first set, they took the second 6-3. The same was true for Inara and Abby at number three. Emma C and Maddie found their stride after losing a close first set. Emma was hitting some strong ground strokes which enabled Maddie to finish for points at the net,” Landes said. NEXT UP Piedmont (7-9 overall) hosts Castro Valley at home tomorrow, Thursday, October 17 at 3:30 p.m. Staff Photos Emma Eisemon helped reel in a win at No. 1 doubles against Bishop O’Dowd with doubles partner Samantha Huynh. Kate Jumper won a three-set match against Bishop O’Dowd at No. 2 singles.

articles.text: Piedmont’s flag football team suffered a 22-6 loss to Encinal. Piedmont High’s flag football team suffered a 22-6 loss at Encinal on Thursday, October 10. It marked Piedmont’s second game of the season against the Jets, where they played significantly better than a 69-12 loss on September 17. PHS was notably without top receiver Dorothy Nemeth. “I thought we played well. We stayed in the game, especially after the first time we played them. They never looked behind and I appreciate that tonight. Dorothy wasn’t here and she’s a main go-to at receiver, so our quarterback Edie Elmquist found her other weapons,” coach Beth Black said. One bright spot continues to be the pass rushing presence by Elspeth Grippando. She recorded three sacks against Encinal and is proving to be a nuisance for opposing quarterbacks. “Elpeth keeps getting stronger. articles.text: After coming off a threegame win streak, Piedmont JV Scots traveled to Hayward High on Friday, October 11 for its first away game of the season. Dealing with multiple injuries, Piedmont lost 28-8 while playing on unfamiliar ground. The first half of the game was rough for the Highlanders. After being held to no yards on the first drive, the Highlanders were forced to punt. The Farmers scored on their first drive on a pass over the middle. After an interception thrown by Piedmont, the Farmers jumped out to a 21-0 lead by halftime. Coming out of the locker room, the Highlanders showed energy to try and get back into the game. On the Farmers’ first play of the second half, sophomore defensive back Owen Curran snatched an interception, taking it back to the house for a 30 yard pick-six. It marked Curran’s third interception on the season and first touchdown. Starting quarterback Jimmy Lagios had to leave the action in the first half due to a head injury, with backup quarterback Jonah Cha-Foster taking over. He helped convert the two-point conversion on a pass to Max Fujimoto. Although the Highlanders had a glimpse of hope, the rest of the second half was not enough to overtake the Farmers They allowed one more touchdown in the final minutes. Injuries proved to be a factor: Three of the four captains were forced to sit out most of the second half. George Saunders suffered a wrist injury, and Fujimoto also had to exit the game. articles.text: An exhibit of painter Mary Lovelace O’Neal’s first return to the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art in 45 years remains open until Sunday, October 20. The solo exhibition, “New Work: Mary Lovelace O’Neal,” opened on March 16. In a career spanning six decades, O’Neal has used unorthodox materials and color to show both abstraction and figuration. Her paintings blend worlds of personal details and shared historical narratives, from her beloved dachshund Tillie to her involvement in the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee. Her early works from the 1960s utilized “lampblack” pigment — powdered soot made from burning oil, which she rubbed into her canvases. She used this technique to address three subjects at the fore of art and culture at that moment, which she has described as “surface flatness, black as a color, and blackness as an existential, racial experience.” O’Neal would then inscribe the velvety black expanses with materials including paint, gasoline, masking tape and glitter, introducing an element of play. In time, representational elements emerged from her abstractions, offering new narrative possibilities within a constellation of references across music, literature and social movements. In 1979, O’Neal was hired at the University of California, Berkeley, where she became the first African American professor awarded tenure in the Department of Art in 1985; she became chair of the department in 1999 and professor emerita in 2006. She now splits her time between Oakland and Mérida, Mexico, where her at currently on display was created. Although her paintings begin with a black background, color remains foundational to her practice. Describing the seven 7-foottall canvases on view in this exhibition, O’Neal said, “Painting with color was always a surprise … like dancing with the paint.” SFMOMA (151 Third Street in San Francusci) is open 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Friday through Tuesday, and 12 p.m. through 8 p.m. on Thursdays. Tickets ($30 general, $25 senior, $23 student, free 18 and younger) are available at sfmoma. org/visit. Mary Lovelace O’Neal, MARDI GRAS UMBRELLAS & FIREFLIES, 2021-23. This Sunday, October 20, is the last day of the artist’s SFMOMA solo exhibition.
articles.title: Mary Lovelace O’Neal exhibit at SFMOMA closes on Sunday

articles.text: San Francisco’s de Young Museum will be the sole West Coast venue for the exhibition “Art and War in the Renaissance” this Saturday through January 12. The exhibit will feature monumental tapestries and superb examples of arms and armor on loan from the Capodimonte Museum in Naples, Italy. The dazzling centerpiece will be the newly conserved, complete seven-part cycle of the “Battle of Pavia” tapestries. These colossal woven artworks will immerse visitors in the world of Renaissance politics, history, and art. These tapestries will be on view with original preparatory drawings lent by the Louvre Museum, alongside a selection of 16th and 17th century arms and armor from the Farnese Armory at the Capodimonte Museum. Combined, the works will give visitors insight into the artistry and craftsmanship required to transform Renaissance tapestries from initial designs into glittering propagandistic luxuries. The “Battle of Pavia” tapestries celebrate the decisive victory of Holy Roman Emperor Charles V and the imperial army over the French army led by King Francis I. This decisive moment in European history took place five centuries ago on February 24, 1525, around the town of Pavia, outside Milan. The pivotal battle ended the Italian war, which had begun in 1521, and stopped the French from encroaching into Italian territories. “Monumental in scale, tapestries were the grandest form of art and propaganda in the Renaissance and kings and popes spent vast sums to commission them. Yet, few of these great sets have survived and even fewer are on display. The fact that the ‘Battle of Pavia’ tapestries have survived, complete and in good condition, is little short of extraordinary,” said Thomas P. Campbell, director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco and one of the world’s leading authorities on European tapestries. During the Renaissance, tapestries were the art form of kings, prized by rulers as lavish displays of wealth and power. The works were woven on a grand scale by vast workshops, using precious materials costing exponentially more than paintings. The grand “Battle of Pavia” tapestries were made with silver- and goldwrapped thread, interwoven with expensive wool and silk from across the globe. The manufacture of tapestries was a huge collaborative endeavor and necessitated years of work to produce one set. A single panel of the “Battle of Pavia” tapestries would have taken roughly 18 months to create. “The scale of these tapestries is staggering, as is the sheer profusion of detail. You can find something new and exciting every time you look,” said Jeffrey Fraiman, Assistant Curator of European Decorative Arts and Sculpture, and organizing curator of the exhibition. “But it is also the freshness, the immediacy of them, that hits you,” he added. “These are half a millennium old, and their survival feels miraculous. I think audiences will be awestruck.” The de Young Museum (50 Hagiwara Tea Garden Drive, Golden Gate Park) is open from 9:30 a.m. to 5:15 p.m., Tuesday through Sunday. Tickets ($20 adult, $17 senior, $11 student, free under 18) are available at ticketing.famsf.org/events.
articles.title: Legendary “Battle of Pavia” tapestries come to de Young Museum Oct. 19

articles.text: In a first-ever trio tour, violinist Tessa Lark, cellist Joshua Roman and double bassist Edgar Meyer will perform the work of Meyer and J.S. Bach at UC Berkeley’s Hertz Hall this Sunday. Cal Performances at UC Berkeley presents the trio of Grammy-winning double bassist Edgar Meyer, genre-crossing violinist Tessa Lark and eclectic cellist Joshua Roman for a performance at Hertz Hall this Sunday, October 13 at 3 p.m. This new collaboration brings together three singular figures in American concert music — virtuoso instrumentalists with both strong classical backgrounds and deep connections to roots and fiddle music. The concert will open with J.S. Bach’s Sonata for Viola da Gamba in G Major, arranged specially for this string instrumentation. The trio will then perform the Bay Area premiere of Meyer’s new work, commissioned by Cal Performances, as well as his Trio 1986 and Trio 1988. This engagement is part of the trio’s first-ever tour. “In 1986 to 1988 I wrote a series of three string trios that I premiered at the Santa Fe Chamber Music Festival,” said Meyer. These were the first longer pieces that I had conceived as such, and they set the tone for my next four decades. After meeting Tessa Lark and Joshua Roman a few years ago, I realized that they were perfect for helping me document this personal milestone.” Violinist Tessa Lark is recognized for her mastery of both classical and bluegrass music. She was nominated for a 2020 Grammy in the Best Classical Instrumental Solo category and received one of the Lincoln Center’s prestigious emerging artist awards, the Hunt Family Award. She is the recipient of a Borletti– Buitoni Trust Fellowship, serves as Artistic Director of Musical Masterworks and co-hosts NPR’s classical podcast “From the Top.” Cellist and composer Joshua Roman is known for blending precision with improvisatory freedom. He has performed with leading orchestras worldwide and opened the 2017 TED Conference, where his performance of Bach’s solo Cello Suites became TED’s most-viewed event. His 2023–24 season included his role as the Las Vegas Philharmonic’s inaugural Artist in Residence, alongside performances with several U.S. symphony orchestras. Virtuoso and composer Edgar Meyer has carved out a unique niche in the musical world by bridging classical and Americana genres. Recognized with a MacArthur Award, he has performed and recorded extensively, including collaborations with Yo-Yo Ma, Chris Thile, Joshua Bell and Béla Fleck. Meyer’s compositions have been premiered by the Los Angeles Philharmonic, Boston Symphony Orchestra, Detroit Symphony Orchestra and Minnesota Orchestra, while his genre-bending recordings, such as “The Goat Rodeo Sessions,” have garnered critical acclaim and Grammy Awards. Tickets ($68) for the performance at UC Berkeley’s Hertz Hall (101 Cross-Sproul Path) are available at calperformances.org, or by phone at 642-9988.
articles.title: Cal Performances brings string trio to Berkeley Oct. 20

articles.text: As the well-to-do Birlings celebrate an engagement in the family, the festive evening is punctured by an uninvited visitor: an inspector looking into a young woman’s death, in the whodunnit, An Inspector Calls, at San Jose’s City Lights Theatre this weekend. The final performance is Sunday, October 20. Questions multiply and guilt mounts as Inspector Goole’s grim revelations begin to crack the foundations of the Birlings’ comfortable lives. Before long, they are all challenged to examine their decisions and consciences in J.B. Priestley’s timeless drama. Eric Birling (played by Myles Kenyon Rowland) is affected by the dark revelations in J.B. Priestley’s thriller An Inspector Calls, closing at San Jose’s City Lights Theatre this Sunday, October 20. Filled with Hitchcockian suspense, this production brings back acclaimed director Mark Anderson Phillips (Blithe Spirit, Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde) to the City Lights stage. As the U.S. nears the 2024 presidential election, this play is especially timely. Besides being a taut thriller, it’s also “a passionate plea for a more just and compassionate society,” according to The Guardian. Written by the English playwright, novelist and journalist J.B. Priestley, An Inspector Calls is one of his many compelling stories that take seemingly ordinary people in home or office settings and illustrate universally human issues of compassion. After debuting in the Soviet Union in 1945, “An Inspector Calls” opened at the New Theatre in London in 1946. It has reaped considerable praise with numerous revivals and regional productions over the decades. Tickets ($31-$70) at City Lights (529 S. Second Street, San Jose) are available online at cltc. org, or by phone at 408-295-4200.
articles.title: An Inspector Calls at City Lights Theatre this weekend

articles.text: This Sunday, October 20, will be the last chance to see the West Coast premiere of Mexodus, the musical which is opening Berkeley Repertory Theatre’s 2024- 2025 season. Me xodu s explores t he often-untold stories of the Underground Railroad that led south into Mexico during the Civil War in the 1860s. History meets hip-hop in this electrifying story of resilience, resistance and Black-Latino solidarity, composed by multi-talented writer-performers Brian Quijada and Nygel D. Robinson. “I’m thrilled to bring Mexodus to Berkeley Rep and introduce our audience to the incredible artistry of Brian Quijada and Nygel D. Robinson,” said director David Mendizábal. “Their technical prowess and the passion they bring to the stage each night is sure to entertain and excite audiences,” he added. “In a moment where our country is Nygel D. Robinson and Brian Quijada in Mexodus, a musical that premieres at Berkeley Repertory Theatre. The show closes this Sunday, October 20. experiencing such division, I hope that this story about the power of reaching across divides to support the liberation of each other will fill our audiences with hope.” “As we enter into a season of change in this country, we hope that this show can play a part in combating divisive extremist ideologies,” said Quijada and Robinson. “We want to welcome audiences into our world with the hope that we will all be a little kinder when we walk out of the theater.” Tickets ($22.50+) and showtimes for performances at Berkeley Rep (2025 Addison Street) are available online at berkeleyrep. org, or by phone at 647-2949.
articles.title: Mexodus closes at Berkeley Rep Oct. 20

articles.text: Shotgun Players’ newest production Choir Boy is onstage through October 20 at the Ashby Stage in Berkeley. The play follows main character Pharus, who attends an all-boys preparatory school and is the lead singer for their renowned choir. He is open about his queer identity while also questioning long-held traditions. The show includes arrangements of traditional African American spirituals and dance in Choir Boy, with Tony Award-winning vocal arrangements by Jason Michael Webb. The cast includes Wesley Barker, Chachi Delgado, Miles Meckling, Brandon DiPaola, Fred Pitts, Malcolm Rodgers, William Schmidt and Omar Stewart. For a list of showtimes and to purchase tickets, visit https://shotgunplayers.org/.

articles.text: Berkeley Symphony will open its 2024–25 season with a concert at Zallerbach Hall on the UC Berkeley campus on Sunday, November 10 at 4 p.m. The concert will be dedicated to composer Gordon Getty for his long and significant support of the symphony. After the opening concert, the symphony will honor Getty at the Opening Night Dinner fundraising event. Getty has supported Berkeley Symphony for over 25 years, and made a gift of $1.5 million in 2023 to ensure the symphony’s stability as the organization navigated the difficult challenges of rebuilding after the pandemic. The opening concert – the first in a series of four – is titled Stories From Home. The opening program of Berkeley Symphony’s 53rd season answers the question, “‘What does a story sound like?’ “It sounds like Leonard Bernstein’s jazzy, syncopated Symphonic Dances from West Side Story: you can hear the streets of New York and feel the longing of star-crossed lovers,” said Berkeley Symphony Music Director Joseph Young. “It sounds like the whispering breeze of Samuel Barber’s Knoxville: Summer of 1915, or like the crashing of waves in Silvestre Revueltas’s Redes Suite, or the violin soaring over the orchestra, as it does in Kris Bowers’ concerto For A Younger Self.” Stories From Home will showcase soprano Lisa Delan in Samuel Barber’s Knoxville: Summer of 1915. Delan has performed, commissioned and recorded music by Philip Glass, Jake Heggie, John Corigliano, and Gordon Getty. Grammy-winning violinist Charles Yang will perform in the Bay Area premiere of For A Younger Self by Kris Bowers. Yang has performed as a soloist throughout the United States, Europe, Brazil, Russia, China and Taiwan. In 2016 he became the violinist and lead singer of the multi-genre string band “Time for Three,” which won the 2023 Grammy Award for Best Classical Instrumental Solo. “This is music that takes you somewhere, that grabs hold, and puts you in a specific time and place,” Yang said. Leonard Bernstein’s Symphonic Dances from West Side Story and Silvestre Revueltas’s Redes Suite round out the symphony’s exploration of North America’s cultural and musical heritage. Created in 1971, the Berkeley Symphony is committed to performing, premiering and commissioning new music. Subscriptions and single tickets and tickets to the Opening Night Dinner fundraising event are available at berkeleysymphony.org or by phone at (510) 841-2800. Berkeley Symphony, headed by Music Director Joseph Young, will perform its opening concert at Zellerbach Hall on November 10.
articles.title: Berkeley Symphony to honor Gordon Getty in season-opening concert Nov. 10

articles.text: This Sunday at 4:30 p.m., the piano trio In the Tradition — featuring Bill Jackman, Michael Jones and Dr. Albert Brooks — will play a tribute to Jimmy van Heusen at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. Van Heusen composed nearly 1,000 songs between 1930 and 1970, of which at least 50 have become American standards. Many Americans have heard of classic popular music composers like George Gershwin, Cole Porter and Hoagy Carmichael; although van Heusen doesn’t share their name recognition among the general public, he was every bit their equal. He certainly lays claim to this fame among the jazz musicians who continue to play the many timeless tunes that he composed. These songs include jazz standards such as “Polka Dots and Moonbeams” (1940) and “Like Someone in Love” (1944). Although van Heusen wrote music mainly for film and the stage, his rich use of melody, harmony and complex bass lines makes his work ideal for jazz musicians like pianist Jackman, bassist Jones and drummer Brooks. The musical format of the jazz piano trio, which developed during the modern jazz era of the 1940s and 1950s, flourished in Oakland and the East Bay during the 1950s, most famously with the Dave Brubeck trio — but has since nearly disappeared. In fact, In the Tradition is the last classic jazz piano trio — with a piano, bass and drums — still active in the East Bay. Bill Jackman, playing with the trio for the past 30 years, was a student of the late Oakland jazz pianist Art Fletcher, who for several decades presided over the grand piano at the former Solomon Grundy’s (now Skates) on the Berkeley Marina. Jackman is also a Lupita Records musician who has recorded six CDs in the piano trio format. Michael Jones is a bassist and band leader who has played throughout the Bay Area for over 30 years. After studying music at the University of Northern Colorado, he moved to the Bay Area in the mid-1970s, where he played with many icons including Al Tanner, Faye Carroll, Ed Kelley, Donald Bailey, Pharoah Sanders and Buddy Montgomery. As a sideman and bandleader, Jones has served as the music director for the Golden Gate Library Summer Concert and Jam Session series in Oakland for the past 23 years. Dr. Albert Brooks grew up dancing to Latin music in the South Bronx, playing these rhythms on any percussion instrument he could get his hands on. Alongside Latin drumming, he added trap drums to his musical offerings several decades ago and fluently melds these with swing rhythms. He has juggled his growth as a drummer with the demands of being a practicing obstetrician-gynecologist in the East Bay for nearly 30 years, having graduated in 1974 from the Albert Einstein College of Medicine of Yeshiva University in New York City. Tickets ($25) for the show at PCA (801 Magnolia Ave.) are available at bpt.me/6214927. This Sunday In the Tradition Piano Trio will pay tribute to composer Jimmy van Heusen at the Piedmont Center for the Arts.
articles.title: Jimmy van Heusen tribute at PCA Oct. 20

articles.text: A scene from the Paramont+ series 1883 1883 (Season 1), streaming on various platforms, is an extraordinary, richly produced episodic origin series that is, from the opening scenes, relentlessly engaging, wonderfully cast and superbly acted. The writing and photography are inspired. We soon come to realize that episodic storytelling can transcend the familiar two-hour cinema format, which for more than a century has defined the movie-going experience. The series is set during those early post-civil war years when the nation and its denizens are just beginning to recover from the trauma and loss. The opening scene is of a man, Shea Brennan (Sam Elliot), sitting alone on the porch of his farmhouse, lost in grief. He goes inside, carries his lifeless daughter (small pox we assume) upstairs, places her on a bed next to her deceased mother, and grimly returns to the front of the house and throws a kerosene lamp through a window. He stands back watching all that he cares about consumed by fire. The narrative then cuts to Ft. Worth, Texas, 1883, referred to as “Hell’s Half Acre,” the wide dirt street, bordered by stores, a saloon with hardscrabble people, wagons, horses, all seeming on the verge of chaos and lawlessness. It’s there that we’re introduced to James Dutton (Tim McGraw), arriving alone in Ft. Worth in a covered wagon. His appearance is frayed, heavily bearded, well armed, clearly not intimidated by what he sees. He’s in Ft. Worth to await the arrival of his wife, Margaret (Faith Hill), teenage daughter, Elsa (Isabel May), and young son, John (Rick Audie), arriving by train from Tennessee. We soon learn that the Dutton family intends to travel by wagon West in search of land and a new life. Circumstances lead to James meeting Shea (aka Captain, his rank in the Union Army), and

articles.text: It is no small thing to make a good film about adolescence, to create a sense of verisimilitude and avoid what are often a series of clichés that are too cute by half. It’s like trying to capture lightning in a jar, and Hollywood is strewn with teen movies that imploded from terminal triteness. Adapted from the book by Jesse Andrews, Me and Earl and the Dying Girl manages to get it just right and finds that elusive, emotional sweet spot. Above all, it manages to avoid becoming maudlin or sentimental while making every good faith effort to distract the audience from the last three words of the title. Even to the point of insisting in voice over that the story about to unfold has a happy ending. No worries. The story’s narrator is Greg (Thomas Mann), a senior, who has managed to navigate the clique-driven social mine field that is high school relatively unscathed. He’s self-centered, awkward, bright, sardonic and, along with his best friend, Earl (R.J. Cyler), has spent four years either immersed in schoolwork or making very short Criterion Collection videos, each title a knockoff pun such as “Eyes Wide Butt.” Me and Earl opens with Greg’s mom (Connie Britton) telling him that one of his classmates, Rachel (Olivia Cooke), has just received a diagnosis of leukemia. She suggests that he go and see her. He argues that he barely knows her, they haven’t spoken since kindergarten, and he’ll pass. But his mom insists and relentlessly guilts him into stopping in to say hello, just one time. Olivia Cooke, Thomas Mann and RJ Cyler in Me and Earl and the Dying Girl

But Merida, as wild as her red mane, snorts when she laughs, scoops up food from the pantry, and is a tomboyish, headstrong teenager who has her own ideas regarding gender But Queen Elinor is not to be deterred in her efforts to civilize Merida in the image of a domesticated princess, marriage being at the fore. She therefore invites three suitors to the yearly Highland Games, deciding that the best of the three will win her Merida, however, has other plans, finding the three definitely unsuitable as prospective husbands, and defiantly declares to her mother that she’ll not marry, period, followed by an age appropriate tantrum to make her point. The idea, which comprises the essence of Pixar’s Inside Out, is inspired. The filmmakers, who have an extraordinary history of animated films (Up, Wall-E, Toy Story, Finding Nemo), are able to break what is known as the third dimension. This is, after all, a world wherein the animators can take a step that is rarely used in photographed feature films. Here’s what they did: knowing that a filmed narrative cannot penetrate a character’s mind they tell what is a familiar story of an 11-year-old girl named Riley (Kaitlyn Dias). She lives happily in the embrace of her parents in Minnesota, has loads of friends and plays on a hockey team. For Riley life is better than good. That is until her father takes a new job and they must relocate to San Francisco. Up until this point, Riley’s default setting is contentment and joy – school, friends, sports all fit into a much-enjoyed spectrum of childhood on the cusp of being a teenager (Riley defines the word tween). With this move, Riley’s world is rocked. She is confronted with challenges that are new to her. Her new house is a bit grim, as is her neighborhood. She tries out for hockey and it doesn’t go well. Suddenly Riley begins to slide into a funk. And though her parents ask her if everything is all right (of course, Riley grumA scene from Inside Out bles that all is fine), the emotions taking place inside are a different story. Now here is where the Pixar storytellers create another world (the previously mentioned third dimension) because they can. They craft a kind of emotional wheelhouse (in Riley’s head, so to speak) and therein personify all of Riley’s emotions. It’s wonderful. There’s Joy (Amy Poehler), Fear (Bill Hader), Anger (Lewis Black), Disgust (Mindy Kaling) and Sadness (Phyllis Smith). Each is a unique and funny and engaging character, and all, in their own way, are coping with Riley’s new world and a bevy of feelings that are at first decidedly unsettling. Riley has always been encouraged to be happy. To smile. But then she has been grounded in a spiffy life. Hence Joy, vivacious and energetic, has always had her hand on the tiller, so to speak. But suddenly Anger and Fear and most especially Sadness find that their roles in Riley’s emotions are growing. Meanwhile, Joy, becomes lost in a labyrinth of Riley’s mind and must struggle to find its way back to emotion central before things get really awful for Riley. You have to see the crew in action (Anger is a squat, red, short-fused guy) to get a complete understanding of what Pixar has accomplished as they tell a compelling story, one that kids will relate to and one that parents will quickly recognize, given their more extensive life experience. articles.text: Long time Piedmont residents Connie and Mark Herrick have published the third installment of their children’s book series, Ripley’s Road Trip. The couple wrote and illustrated the book which delivers funny, happy reading for elementary school readers. Ripley’s Road Trip brings back the Herricks’ calico cat yet again and Ripley’s propensity for adventure comes to life in vibrant watercolor illustrations. Ripley joins four legged pals Pele and Kapo on the open road in the family’s converted electric van. The Herricks began the Ripley and Friendz Collection in 2021 with Ripley’s World, and followed with Ripley’s Missing Locket, a sequel that hit bookshelves in 2022. The third installment takes readers on a journey up the Pacific Coast, from San Francisco to Vancouver. The books are created by Connie as the story-teller and Mark as illustrator. “We wanted to create stories that not only entertain but also foster a love of nature, adventure, and friendship,” said Connie. “Ripley’s Road Trip is all about exploring new places, making new friends and discovering the magic within us. It’s a celebration of the beauty of our world and the joy of discovery.” Ripley’s Road Trip is available worldwide in hardcover ($28.95), paperback ($19.95), and eBook ($9.99) on Apple Books, Barnes & Noble, Rakuten-Kobo, eBooks, Indigo, Adlibris, and more. Profits from book sales contribute to animal adoption and wildlife preservation efforts. For more information visit RipleyandFriendz.com. Piedmont residents Connie and Mark Herrick, an author-illustrator duo, have published their latest children’s book, Ripley’s Road Trip. RIPLEY'S ROAD TRIP Book Three in the Ripley and Friendz Collection Ripley’s First Road Trip "Ripley had never seen the ocean or anything like it. The bright sunshine sprinkled the waves with a blanket of sparkly silver glitter. She could not stop looking at it. “The ocean is so beautiful. It's as big as the sky! Does Hariel know there is this much water to swim in?”wondered Ripley. Lots of Fun Destinations “We’re off to Capilano Suspension Bridge Park, ” announced The Boy. “I can’t wait to drive over the bridge, ” woofed Kapo. “We’re not going to drive over it, Kapo. We’re going to walk over it!” said The Boy. “And remember Kapo, that’s walk, not run, ” said Pele. Contact Us Connie & Mark Herrick RipleyandFriendz.com editor@herrickpublishing.com

articles.text: It was still hot on October 7th when the First Mondays Reading Group met for their monthly discussion, so they assembled inside the Community Hall. There was a good turnout of 17 readers on hand. Discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus couldn’t be with them, so Dick Carter, who had suggested this month’s book, led the conversation. Before they got started on their discussion, it was shared that there will be a Piedmont Adult Recreation Expo on Sunday, November 17th, from 2 to 4:30 PM at the Veterans Building. Representatives from groups that provide recreation in Piedmont for adults, including the reading group, will be there to tell attendees about their activities and how to get involved. The book for this day’s discussion was Outliers: The Story of Success by Malcom Gladwell. The author wants us to better understand the world of “outliers.” These are the best and the brightest, the most famous and the most successful people. What makes them different? Gladwell says we pay too much attention to what successful people are like, and too little attention to where they are from. He explains why some people become software billionaires, what it takes to be a great soccer player, why Asians are good at math, and what made the Beatles the greatest rock band. Gladwell believes the idea of the “self-made man” is a myth, and that once you reach a certain threshold, increased abilities no longer help you succeed. He says world-class mastery of anything demands around 10,000 hours of practice. The month and year you’re born in can have a huge effect on what you achieve. How you are raised can radically impact how successful you become. Where you’re from geographically and culturally is important for success and recognizing it can prevent failure. Gladwell contends if we understand this, we can create more opportunities for people to succeed. The readers generally liked Outliers. They found it interesting and easy to read, and agreed Gladwell is an excellent storyteller. They liked his premise and could relate to the different stories and the lessons he is trying to communicate. The book provides a fuller picture of what is going on in life, and the group could personally relate to examples Gladwell presents. They knew of “redshirting kindergarteners” where parents hold their children back a year so they can be the oldest and most mature members of their classes. It was also helpful to understand cultural environments, and how junior Korean pilots would be reluctant to voice a concern to their older co-pilots with disastrous consequences. There was a significant backlash to the book. While some readers liked some aspects of the book, they didn’t care for others. Gladwell mainly presents others’ research, and they felt he cherry picks examples and research that supports his positions. Gladwell recognizes outliers are talented people, but it seemed underplayed to some, as is just plain luck and being in the right place at the right time. What would Bill Gates have been if he didn’t have a high school situation that let him have practically unlimited access to computer programming time? Probably successful too. Other interesting questions also came out of the conversation. The success of Chinese Olympic divers, who are identified at a very young age and do little else for the next 10 plus years of their lives, raised the question, do we need diverse educations or just concentrated study for success? Bob Hall observed that the group will have the opportunity to learn more about the factors behind the success of four American presidents in the group’s selection of Leadership: In Turbulent Times by historian Doris Kearns Goodwin as the selection for December. The readers had also previously selected North Woods by Danile Mason for November. After hearing reviews of three fiction possibilities, the group selected the classic A Farewell to Arms by Ernest Hemingway for the first book of 2025. The group’s next discussion will be on November 4 at 1:30 PM. Weather permitting, it will be outside the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. New readers are welcome to join and there is no fee. Register at https:// bit.ly/3R86PP4. Participants at the First Mondays Reading Group gathering on October 7 included Albert Chen, Adrienne Hamlin, Judy Love, Ken Young, Darby and Gerry Gregg, Laura Goldman, Carol Long, Bob Hall, Nancy Henn, Claudine Bach, Martin Levy, Phyllis Van Kranenburgh, Melba Yee, Mike Henn, Karin Fetherston, and Dick Carter.

pages.text: Wednesday, October 16, 2024 27 It’s October – a time for Squash & Sprouts By Deborah Quok Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on October 7, 2020. Oven-roasted Brussels sprouts and delicata squash are a clear signal we’re transitioning from summer to autumn meals. This is my third published recipe using delicata squash in as many years. We enjoy this seasonal favorite countless times throughout fall and winter. Creating dishes using minimal ingredients with maximal taste is the key in these days of home cooking. A spice blend will do the heavy lifting on seasoning this dish. It’s the key behind this five-ingredient recipe. In addition to a chile blend, I’ve prepared versions of roasted vegetables using curry blends, harissa, Ras el Hanout, and Chinese Five Spice. You get to take your pick. This recipe has endless adaptations with vegetables, aromatics, spices and herbs. I happen to have a favorite spicery where I’ve purchased freshly milled herbs, chiles, and spices for years, Local Spicery. It’s important to like the spice blends right out of the jar to minimize fussing and doctoring them to suit your taste buds. The idea is that they make things easy, so go with a brand that works for you. There is no shortage of local spice shops for that personal touch, and there is an abundant variety of spice blends at local markets. Any flavor profile you enjoy will work here. So will a simple dusting of sea salt and freshly ground pepper. Five ingredients deliver an outstanding result. F-I-V-E! Chile Roasted Brussels Sprouts and Delicata Squash Makes about four cups INGREDIENTS • 1 pound Brussels sprouts, deep green, sliced in half lengthwise • 1 pound delicata squash, ends trimmed, halved and seeds removed; sliced into 1/2-inch thick pieces • 1 tablespoon olive oil • 1 tablespoon chile powder blend, or substitute any preferred spice blend • 1/2 teaspoon sea salt, to taste if your spice blend is salt-free INSTRUCTIONS Place an oven rack on the middle rack of the oven and preheat the oven to either 350° F on the “convection-roast” setting, or 400° F on the “bake” setting. Place the sliced Brussels sprouts and delicata squash on a sheet pan and drizzle with 1 tablespoons of olive oil. Stir the Brussels sprouts and squash pieces around to cover each with olive oil. Add more oil if needed. Arrange the slices into a single layer. Place the pan of Brussels sprouts and squash into the oven and roast for about 12 – 15 minutes, when you see some browning on them, remove the pan from the oven. Using a spatula, move the pieces close together and sprinkle with chile powder blend (or other spice blend) and salt to taste. Stir to mix, then spread out into an even layer and return the pan to the oven. Roast an additional 5 – 7 minutes until both the Brussels sprouts and squash are golden-brown. Test the vegetables with a fork to check they are tender but still provide slight resistance. You don’t want them mushy. Walkers take a stroll on Kingston and Rose By Dick Carter The heat wave finally broke last Wednesday, just in time for the Walking on Wednesdays group’s weekly walk. They decided to see Rose and Kingston Avenues on for the first time this year. These streets are some of Piedmont’s earliest with many old homes and some beautiful Victorians. The group headed off going down Highland Avenue to Park Way. onto Ramona and Ronada Avenues to Grand Avenue just before it becomes Oakland’s Pleasant Valley Road at Moraga Avenue. The walkers couldn’t resist walking the rarely visited Parkside Drive cul-de-sac. Then, it was across Grand Avenue and on to Rose Avenue to where homes on the right side are in Oakland and homes on the left are in Piedmont. They enjoyed seeing Rose’s many old, lovely homes that were built between 1890 and 1930. They went past three especially charming Victorians on Rose, including one dating to 1895. Then they crossed Linda to go up Kingston. In this 700 block of Kingston the homes on the north side are also in Oakland and the homes on the south side are in Piedmont. To their surprise on Kingston they saw walker and local historian Meghan Bennett, who grew up at 780 Kingston. Research by Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombard provided the story of Meghan’s old home and that of the house next door at 778. These two homes were built in 1892 by William Vickery and his sister, Elizabeth Vickery Hadden, at costs of $4,300 and $3,300. They were the first homes on the street which was then called Summit Avenue. Meghan shared an article from a 1904 issue of the Oakland Enquirer that said 10 property owners had sent a petition to the City Council asking to change the street’s name from Summit to Kingston. These houses were built in the fashionable shingle style of the 1890s. The backyard of the house at 778 is one of the deepest lots in Piedmont, 220 feet deep. Google Maps shows the backyard of the home at 784 is even deeper. Neighborhood lore says the two houses once shared a kitchen and the two families ate their meals together. There are many wonderful homes on Kingston, but the classic Victoria at 836 is one of the best. It was built in 1885 on nearby Monte Vista Avenue in Oakland and moved one block in 1910 to its current location. Nancy DeRoche wanted the group to see an historic brick home a little further up Kingston that was designed by Albert Farr, built in 1908m and currently occupied by Chad Olcott and Laura Pochop, owners of Mulberry’s Market. Going to the far reaches of Piedmont was a longer walk than usual, and it was time for them to make their return to the Exedra. They went back up Kingston, down Greenbank Avenue, across Grand Avenue, up to Oakland, El Cerrito, and Magnolia Avenues. They had a good, long walk with wonderful, old homes, some history, and lots of friends on a lovely morning. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are welcome. Register ar https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. articles.text: • Hope Hope is more than wishful thinking; it’s the perceived ability to set goals, find pathways to achieve them, and maintain the motivation to follow those paths. It’s about helping them see possibilities rather than limitations. Encouraging goal-setting and helping young people develop strategies to overcome obstacles can nurture hope. • WOOP (Wish-Outcome-Obstacle-Plan): Developed by researcher Gabriele Oettingen and her colleagues, WOOP is a dynamic, evidence supported approach to increasing follow-through on goals. WOOP is the process of “mental contrasting with implementation intentions,” meaning it involves both visualizing your obstacles and planning for them. • There are various worksheet online, including a website section on hope overall here: https://ameaningoflife.org/enablers/hope/ • Utilize stories of fictional or real characters/people and use WOOP on them to practice • Set Achievable Goals Together: Work with your child to outline short-term and long-term goals. Break them down into manageable steps and celebrate milestones along the way. • Model Optimism: Demonstrate a positive outlook when facing your own challenges. Share stories of how you’ve overcome obstacles, emphasizing the strategies you used. • Teach Problem-Solving Skills: Equip them with tools like brainstorming, pros and cons lists, or mind mapping to navigate hurdles. • Encourage Perseverance: Praise their effort and determination, especially when they persist after setbacks. Reinforce the idea that challenges are opportunities for growth. • Encourage Problem-Solving: When faced with challenges, guide them to find solutions rather than providing answers. Ask open-ended questions like, “What do you think would happen if you tried this?” Assign Responsibilities: Give them age-appropriate tasks that contribute to the household, such as managing a budget for their school supplies or planning a family outing. This fosters ownership and accountability. Self-Esteem It involves recognizing one’s worth and competence in areas that matter to the individual. It’s about recognizing genuine efforts and achievements, helping children understand their unique strengths. • Provide Specific Praise: Instead of generic compliments, offer detailed feedback like, “I’m impressed with how carefully you researched your project.” Offering genuine, specific praise can help build healthy self-esteem. • Highlight Strengths: Help your child identify their talents and passions. Encourage activities that allow them to develop these areas further. • Create Opportunities for Success: Set them up for mastery by introducing tasks that are challenging yet attainable. Success boosts confidence. • Create Opportunities for Failure: A healthy sense of self includes recognizing one’s failures and limitations, and their impacts, without sugar coating. • Promote Self-Reflection: Encourage journaling or discussions about their experiences, focusing on what they’ve learned and accomplished. Please note that REACH Codes pertain only to energy efficiency measures for existing buildings and were not impacted by the recent code changes. Through the City’s REACH Codes, renovations over $30,000 and $115,000 trigger requirements for additional energy efficiency measures into the home. In January 2023, the Sustainability Division presented a Climate Action Plan 2.0 priority implementation areas for 2024/2025, including: The development of an Existing Building Electrification Strategy with the help of a community Task Force. The Task Force has been formed and is working to complete this goal. James Green, Candidate Piedmont has been and can continue to be a regional leader in sustainability. The City needs to continue to take a multifaceted approach to reduce greenhouse gasses from City-owned buildings and vehicles – and more importantly cars and activities of Piedmont residents. One way to mitigate GHG from new housing is to incentivize installing electric equipment (kitchen range, water heater, EV charger) and renewable energy sources (like solar) to power these appliances. Increasing the number of City vehicles that are EVs should continue to be an area of exploration, although the vast majority of emissions in Piedmont are from personal vehicles, so that effort should be seen as a signal of the City’s commitment to reducing GHG, not as a solution to the problem. articles.text: Have you heard about Piedmont Cub Scouts? Piedmont is home to a richly historic and active Scouting council that dates back to 1910 to the founding of Scouts in America. Recently last year’s kindergarten Lion Scouts have experienced rock climbing, toured the Piedmont Police station, and practiced camping in the park, not to mention racing in the Pinewood Derby. Piedmont’s Scouting program strives to build character, leadership skills, and confidence in the outdoors through community service and adventure. And Scouts is really fun! Parent involvement is strongly encouraged to jumpstart children towards experiencing the joy that is Scouting. articles.text: The Piedmont Planning Commission met at City Hall on Monday, October 14, to analyze a pair of draft plans for two possible build sites related to the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan. Prior to the meeting, University of California professor and Piedmont resident Ralph Catalano raised concerns that sight distances for vehicles on roads in the proposed area of construction did not comply with Caltrans safety guidelines. Catalano urged city officials not to make a decision on the proposed plans until a comprehensive review of sight lines and stopping distances are conducted to ensure the highest degree of public safety. The commission noted that the Monday meeting was a study session held as a preliminary step prior to the completion of a draft specific plan. The completed draft plan is expected by city officials to be released for public review and comment in late 2024. During the meeting, members of the Piedmont Planning Commission reviewed landscape design requirements for new multifamily housing and requirements for public services, utilities and infrastructure in the proposed build area for the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan. Among the priorities and considerations for the commission regarding the project were construction with the existing landscape of Moraga Canyon to encourage the siting of future development, enacting architectural standards that integrate building design, access and site improvements for market-rate and affordable multifamily developments and providing flexibility in building and land use design while describing Piedmont’s and it residents’ preferences for future development. The commission noted that final determination of the build plan will rely heavily on contractor input to ensure that the city of Piedmont gets the best available deal when undertaking the construction project. The Moraga Canyon Specific Plan is a construction effort by the city to comply with a state mandate for more housing by incorporating between 132 and 199 units of new housing, 60 units of which are slated to be reserved for households earning lower incomes. The city anticipates the project to include development of multifamily residential buildings that would stand between four and six stories in the canyon. The project is studying all cityowned land in Moraga Canyon, including Blair Park, Coaches Field, Kennelly Skate Park and the city’s Corporation Yard. The city owns five parcels of land totaling about 18 acres on both the north and south sides of Moraga Avenue near Red Rock Road. The Moraga Canyon Specific Plan also seeks to develop detailed methods to maintain and improve existing city facilities, recreational amenities and open space and improve bicycle, pedestrian and traffic safety. The plan also seeks to enhance wildfire safety and evacuation protocols. articles.text: The City of Piedmont is currently pondering two options for the ongoing Moraga Canyon Specific Plan project, which seeks to add new housing to city-owned property. City Planning Director Kevin Jackson said the city has two available sites on either side of Moraga Avenue. Jackson said the two sites would offer opportunities to build new housing. “The city will need to seek proposals from developers, and that will help inform which side it goes on,” Jackson said. “The developers may prefer one site or the other. The city may find one to be more beneficial than the other, depending on what the developers put forward.” Jackson said the challenge to build on the site is due to its hilly and uneven nature, but added several developers have expressed interest in the building project. The city hopes to have a draft of a completed plan for public review and comment later this year. “We’re getting some feedback from the public and the commission on the preliminary content that will help inform a draft we’ve got for public review,” he said. Jackson said the community has also expressed interest in the development of the project. articles.text: The Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) presented a check for $4,039,957 to Piedmont School District during a school board meeting on Wednesday, September 25. This substantial grant represents a year’s worth of dedicated fundraising by PEF members and demonstrates the community’s unwavering support for local education. The funds were raised through the annual Giving Campaign, Spring Fling, Harvest Festival, Dress Best for Less, business sponsorships, a the PEF endowment fund, and generous bequest from Pamela Wells Rafanelli. A former Piedmont resident and teacher at Havens and Beach schools, Rafanelli left a legacy gift to support professional development opportunities for Piedmont educators. PEF raised $321,660 through last year’s Spring Fling and Harvest Festival, which is being allocated to fund critical projects such as classroom technology, decodable books for the phonics curriculum, and initiatives to promote a positive playground culture at Beach, Havens, and Wildwood schools. The remaining $3,693,297 is Giving Campaign co-chairs Kim Hunter and Catie Osborn present a $4 million check to Piedmont’s School Board on September 25.
articles.title: Education Foundation presents $4 million check to School District

articles.text: Editor: I am writing to express my enthusiastic support for Lorrel Plimier in her candidacy for Piedmont City Council. As both a friend and campaign volunteer, I have seen firsthand the qualities that make her the ideal choice for this role: her leadership, commitment to service, and sharp intelligence. Lorrel’s leadership is rooted in her experience as an Army veteran, where she learned how to make tough decisions under pressure. She’s led with integrity and vision in every sphere, whether managing her own business or serving in leadership roles with the League of Women Voters. Her dedication to service is unwavering. Lorrel has spent years volunteering in our community, stepping up when others needed her. From participating in Wildwood School involvement, to keeping the League of Women Voters of Piedmont operational during the pandemic, to mentoring youth, she’s committed to improving the lives of everyone in Piedmont. Finally, Lorrel’s intelligence is remarkable. She understands the complexities of local government, and her thoughtful, solution-oriented approach makes her uniquely qualified to tackle the challenges our city faces. She’s Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. Subscribe to the Post and we’ll deliver
articles.title: In support of Lorrel Plimier for City Council

articles.text: Piedmont Community Church will host a free showing in October of the documentary, Join or Die. Directed by Pete and Rebecca Davis, the film explains the benefits of joining a club or an organization. The screening will be at Piedmont Church, 400 Highland Avenue at 7 p.m. on Friday, October 25. “At a time when American society is more and more fractured – and our politics are increasingly fractious – the need for people to get together with others in face-to-face groups has never been stronger,” the church wrote in a press release. The film follows the journey of social scientist Robert Putnam, whose groundbreaking research, Bowling Alone: The Collapse and Revival of American Community, examines America’s decades-long decline in community connections. For more information contact Rev. Don Ashburn at Don@ PiedmontChurch.org.
articles.title: Community Church to host film screening in October.

articles.text: Piedmont is hosting its first ever Adult Recreation Expo this coming November, and the city is currently encouraging local organizations to attend. The Expo will take place on Sunday, November 17, from 2:00 to 4:30 p.m. at the Veterans Memorial Building. 401 Highland Avenue. Its goal is to help publicize adult recreational activities available to residents. Current participants include Piedmont Adult School, Piedmont Center for the Arts, League of Women Voters, and Piedmont Recreation Department. To sign up and for more information e-mail AdultRecreationExpo@piedmont.ca.gov. There is no cost. Organizers will be provided with tables and chairs at the event. The Expo was conceived by members of the Recreation Commission and is the result of a survey that was conducted. The deadline to register is October 18.
articles.title: Adult Recreation Expo deadline for signups is Oct. 18

His owner fell on hard times and had to surrender him and now Babyn is looking for a new home. Could that home be with you? He is medium energy level and has been gentle around other dogs indicating he might do well living with another dog with well matched energy. He would also be happy to be your only dog. In the shelter setting, Babyn can be a little wary of strangers at first. However, as a foodie he is easily won over with treats. Come meet Babyn at Oakland Animal Services this Thursday from 12 - 7 p.m., or Meet Babyn, a young Rottweiler mix ready for adoption. this Friday, Saturday, or Sunday between 12 and 3 p.m. Potential adopters with a child younger than 12 or a dog that weighs 25 pounds more or less than Babyn must bring them to the shelter for the meeting. articles.text: It seems that part of the rules for being a home beer brewer are that when naming your beer there are no rules. Unlike the character, Tyler Durden whose first rule was never to mention Fight Club, our brewers seem to enjoy naming their creations as much as they do making them. Looking at the names of some of the past year’s Artisanal Beer Festival names, one could conclude that coming up with a clever name for one’s beer is as important as the beer itself. To patrons of prior PCA beer festivals this is no surprise. Some of last year’s entrants included Stub Your Toein-the-Dark Ale, Cognitive Dissonance, Paul the Pilsner and the still mysterious Oaxacan Green Corn Saison. Fortunately, all the brewers who pour their beers stand ready to translate what the creative names have to do with the styles of beers they are pouring. It should come as no surprise that this year’s brewers have again produced creative and unique names for the beers they will serve on Friday, October 18, at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. Of this year’s returning brewers, multi-year entrant Matt Gerhart will be presenting Jazzman, a rice lager, and Leprechaun Merlot, an Irish red ale. Multiple year entrant Kyle Blomseth will be pouring a spiced saison called Mashing Pumpkins and a Double IPA which apparently needs no name. Jon Rhodin, a brewer for eight years, will present a double IPA named Ah, Bitter Dregs. You know it must be good with a name like that. Reyes will present a Mate Stout, a Passion Blonde and a Potato Saison. Patrons will need to taste all three to know what styles they represent. Trevor Fleshman, whose prior beers have leaned towards the exploratory side, this year presents Nipple Confusion, a single batch American IPA, one half containing 5% lactose, and the other half an unadulterated American IPA. Patrons will be challenged to pick which is which. Piedmont native Jessica Falarski Cross, once Trevor’s babysitter, is back for her second year. She and husband Kevin have created an anchor steam beer called California Common, which it certainly won’t be. Carter Dunlap, PCA board member, a home brewer, and the event organizer, plans to play it safe with Fifth Generation Cali, an American Red Ale with a West Coast twist and a nod to his California heritage. While most of the brewers have taken part before, this year Piedmont resident Michael Fodor a craft brewer for 20 years makes his debut at the festival. His entrant rounds out this year’s beers with a nod to P-town with his Dracena Haze, a West Coast Hazy Pale Ale made with hops harvested believe it or not near Dracena Park. As you can see, there is no limit to the styles of beers or at least what they are named for this year’s festival. Tickets are most easily purchased ahead of time at www. eventbrite.com/e/948562324447 or at the door on the night of the event. For further information, contact Carter Dunlap at carter@ dunlapclan.net. Aaron Bagnell, a home brewer with his Prime Ordinal beer, is shown tasting his product which will be at this year’s Artisanal Brewing Competition at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. Robert Davis, a prolific, longtime festival entrant also has his own imaginary brewery named Happy Girl. This year he presents: Ukrainian Anti-Imperial Stout, created for the International Red Cross. It includes beets for a Ukrainian vibe. Davis will also present Box of Birds, a New Zealand Strong Pilsner; and Occam’s Razor, a traditional Kolsch. Last year’s best in show winner, Kyle Killion, returns to the PCA this year with Sake to Me (yikes), a white koji ale and a repeat of his Saison Du Poe, a super saison. The team of Aaron Bagnell and Anna Haefele, who have been brewing for eight and five years respectively, will present an Irish Red Ale, Deoch of Kells (ask him the joke) and Prime Ordinal, an English “Amber” ale. Veteran brewer Alan Bernales returns this year. He and his co-brewers Ben Mand, Francis Hoang, and Carlos Newsstand copies of the Piedmont Post are available at ­ Mulberry’s Market. articles.text: Several Piedmont ladies and local friends participated in Santa Rosa Cycling Club’s inaugural Women on Wheels 50K ride through the beautiful wine country of Sebastopol on the weekend of October 5. The morning started with breakfast and yoga at the Sebastopol Arts Center, then embarked on the route which crossed the Hacienda Bridge and meandered through Russian River Valley Vineyards. articles.text: Staff photo Gary Randolph, 31, joined the Piedmont Fire Department as a paramedic in January and became a certified firefighter in July. When Gary Randolph was forced to evacuate his new home in Healdsburg with his wife during the 2019 Kincaid Fire, he remembered feeling completely helpless. Randolph, 31, had just moved into the house three months prior to the blaze, and while he was staying with relatives in the Sacramento area after the fire, he had an epiphany: He realized that he wanted to do whatever he could to fight a feeling of powerlessness in the face of disaster. “It was honestly right then and there I realized, ‘You know what? This is something that I want to do. I want to get into firefighting. I want to be able to help,’” Randolph said. Randolph said he took that inspiration and started asking associates who worked as firefighters what he could do to break into the service. That’s when he learned of the vast need for paramedics. “Every department, especially in California, is really looking for paramedics. That’s kind of the standard now,” Randolph said. “So in January 2020 I took my first EMT class, I got my certification and went straight from EMT into paramedic school.” He initially worked as a reserve firefighter in Healdsburg and as a paramedic with a private ambulance company for a year before he made his way to the Piedmont Fire Department, where he landed a job as a paramedic in January 2024. In March, he and two other Piedmont recruits were sent to the Las Positas College Fire Academy to become firefighters. Randolph and his colleagues graduated from the fire academy in July this summer and are now full-fledged firefighters with the Piedmont Fire Department. In addition to his new certifications, Randolph welcomed his first child – a baby boy named Hayden – on September 5. Randolph and his wife and son reside in Healdsburg, where his family has lived for four generations. HEATING AND AIR CONDITIONING COMPANY

articles.text: Association of Piedmont Teachers (APT) representatives spoke to the Piedmont School Board about overcrowded classrooms at the high school and middle school on September 25. Kate Waldron of Piedmont Middle School and high school teacher Mercedes Foster described the current conditions at their schools in a discussion at the last school board meeting. They want the board and the community to be aware of the impacts the budget cuts have made to schools this year. The duo read their reports in alternating fashion, which detailed where the cutbacks hit at the two schools. The teachers stood before the school board and reported large class size numbers in some classes. Waldron, a PMS Math teacher, stated that Compression Math for eighth graders has an average of 33 students, and sixth graders in advanced math classes have an average of 31 students. “This year in many departments and for many specific courses, 30 or more students in the room has become the norm at Piedmont Middle School,” Teachers tell the district that some Piedmont Middle and High School classes are too crowded. explained Waldron. Foster reported larger numbers in some classes at the high school that at times have created a need to crawl over desks to go to the restroom. Calculus classes have 34 or more students, and Statistics and AP Spanish have classes with 35 students. “Larger classes change the behavior of students. Some check out, while others act out,” Foster said. “All of this gets in the way of learning.” Classroom size caps contained in teacher contracts only say that the staffing ratio for each elemen-

articles.text: Part 4 in a series All three school board candidates continue to participate in the Post’s weekly questions posed to candidates for public office. One question was sent out on Thursday with a request to limit answers to 200 words. School Board, 4-year terms 3 open seats; 3 candidates Week 4 Question Please give an example of something you think is an underutilized resource for Piedmont students. Explain how it could benefit them. SUSY STRUBLE, Candidate PUSD graduates and the broader Piedmont community are valuable yet underutilized resources. The District is starting to develop programs, such as the PUSD Alumni Network, that go beyond traditional career day discussions. As this network matures, I hope it will noy only help students in exploring career and continued learning paths but also in navigating the transition from Piedmont into the wider world. I’m especially excited to see how the Alumni Network can help our kids understand that there are many paths to fulfillment and how to build their own flexible, healthy scaffolding for success in an ever-changing world. Insight from peers on these points carries more weight than anything parents and teachers might say. MICHAEL MALIONE, Candidate I think the most underutilized resource for Piedmont students is the career-related expertise of the parents, families, and retirees who live here. The PHS College and Career Center is doing a much bigger program this year, and it would be great to have broader community involvement in Career Day. Though parents volunteer their time at the schools in a variety of ways, the district underutilizes this resource in projects that are more directly on point to a particular community member’s skills and experience. Having more community involvement and better-coordinated community involvement would go a long way. The district recently launched a Piedmont Alumni Network, and I fully support such efforts. Further development to include parents and a volunteering aspect would continue the support of long-time parent volunteers, strengthen community in Piedmont, and most importantly, help PUSD students make better decisions in their preparations for life after graduation. MAX ROMAN, Candidate I think an underutilized resource for Piedmont students is the community. There are a lot of people who are experts in all sorts of fields who live here, and I think it would be terrific if there was some kind of program to connect students with experts in whatever they are studying in the community.

articles.text: Forty-seven Piedmont Middle School students will perform Legally Blonde Jr. the musical, based on the award-winning Broadway show and the smash hit motion picture. This fun journey of self-empowerment and expanding horizons is appropriate for the entire family and will run October 18-20. Legally Blonde Jr. follows the transformation of Elle Woods as she tackles stereotypes, snobbery and scandal in pursuit of her dreams. When Elle’s boyfriend, Warner, dumps her and heads to Harvard, claiming she’s not “serious” enough, Elle takes matters into her own hands. Now a Harvard Law student, Elle begins outsmarting her peers and realizes that law may be her natural calling after all. All performances will be held in the Alan Harvey Theater on the high school campus, 800 Magnolia Avenue. Music and lyrics are by Laurence O’Keefe and Nell Benjamin. Tickets go on sale in early October. Tickets are $8-$18 and are available online at Pmslegallyblondejr.ludus. com. Contact Amy Moorhead at amoorhead@piedmont.k12.ca.us for more information.

articles.text: Miranda Liu, a junior at Piedmont High School, participated in the Global Asian Moon Festival & Creator Summit on September 20 in Los Angeles. Liu was a part of a team of high school students that presented their short documentary “Crisis in Alviso,” which was featured at the event. The documentary cues in on environmental justice issues that have arisen in the northern San Jose district of Alviso, which lies on the southern shores of the Bay. Alviso is a small community where Hispanics and Asians make up nearly 75% of its population. Alviso was once a thriving port city shipping goods and produce to San Francisco, but Alviso has taken a concerning turn in recent decades. The Global Asian Moon Festival and Creator Summit showcased the creative power of Asia Americans, attracting cultural-minded audiences from around the world to celebrate the thriving of Asian cultural and creative industries. The event attracted many creative talents including Liu’s group which is mentored by CP Mentorship, a non-profit organization based in Sunnyvale, CA. Other highlights of the event included the stand-up comedy of Joe Wong, Taoist calligraphy, Miranda Liu, PHS student, at Global Asian Moon Fest

articles.text: On Saturday, October 26, the Bay Area’s most spooktacular all-ages Halloween party returns to the California Academy of Sciences in Golden Gate Park. SuperNatural opens at 6:30 p.m., with VIP entry at 5 p.m. Goblins and ghouls of all ages can don their costumes for the beloved annual family-friendly Halloween party. Kids can satisfy their sweet tooth at trick-or-treat stations throughout the museum and amp up their costumes with face painting. A silent disco in the aquarium provides the perfect outlet for those looking to get out some of that candy-fueled energy. Curious to see what’s slithering and scuttling throughout the museum? See live animals in demonstrations from the Lindsay Wildlife Experience, meet mad scientists and ogle unusual specimens, then channel that inspiration into Halloween crafts. The exclusive Teen Lounge also returns with retro video games from the Museum of Art and Digital Entertainment, arcade games, sweet treats. For kids perhaps the best news us that no adults are allowed. Check out sponsor Zenni Optical’s Zenni Zone to get a complimentary vision test plus some special giveaways. SuperNatural tickets start at $45, with discounts available for Academy members. And for adults age 21 and older don’t miss the Academy’s popular annual NightLife Halloween Families and science fans of all ages bring their most inventive costumes and Halloween excitement to SuperNatural at the California Academy of Sciences in Golden Gate Park on Saturday October 26. bash, October 31 from 6-10 p.m. Sip cocktails while exploring the museum in costume, and a special drag performance by Oaklash is not to be missed. articles.text: This past July Troop 15 went to Camp Wente summer camp. There, Scouts checked off requirements, completed merit badges, and had tons of fun during the evening. Even the mosquitos and the deathly heat didn’t stop the Scouts from having a blast. The daily Scout schedule consisted of breakfast, merit badges, lunch, merit badges, dinner and evening activities. Scouts could choose from 85 different merit badges like archery, astronomy, emergency preparedness, kayaking, photography and many more. Theo said “I had fun doing the merit badges. I would go to Camp Wente again in a heart beat.” A merit badge many Scouts found very enjoyable was Riflery. The merit badge consisted of grouping three and five shots together five times each in the area of a quarter. Many found it exciting to learn how to handle a rifle and to see their progress in shooting. Scouts don’t need to shoot in consecutive rounds which makes the merit badge less stressful and you can complete it in the span of four days at the minimum. If the Scouts wanted an extra challenge they could try to get into, The Dime club. This is a club Scouts can only get it in if they group five shots together in the area of a dime. In addition to merit badges, Scouts had time to enjoy hanging out at the campsite, meeting Scouts from other Troops and trying to stay cool. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart.
