articles.text: Photos by Lynne Wright Piedmont’s win over Lick-Wilmerding brings their record to 7-7, the school’s most since 2019. Piedmont High’s girls’ water polo continues its winning ways, this time with a 17-11 win over Lick-Wilmerding in San Francisco on Thursday, October 3. The victory improves the team’s record to 7-7, the most wins since 2019. The Highlanders have three matches left in the regular season. They have an opportunity to notch the most wins in a season since 2017, which went 10-13 and was led by the school’s AllTime leading goal-scorer, Annika Disney, who went on to play for Santa Clara. Thursday’s win marked another strong performance by Abigail Jacoby, who had three goals and five assists. Goalie Zoe Waitkus was critical with six saves and two assists on long throws. Game Recap Piedmont led 4-3 through the first quarter and continued a narrow one-goal advantage up 7-6 going into halftime. The Highlanders extended their lead to 13-8 in the third quarter and scored four while allowing three in the final going, 17-11. Lick-Wilmerding actually scored the game’s first goal just 51 seconds into the game, but Piedmont went up with three unanswered goals by Sydney Olson, Viviane Burke, and Julian Montes to lead 3-1 with 2:34 left in the first quarter. Lick came back to tie it at 3-3 with a minute left, but Rachel Young got PHS back on top by scoring just 20 seconds later on the ensuing possession. Olson got her second goal a minute and a half into the second quarter, while Abigail Jacoby made it 6-3 after Piedmont’s defense forced a change of possession with 5:06 left. After a Tigers goal, Jacoby scored again with 4:32 left in the half. Lick-Wilmerding added two goals prior to halftime, making it 7-6. I n t he t h i rd qu a r ter, Lick-Wilmerding tied the game at 7-7 with a goal with 5:44 remaining, but Burke and Celeste Dickason created a two-goal cushion with 3:16 on the clock. Piedmont added four straight goals to end the quarter up 13-8 by Esme Krumins, Jacoby, Olson, and Sonja ten Grotenhuis. PHS continued on the throttle in the fourth quarter, scoring after 20 seconds by #2 followed by Mari Pisani with 5:22 remaining in the game. After conceding Viviane Burke scored twice in Piedmont’s victory. Abigail Jacoby scored three goals and five assists in Piedmont’s win over Lick-WIlmerding
articles.title: Piedmont beats Lick-Wilmerding 17-11

articles.text: The Highlanders put together another dominant display on Friday, October 4 under the lights of Witter Field, blanking the visiting Dougherty Valley Wildcats 41-0. Piedmont’s football team improves its record to 4-1 and has outscored opponents 167-35 in its four-game winning streak. Piedmont put up 14 points in the first quarter and led 21-0 by halftime. Coach Jordan Seiden said it was their most complete performance this season and was glad to see his players remain hungry for more in the second half. “When the guys go into the locker room at halftime and they are disappointed, saying ‘We should be up more,’ that tells me that they know we can be even better. This was the most complete game we’ve played all season,” Seiden said. The Highlanders had 464 yards of total offense, with receiver Sam Shelby accounting for nearly half of it with 214 total receiving yards. Quarterback Markos Lagios accounted for four passing touchdowns and added another on the ground. “We expected a much more physical team and we just came out with that fire. Sam was doing his thing, he got me all those passing yards on little screens,” Lagios said. PHS now moves into the final stretch of the season with its five-game league schedule in the Western Alameda County Conference Mission Division. Piedmont received a promotion from the Shoreline Division last season after winning the title. It aims to win back-to-back league banners. “We have a big game next week in Hayward. I think this matchup has a lot of buzz around the league. After winning the Shoreline last year, we have some really tough competition in the Mission [Division]. Irvington is looking a lot better; Washington looks good. No one is going to hand us anything and we’re not sneaking up on anyone,” Seiden said. Game Recap After trading possession twice, Piedmont got on the board with Staff Photos Quarterback Markos Lagios pushes into the end zone for one of his five touchdowns against Dougherty Valley. 5:04 left in the first quarter with Shelby on 15 and 20-yard receptions, a 16-yard reception by Xavier Henderson, and a 20-yard touchdown run by Tommy Ashton. Miles Silver then recovered a chip kick over a Wildcats players’ head at the DVHS 23-yard line. Shelby helped convert a 4th-and-7 with a nine-yard reception to the 11, followed by Lagios tucking and running in a touchdown on a broken pass play with 2:11 left in the first. PHS’ next touchdown came on a seven-play drive, where Lagios took a carry 47 yards to the DV 22-yard line. The next play Lagios found Jack Meyjes on a crossing route underneath, running it into the end zone for his first varsity touchdown with 8:56 left in the second quarter. Piedmont put up 14 more points in the third quarter. Shelby turned a screen pass 65 yards down the sideline for a touchdown with 7:42 on the clock, then scored an 80-yard touchdown including a broken tackle with 4:02 left. After Miguel Long grabbed an interception, PHS scored in 13 plays on a 4th-and-Goal at the Wildcats’ three yard line, when Henderson caught a pass in the flat and ran it in easily, making it 41-0 after a missed extra point with 8:21 left in the game. Final stats: Lagios completed 20-25 passes for 279 yards and four touchdowns, to go along with 89 rushing yards and a touchdown. Shelby had 193 yards on nine receptions and two touchdowns, plus 21 rushing yards on two carries. Ashton had 68 rushing yards on nine carries and a touchdown. Henderson and Meyjes both had touchdown receptions. Defensively, Brandon Dicke had two tackles for loss; Henderson had one tackle for loss. Silver had a pass defense and fumble recovery. Long had an interception. NEXT UP Piedmont (4-1) heads to Hayward on Friday, October 11 for a 7:00 p.m. game. Sam Shelby had 193 receiving yards and touchdown runs of 80 and 65 yards. Jack Meyjes (14) celebrates a touchdown reception with Cash Elmquist.
articles.title: QB Lagios scores 5 touchdowns

pages.text: 12 Wednesday, October 9, 2024 Sports Piedmont shuts out Dougherty Valley 41-0 QB Lagios scores 5 touchdowns Piedmont beats Lick-Wilmerding 17-11 By Jonathan Comeaux The Highlanders put together another dominant display on Friday, October 4 under the lights of Witter Field, blanking the visiting Dougherty Valley Wildcats 41-0. Piedmont’s football team improves its record to 4-1 and has outscored opponents 167-35 in its four-game winning streak. Piedmont put up 14 points in the first quarter and led 21-0 by halftime. Coach Jordan Seiden said it was their most complete performance this season and was glad to see his players remain hungry for more in the second half. “When the guys go into the locker room at halftime and they are disappointed, saying ‘We should be up more,’ that tells me that they know we can be even better. This was the most complete game we’ve played all season,” Seiden said. The Highlanders had 464 yards of total offense, with receiver Sam Shelby accounting for nearly half of it with 214 total receiving yards. Quarterback Markos Lagios accounted for four passing touchdowns and added another on the ground. “We expected a much more physical team and we just came out with that fire. Sam was doing his thing, he got me all those passing yards on little screens,” Lagios said. PHS now moves into the final stretch of the season with its five-game league schedule in the Western Alameda County Conference Mission Division. Piedmont received a promotion from the Shoreline Division last season after winning the title. It aims to win back-to-back league banners. “We have a big game next week in Hayward. I think this matchup has a lot of buzz around the league. After winning the Shoreline last year, we have some really tough competition in the Mission [Division]. Irvington is looking a lot better; Washington looks good. No one is going to hand us anything and we’re not sneaking up on anyone,” Seiden said. Game Recap After trading possession twice, Piedmont got on the board with Staff Photos Quarterback Markos Lagios pushes into the end zone for one of his five touchdowns against Dougherty Valley. 5:04 left in the first quarter with Shelby on 15 and 20-yard receptions, a 16-yard reception by Xavier Henderson, and a 20-yard touchdown run by Tommy Ashton. Miles Silver then recovered a chip kick over a Wildcats players’ head at the DVHS 23-yard line. Shelby helped convert a 4th-and-7 with a nine-yard reception to the 11, followed by Lagios tucking and running in a touchdown on a broken pass play with 2:11 left in the first. PHS’ next touchdown came on a seven-play drive, where Lagios took a carry 47 yards to the DV 22-yard line. The next play Lagios found Jack Meyjes on a crossing route underneath, running it into the end zone for his first varsity touchdown with 8:56 left in the second quarter. Piedmont put up 14 more points in the third quarter. Shelby turned a screen pass 65 yards down the sideline for a touchdown with 7:42 on the clock, then scored an 80-yard touchdown including a broken tackle with 4:02 left. After Miguel Long grabbed an interception, PHS scored in 13 plays on a 4th-and-Goal at the Wildcats’ three yard line, when Henderson caught a pass in the flat and ran it in easily, making it 41-0 after a missed extra point with 8:21 left in the game. Final stats: Lagios completed 20-25 passes for 279 yards and four touchdowns, to go along with 89 rushing yards and a touchdown. Shelby had 193 yards on nine receptions and two touchdowns, plus 21 rushing yards on two carries. Ashton had 68 rushing yards on nine carries and a touchdown. Henderson and Meyjes both had touchdown receptions. Defensively, Brandon Dicke had two tackles for loss; Henderson had one tackle for loss. Silver had a pass defense and fumble recovery. Long had an interception. NEXT UP Piedmont (4-1) heads to Hayward on Friday, October 11 for a 7:00 p.m. game. Photos by Lynne Wright Piedmont’s win over Lick-Wilmerding brings their record to 7-7, the school’s most since 2019. By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High’s girls’ water polo continues its winning ways, this time with a 17-11 win over Lick-Wilmerding in San Francisco on Thursday, October 3. The victory improves the team’s record to 7-7, the most wins since 2019. The Highlanders have three matches left in the regular season. They have an opportunity to notch the most wins in a season since 2017, which went 10-13 and was led by the school’s AllTime leading goal-scorer, Annika Disney, who went on to play for Santa Clara. Thursday’s win marked another strong performance by Abigail Jacoby, who had three goals and five assists. Goalie Zoe Waitkus was critical with six saves and two assists on long throws. Game Recap Piedmont led 4-3 through the first quarter and continued a narrow one-goal advantage up 7-6 going into halftime. The Highlanders extended their lead to 13-8 in the third quarter and scored four while allowing three in the final going, 17-11. Lick-Wilmerding actually scored the game’s first goal just 51 seconds into the game, but Piedmont went up with three unanswered goals by Sydney Olson, Viviane Burke, and Julian Montes to lead 3-1 with 2:34 left in the first quarter. Lick came back to tie it at 3-3 with a minute left, but Rachel Young got PHS back on top by scoring just 20 seconds later on the ensuing possession. Olson got her second goal a minute and a half into the second quarter, while Abigail Jacoby made it 6-3 after Piedmont’s defense forced a change of possession with 5:06 left. After a Tigers goal, Jacoby scored again with 4:32 left in the half. Lick-Wilmerding added two goals prior to halftime, making it 7-6. I n t he t h i rd qu a r ter, Lick-Wilmerding tied the game at 7-7 with a goal with 5:44 remaining, but Burke and Celeste Dickason created a two-goal cushion with 3:16 on the clock. Piedmont added four straight goals to end the quarter up 13-8 by Esme Krumins, Jacoby, Olson, and Sonja ten Grotenhuis. PHS continued on the throttle in the fourth quarter, scoring after 20 seconds by #2 followed by Mari Pisani with 5:22 remaining in the game. articles.text: Football players Sam Shelby and Markos Lagios, and Leighton Mand of the girls’ cross-country team have been named co-Athletes of the Week by the Post. Lagios was our Athlete of the Month for September and starts October with another strong performance. In the football team’s 41-0 win over Dougherty Valley, Lagios completes passes for 279 yards and four touchdown passes, in addition to gaining 89 rushing yards and one touchdown. Shelby, Piedmont’s star receiver and playmaker, had nine receptions for 193 yards with an eye-popping 21.4 yards per catch. He had two long touchdown runs on screen passes, including scores of 80 and 65 yards. Shelby also had a punt return for a touchdown called back due to a penalty. Sophomore Leighton Mand led the girls’ cross country team to the Artichoke Invitational title with a time of 15:29 on the 2.3 mile course in Half Moon Bay. It was 1 minute and 18 seconds faster than her time at the race last year. Staff Photo Markos Lagios earns Co-Athlete of the Week honors for a 5-touchdown performance. Sam Shelby earns Co-Athlete of the Week honors for 80 and 65 yard touchdown receptions against Dougherty Valley. Leighton Mand earns Athlete of the Week for leading her cross country team to the title at the Artichoke Invitational in Half Moon Bay.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s flag football team improved its record to 5-5 with a pair of heated wins in the heat last week. They defeated Tennyson 7-6 under the lights at Witter Field on Thursday, October 3, and beat Mt. Eden 13-12 in Hayward the previous day. “We had some injuries, which is normal at this point in the season, and everyone stepped up. We’ve played great defense and moving forward with creating turnovers,” coach Beth Black said. It was a defensive battle against the Tennyson Lancers with back-and-forth possessions. Piedmont scored the game’s opening touchdown to go up 7-0 midway through the first half, and Tennyson scored on its first drive of the second half but missed its extra point attempt. The Mt. Eden win, similarly, required strong defense with frequent blitzes by Elspeth Grippando and am interception and touchdown by Mary Schickedanz. “We’ve been using Elspeth and our outside players really patiently. They are getting there and making plays. Elspeth keeps pushing and pushing; her role is really something that has developed as the season has gone on,” Black said. Making her mark on the defensive side is junior leader Dahlia Osman. She’s the team leader in tackles and notable made the switch from outside cornerback to the safety role. It’s a move that has better utilized her consistent flag-pulling ability. “I switched to safety this season. At cornerback, I was really stuck to just one side, so now I can play to both sides. The safety spot allows me to run around; I definitely like it, it gives me a lot more room to move up, move back, or make a play on the ball,” Staff Photos Elspeth Grippando pulls a flag on Tennyson’s running back. She had one QB sack and one tackle for loss against Tennyson and two sacks against Mt. Eden Osman said. On offense, tall receiver Dorothy Nemeth, a senior, is proving to be a key wea[pm for the Highlanders. She scored a touchdown and extra point in the win over Tennyson and recorded an important 28-yard reception to extend their final drive. “We did really well moving around the ball to different players tonight. While it’s fun to get the ball a lot, it’s important to get a lot of people the ball. On that play [28-yard reception], I actually ran the wrong route. I was supposed to run a corner route, but I saw an open space down the middle of the field. I just put my arms up and hoped for the best,” Nemeth said. 7-6 over Tennyson Tennyson’s first drive got them to 1st-and-Goal at the Piedmont 20, but Piedmont turned the tide with a pass defense by Dahlia Osman and a sack by Elspeth Grippando. On 4th-andGoal, quarterback Edie Elmquist found Nemeth for a touchdown reception on a hitch route with 12:58 on the clock. Nemeth also caught the one-point conversion. The Lancers scored quickly in the second half with after just two minutes, but Piedmont’s Eunice Kouadio had a critical pass defense on the one-point conversion to keep the Highlanders’ lead at 7-6. From there, Tennyson punted three times and tossed interceptions to Ella Yassar and Osman. PHS’ final offensive drive ate the clock away from 2:23 down to 4 seconds, including Nemeth’s big 28-yard reception. PHS’ first touchdown came from Malia Williams came on a short catch and run into the end zone. During the drive, Williams also made a critical 11-yard reception on a pass from Elmquist, where Williams ranged to keep one foot in bounds down the sideline. Grippando also recorded two sacks. Offensively, Piedmont drove down to the one-yard line twice, but couldn’t get the ball into the end zone. However, one of those drives was PHS electing to knee the ball in victory formation to wind out the clock. articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ tennis team suffered a tense 4-3 loss to Conference rivals, Berkeley, at the Berkeley Tennis Club on Thursday, October 3. It marked the team’s second league loss after losing to Alameda 5-2 the previous week. “Another nail biter that didn’t go our way, unfortunately,” said PHS coach Jim Landes. “It came down to the third set in the third doubles match; it was the last match on the court. We’ll get Berkeley at home on the 24th and we’re looking forward to it.” The match came down to the No. 3 doubles team of Inara Mehta and Abigail Call, who lost in a narrow three-set contest 3-6, 7-6 (7-4), 6-3. “Abby and Inara started well, but two things happened. They relaxed and gave their opponents hope and then struggled keeping the ball away from Berkeley’s net person,” Landes described. The result brings Piedmont’s record to 6-9 overall and 1-2 in league matches. They look ahead to another critical league match this week when hosting Bishop O’Dowd on Thursday, October 12. Match Recap At singles, Piedmont won one of four matches with Kate Jumper at No. 2 winning a three-set battle, 3-6, 7-6 (7-3), 6-2. “Kate gradually started playing better and better. After, she pulled out the second set tiebreak, she really settled down and went through the third set like a hot knife through butter,” Landes said. Carolina Romanczuk lost a close match, 7-5, 6-4, at No. 1 singles. Arianna Kortum lost at No. 3 singles, 6-4, 6-2. Faith Chin lost 6-3, 6-1 at No. 4. “Carolina had a good match against Sam Lopatin at No. 1. She struck the ball more cleanly and with more power than Sam, but just wasn’t quite consistent enough,” Landes said. Piedmont won two of three doubles matches. At No. 1 Samantha Huynh and Emma Eisemon won in straight sets, 7-6 (7-1), 6-3. Emma Chan and Maddie Tran won 6-3, 6-1 at No. 2. “Emma E. and Samantha had a very tight first set, but they turned on the jets in the tiebreak and won it 7-1. They continued to roll and won the second 6-3. Maddie and Emma C. built on their momentous win the prior week against Alameda and trounced the Berkeley team pretty easily,” Landes said. At No. 3 doubles, Mehta and Call fought to three sets before losing 3-6, 7-6 (7-4), 6-3. NEXT UP Piedmont (6-9 overall, 1-2 league) hosts Bishop O’Dowd on Thursday, October 12 at 3:30 p.m. at the Corey Reich Tennis Courts. Kate Jumper won her No. 2 singles match against Berkeley. Staff Photos Emma Eisemon won her No. 1 doubles match with partner Samantha Huynh. Thursday’s loss to Berkeley came down to No. 3 doubles team of Inara Mehta and Abigail Call (not pictured).

articles.text: MAKENNA THIEL JACK STEIN This week we look at three former Piedmont High athletes who are currently competing in college. tional on September 21 in 24:34.3. Recently on October 4 at the DIV. 3 Pre-Nationals in Indiana, Stein was 13th in a jam-packed field of 405 runners, posting a time of 24:50 to lead his college team to the championship in competition with 45 other schools. In November last year, Stein helped the Sagehens win the Div. 3 NCAA Championship by defeating Wisconsin La Crosse by just one point, 158-159. Stein was Pitzer’s fifth-best runner and his finish was the margin of victory for the team. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team traveled to CSU Monterey Bay for the 2024 Monterey Invitational on Friday and Saturday, October 4-5. They went 2-2, opening with an 11-10 loss to Willow Glen and a 15-3 loss to Archbishop Mitty on the first day, but followed up strongly with an 18-12 win over Morro Bay and 13-12 double-overtime win over Aptos om Day 2. “The team really came together facing some tough competition in the Monterey Invitational, there were a lots of good teams. Our defense dramatically improved as our communication got better,” said assistant coach John Savage. It was a big tournament for senior leader Elles Krieckhaus, who totaled 15 goals in the four matches. He scored five goals in Piedmont’s overtime win over Aptos and seven goals in the win over Morro Bay. “We are really happy with Elles’s progression this year, realizing he can be the best player in the water on both sides of the game; offense and defense,” Savage said. The batch of games brings Piedmont’s record to 11-6 with four matches left on the regular season schedule before the start of the Western alameda County Conference tournament. 13-12 double OT win over Aptos Piedmont went up 2-1 in the first quarter and 6-4 by halftime. PHS maintained the two-goal advantage 10-8 through the third quarter, but Aptos tied the game at 12-12 with just 22 seconds left in the fourth quarter. After a scoreless first period of overtime, Piedmont’s Leo Hurwitz scored the game-winner with just four seconds left in the second OT. In the first, Piedmont’s Krieckhaus scored the opening two goals to put his school up 2-0 with 1:12 left but Aptos added one with 13 seconds left. PHS added another two within the first two minutes of the second quarter by Rylan Patty and Hurwitz, while Krieckhaus made it 5-2 with 3:47 on the clock. Zach Dupree made it 6-3 with 2:29 left in the half before Aptos cut one back before the break. In the third quarter, Piedmont took just 13 seconds to score out of the after winning the throw in, leading to Krieckhaus’ fourth goal. Aptos cut the lead to 7-6, but Dupree scored with 2:58 to go. After another Aptos goal, Patty and Hurwitz scored, 10-7, before Aptos’ next score to end the third. Aptos scored three straight in the fourth quarter to take an 11-10 lead with 2:35 left in the game. But Piedmont’s Krieckhaus tied the match at 11-11 with 1:12 on the clock, then PHS re-took the lead when Patty scored with 44 seconds left. Aptos scored on its last possession to force overtime. In the first period of overtime, Piedmont was able to kill a penalty with 21 seconds left. Then, things turned back in PHS’ direction after drawing a man-advantage with 27 seconds left. After a timeout, Piedmont drew up the play, leading to Hurwitz’s Golden Goal with just four seconds left. Final stats: Krieckhaus scored five goals, one assist, and one steal. Patty and Hurwitz had three goals and a steal. Dupree had two goals and an assist. Henry Stein had two assists and a steal. Goalie Luke McAuliffe had eight saves, one steal, and one assist. 18-12 over Morro Bay PHS actually trailed 5-3 through the first quarter and cut the deficit to 7-6 in the second quarter. articles.text: Legendary jazz fusion guitarist Al Di Meola will play five shows at Yoshi’s in Oakland this weekend, Friday through Sunday, October 11-13. Meola is among the top guitarists of our time. His fascination with complex rhythmic syncopation combined with provocative lyrical melodies and sophisticated harmony has been at the heart of his music throughout a career that has spanned four decades. He has produced four gold albums and two platinum albums, with six million record sales worldwide and five German gold albums. His awards include an Honorary Doctorate Degree from Berklee College of Music, the Honorary Miles Davis Award presented by the Montreal Jazz Festival, a BBC Lifetime Achievement Award presented by Sir George Martin in 2008, Hungarian Foundation for Performing Arts Lyra Award and numerous Grammy awards and nominations and awards. Not only a guitar hero but a prolific composer, Di Meola has amassed over 30 albums as a leader while collaborating on a dozen others with the fusion supergroup Return to Forever Al Di Meola will play at Yoshi’s in Oakland this weekend, Friday through Sunday, October 11-13. (with Chick Corea, Stanley Clarke and Lenny White). The celebrated acoustic Guitar Trio features virtuoso John McLaughlin; and the Rite of Strings trio with bassist Clarke and violinist Jean-Luc Ponty. A pioneer of blending world music and jazz, going back to early Latin-tinged fusion outings like 1976’s Land of the Midnight Sun, 1977’s Elegant Gypsy and 1978’s Casino, the guitar great continues to explore the rich influence of flamenco, tango, Middle Eastern, Brazilian and African music with his World Sinfonia, a global group that he formed in 1991. Tickets for the evening shows ($49-$99) are available at yoshis. com/events/buy-tickets.
articles.title: Guitarist Al Di Meola plays Yoshi’s this weekend

articles.text: This Sunday will mark the last show of the dazzling musical The Prom, which kicked off the 2024-2025 season of Berkeley Playhouse. Set in small-town Indiana, The Prom follows four eccentric Broadway stars who swoop into a conservative community to boost their careers by championing a high school student’s right to bring her girlfriend to the prom. The musical premiered on Broadway in 2018 and earned seven Tony Award nominations. It was followed by a movie (featuring Meryl Streep and Nicole Kidman), a national tour, and productions in top regional theaters across the U.S. Now, for a few more days at the Julia Morgan Theater, audiences can experience this hit Broadway musical, renowned for its infectious energy and poignant storytelling. Co-director Christina Lazo expressed the impor tance of presenting the musical in today’s world: “There have been instances over the years across the country of parents pulling their students from high school productions and local theaters canceling their shows due to the material. We have to do this show and keep doing shows like this. I can’t wait for audiences to see the sparkle and the beauty of the world within The Prom.” “This is a special show that is so much fun with tons of dancing and big numbers, but that is also full of heartfelt moments and important themes of acceptance,” added co-director McGrath. “The best part of the story is at the end where everyone gets to celebrate their truest selves.” For tickets ($19–$55) or more information, the public may call 845-8542 x351 or visit berkeleyplayhouse.org. Group rates are available for 10 or more people. All performances will take place at Berkeley Playhouse, 2640 College Avenue in Berkeley. The company of The Prom performs in Berkeley Playhouse’s production of the musical, co-directed by Christina Lazo and Megan McGrath. The show will play through this Sunday.
articles.title: The Prom closing at Berkeley Playhouse Oct. 13

articles.text: The Left Coast Chamber Ensemble will perform in Berkeley in November, offering music lovers the chance to hear works from the 20th and 21st centuries that combine drama and poetry. The opening concert of its 2024-2025 season will be held on Saturday, November 2 in San Francisco, with a repeat concert on November 3 at the Hillside Club in Berkeley at 4 p.m. The program includes Arnold Schoenberg’s Fall Cabaret: Pierrot Lunaire “This program exists in an atmosphere where melancholy and humor inextricably co-exist,” said Artistic Director Matilda Hofman. Tickets at the door are $38 for general admission and $18 for student admission. Advance tickets are available at $35 for general admission and $15 for students. For details visit www.leftcoastensemble.org/pierrot Founded in 1992, the ensemble is a group of 17 San Francisco Bay Area classical musicians. The ensemble performs a wide variety of musical compositions such as small ensemble, vocal, orchestral, multi-media and operatic productions. The LCCE’s expressed mission is to champion chamber music and new composers, with particular emphasis given to highlighting the contribution of lesser-known composers. The Left Coast Chamber Ensemble Photo by Miles Caliboso
articles.title: Left Coast Ensemble to perform in Berkeley in November

articles.text: From now through February 18, the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art presents Get in the Game: Sports, Art, Culture, exploring the place of sports in our society. Get in the Game, together with six sports-related companion exhibitions, will be the museum’s most expansive presentation dedicated to any one subject to date, covering over 15,000 square feet with over 200 compelling artworks and design objects by over 70 artists. Viewers will discover the sense of community found in depictions including pickup basketball games, minor league baseball teams, neighborhood swimming clubs and surfing groups. Audiences will also encounter artists and designers inspired by athletes promoting conversations about gender and race, as well as artworks responding to the remarkable achievements of sports figures such as Muhammad Ali, Michael Jordan, Diana Nyad and Venus Williams. Woven throughout Get in the Game are stunning works of contemporary art and design, interactive installations and historical videos that reconsider political and cultural issues through the lens of athleticism, competition and play. “Get in the Game explores the confluence of culture and sports and the many ways in which they influence each other. The exhibition creates space for dynamic conversations about identity, physicality, passion, ambition, and resilience”, said Christopher Bedford, SFMOMA Director. Upending our expectations of museums and games, viewers will be able to play interactive artworks by contemporary artists: Maurizio Cattelan’s 22-person foosball table, Stadium (1991), and Gabriel Orozco’s Ping Pond Table (1998), a four-way pingpong table with a square pool in place of a net. Get in the Game features dozens of innovative designs for sports gear, gaming and fashion, including Formula One race car steering wheels, a 2022 ensemble from Virgil Abloh’s final Louis Vuitton collection, Michael Johnson’s gold running shoes, Nike’s original Air Jordan basketball shoes, and the technological advances of surfboards, tennis racquets and football helmets. Reflecting the evolving field of play, the exhibition also integrates designs from more recent years, such as the Cheetah Xceed prosthetic running leg, developed by biomedical engineer Van Phillips an amputee, and the Refugee Nation Flag, designed by artist Yara Said, a Syrian refugee now in Amsterdam. SFMOMA (151 Third Street in San Francisco, is open 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Friday through Tuesday, and 12 p.m. through 8 p.m. on Thursdays. Tickets ($30 general, $25 senior, $23 student, free 18 and younger) are available at sfmoma.org/visit.
articles.title: SFMOMA opens Get in the Game Oct. 19

articles.text: The de Young Museum in San Francisco will open the first major U.S. retrospective of Tamara de Lempicka this Sunday, with over 150 works on display through February 9. Through her glamorous lifestyle, artist Tamara de Lempicka (1894-1980) has become synonymous with the carefree spirit and opulence of the 1920s. Her paintings, combining a classical figural style with the modern energy of avant-garde, have cemented Lempicka as one of Art Deco’s defining painters. Retrospective Tamara de Lempicka, the first exhibition in the United States dedicated to the artist’s full oeuvre, will reveal a new perspective on her life and art practice. In addition to her celebrated portraits, the exhibit will include a number of rarely seen drawings, experimental still lifes from Lempicka’s early Parisian years and melancholic domestic interiors, as well as a selection of Art Deco objects, sculptures and dresses from the museum’s collection. The exhibition is co-curated by Furio Rinaldi and Gioia Mori. “Considering San Francisco’s history as a great Art Deco capital of the world, the exhibition – aptly presented in close proximity to landmarks of the period such as the Golden Gate Bridge and Coit Tower – adds to our understanding not only of Lempicka’s work specifically, but also this influential art and design period at large,” said Thomas P. Campbell, Director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. “The combination of varied artistic influences in Europe during the interwar period constitute the ingredients for Lempicka’s unique visual language, a captivating and unique blend of classicism and modernism,” said Gioia Mori, exhibition co-curator. Tamara de Lempicka unfolds chronologically in four major chapters that mark the stages in the artist’s life through her changing identity: “Tamara Rosa Hurwitz” (her birth name), “Monsieur Łempitzky,” “Tamara de Lempicka,” and “Baroness Kuffner.” These sections include poignant and experimental still lifes from Lempicka’s early Parisian years, figural works inspired by the Russian avant-gardes and Cubist inspirations from her painting teacher André Lhote, while highlighting Lempicka’s appreciation for the work of Neoclassical painters of the 18th century like Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres. The de Young Museum (50 Hagiwara Tea Garden Drive, San Francisco) is open from 9:30 a.m. to 5:15 p.m., Tuesday through Sunday. Tickets ($20 adult, $17 senior, $11 student, free under 18) are available at: ticketing.famsf.org/ events. Tamara de Lempicka, Young Girl with Gloves, detail, 1930–1931. The de Young Museum in San Francisco will open Lempicka’s first major U.S. retrospective this Sunday, October 13.
articles.title: First major U.S. retrospective of Art Deco icon premieres at de Young Oct. 13

Tamara de Lempicka unfolds chronologically in four major chapters that mark the stages in the artist’s life through her changing identity: “Tamara Rosa Hurwitz” (her birth name), “Monsieur Łempitzky,” “Tamara de Lempicka,” and “Baroness Kuffner.” These sections include poignant and experimental still lifes from Lempicka’s early Parisian years, figural works inspired by the Russian avant-gardes and Cubist inspirations from her painting teacher André Lhote, while highlighting Lempicka’s appreciation for the work of Neoclassical painters of the 18th century like Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres. The de Young Museum (50 Hagiwara Tea Garden Drive, San Francisco) is open from 9:30 a.m. to 5:15 p.m., Tuesday through Sunday. Tickets ($20 adult, $17 senior, $11 student, free under 18) are available at: ticketing.famsf.org/ events. Tamara de Lempicka, Young Girl with Gloves, detail, 1930–1931. The de Young Museum in San Francisco will open Lempicka’s first major U.S. retrospective this Sunday, October 13.

I’ve learned a lot about that in the last week. Here are two dishes that you can make without much difficulty: One is a warm dish which they call “complete.” Take a large round cooking dish made of either clay or cast-iron. Use a variety of meats such as chicken, turkey, lamb, and beef – use whatever meat you have. Add a variety of vegetables, including carrots and potatoes and lots of paprika. Use capers in everything you cook. Douse these with some wine. The locals love their local wines, which are high in alcohol but rather light in flavor. Cook in the oven until the flavors blend. articles.text: This Sunday, October 13, the Piedmont Center for the Arts will host the first of three events in a new series, Japanese Internment Camps: Life, Art, and Music. This first event, “My Dad, the Activist,” starts at 4 p.m. and will feature Karen Korematsu, daughter of Oakland-born Fred Korematsu, who was arrested and convicted in Federal Court for resisting military orders to report for transfer to an internment camp in 1942. He appealed this conviction all the way to the Supreme Court, where it was overturned in 1983. Karen will share his father’s story and that of her family during the internment years, She will answer audience questions and take part in a meet-and-greet reception at the Center. The second event in the series, “Remembering, 80 Years Later,” will be held on Sunday, November 2 and feature Wendy Tokuda, a former Piedmont resident and award-winning former News Anchor at KPIX in San Francisco. She will share stories of her family’s time in the camps. Kimi Hill, the granddaughter of famed artist and interned UC Berkeley professor Chiura Obata, will share art produced in the camps, including her father’s. The third event, held on November 23, will feature a screening of Alternative Facts: The Lies of Executive Order 9066, a documentary by John Osaki about the false information and political influence which led to the World War II incarceration of Japanese-Americans. After the screening, Osaki will discuss the film with Piedmont resident Don Tamaki, the attorney instrumental in getting Fred Korematsu’s conviction vacated by the Federal District Court in 1983. Japanese Internment Camps: Life, Art, and Music will feature Karen Korematsu, daughter of Fred Korematsu Tickets and schedules for all three events ($18 one youth admission, $35 one general admission, $85 full series, $125 full series with front row reserved seating) at Piedmont Center for the Arts (801 Magnolia Ave.) are available at bpt.me/6449591.

articles.text: Miles Graber will present the Mila Trio in concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Friday, October 25 at 7:30 p.m. The tiro includes flautist Martha Aarons, violinist Lev Polyakin, and Graber on piano. Advance tickets are $35 in advance and $40 at the door. (https://bpt.me/6465993). The combination of violin, flute, and piano is most unusual in chamber music. Although there are countless works for violin or flute with piano, there are only a handful of works for these three instruments together. In a concert with pianist Miles Graber and the Mila Trio, audience members will be treated to two lovely works for the trio, complemented by three pieces for the individual instruments with piano. The two very stylistically contrasting pieces are J.S. Bach’s Trio Sonata in G major BWV 1038, and “Five Pieces” Op. 56, by the Russian composer Cesar Cui (1835- 1918). Manuel de Falla composed the “Siete Canciones Populares Españolas” for soprano and piano in 1914. He subsequently arranged the set (minus the second song) for violin and piano for the violinist Paul Kochanski, and it is this arrangement that will be performed. Pyotr Tchaikovsky wrote “Meditation” in 1878, originally as the slow movement of his violin concerto. He subsequently transcribed it for violin and piano as the first movement in a set called “Souvenir d’un Lieu Cher,” the “dear place” being the estate of his patroness Nadezhda von Meck. The piece for flute solo and piano is the beloved sonata of Francis Poulenc (1899-1963), a late work written in 1957 and debuted by Jean-Pierre Rampal with the composer at the piano.

articles.text: Festival Opera presents a recital with Sara Couden, contralto and Derek Tam, pianist, on Sunday, October 27, 4:00–5:30 p.m. at Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. What do art song and Halloween have in common? Well… monsters! Beasts without and within, love gone horribly wrong, generalized anxiety and existential crises, conversations with death… The world of classical music is rife with horrors, and contralto Sara Couden is excited to introduce as many of them as possible to the audience this October. She will be working with the fabulous and multi-talented pianist Derek Tam, presenting works by a list of composers including Schubert, Strauss, Wieck, and Weill, as well as modern composers Jordan Rutter-Covatto, Erika Oba, and Chris Castro. Don’t worry, there’s nothing to fear but fear itself. Praised for her “unusually rich and resonant voice” (Opera News), contralto Sara Couden is a premiere interpreter of operatic, concert, and song repertoire. Opera engagements for 2024 include Baba the Turk with Lakes Area Music Festival, as well as her San Francisco Opera debut as Rita in The Handmaid’s Tale. Concerts include Beethoven’s Symphony No. 9 with Seattle Symphony, Mass in B Minor with Santa Cruz Symphony, Duruflé Requiem with the Berkeley Community Chorus and Orchestra, and a concert of art songs and piano chamber music with Jenny Lin and Philip Setzer at the Manchester Music Festival. In previous seasons, Ms. Couden made her Metropolitan Opera debut as Albine in Thais, her Philharmonia Baroque Orchestra debut as Israelitish Man in Judas Maccabaeus, her San Francisco Symphony debut in Beethoven’s Symphony No. 9, and her Cincinnati May Festival debut as alto soloist in Julia Perry’s Stabat Mater. She toured Japan with Maestro Masaaki Suzuki in Bach’s B Minor Mass, and performed Third Lady in Die Zauberflote with the Los Angeles Philharmonic. She has performed numerous Handel roles, including Bradamante, Cornelia, Ino, Juno, Dejainira, Irene, and Narciso. She completed the Lindemann Young Artist Program at the Metropolitan Opera in 2017, and has been a fellow at the Marlboro Music Festival, Music@Menlo, Music Academy of the West, and the Institute for Young Dramatic Voices. Praised not only for his “deft” conducting (San Francisco Chronicle ) but also as “a master of [the harpsichord]” (San Francisco Classical Voice) and “the fortepianist of the beguiling fingers” (Bloomington Herald-Times), Derek Tam appears regularly throughout the Bay Area as a conductor and historical keyboardist. He is the executive director of the San Francisco Early Music Society, and serves as the artistic director of the biennial Berkeley Festival & Exhibition, an internationally-renowned celebration of early music. Tam is the president of the board of Early Music America, a national organization dedicated to strengthening historical performance. All are invited to meet the artists at a complimentary reception immediately following the performance. Tickets are $44.52 at www. Sara Couden, contralto Derek Tam, pianist eventbrite.com/e/913718355197

articles.text: San Francisco’s longest-running literary festival returns to celebrate its 25th year with over 120 literary events throughout the city in just over two weeks. Events running from Thursday, October 10 to Saturday, October 26 include reading series, publisher talks and bookstore exhibitions catering to all ages and tastes. It’s the best single event in the Bay for literature lovers to get a sense of what’s happening locally; nearly 80% of last year’s 570 featured authors, for instance, called the Bay home. A few of this year’s featured authors include Maxine Hong Kingston, Chinese-American novelist and National Book Award for Nonfiction winner; Daniel Handler, alias Lemony Snicket and author of many children’s books including the A Series of Unfortunate Events series; novelist Rachel Kushner, a Guggenheim Foundation Fellow, Prix Médicis winner and the recipient of an American Academy of Arts and Letters award; best-selling author and award-winning neuroscientist Daniel Levitin; and stand-up comedian, essayist and Academy Award-nominated actress Jenny Slate. One highlight of this year’s festival is the Booksellers Ball on October 10 from 7 to 10 p.m. at Club Fugazi in North Beach (678 Green Street), with beer, wine and delicious food; entertainment including music and dancing; and a reading nook with surprise exhibitions. Tickets range from $75 to $100, and all proceeds will support the Litquake Foundation. Another keystone of the festival is Kidquake, consisting of two days of citywide in-person and virtual talks and meet-and-greets with a diverse array of children’s book creators from October 10 to October 11, alongside activities run by the Bay’s top interactive educators. Each student leaves the in-person events with a new book, and teachers receive a bag of books and other goodies for their classrooms. Kidquake is completely free, and serves thousands of Bay Area K-5 public school students every year. A schedule of both days is available at litquake.org/ kidquake. Book lovers are urged to not miss the Litquake Book Fair on Saturday, October 19 from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. at Yerba Buena Gardens (750 Howard Street). A curated spread of 18 small presses and literary magazines will have local literature on offer throughout a day of poetry readings and music. Litquake will culminate with one of the Bay’s most anticipated literary nights of the year, Lit Crawl: a massive, one-night literary pub crawl through San Francisco’s Mission District that will bring together over 250 authors and an estimated 5,000 fans for the world’s largest free pop-up literary event. articles.text: Noomi Rapace and Michael Nyquist star in The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo who should have cared for her. The result is a young woman who is profoundly mistrustful of all authority. There is likely not enough time or therapy to unravel Lisbeth, if she would, even for a moment, consider trying. The question then is: can the first of what will be three films capture the essence of Salander while detailing a complex serial-murder mystery? All in 2 ½ hours. The answer is yes. Filmed in Northern Sweden, the movie has a brooding, stark feel to it, much of it shot in winter, involving a 40-something journalist, Mikael Blomkvist (Michael Nyquist). He is hired by an aging industrialist to find the person who, he assumes, murdered his 16-year-old niece some 40 years before. In every way it is a cold case, a case that at first blush seems intricate and unsolvable. The police tried. Yet, when Lisbeth is recruited, pieces to the jigsaw begin to come together revealing not just one murder, but a series of women, killed horribly and then mutilated, suggesting a terrible pathology at work. The film is wonderfully shot by cinematographer Eric Kress, and well acted by the Swedish ensemble. Of course, the crucial challenge was who to cast as Salander. Rapace is perfect, a slip of a woman, who conveys with her silence and anger and intelligence, her vulnerability while remaining well-defended, with an emotional carapace ever intact. Regarding the book and the film, there’s an inherent conundrum: if you read the book first, then the film will be eminently interesting, though without surprise. The twists at the end will be anticipated. But to watch the film before reading the book will reveal the ending and take some of the punch out of the story. The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo is a wonderful murder mystery, a classic whodunit, and the perpetrator is not disclosed until necessary making for a ripper of a climax as well as a very nice surprise embedded in the denouement. articles.text: Woody Allen is a serial monogamist when it comes to world-class cities. He fell in love with New York, then London, briefly Spain, and now Paris. Ah, Paris. Allen caresses its wide boulevards and avenues, reveals skylines under a startling blue sky, captures the wide sidewalks, damp from rain, the busy outdoor cafes, the lovely restaurants and grand lobbies of hotels. From the first frame of Midnight in Paris, photographed by the gifted cinematographer, Darius Khondji, Allen gives the city of lights a lingering embrace that ripples throughout the film. Gil Pender (Owen Wilson) and his fiancée, Inez (Rachel McAdams), have joined her parents (Kurt Fuller and Mimi Kennedy) in Paris. Gil is enchanted by the city, wants to walk the streets in the rain, especially the rain, and waxes nostalgic about what he believes were the glorious 1920s, the golden age when writers and artists, known as the Lost Generation, took up residence. A screenwriter in Hollywood, Gil tells Inez that he would love to move to Paris, find inspiration, and work on his novel – his protagonist owns a nostalgia shop filled with memorabilia. Inez, a lovely, mercenary young thing with the heart of a philistine, doesn’t grasp anything that Gil is attempting to convey, nor do her suspicious, judgmental parents. So instead of spending time with Inez clubbing, he wanders the streets of Paris into the midnight hours. And it’s on one such late night peregrination, feeling lost, literally and figuratively, that a classic Peugeot town car stops and a couple, formally dressed, insist that he join them. And so begins Gil’s journey back to that period about which he has romanticized, meeting a host of writers and artists to include Gertrude Stein (Kathy Bates), Ernest Hemingway (Corey Stoll) and the Fitgeralds, F. Scott (Tom Hiddleston) and Zelda (Alison Pill). These moments are wonderfully rendered, Gil’s jaw constantly dropping in astonishment, his heart given a tumble when he meets the lovely Adriana (Marion Cottillard), current girlfriend of Pablo Picasso (Marcial Di Fonzo Bo). It’s all pretty heady stuff with background music by Cole Porter. But there is a nugget of Woody Allen wisdom tucked into this engaging narrative, and it has to do with the nudging belief that plagues us all, well perhaps many of us, that the past is always qualitatively better than the present. For Gil it’s Paris of the 20s. For others, it might be pre-industrial America, or the early 40s when America was on the cusp of World War II. Some have referred to those who stepped forward during this period as the “greatest generation.” A nice bit of nostalgia. This slim but important insight offered up by Midnight in Paris – which is seamlessly presented with laugh-out-loud moments – is that we have but one life to live and if it’s going to be lived fully, well, best to live it in the present. A nice thought that resonates, offered up by Gil, who is an uncanny doppelganger for Woody in mannerisms and pacing, conveying just a hint of Allen’s signature nebbish uncertainty. This film is one of Allen’s best since Match Point. It’s richly put together, with a strong sense that the auteur is back on his game. Which is all to the good. Midnight in Paris. Directed by Woody Allen. Starring Owen Wilson, Rachel McAdams, Marion Cotillard. 1 hr., 34 min. Rated PG-13. Streaming on Fandango/ prime/apple tv. Released in 2013. The stories, each over 600 pages, are a tour de force, a cultural phenomenon, combining the thriller-mystery genre with an intensely fascinating character study, each densely layered with multiple characters and labyrinthine plots that are all but impossible to put down. The novels have been read worldwide and continue to spark interest and discussion, bolstered by the release of the film based on the first book. What makes the book and the movie compelling are its central character, Lisbeth Salander (Naomi Rapace), a 24-year-old waif of a young woman, brilliant to the point of genius, possessing a photographic memory and a deep well of courage. On the surface she is painfully asocial and all goth – tattoos, piercings, with ravenwing hair, dark eyes and a strain of individuality that is, in every respect, iron. articles.text: To watch the work of animator and writer Hayao Miyazaki is to be in the presence of creative genius, a master storyteller who invariably finds that engaging sweet spot: always surprising, perhaps a little scary, and consistently filled with mesmerizing wonder. My Neighbor Totoro, an early work, is no exception. Actually, if you, the reader, have yet to sample one of films, and are always in the hunt for a compelling G-rated film for the young ones, Totoro would be a solid beginning. The story is absent rough edged villains. There is no conflict, and it is told from the point of view of two young sisters, Mei and Satsuki (Dakota Fanning and Elle Fanning). It is, as well, an extraordinary co-mingling of fantasy and reality, which defines the essence of childhood. A scene from Hayao Miyazaki’s Princess Mononoke Princess Mononoke is an epic story set in Medieval Japan during its iron-age period. A world order, so to speak, is in transition: the balance between the forces of nature and those trying to bend the natural world to their own purpose is in conflict. However, animator/ director/ and storyteller Miyazaki often blurs the lines between good and evil, creating a sense of compelling ambiguity in this narrative wherein humans, forest animals and nature gods struggle for their share of the changing order. The film opens with a watchtower guard spotting “something wrong in the forest.” Out of this disturbance leaps a remarkable creature, a kind of boar-monster with flesh made of writhing snakes. It attacks the villagers and riding to their defense comes Ashitaka (Billy Crudup), a young prince of an isolated people. He is encouraged to begin a journey west and try and discover what the source of the disturbance is. He rides a Yakkuru, a beast that is part horse, part antelope and part goat. He finally arrives in an area prowled by Moro (Gillian Anderson), a hybrid wolf that is also part God. And it’s then that he sees for the first time a young woman named San (Claire Danes), also known as Princess Mononoke (a mononoke is actually a spirit of a beast). San is a human child, raised as a wolf, and rides a spirit wolf. And so the story continues, a panoramic trip with extraordinary characters and places, reflecting the deep bench imagination of Miyazaki. It’s a multilayered, richly told story. But know that for many young viewers, Princess Mononoke is not only complex, but one of Studio Ghibli’s darkest animated “Strictly Business”, Acrylic on Canvas, 38x40”, 2024

articles.text: Nothing about Totoro is intended to be even remotely spooky. Perhaps touched lightly by sadness, the spare story fits nicely under an umbrella of joy, imagination, and hand-drawn visuals that possess a palate of rich colors and an unfailingly detailed background. The film is set in Japan. The year is 1958. Professor Kusakabe (Tim Daly), a loving father, with his daughters move into an old, creaky house that is filled with enchantment and magic. It sits on the outskirts of a sweeping forest, never forbidding or menacing. The girls immediately take notice of a massive camphor tree that seems to stretch in all directions. The tree, they discover, is the home to a giant, benign creature called a totoro, which can only be described as an amalgam of a penguin, rabbit and owl. The narrative unfolds slowly. A scene from Studio Ghibli’s My Neighbor Totoro
articles.title: My Neighbor Totoro a classic from Studio Ghibli

articles.text: The Piedmont Post is presenting one month of reviews of films by celebrated Japanese animation director Hayao Miyazaki. As a writer, director, and animator he is one of the most revered filmmakers in Japan, and worldwide. His award-wining animated films have been embraced by audiences that have found his beautifully detailed hand-drawn visuals and thematic storytelling compelling. As well, his protagonists are often strong young girls or resilient young women. Miyazaki co-founded the now iconic Studio Ghibli in 1985. In 2012 he was named a Person of Cultural Merit by Japan for his outstanding cultural contributions. He received an Academy Honorary Award for his impact on animation and cinema in 2014. His work continues to serve as an inspiration for countless animators, directors and writers. This week’s reviews are: Princess Mononoke (1997) and My Neighbor Totoro (1988).
articles.title: One month of Hayao Miyazaki films

pages.text: 22 Wednesday, October 9, 2024 MOVIES FOR KIDS One month of Hayao Miyazaki films By Chris Honoré The Piedmont Post is presenting one month of reviews of films by celebrated Japanese animation director Hayao Miyazaki. As a writer, director, and animator he is one of the most revered filmmakers in Japan, and worldwide. His award-wining animated films have been embraced by audiences that have found his beautifully detailed hand-drawn visuals and thematic storytelling compelling. As well, his protagonists are often strong young girls or resilient young women. Miyazaki co-founded the now iconic Studio Ghibli in 1985. In 2012 he was named a Person of Cultural Merit by Japan for his outstanding cultural contributions. He received an Academy Honorary Award for his impact on animation and cinema in 2014. His work continues to serve as an inspiration for countless animators, directors and writers. This week’s reviews are: Princess Mononoke (1997) and My Neighbor Totoro (1988). Princess Mononoke a lovely fable from Japan My Neighbor Totoro a classic from Studio Ghibli By Chris Honoré To watch the work of animator and writer Hayao Miyazaki is to be in the presence of creative genius, a master storyteller who invariably finds that engaging sweet spot: always surprising, perhaps a little scary, and consistently filled with mesmerizing wonder. My Neighbor Totoro, an early work, is no exception. Actually, if you, the reader, have yet to sample one of films, and are always in the hunt for a compelling G-rated film for the young ones, Totoro would be a solid beginning. The story is absent rough edged villains. There is no conflict, and it is told from the point of view of two young sisters, Mei and Satsuki (Dakota Fanning and Elle Fanning). It is, as well, an extraordinary co-mingling of fantasy and reality, which defines the essence of childhood. Nothing about Totoro is intended to be even remotely spooky. Perhaps touched lightly by sadness, the spare story fits nicely under an umbrella of joy, imagination, and hand-drawn visuals that possess a palate of rich colors and an unfailingly detailed background. The film is set in Japan. The year is 1958. Professor Kusakabe (Tim Daly), a loving father, with his daughters move into an old, creaky house that is filled with enchantment and magic. It sits on the outskirts of a sweeping forest, never forbidding or menacing. The girls immediately take notice of a massive camphor tree that seems to stretch in all directions. The tree, they discover, is the home to a giant, benign creature called a totoro, which can only be described as an amalgam of a penguin, rabbit and owl. The narrative unfolds slowly. See My Neighbor Totoro on page 31 A scene from Hayao Miyazaki’s Princess Mononoke By Chris Honoré Princess Mononoke is an epic story set in Medieval Japan during its iron-age period. A world order, so to speak, is in transition: the balance between the forces of nature and those trying to bend the natural world to their own purpose is in conflict. However, animator/ director/ and storyteller Miyazaki often blurs the lines between good and evil, creating a sense of compelling ambiguity in this narrative wherein humans, forest animals and nature gods struggle for their share of the changing order. The film opens with a watchtower guard spotting “something wrong in the forest.” Out of this disturbance leaps a remarkable creature, a kind of boar-monster with flesh made of writhing snakes. It attacks the villagers and riding to their defense comes Ashitaka (Billy Crudup), a young prince of an isolated people. He is encouraged to begin a journey west and try and discover what the source of the disturbance is. He rides a Yakkuru, a beast that is part horse, part antelope and part goat. He finally arrives in an area prowled by Moro (Gillian Anderson), a hybrid wolf that is also part God. And it’s then that he sees for the first time a young woman named San (Claire Danes), also known as Princess Mononoke (a mononoke is actually a spirit of a beast). San is a human child, raised as a wolf, and rides a spirit wolf. And so the story continues, a panoramic trip with extraordinary characters and places, reflecting the deep bench imagination of Miyazaki. It’s a multilayered, richly told story. But know that for many young viewers, Princess Mononoke is not only complex, but one of Studio Ghibli’s darkest animated See Princess Mononoke on page 31 A scene from Studio Ghibli’s My Neighbor Totoro “Strictly Business”, Acrylic on Canvas, 38x40”, 2024 IT’S ALL RELATIVE P Pa ai in nt ti in ng gs s b by y B Bi il ll l P Pr ro oc ch hn no ow w Figurative abstractions using color, form & negative space to comment on and respond to human relations. articles.text: Marty Clubb explains the geography of the Walla Walla vineyards. Part 1 In my 23 years of being a wine journalist I have traveled to many countries and several continents to visit the major wine regions of the world. One region I had missed was the wine growing region of Washington state. I have had many fine wines from Walla Walla and knew their reputation was soaring, but I had yet to visit. This past month that omission was corrected as I journeyed there with my good friends Wine. com founder Mike Osborn and winemaker Kent Rasmussen. Flying into Pasco and the Tri-Cities area and driving east one hour to Walla Walla you pass through vast open spaces of scrubland interlaced with wheat fields. Part of the journey included the Columbia River with its dramatic gorges and beautiful scenery. Walla Walla (“place of many waters” in the Nez Pearce language) is a green oasis of treelined streets, verdant parks and tidy wooden houses. With a population of around 34,000 it seems like a charming, livable city that would be a great place to raise a family. In the last 20 years Walla Walla has morphed from quiet, overlooked wheat town to a vibrant wine capital of Washington state. Leonetti, the area’s first winery, was started in 1973 and for years there were just a handful of wineries in the area. There are now over 120 wineries, and the main street is packed with tasting rooms promoting their wines. There are charming Bed and Breakfast places and Air B&B and trendy restaurants galore. In the early days of the wine industry most of the attention was focused on growing Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon. While those wines continue to thrive, the rising star is the Syrah grape, and the region has been winning major accolades for those wines. Ferguson is L’Ecole No. 41’s flagship Bordeaux Blend.

This third-generation owned winery is now run by Marty and Megan Clubb. Marty, an expert on the geography of the Walla Walla growing region, gave us a fascinating tour of their vineyards and topography. The L’Ecole 41 wines are widely available with national and international distribution. (see lecole.com) • 2022 L’Ecole No.41 Semillon Stillwater Creek, $25 This winery has long been famous for its Semillon, a grape that is in my mind underappreciated and overlooked. Like the excellent examples from Australia’s Hunter Valley, this concentrated wine shows green apple, sage, preserved citrus and lemongrass. The acidity is woven into every fiber of the fruit, carrying it through the long finish. Will benefit from time in the cellar. • 2022 L’Ecole No. 41 Luminesce Seven Hills Vineyard, $28 A blend of 60% Semillon and 40% Sauvignon Blanc this wine reminds me of a fine Bordeaux blanc. It does see a percentage of new French oak which gives a sweet vanilla note to the nose. In the mouth you get peaches, apricots and pears. It has a nice round mouthfeel and a savory finish. Perfect partner to roast chicken.

L’Ecole 41 Winery tasting rooms don’t get much cuter than this. It is housed in the old Frenchtown school just outside of Walla Walla. Purchased in 1983 it was the third winery in Walla Walla. This third-generation owned winery is now run by Marty and Megan Clubb. Marty, an expert on the geography of the Walla Walla growing region, gave us a fascinating tour of their vineyards and topography. The L’Ecole 41 wines are widely available with national and international distribution. (see lecole.com) • 2022 L’Ecole No.41 Semillon Stillwater Creek, $25 This winery has long been famous for its Semillon, a grape that is in my mind underappreciated and overlooked. Like the excellent examples from Australia’s Hunter Valley, this concentrated wine shows green apple, sage, preserved citrus and lemongrass. The acidity is woven into every fiber of the fruit, carrying it through the long finish. Will benefit from time in the cellar. • 2022 L’Ecole No. 41 Luminesce Seven Hills Vineyard, $28 A blend of 60% Semillon and 40% Sauvignon Blanc this wine reminds me of a fine Bordeaux blanc. It does see a percentage of new French oak which gives a sweet vanilla note to the nose. In the mouth you get peaches, apricots and pears. It has a nice round mouthfeel and a savory finish. Perfect partner to roast chicken. The L’Ecole No. 41 tasting room is an old historic schoolhouse. • 2021 L’Ecole No. 41 Syrah Seven Hills Vineyard, $42 The wine is opaque purple-magenta in the glass. It opens with a full-throttle nose of dark fruit aromas, dried herbs black pepper and vanilla. The palate is medium bodied with a seamless, svelte texture transitioning to a savory finish with soft tannins and meaty undertones. • 2021 L’Ecole No. 41 Merlot Estate, $42 The Estate Merlot leads with brambly mintiness, cocoa and dark chocolate plum and herbs. This is a classy wine. It nails the traditional Merlot characters and is impeccably balanced and layered ending with soft inviting tannins. • 2021 L’Ecole No. 41 Apogee, $60 Hailing from the famous Pepperbridge Vineyard, this Bordeaux blend opens with blackcurrants leather and fresh herb aromas. The palate combines sturdy, dusty dark fruit flavors with admirable finesse. It shows judicious use of new wood which gives complexity and sturdiness. The wine should develop beautifully for two decades in the cellar. • 2021 L’Ecole No. 41 Ferguson Estate, $75 This Bordeaux blend uses all five of the traditional Bordeaux varietals in the mix. It offers up aromas of wild berries, cassis, licorice, rose petals and earth followed by a medium to full-bodied velvety and seamless palate, its structuring tannins hidden in an ample core of lively, succulent fruit. A dead ringer for a top growth Bordeaux. K Vintners One of the highlights of our Walla Walla trip was the invitation to have dinner at the home of Charles Smith, founder of K Vintners. Smith lives in a historic wooden house tucked beside a creek behind one of his vineyards. Over Smith’s dinner of fresh oysters, pasta and swordfish steaks we had a chance to sample some of his old K Syrahs and get to know this iconic Washington wine figure. Smith became interested in wine while working in restaurants at age 19. After veering off-track to spend a decade touring Europe as a rock band manager in Denmark, he returned to the U.S. to open a wine shop on Ferguson is L’Ecole No. 41’s flagship Bordeaux Blend. K Vintners in Washington is King of Syrah. Bainbridge Island by Seattle. But Charles’ real calling was not selling wine but making it. He made his way to Walla Walla where he got the opportunity to jump into the business. With almost nothing in his pockets, he found a way to produce his first vintage – 330 cases of 1999 K Syrah in 1999. In the two decades since he has become a celebrity winemaker. He developed (and later sold) iconic brands like House Wine and Kung Fu Girl Riesling. But the heart of Smith’s portfolio remains the Rhone-inspired K Vintners label. (His entire portfolio can be found at Houseofsmith. com.) • 2021 K Vintners M.C.K. (Motor City Kitty), $40 (Best Value) This is 100% Syrah from the Boushey Vineyard in Yakima Valley. The MCK is youthfully dense with aromas of blackcurrant, leather, charcuterie and coffee. The full-bodied palate has a round mouthfeel and mouthwatering acidity to enliven its concentrated, savory fruit and go with the long, lingering finish. This bargain priced Syrah is the best value of the lineup. See Wine Corner on page 31

pages.text: 26 Wednesday, October 9, 2024 Walking on Wednesday Exploring some new territory By Dick Carter Twenty-eight heat resistant members of the Walking on Wednesdays group gathered last Wednesday for a walk, though the forecast was for temperatures in the 90s. One seldom traveled Piedmont street the walkers hadn’t gotten to this year was activity leader Dick Carter’s Florada Avenue. Getting to it would let the walkers have a “fall colors” experience on Wildwood Avenue where its maple trees were almost-New England colorful. Additionally, the group could walk through Wildwood Gardens and check out the controversial vacant lot/house project on Wistaria Way. However, a walkthrough Wildwood Gardens would be incomplete without some history of Frank Colton Havens, the man responsible for it. The walkers went down Highland Avenue, turned up Wildwood Avenue, and stopped to enjoy the red leaves on the maple trees that line both sides of the block. A group photo was taken and some history from Gail Lombardi’s Piedmont Historical Society articles and Meghan Bennett’s History of Piedmont website was told. Frank C. Havens came to San Francisco from New York in 1866 and worked in banking, stocks, insurance, and investments. In 1895 he created the Oakland-based “Realty Syndicate” with F. M. “Borax” Smith. They became major real estate developers in the East Bay, particularly in Oakland, Berkeley, and Piedmont. The Syndicate accumulated at least 13,000 aces of valuable hilltop land that stretched from Mills College to North Berkeley. It built the Claremont Hotel in Berkeley and was also the parent company of the Key System transit company. Ken Hubbert provided some new information from the book Borax Pioneer about Smith. At some point before 1910, Smith and Havens came into conflict, for reasons unknown. One explanation was Smith joined in a water business that competed with a Havens business. Another was that Havens knew where Key System lines were going to be built and tipped off his family and friends to buy the land first at Smith’s expense. On December 9, 1910 it was made public that they had divided their interests, and sadly, after they had created so much together, never met or spoke again. Havens owned all the land from Crocker Avenue to Oakmont Avenue and Oak Road, and wanted to build an estate that he would call “Wildwood.” Havens’ mansion is at 101 Wildwood Gardens, which the walkers went to earlier this year. The group turned into Wildwood Gardens, passing two partially hidden pillars that marked the entrance to Havens’ estate. They walked up to Wistaria Way to a recently cleared lot. It was once part of a home that was donated to a local church and sold in 2022. The walkers were surprised to see work in progress. A large piece of equipment was down the hillside and drilling large holes for piers that will secure the home’s foundation. By chance, the landowner, Geoff Gibson, was there and explained he was dividing the lot into two parcels and constructing two new homes, one for his family, with an ADU alongside one. A new California law, known as “SB9,” which is intended to allow homeowners to divide their lots and construct up to four houses on a On hand for last week’s walk were Jack and Sharona Fischrup, Elizabeth Richter, Martin Levy, Peggy Shultz, Nancy and Dave DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Sherry Jacobs, Chuck Oraftik, Judy Love, Karen Palmer, Lori Austin, Rick Eigenbrode, Joyce Bailey, Noemi Alvarado, Woody Bailey, Claudine Bach, Marianne Jakus, Mike Henn with k-9 best friend Roger, Jim Kuo, Jim Kellogg, Bob Wong, Priscilla Wanerus, Mark Davis, Lorek Haghnazarean, Albert Chen, Charlene Louie with K-9 best friend Archie, Joyce and Woody Bailey from Maryland, and Dick Carter. single-family parcel. The neighbors have issues with it, but the project is moving forward. The walkers emerged on Woodland Way, then over to LaSalle Avenue and down to the little traveled Florada Avenue, the location of the Carters’ home. Further down the street is the Oakland/Piedmont city line where the street becomes Portal Avenue. That was as much Oakland exploration most walkers wanted on such a hot day, But some went on to see an Oakland house with a wonderful cactus garden. By chance the owner was outside and told them about his 15-year gardening project. The return to the city center was on LaSalle, Muir, and Crocker Avenues, Wildwood and Sheridan Avenues. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu

articles.text: Piedmont’s third largest community event, the Harvest Festival, had more going on than immediately met the eye on September 22. The Festival include an art exhibit each year at the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. While the center sounds of Harvest Festival activities saturated the park, the Art Exhibition was a stand-out spectacle of local art talent. Long-time organizer of the exhibit Jane Reed gathered talented Piedmont artists to supply pieces for the show. Adult artists included Jon Schleuning, with some of his drawings, and Bonnie Bonner, aka Joanne Palamountain, displayed some of her more contemporary pieces including Undressing for Winter, a giclee print on canvas of an Aspen sapling. Many different mediums of art were on display, including 7th grader Evan Shim’s crocheted stuffed animals. Shim nearly sold all his pieces during the festival. Another 7th grader, Peter Zee, displayed his croqueted medieval knight’s chest armor. “I was especially proud to see my son have his work displayed this year. He worked on his piece completely by himself whenever he could find free time between soccer or robotics practice. We calculated that it took him 40 hours of work to finish his piece and he designed his own pattern. He also crafted the helmet on his own using cardboard, a glue gun, and paint,” said mom Tracie. “It takes a lot of early mornings or late nights to capture some of these moments, so I’m happy that others can see these too,” said photographer Tracie with Picture Happy Photos. “Some of those unique alignments of the sun or moon to famous Bay Area landmarks were captured from right here in Piedmont.” Art lovers chat with artists at the 2024 Harvest Festival’s Art Exhibit. A wide range of Asian-inspired cuisines helped celebrate the Asian culture and the Mid-Autumn Festival. Liu prepared a presentation and spoke at the festival about the community of Alviso, that lives below sea level due to the history of excessive groundwater pumping for agricultural and residential uses. During the Gold Rush in the mid-19th century, large quantities of mercury were used in the mining process to extract gold from ore. This led to significant mercury contamination in the waterways leading into Alviso. Environmental problems continue as freshwater has been diverted into the Alviso wetlands, lowering critical salt levels, allowing invasive plants to infiltrate, squeezing out the native plants. The documentary introduces the community of Alviso, which also faces gentrification, the loss of affordable housing, and the erosion of the community’s cultural fabric in the wake of rapid urbanization in Silicon Valley. articles.text: Part 3 in a series The Piedmont Post provides extensive coverage each election cycle so voters may learn more about each City Council candidate and make well-informed decisions on election day. In the weeks leading up to the November 5 election, we will continue to publish a regular Q&A segment where candidates will answer questions about their backgrounds, qualifications and policies with a 200-word limit for each response. City Council Two open seats; four candidates. Week 3 Question: What is the most significant issue that the Piedmont City Council faces? Conna McCarthy, Incumbent Since 2017, California lawmakers have passed over 100 pieces of legislation in response to decades of neglect supporting housing affordability and availability. State mandates require cities adopt policies that remove barriers to building in all residential areas, including neighborhoods previously reserved for single family homes. State policy changes increased target numbers for most communities and greatly strengthened tools for enforcement. Piedmont is challenged to meet an allocation of 587 new units. In 2020, Piedmont began a process to meet state mandates by considering lot size minimums, ADU guidelines, multi-family housing, zoning, and other ways to identify options for new housing while maintaining the essential character of Piedmont. A change in policies that traditionally constrained development to policies that remove restrictive local zoning is the source of significant upset in Piedmont. Since 2021, Piedmont Council and Planning staff has hosted 70 public meetings or workshops on housing related issues and published 29 news releases. It is an ongoing struggle to balance community concerns with state mandates. We closely follow court cases and will join any feasible challenges. The housing decisions we make today will impact Piedmont for future decades. Ongoing community participation in problem solving is critical. Lorrel Plimier, Candidate Housing is one of the most significant issues that the Piedmont City Council faces and I expect this will remain true for the foreseeable future. It’s well known that California and the Bay Area are experiencing a housing crisis. The state of California has legislated a number of solutions to allow for housing to be built more quickly to accommodate our growing population. In addition to newer legislation,
