RELIGION CORNER In celebration of World Wide Communion Sunday By Pastor Jim Hopkins In many Protestant churches the first Sunday of October is designated as World Communion Sunday, which celebrates our oneness in Christ with all our brothers and sisters around the world. Paul tells us that we are to “discern the body” when we partake of Holy Communion, mindful that we note our relationship to all siblings in Christ in the celebration. The website of the Presbyterian Church USA notes that the World Communion Sunday (originally called World Wide Communion Sunday) is a gift of the Presbyterian Church to the larger ecumenical church. The first celebration occurred at Shadyside Presbyterian Church in Pittsburgh, PA, in 1933 where Dr. Hugh Thompson Kerr served as pastor. It wasn’t until 1940 when the Department of Evangelism of the Federal Council of Churches (a predecessor body of the National Council of Churches) promoted extending the celebration to a number of churches around the world that the practice became widespread. At Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church we will turn to the Easter story of the walk to Emmaus to celebrate World Communion Sunday this year. On a seven-mile walk from Jerusalem, two of Jesus’ disciples, still grieving his death on the cross, came to recognize their resurrected savior as they walked together, as he explained the teachings of scripture to them and as they shared a meal. We will affirm that gathering at the Table of Communion represents our commitment to walk with people from all over the world, to study the Bible together and to break bread together. We will further affirm that these acts are tangible ways of moving from xenophobia (fear of the stranger) to philoxenia (love of the stranger). In leading our World Wide Communion Sunday service, I will note that as important as table fellowship is as a symbol and act of unity, it is sadly ironic that maligning a culture via its foods is a long-standing American tradition. A recent Associated Press article by Deept Hajela begins, “It’s a practice about as American as See Religion Corner on page 3 HANA THOMAS, 11th grade Adult inaction. If we keep expecting the problem to deal with itself and push it off onto future generations, it will never get taken care of. JOAQUIN GONZALEZ, 11th grade All of the pollution that goes into the air from factories and fossil fuels being burned. ELIZABETH LONG, 11th grade Human technology. The way that humans are producing technology in such high amounts and at such a great rate does not consider the repercussions in the future or right now. articles.text: Editor: As a parent with children at both Havens and Piedmont Middle School, I’ve been consistently impressed by the dedication of our teachers across both schools. Every year I am amazed at what these teachers do daily and accomplish with our children annually. Mrs. Adams, two of my children’s kindergarten teacher, has been exceptional. articles.text: Editor: Moving to Piedmont more than 20 years ago was handsdown the best decision we ever made for our family. In addition to the beautiful homes, parks, and playgrounds, Piedmont has a renewable resource that makes it punch far above its weight: a small army of committed, competent, empathetic and smart volunteers who step up to help guide decision making for our town. Conna McCarthy is a poster child for that army. As a member of the City Council for the past four years, Conna has shown a deep commitment to listen to every member of the Piedmont community, and to transparency and accountability for the decisions made by the City Council that greatly impact the quality of life and safety of the town we all love. As owners of one of Piedmont’s most visible businesses, it’s important to us that the City Council is made up of dedicated volunteers who will put public service ahead of politics and ensure everyone in our community has a voice in important decisions. Over the years, we have both spent countless hours volunteering, parcel-tax wrangling, and event chairing in Piedmont. Or at least to us it felt like countless hours, until we noticed that every single time we were involved in a city-wide effort, Conna was there with us in the trenches, working to ensure our city and our schools thrived. She’s been a part of each and every initiative that makes Piedmont so special, from Tri-School fundraisers to the Piedmont Educational Foundation to securing pickleball in our town. We believe in Conna’s intelligence, empathy, humility and work ethic, and we urge you to relect her to the City Council on November 5th. –Laura Pochop & Chad Olcott She will come on board ready to work, without a learning curve. Lynda has had a constant, passionate involvement with her community and the environment, both in her career as a scientist and in her everyday life. Her life’s work is to preserve the environment and educate the youth. There is no one else who can match the qualifications needed for this job other than Lynda Deschambault. We need people like her. –Kay James, Moraga You may now subscribe online at:

articles.text: I have known Conna McCarthy since our children were in Piedmont Middle School and we were both on the Parent Board. Since then we have worked together on many, many projects and many, many campaigns. Conna is a real people person and she cares deeply about our Piedmont community. She is an enthusiastic and tireless worker and has an impressive resume. But what sets Conna apart is her willingness to roll up her sleeves and dive right in. Thanks to Conna’s leadership on the Seismic Safety Campaign, our schools are much safer. Thanks to Conna’s extensive experience with the Piedmont Education Foundation, she understands how important the City/School relationship is. Thanks to Conna’s role on the Piedmont Recreation Commission, our city has improved pickleball courts. And thanks to Conna’s four years on our City Council, Piedmont is better positioned for the future. She asks the tough questions and makes the tough decisions, always guided by her smarts, true moral compass, and love of Piedmont. –Andrea Swenson Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: Matt Simons Margaret “Maggie” Kane celebrated her 100th birthday in Piedmont over the weekend surrounded by friends, family and neighbors. Kane hosted a tea party prior to the birthday festivities at her home on Sunday, September 29, celebrating a century of life experiences, family ties and community bonds. Born on October 2, 1924, she grew up in Phoenixville outside of Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, with her younger siblings Jimmy and Helen. Her father owned a thriving taxi business, but opportunities were “extremely limited” in the small manufacturing town. She recalled that Phoenixville was home to both a steel mill and a Goodyear rubber plant that offered steady employment, though she eschewed the restricted and physically laborious roles to follow in her parents footsteps and pursue higher education. When it came time for college, she decided to study public relations; a decision she credits to an uncle who lived and worked in the Bay Area. “He was here in San Francisco, and he was quite wellknown and a delightful guy,” Kane said. “And I thought, ‘that’s what I want to do.’ I mean, he was enjoying life to the hilt.” Kane said she remembers her uncle interviewing and socializing with a variety of personalities such as swimmer and actress Esther Williams and radio personality Major Bowes. Her uncle’s gregarious personality and career allowed him to lead an exciting life that she found inspiring. “He was very sharp and he just gravitated to people that were on his intellectual level,” Kane said. Kane attended the Charles Morris Price School of Advertising and Journalism in Philadelphia, where she earned her degree in one year by going to school at night and by day. She graduated in 1944, during World War II. She added the ongoing military draft at the time meant many opportunities that were previously dominated by men had been made available to women. She landed her first job at a print shop in Philadelphia. “I was the only woman they’d ever hired,” Kane said. However, Kane quickly became bored with the setup in Philadelphia and pined for something more. “There were no other women to have lunch with, and there Photos by Johan Quie The Kane residence ready to celebrate a centennial birthday party One-hundred-year-old Maggie Kane celebrating with her one-year-old next door neighbor Berit Quie Maggie Kane blows out candles on her birthday cake. Maggie Kane hosts a tea party for her friends and family. was nobody who was going to give you the time of day,” Kane said. “So I decided I better look around and find something more interesting.” Kane held a number of jobs between 1944 and 1950 and before the Korean War. Kane was hired at a Philadelphia advertising agency, where she discovered on her first day that one of her new colleagues was one of the many enlisted men who had returned from service. “I came in, and lo and behold, there’s a young man who had just been hired and had just returned from the Navy,” Kane recalled. His name was Bill Kane. Little did I know that he was going to be very much in my future.” The two dated for a year-anda-half, during which time he proposed to her on numerous occasions. “One day he came with a diamond ring that was his grandmother’s.” She said she worried that refusing the ring would embarrass him, so she decided to keep the ring for a couple of weeks before returning it to him. “I never gave it back,” Kane said with a smile. They were engaged in 1952 and married the next year. They moved into a brownstone apartment in Philadelphia, and raised a family of five children, Coleman, Lachlann, Nevan, Michael and Caroline. “But we thought with five children to put through college, we’d better get to California,” Kane said. “The state had a reputation that it was so inexpensive to go to college. So we packed them up and out we came.” Kane and her family moved to Piedmont in 1972 for the school systems, and she has been here ever since. And this week she gets to celebrate her 100th birthday with her many friends and family members. Newsstand copies of the Piedmont Post are available at ­ t ­ t ­ t ­ Mulberry’s Market. Kane was hired at a Philadelphia advertising agency, where she discovered on her first day that one of her new colleagues was one of the many enlisted men who had returned from service. “I came in, and lo and behold, there’s a young man who had just been hired and had just returned from the Navy,” Kane recalled. Little did I know that he was going to be very much in my future.” The two dated for a year-anda-half, during which time he proposed to her on numerous occasions. “One day he came with a diamond ring that was his grandmother’s.” She said she worried that refusing the ring would embarrass him, so she decided to keep the ring for a couple of weeks before returning it to him. “I never gave it back,” Kane said with a smile. They were engaged in 1952 and married the next year. They moved into a brownstone apartment in Philadelphia, and raised a family of five children, Coleman, Lachlann, Nevan, Michael and Caroline. “But we thought with five children to put through college, we’d better get to California,” Kane said. “The state had a reputation that it was so inexpensive to go to college. articles.text: As a senior in high school, in the thick of applying to college, balancing homework, being an active member of multiple extracurriculars, and just in general stressed, I forget to breathe. Sometimes I am so focused on what I’m doing, I lose focus of myself. and of what truly matters. For each person, what truly matters is different. For me it’s being a good friend, family member, singer, athlete, and more. Remembering these things and people helps me feel like myself again. Recently I have felt that I’ve been pulled in so many different directions I don’t feel like myself. I don’t feel like a good friend, or like a good daughter. I feel like I’m getting stripped of who I am because people keep telling me who I’m supposed to be and what I’m supposed to do. I don’t like that – I really don’t. I want to be able to decide on my own. Being told that I might not have that choice is heartbreaking. We are all so stretched thin by responsibilities and expectations, we can’t always see the similarities of our situations. I am being faced with the reality that I have to say goodbye to many parts of myself this year. I am saying goodbye to being a high school student and athlete. I am saying goodbye to being a part of a choir that I’ve called home for 14 years. I am saying goodbye to my best friend as she moves away for college. I am saying goodbye to my childhood. I know that seniors have been faced with that question a lot recently. The question of who are we? What will we do? And we are being forced to choose now, when we ourselves are still trying to figure it out. I am scared. Because if I don’t even know who I am, how am I supposed to convince someone else who I am? I recently heard a quote that helped bring me clarity through the fog of my own uncertainty. It went something like this: “I am at a point in my life where I am letting go of things that don’t serve me anymore. And letting go of some of that stuff, I am going to leave claw marks, because I love those things and those people.” I will let go of my childhood because dwelling on the fact that it’s over doesn’t serve me. I will let go of my uncertainty about who I will become, because being scared about it doesn’t serve me. I will let go of my best friend because I can’t make her stay and stop her from finding out who she is going to be and it won’t serve either of us. And I will let go of people telling me who I’m supposed to be because that is meant for me to find out. But I am excited, to see who I will be in six months after I’ve let go and started fresh, because something about meeting a new, happier version of myself is beautiful. As we – especially seniors – are faced with never ending existential questions about our lives, the threat of losing ourselves trying to be someone we’re not for somebody or something else, and the constant letting go, I ask that we remember that we are just starting on our own adventures. That we will end up where we are supposed to be. That we will be OK. That it’s just one day at a time, until we have the courage to look past today and into tomorrow. Larissa Edel is a Piedmont resident and a student at Bentley High School ln Lafayette.
articles.title: Essay: On being yourself

articles.text: Ariel Rodriguez Many high schools throughout the country will be hosting the PSAT this month, but what is the PSAT? PSAT stands for Preliminary Scholastic Aptitude Test, essentially the precursor to the SAT. Like the SAT, the PSAT is a digital, adaptive test that includes a Reading & Writing section and a Math section. Both the SAT and PSAT are 2 hours and 14 minutes long. There are also some major differences between the PSAT and the SAT. The PSAT is only offered once per year, in October, and is typically hosted by your high school. The SAT, on the other hand, is offered seven times per year at test centers throughout the country. The maximum scaled score on each section of the PSAT is 760; the maximum scaled score on each section of the SAT is 800. If you are a junior taking the PSAT, your scores could qualify you for National Merit Commendation or National Merit Semifinalist. Many schools will also allow sophomores to take the PSAT, but only scores from junior year can qualify for national merit recognition. Exact score cutoffs are determined by state in the year following the PSAT taken. So, a junior taking the PSAT Fall 2024 will not find out if they have received national merit commendation or semifinalist status until 2025. Commended students are typically within the top 3-4% of testers; semifinalists are typically within the top 1% of testers. Historically, California has been one of the states with the highest cutoffs. Students who are National Merit Semifinalists can apply to become National Merit Scholars. National Merit Scholar status makes you eligible for different scholarships: some from the National Merit Corporation, some from private corporations, and others from colleges and universities themselves. While there are some perks for students who score in the top percentiles on the PSAT, for the vast majority of students, the PSAT mainly functions as a practice test. If the PSAT is being offered at your school, go ahead and take it and put in a good faith effort, but don’t put undue stress on this test. Instead, use it as an opportunity to gain more information that will empower you to understand how standardized tests may become part of the bigger picture for college admissions. Ariel Rodriguez is the Director of College Counseling and Emily Thompson is the Managing Director at Study Smarter. articles.text: Scouts and parents pause after completing a climb to an altitude of 9381 feet. Pictured are Leo Kansal, Joelle Frechet, Liam King, Charlie Robinson, Tom Robinson, Alex Wolff, and Dante Rodriguez. Three Scouts, including two Eagles, and five adults from Piedmont Troop 4 went on a 50-mile backpacking trip last summer in Desolation Wilderness, a mountainous area near Lake Tahoe. Members of the troop prepared for months in advance to make sure they were prepared for any situation. Overall, the trip was a great success, helped a lot by Troop 4’s Dante Rodriguez, who has led plenty of 50 Milers as a Scout with Troop 4 and now as an adult. The Scouts were well prepared for challenges, including rain, heat, and cold. A typical day on the trip started with breakfast. Breakfasts ranged from granola with dehydrated milk to oatmeal and dried blueberries, but they felt special to be eating in such beautiful places. The day would continue with several miles of hiking, a good view, and a stop for lunch at a place with shade and fresh water to filter. After lunch the Scouts would be back on the trail for a few more miles, before setting up camp for the night. In the afternoon the Scouts would often take a swim in a lake, lay on the warm rocks, and enjoy the beautiful scenery that can only be found in the mountains of the Sierra Nevada range. The crystal clear lakes in the mountainous forests were not warm but were not frigid. As the sun began to set, the Scouts began preparing dinner and would eat their evening meal sitting on warm rocks at their campsite. But as the sun dips behind the horizon, the mosquitoes come out. Scouts have many methods of sleeping outdoors – some choose hammocks, some sleep under the stars on tarps, while others use tents. The important part is getting rested for the next day’s adventure and reducing the weight you carry as much as possible. Some of the most memorable parts of the 50-mile hike were going over Dick’s Pass, eating dinner on the rocks at Middle Velma Lake, swimming at Lake Ropi, and seeing a water snake at Lake of the Woods. On a trip like this, water is important and the Scouts almost always stopped at a lake for lunch and camped at a lake every night. In total the trip took seven days and reached an elevation of 9381 feet. Troop 4 Scouts hike up a valley to reach a lake where they set up camp for the night. Some Scouts chose to use hammocks because for one person they are lighter than tents. Leo Kansal, Liam King and Alex Wolff at Clyde Lake Scouts put on their rain gear when it started raining on the last night of the trip.

articles.text: Dozens of pickleball enthusiasts converged on the middle school courts on Saturday, September 21, to play in a fund-raising tournament to support the school district’s Wellness Center. The “Positively Pickled” tournament proved to be so popular that organizers had to create a waitlist to accommodate would-be entrants. More than $65,000 was generated by the tournament through family and corporate donations, all in support of the Wellness Center, which provides counseling and mental health services to Piedmont students in high school and middle school. Last year the Wellness Center provided more than 2,000 therapy sessions to Piedmont students. The inaugural Wellness Center tournament included beginPickleball enthusiasts Shyla Ranga, Paige Rampton, Madeleine Ewen, Mackenzie Ewen, and Grace Fa at the Wellness Center pickleball tournament Intermediate division winners Reed and Aaron Bennett ner, intermediate and competitive divisions. Twenty-eight intermediate and 12 competitive division teams participated. Father-son duo Reed and Aaron Bennett won the intermediate division, followed by runners-up Cindy and Kris Lynds. Ray Ramillosa and Stefan Schulze won the competitive division, with Beth Barrett and Virginia Davis a close second. For many players, it was their first time participating in a pickleball tournament. Before beginning play, new players received a group lesson from professional pickleball player Carolyn Wei. Coaches advised beginners on scoring and rules. Montclair Sports Tennis & Pickleball donated 10 pickleball rackets to the first five doubles teams registered in the beginners division. “There was a lot of learning and joy on the court,” said tournament chair, Blair Paige. “It really showed how people of all ages can play pickleball together and have fun.” The winners of the intermediate and competitive divisions received $100 Mulberry’s Market gift certificates, and runners-up were awarded $50 gift certificates from Yellow Door in Montclair. Giant jars of pickles served as both trophies and fun photo opportunities. Major corporate donors included Elfster and TPG. In-kind donors included Montclair Sports Tennis & Pickleball, Mulberry’s Market, Yellow Door, and Bay Padel. “It’s so representative of our amazing Piedmont community that people don’t just give for academics but also to support our student’s mental wellness,” said Wellness Center Support Committee chair Neha Gupta. “Student mental health should be prioritized just as much as the library, the arts, and sports,” Gupta added. To support the Wellness Center or to donate, please visit Piedmontwellness.org. articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department hosted its sixth annual Car Show on Saturday, September 21, with hot coffee and even hotter automobiles parked in front of the Exedra. Piedmont Police Officer Tyler Petit once again led the event which has brought cops, coffee and cars to the center of Piedmont as a part of the department’s outreach efforts. The Car Show took place on the last day of summer, which turned out to be a beautiful Saturday morning in Piedmont. Around 85 vintage, classic and muscle cars were on display for public viewing. Upwards of 500 viewers came out for a cup of coffee, chat with a car owners, and to witness a cornucopia of chrome. “When we start throwing these events people get to know us,” said Petit. “It’s not Officer Petit its ‘hey, Tyler.’ For me, as a police officer and someone who wants this kind of customer service in a community, I like to know that people can come to me as a friend.” The set up was slightly different this year because of the ongoing construction at the Piedmont Police Department of a new dispatch center, scheduled to be completed in April 2025. The “La Casita del Guero” taco truck was on hand making breakfast burritos in the morning and super burritos later on. The community center parking lot was also secured for the event, in case An aerial view of the car show from the drone of car show founder retired Piedmont Sergeant Steve DeWarns. A split-window black on black 1963 Chevy Corvette. A white 1954 Chevy Corvette convertible with whitewall tires, owned by Jon Peters. Photos courtesy of Michael Glasser Two pace cars, both Chevy Corvette convertibles, lead a lineup of cars on Highland Avenue in Piedmont’s 6th Annual Car Show. Anthony Dunlap, owner of 1912 Ford Model T converted for military use in the First World War. The interior of a 2002 BMW Turkis. of surprise attendance. While the event was a success, by all accounts Petit is thinking about how to make it grow, and estimated that the event could have up to 250 cars in future shows. “Our contact sheet is up to over 140 vehicles now, so it is Chrome and power under the hood of a yellow 2006 supercharged Chevy Corvette with over 700 horsepower. very evident our car show is expanding,” said Petit. The event was pioneered by now retired Piedmont Police Officer Steve DeWarns in 2018. In its second year, the show had 44 cars and has had around 100 showroom worthy cars since 2021. “These events are important because we are breaking down the walls of ‘police vs. citizen’ and this whole ‘us vs. them’ mentality. It’s about creating new friendship not just amongst us, but between car owners,” said Petit with a smile. A 1967 Jaguar E-Type. A Ford race car is pushed into a trailer at the end of the car show. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. articles.text: Piedmont High’s cross country team traveled to Pinole Point in Richmond for its first Western Alameda County Conference league meet of the season on Wednesday, September 25. The girls’ team finished third of nine teams, and the boys were fifth of 10. “Varsity girls finished third behind two Division 1 teams [Berkeley and Castro Valley], while the boys were fifth. I heard a lot of kids comment on how they loved the scenic quality of the race and great conditions. Lots of “it didn’t feel that long” from new kids who were running three miles for the first time,” said coach Steve Zirkelbach. The girls’ team top runner was junior Skylar Best, who placed fifth in a field of 73 runners with a time of 19:20.02. Trailing Best was sophomore Amalia Gray in ninth with a personal record time of 19:53.96. She topped her previous record by over two minutes. Junior Cora Chun placed 17th in 20:22.07, sophomore Leighton Mand was 19th in 20:30.85, while senior Caroline Taylor rounded of Piedmont’s best five runners in 22nd in 20:33.55. “Amalia Gray continues to demonstrate her focus and is seeing the results of the hard work that she is putting in. Leighton Mand was finally able to race this season, after nursing an injury for the past 3+ weeks which has not allowed her to train with rest of the girls. Even though we talked Photos by Jenni Tsoi Leighton Mand (left), Skylar Best, and Cora Chun helped lead Piedmont to a third place finish. Alex Schleuning legs it to the finish line. He finished 30th of 83 runners. Leighton Mand returned from an injury to finish 19th. about just running at a tempo pace to see how her leg felt, she was able to surge to a 19th place finish overall, despite not truly racing for the first two miles,” Zirkelbach said. The boys’ team was led by standout sophomore Sebastien Swain who missed the team’s first meet. He returned full head of steam, finishing eighth of 83 runners with a time of 16:17.75. It was a two-second improvement than his previous best. Behind Swain was junior Noah Sohn finishing 15th with a personal record time of 16:43.07, marking a 1:21 improvement over his last race. From there, sophomore Alex Schleuning was 30th in 17:29.22, senior Oliver Horsley was 33rd in 17:35.22, while sophomore Thomas Ero rounded out PHS’ best five runners in 37th, 17:36.98. “Of the varsity boys, Noah and Thomas had the most significant improvements over the three-mile distance. Alex Schleuning ran a very competitive race as well,” Zirkelbach said. articles.text: We’ve named Markos Lagios, quarterback on the football team, and water polo player Abigail Jacoby as our Athletes of the Month for September, with honorable mentions going to water polo player Ryan Patty and cross-country runner Skylar Best. MARKOS LAGIOS Lagios has helped Piedmont’s football team start the season with a 3-1 record, including three wins in September. During that time, Piedmont outscored its opponents 126-35. Lagios has totaled 593 yards and scored six touchdowns, to go along with 226 rushing yards on 30 carries (7.5 yards per carry) and seven touchdowns. Perhaps his best performance was in Piedmont’s 42-21 win over Middletown on September 6 with four rushing touchdowns for 107 yards and completing 13 of 15 passes for 188 yards. Staff Photo Quarterback Markos Lagios is the Post’s Athlete of the Month. ABIGAIL JACOBY Jacoby has proven to be a star water polo player, helping Piedmont surpassed last year’s win total and improve to 6-6. She recently notched a hat trick (3 goals) in a game with Foothill on September 30. She also had a hat trick against Castro Valley and had a goal and two assists in Piedmont’s 5-3 win over American on September 23. Photo by Lynne Wright Water polo player Abigail Jacoby earns an honorable mention for her last four matches. season. Still with a lot of meets remaining, Best showed signs of being at the start of a strong 2024 campaign after creating a new three-mile personal best recently on September 25 at their league meet with a time of 19:20.02— topping her previous time set in 2022 when she was our Freshman of the Year after qualifying for the State Championship. Staff Photo Cross-country runner Skylar Best earns an honorable mention for Athlete of the Month for her performance in her second meet of the season. Photo by Lynne Wright
articles.title: Honorable Mention: Rylan Patty & Skylar Best

articles.text: RYAN PATTY Ryan Petty has burst onto the scene as a freshman starter on the water polo team, which is churning along at 7-4 after losing nearly their entire starting lineup from last year’s NCS championship winning team. In a 10-8 win over Marin Catholic for the Napa Tournament title on September 21, Patty caught everyone’s attention with eight goals including converting all four penalty shot attempts. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont’s girls’ volleyball team suffered a 3-0 loss to Alameda. Piedmont High’s girls’ volleyball team took a 3-0 loss on the road to Alameda on Wednesday, September 25 by scores of 25-8, 25-8, 25-13. The result brings Piedmont’s record to 1-9 entering the final month of play with eight matches left. Piedmont now looks ahead to visiting Western Alameda County Conference powerhouse, Bishop O’Dowd, next Tuesday, October 8. Game Recap In the first set, Piedmont got out to a quick 3-2 lead with kills by Hanley Carling, but the set quickly unraveled. At that point, Alameda went on a 10-0 scoring run to jump ahead 12-3 before Piedmont’s Stella Wilk scored a kill. After that, Alameda scored 10 of the next 12 points, including four kills and three aces. Fiona Olsen scored a kill, but alameda finished the set with three straight point. Piedmont similarly won the opening two points of the second set thanks to a kill by Carling and an error by the Hornets. The two sides traded points, including kills by Wilks and Carling, until Alameda held a one-point 7-6 lead. That’s when the Hornets went on another exhausting scoring run, landing eight straight points before Carling scored another spike. Following that, Alameda scored another nine straight points including five kills and two aces. Carling got one more kill before the close of the second set. The Highlanders were competitive for the first half of the third set before falling behind. Piedmont actually battled to an 8-7 lead thanks to kills by Carling, #11 and Sophie Glass, and an ace by Charli Panico. PHS only briefly held the advantage when the Hornets went on a three point scoring run to go up 11-8. PHS then scored two points to cut the deficit to one point at 11-10, but the Hornets then went on another long-lasting streak of points. Alameda scored 11 straight points with four kills and four aces to their credit to go up 22-10. Piedmont’s Olsen and Wilks slammed in spikes to give Piedmont two straight points, but Alameda closed the game with a pair of kills of its own. Final stats: Carling had seven kills, Olsen had two kills, Wilk had four, Julia Stokes had one block, Panico had one ace. NEXT UP Piedmont (1-9 overall, 0-2 league) will play at Bishop O’Dowd on Tuesday, October 8 at 6:30 p.m. Hanley Carling (5) had six kills against Alameda. Also pictured is Allyson Huynh. Stella Wilk had four kills against the Hornets.
articles.title: Piedmont falls 3-0 to Alameda

That’s when Piedmont mounted a comeback, tying the game late at 7-7 but ultimately falling 9-8. In the first quarter, the two sides traded possession for nearly four minutes before Foothill broke the deadlock. Abigail Jacoby cut the deficit to 2-1 with 23 seconds left in the first. Piedmont drew multiple player advantages in the second quarter, but couldn’t find the goal. Sydney Olsen cut the deficit to 4-3 just 30 seconds into the third quarter, followed by Vivian Burke tying the game 4-4 after Piedmont forced a quick turnover to find the goal at 6:09, giving them two goals in the first minute of the second half. articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ tennis team finished a rough week with two defeats. Most recently, they fell 5-2 to Alameda at the Corey Reich Tennis Center on Thursday, September 26 after losing 6-1 at Marin Academy in San Rafael the previous day. Their loss to Alameda comes against a Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division rival. Two of Piedmont’s losses came down to tightly contested three-set matches. Three of their losses to Marin Academy also went to three sets. The Highlanders will get one more chance to defeat Alameda on October 23. “Against Marin Academy, three matches went to third set tiebreaks. Despite winning the first set in each, we lost all of them,” said coach Jim Landes. “We need to avoid letting up after a first set win. With Alameda, four matches went to the third set and we split them. Again, we need to fight against relaxing too much after a good start,” coach Jim Landes said. In the match with Alameda, Piedmont won one singles and one doubles match. Maddie Tran and Emma Chan won their No. 2 match after trailing in the first set and third set, but claimed the win after their opponents had to forfeit the match with the final set tied at 5-5. Tran and Chan won 7-5, 3-6, 5-5 (retire), but were trailing 5-2 in both the first and third sets before mounting momentous comebacks. “We were losing 2-5 in the first set and our mental game was so bad, then we started winning games and building momentum to win the set. It was almost the same in the third set where we went down 2-5. We were thinking back to the first set and knew we could do it again. We brought it back to 5-all and had momentum going again,” Tran said. “A lot of my first serves were going out. In the third set, I started hitting my serves really hard and landing them. We started getting a lot of points when I was landing my first serves. Maddie’s volleys in front of the net were also really good. She was hitting them to where they couldn’t get it,” Chan mentioned. Staff Photos Maddie Tran won her No. 2 doubles match against Alameda alongside Emma Chan. Emma Chan sends a forehand against Alameda in her doubles win. Faith Chin won her No. 4 singles match against Alameda.

articles.text: Mexican-born singer-songwriter Ana Lila Downs Sánchez will perform at the Paramount Theatre in Oakland on Saturday, October 12. A Grammy-winning vocalist, Downs will perform music celebrating Día de los Muertos, Mexico’s Day of the Dead, by highlighting tracks from her latest album, La Sánchez, featuring folklorico dancing, and stunning thematically-inspired visual projections. A native of Oaxaca, Downs’ version of traditional Mexican music blends blues, jazz, soul, African root, and even klezmer music. Downs sings in both English and Spanish and has performed worldwide. Vocalist Lila Downs The concert begins at 8 p.m. Visit https://www.sfjazz.org/ tickets/productions/24-25/liladowns-dia-de-los-muertos/ to purchase tickets.

articles.text: AXIS Dance Company, an acclaimed ensemble of disabled and neurodiverse dancers, will perform Friday through Sunday, October 11-13 at San Francisco’s ODC Theater. The Bay Area-based dance company was founded in 1987 and has performed in more than 100 cities in the U.S., the United Kingdom, Europe and the United Arab Emirates. The company’s mission is to create world-class productions that challenge perceptions and redefine dance and disability. AXIS will perform new choreography for its home season Ecos, with Berkeley-based contemporary dance company, Post:ballet, serving as special guests. “Ecos brings together extraordinary artists to explore the complexities of our shared human experience,” said AXIS Dance Company Artistic Director Nadia Adame. “Each piece in this Home Season reflects a unique perspective, yet together they resonate with a powerful, collective spirit. This season is a heartfelt invitation to connect, reflect, and be moved together.” Tickets for Ecos are available now at www.axisdance.org. AXIS Dance Company artists perform onstage.
articles.title: AXIS Dance performs at ODC theater Oct. 11-13

articles.text: Victoria Hurd will perform a piano concert on Sunday, October 29 at Plymouth Church, 424 Monte Vista Avenue. Titled Beethoven Revisited, the concert will start at 5:30 p.m. It is a benefit for SAVETHECHILDREN.ORG Beethoven Revisited focuses on Beethoven’s pianistic use of the sustaining pedal. He didn’t have one! (He did occasionally use a knee lever to sustain one chord.) Modern pianos sound bare without the pedal, so the concert will adapt early piano techniques to the resonant, powerful sound of modern pianos. Included in the program, for historical context, will be music by Mozart and Chopin. Victoria Hurd studied Performance Practices as a graduate at Stanford University and has played piano and harpsichord for many years. She infuses her playing with a love of dance and song; She also sings with Chora Nova in Berkeley. Admission is your donation receipt to: https://bit.ly/VHurdBeethoven. Pianist Victoria Hurd ®
articles.title: Victoria Hurd piano concert at Plymouth Church Oct. 20

articles.text: Opera Parallèle will open its 2024-25 season with its firstever production at the California Academy of Sciences Planetarium om Golden Gate Park from November 8 through 17. Entitled Everest: Opera in the Planetarium, the production is based on the internationally renowned opera, Everest, composed by Joby Talbot with a libretto by Gene Scheer. The oneact opera retells the 1996 Mount Everest disaster, when several mountaineers died after a severe storm hit during their climb to the summit. It is based on interviews with survivors and shows in the deaths of mountaineers Rob Hall and Doug Hanse. Opera Parallèle’s production uses the Academy of Sciences’ state-of-the-art planetarium to present the opera in bold new iteration. The event is not a live opera, but an immersive operatic experience. Award winning conductor Nicole Paiement leads the orchestra as animations come to life through facial tracking technology. The cast includes features Sasha Cooke, mezzo-soprano; Nathan Granner, tenor; Kevin California Academy of Sciences Planetarium Burdette, bass; Hadleigh Adams, baritone; Charlotte Fanvu, treble; Matt Boehler, bass; Shawnette Sulker, soprano; Whitney Steele, mezzo-soprano; and Kevin Gino, tenor. The launch of the company’s 2024-25 season also coincides with Opera Parallele’s 15th anniversary. “When we launched Opera Parallèle, we knew we were creating something that had the capacity to change the perception of opera as an art form and storytelling mechanism,” explained Artistic Director Nicole Paiement. “After 15 years of pushing artistic boundaries through partnerships with many hundreds of talented and diverse creative collaborators, singers, composers, and musicians, the world of opera has indeed become more varied, more relevant, more innovative. I am very proud that Opera Parallèle has been recognized as a catalyst in that shift.” Everest: Opera at the Planetarium begins Friday, November 8 at 6.30 p.m. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.cityboxoffice.com/ everest.

articles.text: Dateline: Split, Croatia. The view from above as you approach Croatia is spectacular. Thousands of islands appear as stars in a sapphire-colored sky. They are highlighted by occasional whitecaps and sailboats. The Split airport is super clean, neat and orderly. That’s the way things are here. If memory serves me correctly, Croatia resembles California in days long ago. The overwhelming majority of the locals speak English and they speak it quite well. Tourists are everywhere. All the local business owners address you first in English. As beautiful and friendly as things are here, the prices have risen dramatically in the last decade. Split reminds me of Venice, Italy, with tourists everywhere. Rest assured, the food is much better in Croatia than it is in Venice. The architecture is unified in style and in color. All the buildings are made of stone and the roofs are of orange tile. On one side of the island are the very expensive fancy boats, with more modest boats on the other side. Directly opposite the wealthy area is a promenade lined with one restaurant after another. An ancient stone castle guards the harbor. All of the people are friendly, especially those in the stores when they want to sell you things. They look you up and down and if you are reluctant to buy anything, they will give you a “deal”. The food in Croatia is excellent. I haven’t been able to discover an actual Croatian cuisine, but the people assure me everything they serve is Croatian. One thing is for sure, the food is excellent. Fish is the most popular item on the menu, but you can also get beef, lamb, and chicken. I was assured by almost every waiter that a normal green salad is actually Croatian. Tomato soup is on every menu as is a their version of mushroom soup. As for seafood, tuna and swordfish are offered in a variety of ways. My favorite was medallions of tuna with grilled polenta and grilled bread, accompanied by mixed vegetables. It was adorned by a very subtle pesto sauce. Our hotel specializes in a super buffet for breakfast and for dinner also. When I told the hostess that my wife and I were not very hungry, she offered us a huge reduction in price. It didn’t matter how much we ate she gave us a great discount. But you need to remember that prices are very high here. Think prices of San Francisco, New York or London. We were thinking about getting the lobster and then we looked at the price – €130. … Uh…Maybe next time. People bring their pet dogs onto the airplane and into restaurants. Strangely enough, although this area is also known as the Dalmatian Coast, I didn’t see any Dalmatian dogs anywhere. Unfortunately, there is no music to speak of here. However, I’ll have an excellent music story in the next article. It deals with one of the immortals of music who was tempted to sell his soul to the devil. The resulting music was his most famous. Fish is king in Croatia. Here is a delicious plate of medallions of swordfish accompanied by grilled polenta, grilled bread and vegetables. The swordfish was as large as a good sized steak.

articles.text: Kedrick Armstrong will lead the Oakland Symphony on October 18 in his debut as the symphony’s ninth music director. Ar mstrong’s unanimous appointment to the position in April marked the end of a twoyear search since the passing of the symphony’s previous conductor Michael Morgan in August 2021. Before Armstrong’s appointment, the symphony invited a series of guest conductors. “The search committee… was impressed by Armstrong’s demonstrated leadership and community-building abilities along with his passion for and command of an extraordinarily broad range of music,” said publicist Marshall Lam. “All of these qualities were reflected in the programs that he conceived, organized and conducted with the Oakland Symphony.” Armstrong, 30, grew up in Georgetown, South Carolina and established his music career in Chicago. Prior to being named music director in Oakland, he worked as the creative partner and principal conductor of the Knox-Galesburg Symphony in Illinois. Armstrong was named by the Washington Post as one of the “Top 22 Composers and Performers to Watch” in 2022. Armstrong was a guest conductor with Oakland Symphony in 2022 for the Summer Stage at Oakland City Hall, then again in 2023 and early 2024. His new job as music director prompted him to permanently move to the East Bay in August. “The Oakland Symphony community has embraced me with open arms since my first visit. It immediately felt like a place I wanted to call home,” Armstrong said. In his new role, Armstrong will conduct the orchestra’s concerts in and around the Bay Area, participate in the organization’s education and community engagement programs, and be the symphony’s cultural ambassador to Bay Area artists and communities. “Living in the Bay Area now, it’s learning a new community, learning a new area, learning what interests people with cultural items that are significant to the Bay,” said Armstrong. The position with Oakland Symphony is unique in part because the post has long been held by Black conductors, Michael Morgan and Calvin Simmons, who combined led the symphony for more than 40 Photos by Scott Chernis Before he was appointed to his new role, Armstrong was a guest conductor with Oakland Symphony between 2022 and 2024. Photos by Scott Chernis Kedrick Armstrong established his career in Chicago before he was named Music Director for the Oakland Symphony. years. “As an African-American conductor, I find it humbling to stand on the shoulders of both Michael Morgan and Calvin Simmons,” Armstrong said. “Having that legacy of both Simmons and Morgan has been empowering for me. But also it makes it so that my vision and my goals are aligned with the history of this organization.” Armstrong said his experience with the Oakland Symphony has reiterated the strength of the bonds present in classical music. “There are beautiful differences and similarities; one of the similarities is just kind of how tight knit it is,” he said. “On a national scale you realize in classical music just how small the world is and how much we all know each other. I’m trying to learn more about this deep history. I also want to bring everything that I have as a 30-year-old. I pinch myself every day. I truly feel like one of the luckiest people to be able to do this work.” Armstrong’s inaugural performance as music director with the Oakland Symphony will be on Friday, October 18 at the Paramount Theatre in Oakland.
articles.title: Kedrick Armstrong to lead Oakland Symphony in Oct. 18 concert

As beautiful and friendly as things are here, the prices have risen dramatically in the last decade. Split reminds me of Venice, Italy, with tourists everywhere. Rest assured, the food is much better in Croatia than it is in Venice. The architecture is unified in style and in color. All the buildings are made of stone and the roofs are of orange tile. On one side of the island are the very expensive fancy boats, with more modest boats on the other side. Directly opposite the wealthy area is a promenade lined with one restaurant after another. An ancient stone castle guards the harbor. All of the people are friendly, especially those in the stores when they want to sell you things. They look you up and down and if you are reluctant to buy anything, they will give you a “deal”. The food in Croatia is excellent. I haven’t been able to discover an actual Croatian cuisine, but the people assure me everything they serve is Croatian. One thing is for sure, the food is excellent. Fish is the most popular item on the menu, but you can also get beef, lamb, and chicken. I was assured by almost every waiter that a normal green salad is actually Croatian. Tomato soup is on every menu as is a their version of mushroom soup. As for seafood, tuna and swordfish are offered in a variety of ways. My favorite was medallions of tuna with grilled polenta and grilled bread, accompanied by mixed vegetables. It was adorned by a very subtle pesto sauce. Our hotel specializes in a super buffet for breakfast and for dinner also. When I told the hostess that my wife and I were not very hungry, she offered us a huge reduction in price. It didn’t matter how much we ate she gave us a great discount. But you need to remember that prices are very high here. Think prices of San Francisco, New York or London. We were thinking about getting the lobster and then we looked at the price – €130. … Uh…Maybe next time. People bring their pet dogs onto the airplane and into restaurants. Strangely enough, although this area is also known as the Dalmatian Coast, I didn’t see any Dalmatian dogs anywhere. Unfortunately, there is no music to speak of here. However, I’ll have an excellent music story in the next article. It deals with one of the immortals of music who was tempted to sell his soul to the devil. The resulting music was his most famous. Kedrick Armstrong to lead Oakland Symphony in Oct. 18 concert By Andrew Fortin-Caldera Kedrick Armstrong will lead the Oakland Symphony on October 18 in his debut as the symphony’s ninth music director. Ar mstrong’s unanimous appointment to the position in April marked the end of a twoyear search since the passing of the symphony’s previous conductor Michael Morgan in August 2021. Before Armstrong’s appointment, the symphony invited a series of guest conductors. “The search committee… was impressed by Armstrong’s demonstrated leadership and community-building abilities along with his passion for and command of an extraordinarily broad range of music,” said publicist Marshall Lam. “All of these qualities were reflected in the programs that he conceived, organized and conducted with the Oakland Symphony.” Armstrong, 30, grew up in Georgetown, South Carolina and established his music career in Chicago. Prior to being named music director in Oakland, he worked as the creative partner and principal conductor of the Knox-Galesburg Symphony in Illinois. Armstrong was named by the Washington Post as one of the “Top 22 Composers and Performers to Watch” in 2022. Armstrong was a guest conductor with Oakland Symphony in 2022 for the Summer Stage at Oakland City Hall, then again in 2023 and early 2024. His new job as music director prompted him to permanently move to the East Bay in August. “The Oakland Symphony community has embraced me with open arms since my first visit. It immediately felt like a place I wanted to call home,” Armstrong said. In his new role, Armstrong will conduct the orchestra’s concerts in and around the Bay Area, participate in the organization’s education and community engagement programs, and be the symphony’s cultural ambassador to Bay Area artists and communities. “Living in the Bay Area now, it’s learning a new community, learning a new area, learning what interests people with cultural items that are significant to the Bay,” said Armstrong. The position with Oakland Symphony is unique in part because the post has long been held by Black conductors, Michael Morgan and Calvin Simmons, who combined led the symphony for more than 40 Photos by Scott Chernis Before he was appointed to his new role, Armstrong was a guest conductor with Oakland Symphony between 2022 and 2024. Photos by Scott Chernis Kedrick Armstrong established his career in Chicago before he was named Music Director for the Oakland Symphony. years. “As an African-American conductor, I find it humbling to stand on the shoulders of both Michael Morgan and Calvin Simmons,” Armstrong said. “Having that legacy of both Simmons and Morgan has been empowering for me. But also it makes it so that my vision and my goals are aligned with the history of this organization.” Armstrong said his experience with the Oakland Symphony has reiterated the strength of the bonds present in classical music. “There are beautiful differences and similarities; one of the similarities is just kind of how tight knit it is,” he said. “On a national scale you realize in classical music just how small the world is and how much we all know each other. I’m trying to learn more about this deep history. I also want to bring everything that I have as a 30-year-old. I pinch myself every day. I truly feel like one of the luckiest people to be able to do this work.” Armstrong’s inaugural performance as music director with the Oakland Symphony will be on Friday, October 18 at the Paramount Theatre in Oakland. Fish is king in Croatia. Here is a delicious plate of medallions of swordfish accompanied by grilled polenta, grilled bread and vegetables. The swordfish was as large as a good sized steak. articles.text: Kristen Stewart and Julianne Moore in Still Alice Life is fragile, tenuous, and each day is a gamble. Until it isn’t. The idea that bad things happen to good people is an abstraction… and suddenly what we took for granted – another dawn, and all that follows – can no longer hold our weight, like fragile ice on a winter’s pond. Still Alice is about such a life and may be more truth than some viewers want to confront in a film, due in great part to a tour de force performance by Julianne Moore. She portrays Dr. Alice Howland, a professor of linguistics at Colombia University, married to John (Alec Baldwin), a research scientist and the mother of three lovely children (Kristen Stewart, Kate Bosworth and Hunter Parrish). Alice accomplished, cherished by her family and colleagues, just 50, and relishing in every way this moment in her life. But ever so gradually she begins to notice small moments when her memory hits a speed bump and what was automatic eludes her. And so begins a cruel and insidious journey, one in which all that she is, all that she has become, begins to abandon her. With John she visits a neurologist who confirms that she has familial early onset Alzheimer’s disease. It’s a betrayal of her mind that is unexpected and will be, with unyielding certainty, catastrophic and like a flower in full bloom, every pedal vibrant with life, she begins to close ever so slowly. What is so insidious, so tragic, is that Alice – bright, scholarly, educated, loving – is told in detail what awaits her, the path that stretches before her is detailed, like a photograph of familiar colors and images left out in the sunshine that slowly begins to fade. The irony of the film is its title: Still Alice. From the moment of her diagnosis, when she is told that the disease she has is very rare and also genetic (it’s possible that the gene she inherited came from her father, an alcoholic, and she may have passed it on to her children), Alice is no longer still Alice. She is now that person who struggles to find the courage and grace to face each day, to suffer each moment of forgetfulness, clinging to any remnant of who she was and wishes she still could be. Though this subject matter is not unique, what gives Still Alice its deeply human essence is the resonating performance by Julianne Moore, who was nominated for an Oscar as Best Actress. She is remarkable and restrained. The camera lingers on her in tight, intimate shots, her every feature conveying the hope and sheer terror and brief moments of panic and lucidity that are now her life’s experiences. Moore is astonishing. She is just so good. As is the film, which is never gratuitous or maudlin. Still Alice. Directed by Richard Glatzer. Starring Alec Baldwin, Julianne Moore, Kristen Stewart. 1 hr., 39 min. Rated PG-13. Released ln 2014. Now streaming on Fandango/prime/ MAX/apple tv.

articles.text: Ongoing to October 7 Michelle Tholen Original Art Original art by local East Bay artist Michelle Tholen remains on display through this weekend, with a closing reception open to all on Sunday, October 6, from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. Please join Michelle for the reception celebrating her new work, and enjoy bites and beverages, with music by classical pianist Ellen Walker. Inspired by restrained color and order, this artist is challenged to create pop using a color combination that is refined and yet suggests more. In a minimalist Modern style reminiscent of Rothko, the artist paints in acrylic on canvas, and will be present with the gallery open both Saturday and Sunday from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. Sunday, October 13, 4:00 p.m. Japanese Internment Camps: Life, Art & Music The first of three events in a new series created and presented by PCA will include Karen Korematsu, daughter of Fred Korematsu, who was arrested and convicted for not responding to military orders to report for transfer to an internment camp in 1942. He appealed the conviction all the way up to the US Supreme Court, but it was upheld. Karen will detail his story and that of their family during the Camp years, will answer questions from the audience, and will interact with you during a reception. The second event in the series, November 2, will feature Wendy Tokuda, the former News Anchor for KPIX, and Kimi Hill, grandaughter of Chiura Obata, an artist who continued to paint in the camps. The series will finish November 23 with a screening of Alternative Facts: the Lies Behind Exec. Order 9066, the instrument that created the controversial internment of Japanese-Americans. Event and Full Series tickets are now available at https://bpt.me/6449591. Friday, October 18, 5:30 – 7:30 p.m. 12th Annual Artisanal Brewing Competition PCA’s annual Oktoberfest-type celebration, offering tastes of home-brewed beers in a custom PCA beer glass, along with a traditional German dinner on the front lawn, including grilled bratwurst, German potato salad, and red cabbage. The brews will be compared and rated by a panel of judges. All food is donated by Dave Larson and Piedmont Grocery. PHS musicians will provide music on the lawn during dinner. Beer glass and food tickets available at the door, cash, check, or credit card, or in advance at www. eventbrite.com/e/948562324447. October 18 – November 4 “It’s All Relative” Art Exhibition Oakland artist Bill Prochnow presents a show of recent works of figurative abstractions. His paintings and drawings currently center on human relationships and connections. Open gallery hours are Saturdays and Sundays from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m., with an opening reception on Saturday, October 19, from 7–9 p.m. Sunday, October 20, 4:30 p.m. In the Tradition Jazz & Pop Piano Trio The In the Tradition Piano Trio – Bill Jackman, Michael Jones, and Albert Brooks – pays tribute to Jimmy Van Heusen, who composed nearly 1000 songs between 1930 and 1970, including Like Someone in Love (1944) and Polka Dots and Moonbeams (1940). He wrote popular music mainly for film and stage. Don’t miss the relaxed pleasure of a Sunday afternoon in the Classic Jazz Club at the Center for the Arts. Doors open at 4:15 PM. Tickets $25 at https://bpt.me/6214927 or $30, cash or check only at the door. Friday, October 25, 7:30 p.m. Mira Trio Chamber Concert Miles Graber, one of the Bay Area’s most highly respected pianists, brings to Piedmont a trio with which he performs, consisting of Lev Polyakin, an international award-winning violinist originally from Russia, and Martha Aarons, principal flute and soloist for several orchestras in the U.S.

articles.text: A scene from Hayao Miyazaki’s The Wind Rises The Wind Rises was intended to be Hayao Miyazaki’s final film. It would also serve as this intensely creative animator and storyteller’s tribute to Jiro Horikoshi, known in Japan as a master aeronautical engineer and a pioneer in aircraft design during the first half of the 20th century. Through Miyazaki’s prism, Jiro (Joseph Gordon-Levitt) is portrayed as a bookish, bespectacled boy and young man (not dissimilar from Harry Potter) who possessed a dreamy, distracted manner, often lost in his imagination, his visions of airplanes filling his thoughts. Early on, Jiro so loved the idea of flight that he imagines meeting the Italian aeronautical engineer Giovanni Battista Caproni, who encourages him to pursue his love of airplanes and design. As it turns out Jiro cannot be a pilot himself because of his eyesight. And yet fly he does. As part of the story, Miyazaki includes a sad and tender romance between Jiro and a young woman, Naoko Satomi (Emily Blunt). They meet in Tokyo during Japan’s most devastating Great Kanto Earthquake in 1923, a natural disaster that all but leveled Tokyo. It is grippingly captured in the film’s intense images. And it is Naoko who quotes to Jiro the words of poet Paul Valéry, “The wind rises, we must try to live,” and is the source of the film’s title. articles.text: If you are exploring the extraordinary works of Studio Ghibli, you have discovered that the lead character is often a young female who is simultaneously fragile and fearless. When Marnie Was There is based on the 1967 fantasy book by English author Joan G. Robinson. The film’s protagonist is a lonely, androgynous 12-yearold girl named Anna (Kiernan Shipka) who lives in urban Sapporo, Japan. Because she is asthmatic, her foster mother, Mrs. Kadoya (Kathy Bates), sends her to live with relatives in the country – a windswept, marshy, seaside area that will, hopefully, restore Anna’s health. While exploring the marshes, Anna unexpectedly comes across a deserted mansion that seems eerily familiar. It’s there that she encounters a strange, mysterious girl of her own age, very western looking, with striking blonde hair and wearing out-of-date clothes. Unexpectedly, the two develop a friendship and begin to share dreams and diaries which, for Anna, lead to moments of self-discovery and revelation. Gradually she begins to emerge from her reclusive shell, growing more and more captivated with the house and this spectral girl named Marnie. The story, languid and almost wistful, gently pulls the audience into its inherent magic, while adding goosebump moments, especially when the girls wander through a seemingly haunted lighthouse during a rainstorm. The film is compelling in so many ways: softly sinister at A scene from Studio Ghibli’s When Marnie Was There In 1942, soon after the attack on Pearl Harbor, FDR signed Executive Order 9066, requiring that all those of Japanese extraction be removed from West Coast “Military Exclusion Zones,” resulting in the relocation of 120,000 American citizens and legal residents to Internment Camps. 801 MAGNOLIA AVENUE, PIEDMONT TICKETS AVAILABLE AT BROWN PAPER TICKETS https://bpt.me/6449591 “ “N Ne ev ve er r A Ag ga ai in n! !” ” — An exploration of life, art, and music in the Camps — : My Dad, the activist — Sunday, October 13, 2024, 4:00 PM Dr. Karen Korematsu, daughter of Oakland-born Fred Korematsu, who was arrested for resisting the relocation order and convicted in Federal District Court, will tell her father’s story and reveal the life he and his family experienced in the internment camps. : Remembering, 80 years later — Saturday, November 2, 7:00 PM Wendy Tokuda, an award-winning journalist, will share stories of her family’s time in the camps. She was the first Asian American to anchor weekday primetime TV newscasts in SF and one of the first to report on the internment of Japanese-Americans during WWII. Kimi Hill, the granddaughter of famed artist Chiura Obata, a Cal professor interned during the war, will bring you his art and other art produced in the camps, as detailed in her book Topaz Moon : Chiura Obata's Art of the Internment. : Alternative Facts — Saturday, November 23, 7:00 PM After the screening, film-maker Osaki will discuss the case and the film with Don Tamaki, the attorney instrumental in getting Fred Korematsu’s conviction vacated by the Federal District Court in 1983.

articles.text: The Piedmont Post is presenting one month of reviews of films by celebrated Japanese animation director Hayao Miyazaki. As a writer, director, and animator he is one of the most revered filmmakers in Japan, and worldwide. His award-wining animated films have been embraced by audiences that have found his beautifully detailed hand-drawn visuals and thematic storytelling compelling. As well, his protagonists are often strong young girls or resilient young women. Miyazaki co-founded the now iconic Studio Ghibli in 1985. In 2012 he was named a Person of Cultural Merit by Japan for his outstanding cultural contributions. He received an Academy Honorary Award for his impact on animation and cinema in 2014. His work continues to serve as an inspiration for countless animators, directors and writers. This week’s reviews are: The Wind Rises (2013) and When Marnie Was There (2014). articles.text: This nicely proportioned bungalow has a low slope roof correctly surfaced with a sheet membrane roofing system. Originally printed in the Piedmont Post on June 30, 2021. After reviewing the last column, I thought readers might be interested in a little more information on the relationship between building materials, engineering, and architectural expression, especially on roofs, one of the most visually prominent surfaces of a building. Architects want their roof designs to look good, but also not to leak! This is not always as easy as it seems. Complicated building forms and leak-risky layouts like decks over living spaces can make a dry building a challenge. In fact, the number one litigation issue architects and engineers face is water intrusion, i.e., leaks. The roof design process is therefore multi-faceted with structural and waterproofing considerations closely tied to aesthetics. In the roofing world, there are basically two kinds of roofs: sloped roofs and “flat” roofs, each with its own requirements and limitations. Sloped roofs are finished with shingles: asphalt, wood, clay, slate etc. For waterA wonderful variegated (varied colors) variable width slate roof tops off this fine Piedmont home. Like a clay tile roof, the building substructure must be engineered to carry the substantially heavier loads of this kind of roofing material. proofing integrity, all types of shingles require a minimum roof slope of at least 3:12. Otherwise water can creep or be blown back under the shingles. Shingles are indeed used on slopes as low as 2:12, but with special underlayment. How effective these applications are I’m not sure. Generally, the steeper the roof slope, the better. Getting water off the roof quickly is best for water intrusion prevention as well as the durability of the shingles. “Flat” roofs aren’t really flat, but almost always have a low slope that directs water to drains. This system only works with low slope roofing materials like membranes or built-up roofs such as tar and gravel. To complicate things, these low slope roofing materials are the opposite of shingles—they don’t work if the roof slope is too steep. In hot weather for example, low slope tar can actually run down the roof if the slope is too steep. Clearly, in every building design, the type of roofing material to be used must be decided early on so that the appropriate roof characteristics can be designed into the architecture. Another major consideration is the design weight of the roof. This is made up of the “dead loads”—the permanent weight of the beams, rafters, and roofing, and temporary “live loads”, which include construction workers, snow loads, wind and seismic forces. There is an incredible variation in these loads which affect the aesthetics and cost of the building. Heavy materials like slate or clay tile require more extensive structural support systems. pages.text: Wednesday, October 2, 2024 21 PIEDMONT FLIX FEST German music comedy swings into Piedmont Piedmont Flix Fest free movie at PCA on October 10 By Bob Hall Music is a universal language, and perhaps no movie demonstrates this more quirkily than the October offering of Piedmont’s Flix Fest, the 2003’s offbeat comedy, Schultze Gets the Blues. It’s a German film. The music is Cajun. If that sounds a bit far out, it isn’t. I’ve seen Peruvian panflute players performing to pedestrian approval on Parisian streets. And what about those taiko drummers in Berkeley? Why can’t a German guy go cuckoo over Zydeco? That’s what happens in Schultze Gets the Blues. Schultze, played by Horst Krause, is a hefty, recently retired salt-miner. Along with his also laid-off friends Jürgen and Manfred, he finds himself restless with time to spare. For years, he’s played traditional polka music on his accordion, but late in life he’s inspired by an interest in American Zydeco and Cajun music. Despite his initial hesitation about traveling to the U.S., he answers his music club’s call to represent it at a German folk music festival in New Braunfeis, Texas. However, instead of appearing there, he chooses to travel in a small blue boat around the countryside, despite speaking little English. Along the way he immerses himself in the music and culture of the Bayou and has several encounters with friendly locals before the movie comes to a bittersweet end. The tale is a study of an ordinary guy who, inspired by music, finds adventure late in life. Quietly amusing, it has a leisurely pace. The Stockholm International Film Festival awarded it Best Picture, and the German Film Awards nominated Horst Krause for Best actor. Roger Ebert gave it a Jury Award in his Best Movies listing. Schultze Gets the Blues will be screened at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Thursday, October 10 at 1:00 p.m. Doors open at 12:45. The event is free and open to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis. Registration is encouraged and may be done at https://bit.ly/3PJyxkP. Everyone is welcome to bring snacks or lunch. The next movie in the Piedmont Flix Fest series is the Italian romantic comedy, Pane e Tulipani (Bread and Tulips), to be shown at 1 p.m. on Thursday, November 14. Walkers tour Moraga Canyon By Dick Carter The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group had a special walk last Wednesday, and 44 walkers and three K-9 best friends were at the Exedra for it. The Monday before, the Piedmont Planning Commission held a study session to receive a presentation from staff and the consultant team to discuss draft chapters of a Moraga Canyon Specific Plan covering land use regulations, site and building design and roadway improvements. Kevin Jackson, the City’s Planning Director, is leading the project. The walkers wanted to better understand it, so they asked him to meet them at Coaches Field to explain the project and answer their questions. The walkers went up Moraga Avenue and on a boardwalk over the edge of the canyon to Coaches Field, which was dedicated in 1994. Walter Blair, the first European settler in the area, built his “Blair Park” in 1884 on 40 acres of this land between Mountain View Cemetery and Moraga Avenue as a picnic park attraction. He wanted people to come to the Piedmont Springs Hotel he built in 1872, and where the Exedra is today. What is referred to as “Blair Park” today is the land further up Moraga. Before the canyon was filled to create Coaches Field, it was a landfill for Piedmont. Above the field is Kennelly Skate Park that opened in 2001. Kevin explained that Piedmont’s General Plan is a state-mandated document that outlines the city’s long-term policies for land use and development. The Housing Element is part of the General Plan. Development of Piedmont’s 6th Cycle Housing Element started in July 2023 and lays out a plan of policies and regulations that facilitate the construction of 587 new homes by 2031. This is the target mandated by the State and a dramatic increase from its prior mandate of 60 homes. It designates areas along Grand Avenue and in Moraga Canyon as “Priority Development Areas.” The City began work on the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan in summer 2023, with the goal of completing it by the end of 2025. It anticipates development of multifamily residential buildings with up to 199 units of new housing with 60 reserved for lower income households. The Specific Plan also includes improvements to the City’s recreation and public works facilities and the Moraga Avenue roadway. The plan will also include standards governing development. The City Council chose two of four options to be considered for where buildings could be located, either on the north side or the south side of Moraga. Housing could be developed on either side, but it’s required that all housing, both affordable and market rate, be on the same side of Moraga. The housing could be up to 60 feet, or between 4 and 6 stories high. Additionally, two single family home sites near Abbott Way and Maxwelton Road could be built under either option. Option 1 has housing on the current Blair Park open space. It preserves and expands Coaches Field and the Corporation Yard in their current locations and increases parking and transit access. Option 2 has hillside housing development on the open land above Coaches Field and moves the Corporation Yard to Blair Park. It would improve the soccer field and skate spot, increase parking and transit access, and avoid infrastructure relocation. In addition to the housing development, the Specific Plan includes roadway improvements including new sidewalks and bike lanes, and a traffic signal at the intersection with Red Rock Road. Kevin said the project team is currently developing a Draft Plan. Another study session is tentatively scheduled for the Planning Commission’s regular meeting on October 14, 2024. The completed draft is expected to be released for public review and comment late this year. It will be followed by a series of City Council study sessions, anticipated to begin in January or February. The Specific Plan would then be returned to the Planning Commission for recommendation, then to the City Council for adoption in the spring next year. The City will seek proposals from developers and negotiate an agreement with one towards the end of 2025 to build and operate the housing. Kevin said there is interest in the project by developers, but the biggest challenges are the site and making the numbers work. The walkers appreciated the information and Kevin taking time to be with them. The walkers finished their walk with a climb up to the skate park for a view of the site and San Francisco before retracing their steps back to the Exedra. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. articles.text: Walter Blair’s horsecars at the entrance to Blair’s Park, currently the corner of Highland and Moraga avenues. that “upwards of 400 people rambled through the delightful groves and wooded slopes, enjoying the beauties of nature and the magnificent scenery and views.” With visitors headed for Blair’s Park and the Piedmont Springs Hotel, newspapers soon reported that 700 to 800 passengers rode Walter Blair’s horsecar weekly. The park quickly became a popular spot for Sunday School picnics and school field trips. In the summer of 1882, a reported 5,000 to 7,000 passengers rode Blair’s horsecar per month. At the end of Highland Avenue, a large wooden arch spanned the entrance to the park. Admission was free to those who travelled in their own carriages, but there was a ten-cent fare to ride Blair’s horsecar. Benches near the lakes and picnic tables in shady nooks provided pleasant spots to picnic. There were even swings for children. No refreshments were available at Blair’s Park, and picnickers were encouraged to bring their own baskets. A lively stream cascaded down Moraga Canyon and spilled in a beautiful waterfall into the park. Rustic bridges crisscrossed the falls and stream. The more adventuresome could climb up to Inspiration Point on the knoll above Mountain View Cemetery. Young boys called it “Perspiration Point.” From this 700-foot elevation, hikers were rewarded with expansive views of Oakland, Alameda, Berkeley, San Francisco, the Golden Gate without a bridge, and Mt. Tamalpais. A spring provided fresh water for picnickers and hikers and is the probable namesake of Spring Path, just east of the Corporation Yard. Blair’s Park was a popular destination. After Walter Blair died in 1888, the park was purchased in 1890 by the company that would operate a cable car up Oakland Avenue. …But that’s another story. Today that lively stream and waterfall are under Coaches Field. Mountain View Cemetery bought the northern half of Blair’s Park, including the lakes. In 1917 and 1922, contractor Guy Taylor built houses on the southern half. Today, the name “Blair Park” continues to live on current maps of Piedmont. The City now calls the land on the south side of Moraga Avenue opposite Maxwelton Road “Blair Park.” Blair’s Park began as a picnic park where visitors came to enjoy being outdoors. It is fitting that today the tradition continues with the play field and baseball/ softball diamond at Coaches Field and the Kennelly Skate Park. For more on Piedmont’s history and the Piedmont Historical Society, visit the website, Piedmonthistorical.org. Originally published in the Post on May 9, 2018.
