articles.text: In the 1870s, Walter Blair was already a successful dairyman, quarryman and extensive land owner. Blair then turned his energy to transportation and developing horsecar lines. After partnering with investors to build a horsecar line from downtown Oakland to the end of Piedmont Avenue, Blair built his own line in 1878. The Ride to Blair’s Park Blair’s Piedmont Railway began where the Piedmont Avenue line ended and travelled from the gates of Mountain View Cemetery, through Blair’s grain fields, up to Vernal Avenue (now Highland Avenue) and on to the Piedmont Springs Hotel (currently Piedmont Park). Blair had the finest horsecar, with upholstered seats, a carpet on the floor and even a fringe on the top. He called it the “Palace Car.” It ran hourly and was the only public transportation to Piedmont. Newspapers of the day described a ride on Blair’s horsecar as a pleasant even romantic one, winding through fields of grain and up hillsides with birds singing, brooks murmuring, balmy air and gentle breezes. Blair’s Park To increase the number of passengers on his Piedmont Railway, Blair created Blair’s Park where families could escape the dusty streets of downtown Oakland and “spend a pleasant day rambling in the country.” He developed 40 acres of his own land between Mountain View Cemetery and Moraga Road as a picnic park. He began by thinning out some of the eucalyptus trees that grew as a border between his land and the cemetery’s. (Some of Blair’s original eucalyptus trees still grow along the cemetery border near the lakes.) Blair graded pathways and built several bridges over the stream that ran through his park. The paths led picnickers along the stream, through the ravine and up the hillsides among trees and wildflowers. He also constructed several dams and created small lakes. (The lakes in Mountain View Cemetery date back to Blair’s Park.) Walter Blair dedicated his park on June 4, 1884, and the Oakland Daily Evening Tribune reported eucalyptus trees, now fully mature and more than 100 years old.

articles.text: About two hours east of the Bay Area, a rancher with Piedmont family roots manages an upstart family business, a regenerative ranch called Sweet Water Farm and Ranch Company. The Post was invited to the historic town of Columbia, California, near Sonora to learn the ways of the land and what makes pasture-raised California Berkshire pork first-rate. Cary Knowland graduated from Piedmont High in 1985 and then bought 40 acres in 2000 for her family, huskies and horses. Her two sons, Sam and Jack Santry, grew up close to the land and continue Cary’s propensity for adventure and living surrounded by nature. Sweet Water delivers its products to Piedmont every Tuesday. Sweet Water’s California Berkshire bacon, pork belly, ham and ham hocks know no competition in quality. Restaurant goers may have already tried their products at high-end Bay Area restaurants, such as North Beach’s Che Fico, Boulevard in the San Francisco Embarcadero and Chez Panisse in Berkeley. The Santry brothers began their business in 2017 and expanded it with the help of friends. In March 2022 they hired the first farm hands. A day on the ranch can start around 2:00 a.m. when the sounds of farm animals or coyotes in the woods are heard. Most days start by 4:30 – with plenty of coffee – to check on the animals at first light. “Caring for our pigs is a labor of love. We monitor them closely, California Berkshire hogs have a short snout with an upturned nose. Berkshire pigs originate from the English county of the same name and are a short-legged breed. ensuring they are healthy, happy, and stress-free. This means we’re out in the pastures every day,” said Sam Santry. “Early mornings and late nights are often necessary to ensure the health and well-being of the herd. We have to focus on managing the feed quantities, calculate growth rates, and track their well-being. Physical strength is vital too, as handling 700-pound hogs in the dark can be dangerous,” explained Santry. Each hog has ample space to roam, root, and wallow with a diet of organic grains, grasses, and roots. The farm produces a product line that includes a variety of cuts, from succulent pork chops and tenderloins to hearty sausages and bacon. Each cut is chosen with care. Sweet Water has provided their pork to Michelin star restaurants including The Progress and State Bird Provisions in San Francisco. Clint and Yoko Tan, owners of San Francisco’s ramen sensation Noodle in a Haystack gave glowing reviews. “My wife isn’t a big fan of pork here, but she was raving about it,” said Clint. “Super clean flavor, even the fat wasn’t greasy or clotting! Can’t wait to get our hands on those boneless roast portions when you get them back in stock.” The hands-on approach by the staff at Sweet Water reflects the time honored traditions of Spanish Iberico pork, from which they coined the term California Berkshire Pork. “Our pork is rich in omega-3 fatty acids, vitamins, and minerals that are often lacking in conHeading home for dinner

articles.text: As cool weather rolls in and sweaters come on, many of us gardeners feel the seasonal urge to put the garden to bed. Your plants are probably feeling the seasonal shift by dropping leaves and slowing production. With all the browning plant material, it’s the perfect time to start a low maintenance compost bin for the benefit of garden seasons to Hands down the easiest composting method is cold composting. This requires little work to set up, almost no monitoring, Cold composting requires little work and results in nutritious, and you end up with wonderfully nutritious compost in six months or sooner. Start by purchasing or building either a cedar wood or plastic compost bin. Next, grab your carbon and nitrogen plant materials. Think of carbon as any material that’s brown and crispy, including cardboard or scrap paper. For nitrogen you can think of greens, like fresh foliage clippings, or anything that’s wet. In your compost bin, add these materials in a two to one ratio of carbon to nitrogen until the bin is full. The best compost is made from an assortment of materials as opposed to all one plant. If your garden doesn’t produce enough scraps, ask a neighbor who uses organic practices if they don’t mind contributing plant material to your bin. Once your bin is full, add enough water to the pile so it feels like a wrung out sponge. We placed our compost bin near a garden hose for easy access. Then you simply turn it with a garden fork when you feel like it. If you want compost created in the next few months, turn your pile once a week with a spray of water. If you’re okay with waiting and like the idea of stress free composting, truly only turn it when you remember, such as every few weeks. If your bin starts to get smelly, that’s a sign there are too many greens, so add more carbonaceous material like dry leaves. If your materials aren’t breaking down and it feels dry, try supplementing with fresh green clippings and more water. Since this is a cold composting method, meaning your bin won’t heat up to temperatures that kill weed seeds and disease, avoid adding any diseased plants or weeds from the garden. My biggest tip for successful composting is just trusting the process. It’s decomposition so you really can’t mess up that bad. Even if your ratios are off, it’s an easy fix of adding more nitrogen or more carbon and waiting for them to break down. With this method, you should have dark, nutritious, earthy scented compost to use in your garden in six months. So if you start your bin now, you’ll have fresh homemade compost for your spring garden. Girl And Her Dog Farm is run by backyard farmer Michelle Docter in Albany. articles.text: Born in 1925, long time Piedmont resident Jim Meagher passed away in September 2024 at the age of 98. Born James Francis Meagher in Oakland, he was the youngest of three boys and grew up in an era where the milkman came in a horse drawn cart down Grand Avenue. In his early teens during the Great Depression Jim recalled that he would go door-to-door collecting coat hangers to sell for a penny or two. Always on the move Jim learned how to use a metal lathe at age 13 at Stonehurst Iron Works, and later was employed at age 16 in the family business, Independent Iron Works. He entered St. Mary’s High School in Berkeley and graduated with the class of 1943. Outside of school hours during WWII, “Jimmy” machined components for H.J. Kaiser’s Liberty Ships and was drafted as the war ended. He graduated from the University of California in Berkeley as a Mechanical Engineer in 1952 and started his career at San Francisco’s Hunter’s Point Shipyard. As a young man living on San Francisco’s Nob Hill, Jim was an equestrian and played polo in Golden Gate Park. Among his many interests were learning to sail and ski, and for many years he was a student of Judo. In 1953 Jim received his pilot’s license, becoming a twin-engine certified private pilot. Jim would tell colorful stories of his adventures, including flying to Pasadena to watch Cal in the 1959 Rose Bowl. In the mid-1950’s, Jim joined the family business and led notable projects for Independent Iron Works, including the James Lick Freeway in San Francisco, bridges throughout California, and the Union Oil Center in Los Angeles. It was while working at Independent Iron Works that Jim met the lovely Sharon Bounds (Cal class of ‘58). They were married in August 1960 at St. Leo’s Church in Oakland. In 1967, Jim and Sharon and the three boys moved to Piedmont where Jim resided the rest of his life. After the closure of Independent Iron Works in 1960, Jim’s entrepreneurship targeted specialized drayage services for numerous projects in the Bay Area and Northern California. Jim was a fixture at his company, Allied Crane and Rigging, through 2001, personally operating large cranes for construction projects. Jim had a generous disposiJim and Sharon Meagher enjoying the Oktoberfest in Germany in May 1971. Jim Meagher, a resident of Piedmont for 57 years, passed away in September 2024 at age 98. tion, a warm smile, and boundless energy to work and help others. With his three sons Jim became a dedicated Scouter, traveling on many trips and mentoring youth along the way. Scouting became a passion for Jim, and his years of dedication as Scoutmaster and Council member encompassed the Scouting experience. These included: National Jamboree, Woodbadge, Order of the Arrow, The Christmas Tree Lot and many 4th of July Parades. In honor of his impact on the lives of the youth in Piedmont, Jim received the Silver Beaver Award in 1987, Scouting’s highest award for volunteer leaders. It is not well known that among Jim’s other volunteer efforts he was an 18-year veteran of the Alameda County Deputy Sheriff’s Reserve (1966- 1984), where he won a handful of trophies as a sharpshooter. His sons enjoyed the story where he stopped a purse snatcher red handed and recovered the purse for a grateful mother. In 2001, at the age of 75, Jim closed his drayage business and pivoted his energy to other interests. In his later years he became a docent at the Oakland Zoo and a Level 1 archery instructor. Into his mid 80’s, he could be seen unloading trees from trucks to open the Piedmont Scout Christmas Tree lot. At the age of 82, Jim was elected President of Oakland’s Bellevue Club (2007-2009), where he and Sharon were longtime members. Jim was notably the first male President of the Bellevue Club, known for almost 60 years as the Women’s Athletic Club. Jim was also a longtime member of the Lake Merritt Breakfast Club, Toastmasters International, and a parishioner of Corpus Christi Church for more than 50 years. A quintessential Renaissance man, Jim Meagher embraced life, fellowship and God. His generous and cheerful personality, a cornerstone of his character, stayed with him to the end. He was preceded into God’s hands by his wife, Sharon B. Meagher and his sisters-in-law, Sally B. Cardiff and Elizabeth M. Meagher, by his parents, and his brothers, William G. Meagher, Jr. and Dr. Thomas R. Meagher. Jim is survived by three sons, Dai Bounds Meagher (Susan), Thomas J. Meagher (wife Debra), Seamus Meagher, (wife Fernanda), and his brother-in-law Dr. Robert Cardiff of Davis. Jim is survived by nine grandchildren: Patrick Meagher; Isabella and Veronica Meagher; Lillian, James, Margaret, Meredith, Seamus, Fernanda Meagher, and many loving nieces and nephews. Jim and the family are incredibly grateful for the loving care offered him in his final years especially by Maritess Tano, Rose M. Espinosa, Diana Villeta, Alema Rayman, Karen Villarosa, Katie Katoa and Tally Talanoa. All who knew him could say he was happy to the end due to their attentive care. A memorial service will be held at Corpus Christi Church in Piedmont on Friday, October 11, at 10 a.m. A Vigil will be held on Thursday, October 10, from 4 pm to 8 p.m. at Grant Miller Cox Mortuary, 2850 Telegraph Avenue, Oakland. A Rosary starts at 6 pm. In lieu of flowers the family recommends donating to Corpus Christi School or the Lake Merrit Breakfast Club.

articles.text: As the leaves fall, pumpkins have resurfaced at Coaches Field in the form of the Wildwood Dads Club’s annual Pumpkin Patch.
